View from the Rear At last, the winter is over (well, nearly) and the sailing season will be upon us by the time you are reading this edition of Navigans. Sailing Matters: I have just spent a day on the water with a team of Sailboarders in the Club's Orkney which will, (among its many other uses), be a support facility for the sailboarders when they are out during in the winter or during the week when other members or an OOD are not around. Arrangements have been made so that specific members of the sailboard fleet have access to appropriate keys and will be able to launch the Orkney in the case of an emergency. We spent a very useful day going through the launching / recovery process and practising boat handling, man overboard skills and how to tow windsurfing kit in the safest manner. I am delighted that we are able to maximise the use of the club’s property in this way to enhance the safety of more of our members when they are sailing. On the subject of safety, | have been in discussions with Stone Sailing Club about the positioning of our race marks. As many of you may be aware, the Stone No.2 mark was very close to our F mark last year - and there were a number of close shaves when the two fleets happened to be rounding the marks at the same time. As F mark is a Fisheries buoy, we are not able to change its location and Stone have therefore kindly agreed to lay their No.2 mark further east this year. In return, I have agreed to review the position of our B mark which is quite close to another Stone race mark. Hopefully, with this co-operation, we should have safer race courses and be able to avoid some of the near-miss situations we had last year, Dinghy / Cat Park Matters: Some of you may be aware that I have spent some time reviewing both the Cat and Dinghy Parks this winter - mainly in an attempt to identify those boats / equipment whose owners are no longer fee-paying members and asking their owners to have it removed. One important thing | noticed was that hardly any of the boats (both dinghies and catamarans) are marked with their owner’s name or contact details. This has rendered my intent of clearing unwanted kit virtually impossible. Could I take this opportunity to remind you that all boats stored at Marconi Sailing Club must be clearly identified for the following reasons: e Your boat may be damaged eg. by storms or another boat and another club member needs to let you know. e Your boat may need to be moved from its current location and a club official would need to advise you of this. e It identifies that your boat has not been “abandoned” at the club. None of us would want to come to the club and find that our boat had been moved or damaged and no-one had bothered to let us know. However, there are a large number of boats where we would not be able to contact the owner because there is no form of identification. I have put a note to this effect on those boats that do not appear to have their owners’ details displayed. I would be very grateful if you could mark up your boats accordingly. If you have any queries regarding this, please do not hesitate to discuss it with myself or your fleet captain. Thanks! Finally, a big thank you to those sailors who turned up to the Working Party on 20th February. With the help of delightful weather, a substantial amount of work was completed - including the much needed clearing of ditches, building of concrete steps, work on the club support boats etc. Thank you! See you on the water! Jenny Ball Rear Commodore [redacted] 3

Sally Jones [redacted] Those of you with good memories will recall the RYA advice that Sailing Clubs like ours need to address the issue of safety. If you read Navigans you will have seen that the Safety Committee reports at each Main Committee meeting. In a nut shell Malcolm Robertson, a qualified marine safety engineer, has been assessing the hazards in activities associated with cruiser launch and recovery and moorings laying and recovery. Following these assessments the Safety Committee discuss his observations and use the information to draw up Codes of Practice for the different operations. I will be monitoring practices at the club during the coming season to see if we are doing what we say we should be doing! An activity which may affect club members at the start and end of the season is the launch and recovery of cruisers, particularly on a Sunday when dinghy racing is taking place, and I would like to remind all club members of the agreed practice for this activity. I have extracted the relevant section from the ‘Dinghy Code of Practice and would ask all members to read this extract carefully and bear it in mind when using the hard when dinghy racing and cruiser launching or recovery is taking place. I hope you agree that this code of practice allows all club members to use the hard safely for their preferred activity. If you have any observations or suggestions which you think will improve safety during these operations please pass them to me. Telephone [redacted] e-mail [redacted]

Agreed Code of Practice for Beach master during Launch / Recovery of Cruisers which all Club Members should understand and accept. Beach master role as defined in the Dinghy Code of Practice 1999 MSC P0102 2.1 Access to the hard through the gap in the sea wall and a 3.6 metre (12 ft) strip from this gap to the low water mark should be kept free of parked dinghies and launching trolleys at all times. Dinghies can be launched or landed on any part of the hard except during launching and recovery of cruisers. 2.2 When cruisers. are being launched or recovered on a Sunday or at any time when club dinghy racing is scheduled in the year book, a member of the cruiser fleet will act as Beach master and oversee activities on the hard. Members must comply with the Beach master’s instructions at all times. The cast side of the hard MUST NOT be used by sailing dinghies when cruisers are being launched or recovered. 2.3 It is important to be particularly aware of cruisers being launched or recovered when approaching the hard to land because of. 2.3.1. the risk of a serious accident should the cruiser be lowered onto a boat and crew 2.3.2. the risk of striking a partially submerged cruiser trailer and resultant injury to crew or damage to sailing dinghy. The support frames of the cruiser trailer will be visible above the surface of the water to provide warning of the trailer being partially submerged 2.3.3 the risk from stecl wire ropes when winches or tractors are in use, Personnel who are not directly involved with the launching or recovery of cruisers should stay well clear of the operation. 2.4 During lunch breaks between races when the hard becomes a large dinghy parking lot, safe parking of Dinghies is available at some states of tide on the east side of the scrubbing posts towards the club race box. At times when, due to high tide, space is restricted early finishers of races should take their craft into the dinghy/cat parks. It was agreed, at the last Safety Committee Meeting. that the practice of launching/ recovery of cruisers should not take place when dinghies or cats were launching or returning from racing. Where a launch / recovery operation was in progress and this clashed with the departure or return of dinghies or cats then the launch or recovery of the cruiser should be halted where this was practical and safe to do so. Where an operation was in progress and could not be stopped then dinghy or cat owners should be warned and be asked to keep clear. This warning and request should be given by the Beach Master.

MARCONI SAILING CLUB Code of Practice for Dinghy Owners. Revised 15th February 2000 1, General 1.1 This code of conduct has been produced to provide club members who sail dinghies with guidance. A similar document has been produced for Cruiser sailors. By following the advice given all club members will find the club will operate smoothly and provide a better environment for us all to gain benefits from the club facilities. "Dinghy" is used in this document to encompass Dinghies, Catamarans, and Sailboards unless otherwise specified. 2. Use of Hard 2.1 Access to the hard through the gap in the sea wall and a 3.6 metre (12 ft) strip from this gap to the low water mark should be kept free of parked dinghies and launching trolleys at all times. Dinghies can be launched or landed on any part of the hard except during launching and recovery of cruisers. 2.2 When cruisers are being launched or recovered on a Sunday or at any time when club dinghy racing is scheduled in the year book, a member of the cruiser fleet will act as Beach master and oversee activities on the hard. Members must comply with the Beach master’s instructions at all times. The east side of the hard MUST NOT be used by sailing dinghies when cruisers are being launched or recovered. 2.3 It is important to be particularly aware of cruisers being launched or recovered when approaching the hard to land because of: 2.3.1. the risk of a serious accident should the cruiser be lowered onto a boat and crew. 2.3.2. the risk of striking a partially submerged cruiser trailer and resultant injury to crew or damage to sailing dinghy The support frames of the cruiser trailer will be visible above the surface of the water to provide warning of the trailer being partially submerged 2.3.3 the risk from steel wire ropes when winches or tractors are in use. Personnel who are not directly involved with the launching or recovery of cruisers should stay well clear of the operation. 2.4 During lunch breaks between races when the hard becomes a large dinghy parking lot. safe parking of dinghies is available at some states of tide on the east side of the scrubbing posts towards the club race box. At times when, due to high tide, space is restricted early finishers of races should take their craft into the dinghy/cat parks. 3, Storage of Dinghies and Catamarans. 3,1 No boats may be brought to the club before registration and payment of the appropriate fees. unless specific permission is granted by the Club Secretary. All trailers and launching trolleys must be clearly marked with owners name, boat number, and telephone number. Boats should also carry some means of identification, eg. boat number. 3.2 Boats which are not clearly marked and show signs of neglect and could cause damage to other members boats will be moved by representatives of the club to an areca away from other members boats. 3.3 Dinghy Park (Monohulls) 3.3.1 The Dinghy Park is available for occupation as soon as it is marked out pre-season and allocation sheets are shown on the notice board. This is normally in early March. If in doubt call the Dinghy Park officer. At end of season the boats must be removed when requested in Navigans. 3.3.2 Particular positions are taken up on a first-come, first-served basis, although dedicated areas are reserved for recognised fleets and larger boats. These segregations should be adhered to. 3.3.3 Members shall park their boats in an appropriate area and write their name and boat details on the allocation shects on the Club Notice Board.

3.3.4 Members shall keep their allocated boat parking space tidy and the grass cut. Motor vehicles must not be brought into the boat parking area. Road trailers must be stored in the trailer parking area, fitted with a locking device to prevent theft, and marked in accordance with 3.1, 3.3.5 All dinghies WILL be securely tied down with no projections above ground leyel. Fixings shall be able to with stand all possible wind conditions to prevent the dinghy from falling onto other boats. It is the club members own responsibility to ensure the anchor attachments are adequate. Experience has shown that anchors 500 mm (18 inches) long formed from 50 mm x 50 mm (2"x2") angle iron is the minimum suitable. The whole of the anchor must be below ground level to allow for grass cutting and to avoid injury to bare feet. The anchor should be shared between adjacent boats. It is also necessary to ensure that the front of trolleys are secured if raised. 3.3.6 Dinghies, trolleys, and sails should not be left between parking lines obstructing access to the dinghy park for other members, 3.3.7 All dinghies left at Stansgate during the winter months must move from their summer position to a winter position along the hedge at the end of the season as announced in Navigans. (See 3.3.1) Winter storage can be paid in advance at the renewal of annual subscription. In addition to the standards set out in 3.3.5 all dinghies must have their masts lowered before being left for the winter. 3.3.8 A check will be made before the 1 December to ensure that owners of boats remaining in the Dinghy Park have paid a winter storage fee. 3.3.9 Late payment of the winter storage fee will involve payment of a late fee determined by the Committee. 3.4 Catamaran Park 3.4.1 Each catamaran will be allocated a spot by the cat fleet captain. Members shall keep their allocated boat parking space tidy and grass cut. Motor vehicles must not be brought into the boat parking area. Road trailers must be stored in the trailer parking area and fitted with a locking device to reduce the risk of theft, and marked in accordance with 3.1. 3.4.2 All catamarans WILL be securely tied down. Fixings shall be able to withstand all possible wind conditions to prevent the catamaran from falling onto other boats. It is the club members own responsibility to ensure the anchor attachments are adequate. Experience from the 1987 hurricane has shown that anchors and tie-downs must be able to withstand forces estimated at 1Ton. Boats not secured with suitable high standard anchors and tie-downs may be stripped of mast and trampoline by representatives of the club to reduce the risk of damage to other club member's boats. IT IS RECOMMENDED THAT DUCKBILLED GROUND ANCHORS ARE USED TO SECURE CATAMARANS. THESE ARE AVAILABLE FROM THE CLUB THROUGH THE FLEET CAPTAIN. 3.4.3 All catamarans left at Stansgate during the winter, unless sailed regularly, must have their trampolines removed and masts lowered before being left at the end of the season as announced in Navigans. Winter storage can be paid in advance at the renewal of annual subscription. 3.4.4 A check will be made before the 1 December to ensure that owners of boats remaining in the Cat Park have paid a winter storage fee. 3.4.5. A late fee determined by the committee is payable. 3.5 Wind surfers. 3.5.1 Sailboards should be rigged in the area in the dinghy park to the south of the Tractor Shed. Members should park their cars in the Sail board car park after driving through the dinghy car park. The Sail board car park may be accessed via the hard road in front of the clubhouse between 30 November and the first dinghy racing Sunday in March. Access to the water is directly over the sea wall. 3.5.2 It recommended by the Coast Guard that wind surfers carry an orange distress flag when sailing. This flag should be used when individuals require assistance. If the inshore rescue boat is called this flag will help the crew rapidly locate individual(s) needing assistance. 3.5.3 The Coast Guard recommend that they are contacted (Ring 999) if a rescue is instigated by Club members so that they are prepared to help if necessary. INFORM COAST GUARD OF THE OUTCOME. If personnel are 10

rescued but equipment is NOT RECOVERED then the Coast Guard MUST be informed so that fruitless searches for personnel are not made. 3.5.4 If you are wind surfing on a day when racing is not taking place, it 1s strongly recommended that Windsurfers sail in a group comprising at least three people. Should one person need help it will require at least two people to launch a support boat to provide assistance. 3.5.5 In order to provide a level of support for Windsurfers on days when the Club dinghy racing programme is not taking place, the following arrangements have been made'- Keys to access the Orkney (Garage No.5) and the Fuel Store have been placed in a security box at the back of the Clubhouse lounge. A number of regular Windsurfing Members have access to these keys, and have undergone a familiarisation session with the Orkney, 3.5.6 Before sailing - identify who you will need to approach if the Orkney needs to be launched during the day. Do not wait until there is an emergency to do this - it will only delay you and waste valuable time. This will either be the OOD (on Saturdays or Sundays) or one of the Windsurfers with access to the security box - (list of names posted on the Clubhouse notice boards). 3.5.7 If you are sailing during the winter. check the availability of the Orkney as the boat or engine may require a service during this time. Ring the Rear Commodore. 3.5.8 If the Orkney is used, then full details must be entered in the Log Book which is kept in garage No.5 with the Orkney 4, Personal Safety 4.1 Members, their families and guests are responsible for their own personal safety and the MSC, Committee and the MASC cannot be held responsible for the actions of an individual. Advice given by any official of the Club is of an advisory nature only, ’ 4.2 Parents and guardians are warned that the Club is only able to provide support facilities for Club racing. Parents and guardians have sole responsibility for their children and wards and must appreciate that the Club cannot be expected to exercise supervision or control. 4.3 Club support boats have a prime responsibility to assist in protection of human life. The Duty Coxswain is in charge of each rescue operation and dinghy crews are asked to assist the Rescue Services by following their instructions completely Members boats will only be recovered if the operation will not place human life at risk. 4.4 All dinghies used from the Club shall be fitted with buoyancy to Class rules, or as the Committee may require. 4.5 It is recommended that members and their guests shall wear personal buoyancy when sailing. A wetsuit is not considered to be adequate personal buoyancy. The wearing of this buoyancy shall be the personal decision of the individual. Members and their guests are advised to wear Wet/Dry suits between the end of October and end of May (Winter and Spring) whilst sailing. 4.6 It is strongly recommended that all sailors should carry a sailing knife which has a sharp blade and a shackle key If you are sailing alone it is recommended that hand held flares are carried. These are available at the club and can be purchased from the Officer of the Day or the Rear Commodore. 4.7 Under 18 year olds using Club dinghies shall wear personal buoyancy at all times, and between the end of October and end of May (Winter and Spring) shall wear Wet/Dry suit whilst sailing. 4.8 Flag N flown from the Club house mast-head will provide the following information to members. 4.8.1. Flag N (Blue and White check) : All club racing abandoned. We advise NO SAILING AT ALL. 5. Speed Limit 5.1 An 8 knot speed limit exists along the full length of the southern shore of the river. Members are reminded to be particularly cautious when leaving or approaching, the hard where swimmers are liable to be in the water and to cxercise caution when in the yicinity of moored boats. This warning applics particularly to calamarans. Any racing dinghy/catamaran exceeding this limit may be protested and could be disqualified.

5.2 Any boat/dinghy/catamaran sailing within the cruiser moorings should exercise extreme caution, particularly with regard to laden tenders manoeuvring around such boats. 6. Collisions 6.1 Any collision between boats sailing from the club must be reported to the owner of the vessel within 7 days of the incident and reported to the OOD so that a record can be made in the OOD log. If a collision takes place when there 1s no OOD on duty the helmsperson must contact an officer of the club and provide the name or sail number of any boat with which they collide and brief details of damage. The only exception will be when all the vessels involved are racing from the club and the appropriate penalty is complied with. There is an up to date membership list in the upstairs bar where members should find addresses and telephone numbers to assist when making contact. In case of difficulty please contact the Membership Secretary for help. 6.2 While racing, any dinghy/catamaran in collision with a moored cruiser shall retire. In the event of a helm not voluntarily retiring and being subject to a protest, he/she will be disqualified. In this case the DSQ becomes a DND 6gaets - Cadef. Working Party . eynday 20th February 202 Once again the weather was fine although not so many bodies turned up compared to November 1999, nevertheless a great deal of work was completed. All the cruiser park and adjacent cat field hedges are now cut and the scrub grass and rubbish cleared from the space in between. The entrance roadway ditch clearance was a magnificent effort - it has been at least two years since it was done, consequently it was very overgrown. An end of day battle ensued to clear the brambles in the corner of the 'cat' field near the main gate. All the rubbish was cleared earlier in the day but it required bramble clearance to expose the young trees growing there. What a fight it turned out to be - nobody escaped the vicious thorns and I swear one of the vines was fifteen feet long! A bloodied and weary band of warriers completed the job and there is now what should be a pleasant woodland area for our campers. Most of the hedge and ditch cuttings have been burnt in the 'cat' field and it now remains to clear the ashes. With just a few notable exceptions the 'cat' fleet was not around on the day so would the volunteers please contact me to help clear the bonfire debris to the skip. I can be contacted on [redacted]. Much other work was also going on in other places i.e. Galley cleaning by a happy band of ladies - ages ranging from young to very young, Windsurfers laid a concrete base for the fuel shed entrance steps. Boiler house door painted blue to match the other club house doors. Emergency telephone wiring tidied up Continued re-furbishing of our + wheel drive tractor under the guidance of Murray Bates. On-going work to upgrade the cruiser park service points including paved areas. Work carried out by Malcolm Yeoman and his group of assistants. It was a very busy day so my apologies if 1 missed something There is always work to be done in maintaining our club assets and I can put names of volunteers for a few items as follows:- Creosoting main tractor shed. Joe Crumpen Steps for fuel store entrance. Windsurfers Roofing felt over tractor shed extension. Mike Smith. Further volunteers are needed for the following tasks - please contact me if you can help. Tractor Shed Creosote on extension, | Replace missing gutter. _ Repairs to roofing felt to stop leakage Clubhouse Replace missing fascia panel on west wall, Replace broken toilet seat. Security lights - replace lighting elements. Fuel Shed Build brick plinth to support the lubricating oil storage drum. Peter Bloomfield - Vice Commodore Telephone, (01621) -[redacted] STOP PRESS..The Windsurfers have now completed the steps for the fuel store entrance. 13

Minutes of the Main Committee Meeting 8°" February 2000 at MASC Executive Meeting. The Executive discussed the following items; Calor gas, 5-year plan, Windsurfer rigging area, MASC, Orkney operation, Dinghy and catamaran winter parking, Camping and fires. Safety. Mr C Kidner tabled an extract from the Safety Committee Meeting. Proposals to monitor club procedures during the season, Mr C Kidner to conduct the monitoring and submit reports to the safety Committee for discussion. The Safety Committee may recommend to the Main Committee that sanctions be brought to bear against persistent offenders of the procedures. The Beach Master role as published in the Dinghy Code of Practice is to be amended, Para 2.2 words “and be responsible for” to be replaced with “oversee”. Mr Kidner suggested that all dinghy and catamaran owners should receive a copy of the Dinghy Code of Practice. Finally Mr Kidner asked the committee to accept his proposal. Proposed N Pembleton, seconded D Kirby, carried. Clubhouse and Site. P Bloomfield. Road, quotations received for road repairs, P Bloomfield and the contractors to walk the road before placing the contract. Proposed P Black, seconded S Glynn. Mr Klingsick (the farmer) has kindly promised to cut back the hedges bordering the road and also the Cruiser Park hedges. Part of the clubhouse fascia on the western end is damaged. The Windsurfer Fleet has completed the concrete base for the new gas storage cylinder. The gas suppliers have now discovered a problem, action continues. J Ball. Club timber burned during 1999 camping weeks. Following enquiry’s it was not possible to positively identify the culprits other than that they were not cadets. It was proposed by C Kidner and seconded by N Pembleton that a disused trailer at the far end of the cat field is designated as a store upon which fuel for all future fires will be placed. Carried Mr D Thomas. Windsurfers now using area to the east of the clubhouse for rigging, thus avoiding driving cars on the grass. Mr Thomas said that there were a number of dogs running free about the site, there was a possibility that they could damage windsurfer sails, there was also a health risk. The Committee agreed that there was a rule requiring dogs to be kept on a lead whilst on the site, Club rules must be observed. Social. Barn Dance, successful evening, £60.0 raised for the RNLI. Fitting Out Party 07/04/00: Laying up Supper confirmed for the 18/11/00 Moorings Sub Committee. P Clayton. Cruiser Handbook completed and published. Jack B repairs in hand but rudder shaft needs replacement and raw water pump impeller requires replacement. M Richardson suggested fitting a raw water alarm. Sailing Sub Committee. J Ball. Orkney refit complete. ECPR first aid cover has been arranged. Check carried out on boats stored during winter, persons suspected of not paying winter storage fees to be invoiced. Cadet meetings, 20/02/00 model 14

yacht racing, 11 and 25/03/00 fitting out instructions. Cadet week events being planned. P Clayton asked if additional camping slots could be arranged for cadet week weekends in order to stop people booking the whole week in order be present for the weekend only, the committee agreed to permit five extra weekend slots. S Glynn asked about the donation received towards the cadet cabin. Bar Manager. The position of bar manager remains vacant. Membership. Four applications received, all accepted. Five Year Plan. C Shenton tabled an updated version of the Wish List (Feb 2000), each Committee member was requested to identify the first and second most important items on the list. C Shenton will rationalise the abbreviated list for presentation at the next meeting. Any Other Business. M Bates, the hydraulic jack will cost £100.0 to repair. P Black said that a change in the VAT Rules meant that for the club to continue to enjoy exemption from VAT we had to have words in our constitution stating that we are a non profit making organisation and that no profit or surplus will be distributed. C Kidner said that the un-official website is now closed P Black 15

ECPR - Getting Closer Charles Anderson Cruiser Help All sorts of plans are developing for this years race. As you will have seen, the weekend set aside for this year’s event is Saturday 22"? and Sunday 23" July, the latter being the actual ECPR. | am on the trawl once more for around 20+ cruiser owners to join the support craft fleet. Despite a slight last minute panic we made it in the end last year and it would be an enormous help if individuals were able to make a commitment a little carlier this year, It would certainly spare my shredded nerves! For those that are not familiar with the ECPR, the club is unique in putting on this annual event. The race is the only one of its kind offering 2 man-cat sailors a water-borne version of the London Marathon. The charity we support is local to Essex and based in Maldon. Many of you I know will have seen their vessels moored in Maldon or you may well be more familiar with the Hartlepool Renaissence, Duet, The Queen Galadriel and the sailing barge. Xylonite all of which are often out on the Blackwater. The Cirdan Sailing Trust provides sailing breaks for the disabled, disadvantaged as well as their helpers (not necessarily together). The money we raise goes towards bursaries which help those less able to pay make use of the charity’s services. I know the Trust’s Chief Executive has sent some sample letters to our Commodore from recipients of our bursaries; 1 am sure they will appear if not in this issue a subsequent one and they make touching reading. Again as usual. a copy of the Weekend’s questionnaire is in this issue, please don’t forget that if you do respond, your offer will be taken up so keep an eye on Navigans news about the weekend and definitely please do turn up at the weekend. A note about radio frequencies, we would dearly like to change to using MII/ch80 so if you do have it please make sure you indicate accordingly or if you have been thinking about getting a chip for it, perhaps this might help you make the change? Barge Trips There will be more on this in a later issue but ........it is hoped that on Saturday 22TM July, we will be organising trips down river. The duration of the cruises will be subject to prevailing conditions but we envisage one in the morning and one in the afternoon. They will be organised on a first come first served basis. All the money raised will go to the Cirdan Trust and for those of you that have not been on a barge it is an experience well worth taking advantage of. At the moment tickets will be £10/person, While it may seem a lot look at it as a donation to charity ............80 watch this space for further details. 16

Commodore's Notes After good weather in February and early March, the sailing season starts and what do we get? Snow! There's a message there somewhere. I am pleased to be able to tell you that we have had a volunteer for the vacant Bar Manager role. His name - Neil Pembleton. We are seeking to arrange for bar supplies to be delivered to the Club, so that will lighten the load. Also Neil has announced his intention to manage, not do all the work himself and to this end the Main Committee believes that each fleet should provide one person to join the bar committee to share the load of running the bar. This does not mean that they will become glorified bartenders, far from it, the bar will continue to be staffed by the OOD and other designated members. The members of the Bar Committee will each contribute to the smooth running of this facility. If you think you would like to join the bar committee please contact me or Neil, we need your help. Those of you who have been at the Club in the last few weeks could not help but notice that we have a new tractor. Well its not new but the old 4 wheel drive tractor that has been the subject of major refurbishment. Thanks go to Jack Goody, Gerry Champion, Harold Griffiths and Russell Hadley, not forgetting the ever present Murray Bates for a hard winter's work. Well done gentlemen. I now wish to talk about the Five Year Plan. You will recall that we carried out a major consultation with the members last year, which | have sifted, interpreted and categorised. The raw list of suggestions would fill four Navigans but my summary of your suggestions is given elsewhere in this edition of Navigans. If you don't recognise your suggestion its probably because I have included it under a slightly different description, but its there some where I assure you. A word of caution, every suggestion on the list has been made by a fellow member, in writing. Plainly it was important enough for that member to take the time to do so. If the suggestions do not accord with your vision for the Club, please respect the members right to hold a different view. From this long list the Main Committee first arrived at accurate budget figures, and then began a winter of discussion and analysis, We have reached consensus within Main Committee and it is now time to open the debate to a wider audience. It is my intention to publish the summary of the Main Committee's deliberations in the next Navigans. This will be prioritised, costed and have a program for its delivery. In the next edition I will set a date in mid June for an open meeting to which all members will be invited to give their views on the Plan. We may well need more than one such meeting, but our intention is to reach consensus within the whole Club, before putting the proposals to a vote of the entire membership. Have a good spring of sailing, Clive Shenton PLEASE --- No Parking in the cruiser park or surrounding area. The travel hoist will need sufficient room to manoeuvre, recently valuable time has been wasted tracing vehicle owners.

Viewirom the Rear At last the season has started and we will be well into it by the time you are reading this. Goodbye to Sunday moming lie- ins but hopefully we will be rewarded with some good wind and weather, Some of you will have noticed that the RIB has been out of action for a few weeks. If you would like to know more, please contact one of the Cadet Committee or their fleet captains - Bekki Tovey and Andrew Dowley - (who usually have a Cadet page somewhere in this magazine!), See you on the water! Minutes of the Main Committee Meeting held on the 6TM March 2000 General Meeting. Before commencing the normal business of the evening a General Meeting was called to consider a proposal by the MSC Main Committee: Proposal Constitution and Rules Section 1. Proposal to add new paragraph 3 x The Club is a non-profit making organisation. All profits and surpluses will be used to maintain or improve the Club’s facilities. No profit or surplus will be distributed. The motion was carried unanimously. Any Other Business Mr J. Salmon enquired about the progress of the five-year plan. Mr C Shenton in reply said that the Main Committee was nearing a point where they will be able to recommend a plan to the membership. Thirty-seven members attended the meeting, which closed at 1945 hrs. | Main Committee Business Executive Meeting. The Executive Committee met on the 01/03/00 when the following items were discussed. MASC Contribution Charge, General Meeting, Camping arrangements for 2000, Corrections to year book, Cruiser park track, Road repairs, Late payment of Winter storage fees. Finance. Commodore's Notes Also See Pages 22 - 24 { would like to dedicate all of my contribution this month to the Five Year Plan. Firstly, | refer you to last month's Navigans when we printed the complete list of suggestions from members that constituted the Wish List that was considered by the Main Committee. We took that list and struck off the items that we thought were desirable but would always be beyond our ability to afford. So out went the marina, the total rebuild of the Clubhouse and the first floor extension above the toilet block. After some debate we decided not to proceed with the ‘wet bar at ground floor’ proposal, as when I floated it in Navigans last year, there was a large ‘anti’ reaction. There were several suggestions concerning our Hard, varying from the minor to the major. I think we all realise that without the hard the Club would cease to exist. What is not so widely known is that I produced a report on the hard about five years ago. The report was comprehensive, but the main conclusion was that the hard should not be rebuilt but be continually maintained and improved as a facilities maintenance matter. You will see that all the Plans include the sum of £750 per year to achieve this maintenance. Several items were combined under one heading, such as refurbishment of the Upper Saloon, to help simplify our thought processes. Then each Committee member gave their first and second preference from the Wish List and these were rated on a simple points system by myself. There was a surprise number one choice - a veranda with river views to the west of the clubhouse. We tested this in discussion and agreed that this was indeed the Main Committee's first choice. This, and all other choices are shown on the following pages headed Plan A, Plan B and Plan C. Each Plan starts with the assumption that the sum of £5000 will be available each year as surplus income after all other expenses including depreciation have been accounted for, but there are big differences between the Plans. Plan A Plan A shows what we believe we can achieve at the current subscription rates. Plan B Plan B shows what we believe we can achieve with a subscription rate increase of £50 per year. Plan C Plan C shows what we believe we can achieve with a subscription rate rise of £100 per year. Each Plan is shown at current rates. The assumption being that inflation in the costs of the Plans will be offset by inflationary rises in the subscription rates. HEALTH WARNING These Plans represent the best projections and priorities that the Main Committee can reach based on current information, but this is an uncertain world. It is possible that unforeseen circumstances may develop that demand a radical change in direction. It is also possible that our membership numbers may decrease thus reducing the money available which would slow the implementation of the Plan. In these extraordinary circumstances, we would need freedom to act in he best interests of the Club. MEETING Sunday 18" June at the Sailing Club at 4.00 p.m. The Main Committee and myself would now like to open the Plans for discussion amongst the membership. | invite you to attend a meeting for that purpose, when I, and several other Committee members will be on hand to explain our recommendations and to answer your questions, Please bring your copies of this month's and last month's copy of Navigans so you have the information at hand.

Clive Shenton View from the Rear We have had a busy start to our sailing season - which, although it has not been without problems, has been very successful so far - here are some of the highlights! Dart 15 Open It may as well have been April Ist for the disasters we encountered at the start of the Dart 15 open. [| arrived at the club to find 1t was blowing a bitterly cold, strong north-easterly wind complete with rain, which no doubt contributed to the reduced number of visitors this year. Brian Spencer told me that he had had to tow the catering team's car to the club as it had taken an aversion to the rain and broke down en route. Mick Richardson and Clive Shenton had spent a considerable amount of time and effort trying to ensure that the RIB trolley would be back and the RIB re-assembled in time for the Saturday racing. Due to their efforts the RIB was ready for launch on the Saturday morning and the engine promptly conked out! - (it is still not running as I write). Fortunately, the Glynn family had kindly come to our aid and provided additional support cover with their RIB over the weekend - and we are very grateful to them for helping out. However, despite the chaos, everyone pulled together to make the event a success and we achieved the following: * Catering and bar facilities all weekend including an evening meal on the Saturday - (and yes, some of us were mad enough to camp down!!) * Four excellent races (with support cover) in a whole range of conditions - (as is usual in Bntain, Sunday dawned in complete contrast - sunny with light airs!) * Four out of the top five prizes being awarded to Marconi sailors. ] apologise if | am duplicating coverage of this event with other write-ups which may appear in Navigans - but I wanted to take the opportunity to thank the many club members who supported this event and overcame all the problems. The names are too numerous to mention but | would like to thank the Race Officer and his team, all the support crews and the shore based team who ran the reception, sorted out trolleys etc. etc. The Dart 15 Fleet isvery grateful!! Bank Holiday Series As usual the weathermen got it completely wrong for both Easter and the first May Bank Holiday! The Easter weekend provided beautiful weather, if not much wind on the Sunday and Monday - but it was good to be sailing in the sunshine again! On the Saturday of the May Bank Holiday - we allowed the unthinkable to happen. Several thousand Cadets - (OK slight exaggeration) - were let loose with green paint and brushes and set upon the Cadet cabin to transform its appearance - a truly terrifying prospect. Not surpnsingly , most of the Cadets ended up the same colour as the cabin (although they managed to avoid painting any unsuspecting catermeran or passer-by) - but the end was result is very good and a considerable improvement on its previous colour scheme. A lot of electrics and other work was carned out to improve the cabin facilities and my thanks to Kevin Dowley, the Monks family and John Bird for organising this work Support Boats As J mentioned above, we are still having a few problems with the RIB engine as I write, which we hope will be resolved shortly. I would like to thank Clive Shenton, Mick Richardson and Roy Hardwicke for their continued efforts on the RIB - they have given up a lot of their time and effort and it is very frustrating that we have encountered these additional problems. I would ask for your continued patience if you have been allocated as a RIB Helm or Crew and that you support the races by taking the Orkney out instead. The Orkney is proving to be a very capable support boat and it is important (sometimes essential) that we have two support boats out. Request for help - Support Boat Duties Which brings me to my next point - I always seem to be nagging about the need for help (1 apologise!) - but there have been a number of occasions when support boat crews have not turned up to do their duty or have not arranged a swap. | know that there are usually good reasons for this - but it would be very unfair on the sailors if we have to cancel racing due to lack of support boats, particularly when most of them have carried out their own duties. 3

A list of support duties appears elsewhere in this Navigans - could you kindly check the list and make sure you have made a note of the dates you have been allocated. If you are unable to make a date, can [ remind you that you should arrange a swap with an alternative person and then advise Tony Ferguson / Barry Hutt / Dennis Gilbey. Please do not expect them to find an alternative person to cover your duty for you - their task is difficult enough as it is!! See you on the water!! Amyjack Thanks Thank you to all who helped over the weekend of 6th and 7th May when Ray discovered that Amyjack had spent her first week of the season on her mooring, happily leaking in sea water up to cabin floorboard level. This meant she had to be hauled out again asap on Saturday to be drained and dried. We lowered her into the water on her trailer for an hour on Sunday in an attempt to find out quickly what the source of the leak was - result unproven. Thanks go to the tractor drivers who fitted AJ's problems into their existing work schedules: to fellow members for their practical help with hauling out, sympathy and voices of experience, help with leak detection and thanks also to the dinghy and cat sailors, particularly on Sunday, who had an extra obstruction to avoid on the hard The latter is something we try to avoid if we possibly can, but we're finding that a stroppy cruiser ideally needs a retired owner and we haven't got there yet! 62 members attended the Cruiser Fitting Out Supper held at Stansgate on Saturday 6th May and what a splendid night it was, with an excellent meal provided by Lorraine ably assisted by Elaine and Helen. After the meal we were entertained with songs and ditties sung by "The Marconi Buoys" assisted by Margaret Yeoman on the tambourine, as well as members of the Erith Yacht Club who treated us to songs and monologues, Such was the talent I was wondering if I could act as their agent! Mona's Meanderings Continued Part Six - Meandering Around the Madeiras The first thing | noticed when | looked through the porthole in the morning was that we were anchored night next to a mountain. More accurately perhaps we were very near the top of a mountain, with just the peak towering above our heads. The Madeiras consists of Madeira itself, Porto Santo where we now were and several uninhabited islands. We had made for Porto Santo as it has the best harbour. Later in the morning we launched the dinghy and set about completing formalities. This was a lengthy process involving Immigration. Customs, Maritime Police and the Harbour Authorities. Each of these needed to see passports and all the ships papers. While we were in the middle of this a dashing fellow, who turned out to be Miguel the Harbourmaster, stopped his landrover and asked Helen if we were looking for a marina berth. When she said that we were he told us that there might be room later that day. When he discovered that our length was only 10.5 metres he said he could fit us in right away which he duly did. Porto Santo is a fascinating island. Largely arid, very little is now grown there. Rows of terraces on the steep hillsides give evidence of how an earlier generation of islanders eked out a meagre existence form the land. A feature that made our stay there particularly pleasant was the three mile long sandy beach that started just the other side of the harbour wall. A swim in the warm, crystal clear water followed by a shower, then breakfast back on the boat made a very pleasant start to the day. We had great fun exploring the island in a variety of ways. Laura and Katie from Fanai, another boat that we kept meeting us with, seemed determined to explore every inch of the island by foot. Helen and | did manage to clamber up the steep hillside nearest to the harbour. We had started by following a rough track which rapidly faded away to nothing leaving us to scramble as best we could over the remains of old terraces and craggy frock faces. We did eventually reach the top, where the view over the island made the effort worthwhile.. We also did the tourists bit and allowed ourselves to be persuaded to join in a mini bus tour of the island. It proved to be a very good way of seeing the island. Some of the view, were spectacular, although I will admit to having my eyes shut on the way down some of the mountain passes. A couple of days after we had arrived in Porto Santo Pat and Chris decided to organise another mass dinner along the lines of the one we had had in Leixoes. I decided that this would be and ideal opportunity to get my own back on Pat. On the way across to Porto Santo Helen had one night heard strange noises coming from on deck. She tracked this down to Laura who was passing her night watch by making up new words to 'All Things Bright and Beautiful’. It went on the lines of:- All boats bright and beautiful All ARC yachts great and small All crews weird and wonderful Pat Murphy knows them all. I decided that this was a perfect vehicle. All that was needed was to write some verses which | duly did. After the meal which was a great success with over fifty people taking over one of the local restaurants, I told the story or our arrival in Porto Santo and Pat's commentary. I handed out photocopies of the song and encouraged wholehearted support to cover my own inadequacies in the vocal department. I needn't have worried. | thought that we would at least need a practice. Afier the first chorus and verse | just said carry on. It was a superb performance. After a few days in this wonderful place we began to contemplate our next moves. Helen was keen to visit Madeira itself. The main drawback to going there was the fact that Funchal its only harbour, had very little space for visiting yachts and the anchorage immediately outside the harbour was not reputed to be particularly good one. A popular option was to leave the boat at Porto Santo and visit Madeira by ferry. Several crews were oscillating between these options. In addition I was still trying to sort out the problems with our VHF radio. Back in Leixoes when it had already stopped transmitting | had contacted Tolley Marine again. This time they said that Sailor had agreed to send a new handset out to us, as long as I agreed to return the old one, once I had the new one. The only thing that was needed was a forwarding address. I never like being too definite about future ports of call. There are just too many imponderables. However on this occasion I had little choice if I wanted a new radio and had selected Porto Santo. I had at the same time ordered a new back up GPS to replace our existing back up, an ageing Garmin that had gone down in the rollover in August. (I had incidentally got Gamin going again after contacting the manufacturer's who explained the procedure). When we arrived at Porto Santo there was no sign of the expected parcel. I phoned Tolley Marine but could get no answer. My parents who live near Tolley Marine in Poole went round there only to find that they had gone bust. Enquiries to Visa produced the 15 SE — —E ———

disturbing news that my account had been debited. I made further investigations to try and discover just what was going on. Eventually while all this was going on the parcel arrived. Unfortunately when | fitted the new handset it still didn't work. Part Seven - Canary Bound We left Porto Santo on Monday 18th October. There was very little wind and for once Laura wasn't keen to leave, but for some reason both Helen and I felt that we should go. Once clear of the harbour we raised sail and with a westerly just aft of the beam made reasonable progress. Aldebaran had left harbour about an hour after us and as the afternoon wore on were gradually gaining on us. By early evening, just before Aldebaran caught up with us, we changed to our downward rig. Eventually Pat started his engine and motored away, We persevered for two or three more hours, then as our speed dropped to two knots or less we too started our engine. At this time we could just see Aldebaran's stern light in the distance. We carried on motorsailing all night with the monitor once again proving it could handle the situation. In the morning we could just made out Aldebaran's mast through the binoculars. It was then time for the ARC net. Pat did his usual faultless performance as morning DJ. A little later Helen drew my attention to a yacht abeam of us that we hadn't previously seen. It was a while before we realised that it was Aldebaran. Pat's story that we later heard was that at the start of the ARC net the autopilot was steering. While he was conductiong the net the autopilot took exception the amount of power the SSB was taking and did a 180 degree turn. Both Pat and Olivia who was sitting in the cockpit reading at the time were completely unaware of this. When Pat had finished the net he came back on deck and staring over the stern asked Olivia what had happened to Mona. Turning round he then saw a boat passing in the other direction on the port side. Sensing something familiar about it he looked through the binoculars and realised that it was us. When we discussed this incident at the next opportunity on the SSB I promised not to tell anybody about it. Trust me Pat, trust me!! We then reverted to sail as Aldebaran steamed off in the right direction ahead. Progress was slow all day. Later that afternoon the wind died away completely. Once again we resorted to the engine. This seemed to encourage the attention of dolphins who swam alongside us for some considerable time. A little later we also saw a turtle swimming placidly by. Before dark the wind had returned sufficiently for us to rely on sail again. From then on we had light but steady north westerly winds all the way to Lanzarote which we sighted at dawn on the Thursday morning having slowed down the previous night to ensure a daylight arrival. This is yet one more advantage of our much vaunted downwind ng. When you want to slow down all you have to do is roll it up a bit. All in all it had been a superb passage. Slowish but sunny calm and steady. We had all slept well. even Helen who is notoriously bad at sleeping at sea and were all fresh enough to appreciate the breathtaking landfall. Having never visited the Canaries before, I had a rather jaundiced preconception based on lager louts and fish and chips. That first sighting of Lanzarote's craggy skyline rising majestically from the morning mist did a lot to wash away that preconception. We sailed straight into the channel between Lanzarote and Graciousa, a small island just to its north. Motoring the last couple of miles to Sociedad the small harbour on the island of Graciosa, we initially thought that there was no room on the only pontoon and left the harbour intending to anchor. Pat had then called up on our VHF which for a very short time had decided to function, to tell us that a boat was just leaving and that there would be room on the pontoon. Returning to the harbour we manoeuvred successfully into an awkward berth thanks to the combined efforts of this little pontoon community. Once safely ensconced, we quickly fell in love with Graciosa. I decided that it was a safe bet that this would be one of the places that we would look back on with particular affection. I was therefore determined it wasn't going to be a place that we would leave too soon, Part Eight - Isla Graciosa We spent two weeks on Graciosa. An idyllic spot, it provided us with a perfect combination of restfulness and interest. There are no roads on the island, only sandy tracks. The streets in the small town are sand. The single pontoon for yachts in the harbour had no electricity or water but no charges either. so nobody was complaining. The transient community on the pontoon was an extremely close knit and friendly one and it was great fun catching up with what by now felt like old friends and making new ones. Before we came away we'd never realised what a sociable life it would prove to be. One young couple sailing a Halcyon 27 couldn't get over it. "When we walk down the pontoon everyone we see talks to us. Back home in Lymington we could walk right through the marina and nobody would say a word". 16

Laura and Katie did some more energetic exploring, until Fanai moved on to Lanzarote. During the time we were there Helen and managed to get round most of the island. Although largely arid it was a surprisingly interesting place. We found a wide variety 0 volcanic rock. The beaches closest to the harbour weren't particularly good for swimming, but further afield we found some superb secluded, sandy beaches. The water was even warmer than it had been at Porto Santo. We tried to time our walks, not alway successfully, to coincide with the cooler parts of the day. The single pontoon in the harbour brought with it certain problems. Unlike commercially operated set ups there were no handy ster lines ready to be picked up. Instead there were simply concrete blocks with eyes let into them lying on the harbour bed. Securin; stern lines involved diving with your line down to one of these blocks. While we were there three lads on a French boat ‘Jonathon liked nothing better than having an excuse to go diving. Another complication was that whatever the wind was doing elsewhere 01 the island, it always seemed to be blowing half a gale in the harbour. For the first few days that we were there the wind was blowin; our bows on to the pontoon. The trick was in getting the stern lines tight enough to keep our bows off the pontoon but not so tight a: to make boarding impossible. To help with boarding | rigged up a system with our wooden boarding ladder hung over the stemhea and our plank strung between the ladder and the pontoon. This worked reasonably well until, while we were away, the bows rode uj over the pontoon trapping and damaging the ladder. The next day I experimented with a mark two version, using our plastic foldin; ladder. It just happened that Pat was out and about videoing the harbour. I was balanced between the pontoon and the boat, kneelin; on the plank, attempting to secure it to the plastic ladder on which is was resting, when the end slipped off the ladder. 1 emergec splattering from the water to be greeted by the sight of Pat pointing his video camera in my direction with his commentary on th incident already in full swing. A crowd soon gathered. most of whom were too amused to be of much help. It was left to one of the French lads to actually attempt to get me out of the water. The next day we thought is was about time we tried out Little Mu, our Seahopper folding dinghy that I had built from a kit the previous winter. More accurately Katie supported by Laura decided that we should try it out. It was the first time we'd sailed it o: even had it out of its bag since Tollesbury. By the time we started rigging it, Maffick decided that they would have to get the rig up o1 their dinghy. It was a particularly windy day and we ended up having a mini regatta, with the dinghies charging across the harbour with a different crew on every outing. We had a few teething problems, which resulted in me losing the mast and rudder on my firs time out. Running repairs on the pontoon soon had us up an away again. Little Mu did very well, especially with Katie on board. got rather anxious when one of the French lads insisted on standing up every time he tacked, but everyone got back safely and a gooc time was had by all. Garciosa is blessed with five volcanic mountains of modest size, but very steep sided, that rise abruptly from the sandy landscape. Fo: the time we were on the island, Helen was determined to climb at least one. I was less keen, deciding that some challenges were bes left unconquered. Helen persisted however and eventually we arrived at the base of the highest of these hills. The going was quit hard and I decided that I needed to lie down in the heat that was already building up. When | finally got up Helen was some way ut the steep incline, investigating possible routes. As | walked towards her, she shouted down that it didn't look very promising Accordingly I went a bit further round and started climbing. It was hard going, but the higher | got the less | felt like coming down th« way I'd gone up. So I went on, thinking that it must get better soon and that there must be an easier way to come down, as I did so. _ found myself at the highest point of the island, but more alone than I had intended to be. After waiting some time for Helen to arrive I started looking for easier routes back down. This wasn't as easy as I thought it might be and I eventually scrambled down a rathe precarious route that half way down led me through a deep crevice. At one point during this descent I was extremely relieved to catch a glimpse of Helen at the foot of the hill. When I reached the bottom, Helen having made several unsuccessful attempts to find a route to the top, was less than pleased tha’ after all my complaints and protests I had made it. One afternoon we were having a drink on board with an Australian couple. who had sailed their 27 footer from Australia to Norway) via South Africa and were now slowly heading home, when we were haled from the pontoon. Looking up we were amazed to see Phi from Tollesbury standing there, It turned out that he had been crewing for another ecastcoaster who had recently bought a boat in Spain and was in the process of sailing her to Brazil. The next day we decided that we really should be moving on. We had to pick up yet another VHF radio in Puerto Calero on Lanzarote. In addition we were having problems with the single lever control on the engine. It had started playing up as we had lef our marina berth in Porto Santo. Reversing out of the berth I had gone from astern to forward only to discover that as the lever passed neutral, the engine slipped out of gear. I only managed to engage forward gear with great difficulty and in the nick of time. We knew that leaving our berth in Graciosa was going to be interesting to say the least. Everyone turned out in force to help us on our way. In spite of all this assistance Mona swung the wrong way desperately close to the shallows and the countless moorings and lines 17

that surround the pontoon. As we had swung away from the berth I was on my hands and knees in the cockpit attempting to engage reverse. As I did so I realised that we were now facing the wrong way, so carried on attempting to steer Mona in reverse. For one of the few times in living memory she responded beautifully and we wove our way through the closely packed moorings until there was sufficient space for us to round up and leave the harbour in grand style, to the accompaniment of applause and klaxons from the pontoon. As we left the harbour I was visibly shaking. Part Nine - Puerto Calero Leaving the harbour of La Sociodad on Graciosa we motored over a heavy swell into the strong north easterly. Once clear of the headland we were able to shape course down the east side of Lanzarote and bring the wind aft of the beam. We had a superb sail making between six and a half and seven and a half knots. Our arrival in Puerto Calero was almost as interesting as our departure from Graciosa had been. I took Mona as slowly as I could down the long pontoon towards our allocated berth. As we reached it I gave her a quick burst forward to turn her into the berth, Then I collapsed onto the cockpit sole desperately trying to engage reverse gear before we rammed the pontoon. Unable to see what was going on I carried on steering blind expecting at any moement cries of anguish from the foredeck. in their absence | engaged reverse then reverted to neutral. As I straightened up I found that we were neatly alongside the finger pontoon. Helen and Laura were already tying up unaware that I hadn't been able to see anything as we had come in. Perhaps | ought to do it like that more often. We had barely tied up before an extremely helpful French mechanic had arrived to start sorting out our gear change problems. Having dismantled the single lever control, it was found to be beyond repair. A new one was duly ordered. When this arrived a few days later and had been fitted with some difficulty (it had been impossible to get a morse control and the volvo control necessitated a bit of surgery in the cockpit), we discovered that the gearbox had also suffered some damage. We were therefore committed to a longer stay here than we had originally intended. We made use of this time by sorting out some of the other problems that had developed along the way. A new company in the marine M.A.S.T. run by an Englishman Brian and his Irish secretary Marie, proved to be extremely effective in finally locating our replacment radio, which seemed to have been flying around Lanzarote for at least two weeks without actually finding its way to Puerto Calero. Brian managed to get the VHF working, although out of a total of three handsets that we now had in our possession, he could only get one to work! He also sorted out some connection problems we had experienced with the autohelm. While all of this was going on we hired a car for three days and had a good time seeing the sights. It proved to be a fascinating island much less spoilt by tourism than we had anticipated. Only one place had really suffered with an over abundance of fish and chips and English pubs. We were intrigued by the fire mountains that steam continuously and can cause spontancous combustion and the large areas of volcanic deposits. The only problem with Puerto Calero is that without a car you could feel rather cut off there. An entirely recent, totally artificial harbour it had a very opulent but rather contrived feel about it. Spotlessly clean, with brass bollards and palm trees, we were never quite sure whether the uniformed and armed security guards were there to protect us and our yachts or to keep an eye on us. In fact the marina was so difficult to leave on foot that it sometimes felt as if the guards were there to keep us in. Either way we did find their presence somewhat intimidating. One night I was having one of my customary wanders up the pontoon before turning in for the night, when I realised that I was coming under rather close scrutiny. As I climbed back on board Mona, this guard approached and asked if this was my boat. Helen and Laura both thought the incident was hilarious. Helen said it was my fault for looking suspicious. It was just as well that the guard didn't ask them if they knew me as they probably would have denied all knowledge of me. While we were there we realised that the bilges were getting a bit smelly and needed a good clean. Pumping out bilges here was strictly taboo along with hanging out washing and various other activities. The only answer was to secrete buckets of dirty water ashore. The first time I did this | thought I had been very clever tipping the bucketful down a drain the car park. As I walked back down the gangway I was a bit disconcerted to see my dirty bilge water pouring out of a pipe right next to me and pouring straight into the marina. Subsequent trips took me further and further afield with my buckets of water, while Laura had the bright idea of watering the palm trees which didn't seem to suffer unduly. All in all we managed to get a fair bit of general cleaning, sorting out and maintenance done during our stay. We also managed to catch up with yet more people we had met along the way as well as making new friends. One thing that surprised us was that having felt rather dwarfed by a lot of English boats we were meeting up with, we were now finding that a lot of American boats were our size or smaller. Up to now [| had thought of things American as tending to be rather big and brash, but this is certainly not the case with their boats which also tend to be traditional in concept with long keels and generous displacement. 18

As I write this we are still in Puerto Calero awaiting the parts for our gearbox, but | am sure with a bit of luck and good behavior, it won't be too long before we are able to leave and continue our voyaging. Up to now we have in fact been extremely lucky having a great deal of good sailing. It has not been an easy season weather wise and a lot of people leaving both mainland Europe and Porto Santo, just after us, had difficult and unpleasant conditions to deal with. Our problems have been comparatively minor ones and have done little to mar the trip so far. A preoccupation at this time of year, in this part of the world has been the Atlantic crossing. | found it quite unsettling when all the ARC yachts set off. Every day more boats leave. I keep telling myself that it is very early to be going, while hurricanes are still blowing in the Caribbean and before the Trades have had a chance to settle down properly. In fact when we finally leave here, we would still like to see some more of the islands. This should be a bit easier now, because a major problem of cruising the Canaries during October and November is simply one of overcrowding. Nonetheless, however much logic tells you that you are doing the right thing, as day by day boats move on, it is still undecidedly unsettling.

Minutes of the Main Committee Meeting held on 3** April 2000 Previous Minutes. Commodore's Notes After a long discourse on the Five Year Plan last month, its nice to be able to get back to the more mundane things such as weather and sailing. A truly awful Bank Holiday weekend was appreciated by our newest members, the family of ducks swimming in the ponds in the cat field, but not by anyone else. This was made up for, in part, by the following weekend which was reasonably warm and dry and with good sailing breezes. It was good to see many members emerging from their overlong winter hibernation and taking to the water. The imaginative course in the morning caught a few of us out (thanks Howard) but the afternoon race up to Maldon and back more than made up for it. We are now in that part of the season when all the planning over long winter evenings begin to bear fruit. Texel and the Nore Race are imminent and the best race of all, our own East Coast Piers, will soon be upon us. Lee Harrison and Charles Anderson are heading for a record amount this year, with both Ermst & Young and 3Com equal main sponsors. BUT we can't run the race without adequate safety precautions and Charles still needs more mother boats. So all cruiser sailors, please volunteer if you can. You might think that the discomfort of mooring at mile intervals along the course goes unnoticed, I assure you it does not. As a regular competitor, and one who needed to trouble our rescue services last year, I assure you that mother boats are much appreciated. We have hit an unlucky patch with the Rib. No sooner do we fix one problem than another comes along, so that’s why you have not seen it on duty recently. Fortunately the Orkney, much improved after the modifications last year, has been able to stand in. Roy Hardwick, the Rib bosun is on the case and we won't be slow to engage professional help if necessary. It has been a particular pleasure to welcome Ian Caruth back to the Club with his Robber. Mick Richardson and Mike Onyans have also made the conversion from cat to cruiser racing and have already disturbed the established order by getting a first and a second in their first two BJRC Races. Come on everyone, try harder, they are impossible to live with at the moment. Good luck and good sailing to all members, cruising or racing. Particular luck to our Solo fleet whose Open meeting is imminent. I hope the winds are fair but not weak. View from the Rear I hope by the time this goes to print that our delightful British weather has finally sorted itself out. I have clearly been too vocal in my complaints about light airs we were getting as we were treated to full-on gales (and rain to go with it) over the Whitsun Bank Holiday. As far as I am aware, no damage was sustained to boats either on moorings or in the dinghy parks and I hope that this is the case - the only damage I am aware of is the anemometer falling down due to a snapped guy rope. This has been put in place again, hopefully facing the right direction - if it is reading the wrong wind direction then David, Lucy and I definitely did not have anything to do with putting it back up! GULL NATIONALS The Gull Fleet came down to have their National Championships alongside our normal Bank Holiday racing - only to have to sit around for Saturday and Sunday watching the wind and rain abandon all sailing. However, we managed to fit in three races on the Monday to make the championships worthwhile for them - they went away after one good day's sailing with a National Champion and I think they were pleased with the facilities we provided them, in spite of the weather. My sincere thanks go to Mike Helliwell and Hilary Ashley who were Race Officers and had to handle all the extra logistics of three races ( in addtion to the Club's own races) with no warning - ably assisted by Bob Anderson who stepped in to help. My thanks also go to the rescue crews who were on the water for a lot longer than normal - particular thanks to Lucy Boreham and Jan Chaplin who stood in at the last moment when we were short on support crews - Lucy and Ian averted a potentially embarrassing situation where we would have had to cancel the visitor racing due to insufficient support cover. I believe we now have got this situation in hand again. SERIES RACING The Spring Points series is now over with very impressive turnouts for both the Handicap and Cadet Fleets (14 different entries in each class over the series). The Solos continue to have a steady turn out and I am sure the multi-hulls will catch up during the year - not least to get in practice for the East Coast Piers Race which now looms large on the horizon. The rest of the season is now in full swing with Summer Points racing and the Wednesday night series well underway. In the meantime - here's to hot sun and steady Force 3-4s until at least the end of September! Solo - Sailing Downwind Having been asked by numerous people what the secret to my speed was last year, I thought it about time I let you all into a few secrets. Downwind speed is the big difference between the top ten and the rest of the fleet and if you can hang on up the beat you will find that the majority of place changes occur on the reaches and particularly the runs. The key to speed on the sea is surfing and the guy who catches the most waves will almost certainly be the fastest no matter what equipment he uses. Now, I know you are all saying that you've heard it all before but there is far more to surfing than just bearing away down the wave. The most important skill is to try and keep your average speed up. The faster you are going the easier it will be to catch the next wave, which means wallowing in between waves will simply not do. When you feel the boat falling off the back of the wave steer up to increase your speed and go looking for the next wave instead of letting it come to you! Another important skill is being able to pick a path through the wave front. This requires you to look ahead for any gaps which you can plane through and therefore jump the wave. In slower boats like Solos this is sometimes the only way that you can overtake a wave as the boat is not fast enough to plane over the back of it. In these conditions most boats are only separated by one wave and the people on the move are just better at finding the gaps. OK, so you are still finding it difficult to catch those waves. Well that's probably because you're not pumping enough. "“Arrr he mentioned the p word". Now I am sorry to bring up the forbidden subject but in fact is that one pump per wave is legal, so make full use of it. Just as you feel the transom being lifted by the wave give the mainsheet a pump and throw your weight out and back in the boat. This will increase your boat speed enough to catch those tricky little waves in intermediate conditions. Right, now something for all you hot shots out there. In Looe the problem downwind was that the waves were small and close together; this meant that as soon as you caught the waye you planed straight into the one in front. | managed to cope with this by Zig Zagging. This is a technique of getting on the wave and bearing away hard so that you slide across the wave rather than down it. On the runs this means that you will sail by the lee in one direction until you feel yourself falling off the wave, then head up sharply so that you broad reach back which can increase your speed so much that it puts you back on the wave that you have just come off. To do this you will need to let your kicker right off so that the top of your sail twists out in front of the boom. One warning though, it really is tippy!. AR OO IR I kk ok io a ok a ok kk RK kok kk ok oe oe I have only recently started sailing Solo's but I found this tip very useful indeed - especially at my club (Black Swan) where the winds can be a bit fickle between the islands. When sailing downwind in light winds, sit right forward of the centreboard case. Although this pushes the bow down, it has the effect of lifting the rear of the bar clear of the water. It can have quite a dramatic effect - even of the extent of gaining a place or two! Beware that gybing can become a bit tricky. Make sure you get back behind the thwart before gybing. This is for 2 reasons: (a) I found the boat turns too slowly with the bow down and (b) you can get in a real mess as the boom swings across - remember you are sitting right were the kicker comes across plus your arm holding the tiller is in the way of the main sheet! As long as you remember to get behind the thwart before gybing, this technique can help you gain a place or two. Additional Note This technique does not work for all Solos. With our fleet at Lock Venachar, we have found that moving your weight too far forward slows the boat down by allowing the bow to dig in. We have found that in certain boats, Boon and Jolly are good examples, that best results are obtained by keeping your weight on the thwart. It certainly works for Steve Boon - he never goes forward of the thwart. Any other thoughts? Steve Ash - Solo Fleet Captain Telephone: [redacted] Stephen Ash@RSA10 royal-and-sunalliance.com.
