Letter received from The Cirdan Sailing Trust "On behalf of the Cirdan Sailing Trust I would like to extend our heartfelt thanks to the Marconi Sailing Club for their very generous donation of £3,000 towards our work with disadvantaged young people. This donation was used for bursaries, providing groups from the following organisations, the opportunity to sail with us in 1999, 1. Ashford Youth Centre - A group of young people from villages and estates in the Ashford area of Kent. They are all disadvantaged from low-income families. They sailed on Queen Galadriel for 7 days in October. Bursary - £1500 A Canterbury College - The group are all final year 'A' level students from low income families. They traveled from Kent in August to Greenock where they joined Duet and took part in the Cutty Sark Tall Ships Race. They sailed in company from Greenock to Lerwick. 3. Corbets Tey School - All pupils on this trip have a statement of special educational needs. They require a high staff to student ration. Most of the pupils are from low-income families. Without financial assistance trips like this would not be possible. They traveled from Upminster in Essex to sail on Xylonite for 4 days. Bursary - £900. All the above youth organisations have told me they were very grateful for the funding help provided by Marconi Sailing Club. The Cirdan Trust is very grateful for this generous donation, which were the proceeds of the East Coast Three Piers Race. We are also very grateful to Charles Anderson for his help in generating a further £2,300 from sponsors, which we used to help with our vessel refit costs. We would like to take this opportunity to convey our heartfelt thanks to the members of the Marconi Sailing Club for their generosity and hope that you will be able to continue to support the work of The Cirdan Sailing Trust". Nick Back - Chief Executive Extracts from some of the correspondence received by The Cirdan Sailing Trust Corbets Tey School - " I and the pupils of Corbets Tey School would like to thank The Marconi Sailing Club for their kind assistance of bursary funding for our trip on the Xylonite, Without this funding the school could not have run the trip and the pupils would not have been able to enjoy the experience. Some of the pupils who took part were on their first trip away from their parents. The lessons they were able to learn I am sure will be of great assistance in their future lives". KEKKKKKEEKE "At the end of the trip we were able to leave the barge tidy and clean. We had been able to help sail and prepare meals. I feel all apart from one pupil we made good personal progress and had changed as a result of the trip" Canterbury College - "I am writing to thank your organisation for the most generous financial assistance provided to our students. Financial assistance such as yours is without doubt the life-blood of activities such as these. There can be no doubt that without your help we would not be able to undertake this prestigious event and we as a College are most grateful for your help. 10

The students who undertook this event discovered a great deal about themselves and about others. They operated in a very confined and strange environment and undertook tasks, which were, new, strange and in some cases difficult for them. I am convinced that such an event makes them understand more about the world we live in and about the view and opinions of others". Ashford Rural Detached Project - "On behalf of all the young people that sailed aboard Queen Galadriel I offer a very big thank you! In all my years of working with young people it was the most amazing residential experience. Young people are still hassling me in my office and carrying their photographs everywhere to show people. All the young people obtained competent crew certificates with some wondering if it is possible to leave school and cruise the world straight away! It is impossible to thank you enough for your support the reward for me is the young peoples faces after a real taste of adult life on the ocean waves". KKEKEKKEKE "The trip excelled all expectations especially with the gelling of the new crew for the week. To pick the ship up in London added greatly to the excitement as it shortened the journey in the mini bus and was full of people. Most of the young people live in isolated rural areas". KEKKKKKKES The young people always stayed very motivated to the point of not sleeping in case they missed something. There were no upsets in the galley, everybody played by the rota with cooking and washing up and creating wonderful food. The creations were magnificent or do I mean (cremations). KEAKKKKAKES "In total we managed to travel 149 miles from London to Ipswich, the experience of a sailing trip for six days is something I won't forget. There was a lot of hard work to do and if you didn't do it then you were not going anywhere. Team work was important on the trip especially when climbing the crows nest and hoisting someone's boxer shorts up the flag pole" One of the things I found difficult was living out of a bag for a week and also working in cramped conditions. I don't believe that my life has been the same since, as we have all kept in contact and met each other to compare embarrassing photographs. I am very glad I went". KKKKKKKKKK "During the journey me and Martin went up on the bowsprit and had a laugh but it wasn't funny when we had a run in with a few giant waves. Commodore's Notes I have heard that you all enjoyed the Summer Solstice party at the Club when several members were unrecognisable wearing long haired wigs to simulate the decade of ‘big hair’, the 60's. I don't know what the weather was like in England because I was in Holland, meeting my ‘date with destiny’ at Texel. You know, the biggest cat race in the world that I was unable to start last year due to breaking my rudders in the surf before the start. This year Race Day dawned cloudy, windy and cold as forecast. We put on our woolly bears and dry suits in the hotel and were not sorry to have done so. After rigging in the rain, together with the other 700 entrants, we attended the briefing which was late and only said, in three languages, that the weather was pretty awful and come back in an hour. About an hour and a half later, with several TV cameras running, including one on Alex and I (perhaps we look Dutch?) the Race Officer began a long speech. Starting in Dutch he spoke for ages and at the end there was a deep exclamation from most of the crowd. When we heard the English version, we found out why. The wind was already blowing 6, but was expected to rise to 7 in the squalls and ‘while acknowledging that many sailors had the ability to complete the 60 nautical mile course in those conditions, many were not’ Yes you've guessed it, the Race was cancelled. Of course we were disappointed, and some people were angry, but, by the time we had got the boat back on the trailer, the surf was coming in like the North Shore at Wakiki and it required a firm footing to stand in the wind. They definitely made the right decision, but to be thwarted two years running, this time by the weather, was galling. Alex has renewed determination to conquer the course, but I have resolved not to make any decisions until April next year, when I can assess whether the time, money and effort is worth it. The other thing last month was the Five-Year Plan Meeting. I must confess that I was a little disappointed with the turn out, however I would like to thank the 28 members who attended on the hottest day of the year and Father's Day to boot. I started by making a presentation of the Plan and after considerable discussion, we took a non-binding straw poll of those at the meeting. The majority opinion was that Plan B was the best, with strong minority support for Plan A. I have decided to hold another Meeting to discuss the Plan on:- Tuesday 8" August at the Sailing Club starting at 7.30 p.m. I am very keen to get as many of your opinions as possible, and hope you can make the meeting, which, of course, is on the second Tuesday of Camping Fortnight. If you cannot make the meeting but would still like to express an opinion please give me your views in writing. My email is [redacted]. My home address is:- 82, [redacted], Leigh on Sea, Essex [redacted]. Fax is not possible at the moment, sorry. Lastly, this edition should hit your doormat just before the Piers Race. This may not be the biggest cat race in the world, but it is definitely the best and held at the best Club in the country - Ours. What is more, we continue to be the only Club in Europe to channel all the profit from our major event into a Charity. Every member, whether entering or helping with the running, can be rightly proud of this Event, none more so than Lee Harrison, Charles Anderson and their hard working Committee. Now that Steve Monks, Bob Godbold and Mike Smith have fixed up a cellar cooler we can confidently expect a good flow of cold beer as well! I look forward to a good entry of Club boats. Don't forget that you can do the Colne Point Race if you think that Walton is a bit far. Every entry is welcome. See you on the start line. Clive Shenton

Hi folks, its nice to be back having spent the best part of June sailing along the French, Belgium coast to Holland on board "Happy Medium", in company with Malcolm ana Margaret Yeoman on "Suruca". We met up at Ramsgate before going on the Dover, Dunkirk, and Ostend then into Holland via Flushing. For once the weather was generally fine and we had a grand time. Our visit to Dunkirk on the outward leg of our journey coincided with the 60th Anniversary of the "Little Ship" rally and we were there to see them arrive, a truly moving experience. Well that’s enough of my holiday ramblings, what's been going on back at MSC? The trip to Brightlingsea, organised to bid a fond farewell to Harbour Master Peter Copeland was attended by 15 boats plus one crew coming round by road due to the fact that they were not yet launched, a splendid response which showed how much we appreciated the efforts both Peter and his assistant Brian have made on our behalf. 33 sat down to an excellent meal at the Colne Yacht Club with Peter, his wife Francis, Brian and his wife Christine as our guests. A glass tankard engraved with the Clubs emblem was presented to Peter as a memento.

From Your Social Committee The summer solstice celebration has been and gone!!!! Despite the best efforts of the weather the revellers were not to be deterred. It must have been the coldest, windiest evening for weeks. What did we do to deserve this? Should we put the disco on the hard? Would he be playing to himself all evening at great expense to us? Should we eat indoors? Such weighty decisions. We found a string of lights to put round the barbeque. If you ask the right people you will find all sorts of goodies that have not seen the light of day for years. Neil Pembleton to the rescue. We fused the whole club in the process of getting the lights up, but we got there in the end. Peter Clayton helped out by moving the travel hoist (who said it was for lifting boats?) into place to act as a much needed windbreak. By now we had decided to eat outside. Shiver me timbers is an apt description. Thank you Peter. Murray Bates, Mike Smith and family were responsible for getting the meat for us, and jolly good it was too. Thank you for all your efforts, and a big thanks to Eric Cockerton and his wife for running the barbeque on the night. Thank you again to Neil for stocking up the bar, and to Mike Helliwell, Hillary Ashley and Jenny Ball for manning the bars so ably. Eventually we had to move inside or perish. Many of our members entered whole-heartedly into the mid-summer spirit. There was a splendid array of fancy dress. Would you call it imagination or vivid, happy memories of the sixties? Prizes for the best dressed went to Chris and Margaret Harrison, Steve and Debbie Glynn, Michaela Glynn and Anthony Monks. See Debbie for photographs, or pay her for the negatives! They really looked splendid. Did anybody else take any photos? Why not put them on a notice board for a while? Graham, the DJ, commented on how much he had enjoyed himself and what a good crowd we were. He would be happy to come back, but next time he would allow himself more time to find us. Are we really out in the sticks at the back of beyond? When Laura arrived back at the club at some unearthly hour of the morning to go cruiser racing everything had been cleared up. So thank you to that band of merry workers whoever and wherever you are. Anyway, thank you all for your support. We were getting worried when we had only sold 40 tickets with 2 weeks to go. In the end we sold 100 tickets, 15 being bought on the last day. Was this because England was out of the world cup? Whatever the reason we consider this to have been another successful evening. Mona's Travels Continued Part Ten - Tour of the Canaries Eventually the gearbox was pronounced fit, various smaller jobs had been completed and after four and a half weeks we were able to leave Puerto Calero. We left on the sixth of December with grateful thanks to Jean Michel the mechanic and Brian and Marie at MAST who had sorted out a number of electrical problems and been tremendously helpful in getting things sent to the island We drifted down to Papagaya, a superbly picturesque anchorage in the south of Lanzarotte where we celebrated our freedom from marinas by swimming off the boat in crystal clear waters. The next day we had a beam reach across to and down the coast of Fuerteventura to Puerto Castillo. From offshore the most significant features of the island were the wide sandy beaches stretching for miles and the generally volcanic landscape. Puerto Castillo proved to be a pleasant little marina reached by rounding a rather fearsome looking reef and crossing right over some only too visible rocks literally inches below the keel. Around the marina was a modern holiday complex that seemed to stretch forever and completely dominated the immediate area. We hired a car for a couple of days and discovered that much of the island was largely unspoiled. From Fuerteventura we sailed overnight to Puerto Rico in the south of Gran Canaria. We had intended to sail straight onto Tenerife. As we sailed past Gran Canaria the wind having been weak and variable appeared to settle and increase giving us the prospect of a dead run to Tenerife. Laura and I set up the downwind rig only to have the wind fade and die completely within ten minutes. Thoroughly disheartened we started the engine and motored into Puerto Rico. At great expense we were given a berth in a dirty, smelly and noisy part of the harbour. We had a lazy day there and were determined to walk out of the touristy over developed bay. Puerto Rico is surrounded on three sides by high and steep mountainous ridges, we eventually found a way up the steep sides to the bay. We had a wonderful if rather hot walk into the interior with impressive views across this very mountainous island. It was rather depressing however seeing the way the island is being developed. As we walked up a dirt track into the mountains, we were overtaken by a succession of lorries negotiating the steep incline to reach the top and deposit their loads into the deep valley in an attempt to level it off and provide more space for tourist developments. One of these developments already in existence and right next to this dusty track was emblazoned with the name 'TOURISTICA EXPLOITICA' We had an enjoyable beat to Los Cristianos in Tenerife, leaving Puerto Rico before dawn. Anchoring in the harbour we never actually got round to landing on Tenerife but spent a fascinating afternoon watching a succession of weird and wonderful events taking place on the shore close by, with mime artists, bundles of rags that turned into people that then walked away, a series of altercations and much more, In the morning we motored across to La Gomera in a flat calm and were treated to the sight of a large number of pilot whales making slow and stately progress across our track, in marked contrast to the schools of dolphins that we had seen that took great delight in swimming along with us. As far as the pilot whales were concerned, we put the engine into neutral and had a ringside view as they swam past. It was a pleasure to be in La Gomera from the moment we arrived there, it quickly established itself as our favourite Canary Island. Arriving on December 15th we stayed for nine days dividing our time between making final preparations for the Atlantic crossing and exploring the island. Helen and Laura took most of the responsibility for our last minute provisioning, I became obsessed with our water supplies which are not excessive by any standards and seeing how many five litre containers I could squeeze into various comers of the boat. While these preparations were going on we were all trying to get used to the idea of a voyage of nearly three thousand miles. I became convinced that it was inevitable that we would be becalmed for several days at a time. Christmas was fast approaching and we had a festive time meeting up with other yachties and attending a couple of really enjoyable concerts at the very church that Christopher Columbus and his crew prayed at just prior to one of his Atlantic crossings. We set our departure date for the day before Christmas Eve, the allotted day dawned windless so we decided to give ourselves a day off. Christmas Eve morning Helen and Laura did some last minute provisioning at the Christmas market. I checked out with the harbour authorities, topped up the water tanks and we were ready to go. At twenty past two we started the engine and with a number of people helping us out of our berth, made our way to the harbour entrance to the accompaniment of klaxons and cheers. 13

Part Eleven - The Atlantic Crossing. There is always a slight sense of anxiety as you cast off your ties with the shore and head out of harbour. As we left San Sebastion on Christmas Eve 1999, a very real anxiety was mixed with an even stronger sense of relief that we had actually made a start. That morning a young German on a neighbouring boat had showed Laura how to contact a German website at the local internet café, that gave a comprehensive forecast for the area. This showed that we would expect fairly strong winds out of the north for the several days, and while I was convinced that we would suffer calms at some stage of the passage, my nightmare scenario was to be becalmed whilst still in sight of the Canaries. Incidentally, getting forecasts locally and been quite a problem and our Navtex had refused to cooperate whilst in Gomera, due to presumably the fact that we were enclosed on three sides by high cliffs. Within ten minutes of leaving the harbour the engine was off and we were sailing well under just the genny with the wind almost dead astern. I was a bit concerned about committing ourselves too early to the downwind rig whilst we were still coasting along La Gomera, however after an hour or so of sailing under the genny alone, the wind appeared to be fairly settled. Laura andI set up our by now infamous downwind rig with the furling genny poled out on what we thought would be the predominately windward side and the furling Yankee poled out to leeward. Once set up we connected the Monitor self-steering and with seventeen or so knots of wind blowing from astern we were well and truly off. That night we watched the lights of La Gomera receding astern and the wind gradually increased. By Christmas morning it was blowing at about twenty-five knots and we were rattling along at between six and a half and seven and a half knots. During the day the wind increased to the low thirties and Mona was having spurts of eight of nine knots. The seas were building all the time. In spite of the conditions and the fact that Laura and I hadn't quite managed to find our sea legs yet, Helen produced a superb Christmas Dinner, although in the end she decided to reserve the Christmas pudding for a later date. By the evening we were surfing down waves and were jointed for a while by a school of dolphins swimming alongside and leaping out of the saves. Early Boxing Day morning, Helen recorded in the log ‘Another wild night, up to 35 knots of wind, running under reduced sail. Mona going well. We are getting tired but managing OK. L and M have been sick but have both slept a bit so hopefully will recover’, I recorded in the log - ‘We are beginning to settle down to shipboard life. It was quite difficult with the strong winds early on but at least it gave us a good start in terms of progress. It is surprising how long it takes to get into a passage like this. At first all you seem to be doing is feeling tired on watch and then trying desperately to sleep the rest of the time. You gradually unwind and relax and begin to enjoy yourself. Its beginning to happen now. Long may it continue’, It was at this time that I finally managed to get through to Herb on the SSB. Herb is a weather guru who runs a net out of Canada, covering the whole of the Atlantic. Yachts make an initial call giving their position. Herb then groups yachts according to their location in various parts of the Atlantic. He then deals s with each area separately giving every yacht an individual forecast. Not surprisingly this daily procedure can take anything up to three hours, depending on the number of participating vessels. We had been unable to hear Herb at all when we were in La Gomera. Since our departure we had managed to hear him but had not made contact ourselves. Now at last we got through. Up to now we had been heading in a generally southwesterly direction. The perceived wisdom for the crossing is that you should head well south to be more likely to pick up and retain the trades. We had already heard horror stories from this year alone of yachts being becalmed for many days at a time. The other advantage of going well south is that in so doing you pass fairly close to the Cape Verdes and therefore have the option of breaking your journey there should it be necessary. We had decided from the outset that we could call in there if progress was slow. Herb's initial advice was that we should continue heading well south, not so much in search of the trades, which he confirmed we had well and truly found and were likely to retain in abundance, but more to avoid the worst excesses of weather that were about. He was advising yachts still in the Canaries to delay their departure for the time being because of the generally unsettled conditions there. By day six Laura had revived sufficiently to record in the log - "Yes I am still alive. Something was definitely wrong as I had no appetite and even had to force myself to drink water! Mum had achieved great feats in the galley, producing meals to tempt even the most jaded of appetites. Yesterday was a lot calmer while the wind kept up a good speed, so the motion became much steadier and I eventually began to settle in. This evening we have been surrounded by dolphins. They stayed for hours, swimming alongside and mjmping across our bows. Last night was definitely my best night watch so far. We were sailing extremely well at around seven knots with a relatively calm sea. I hardly wanted to go off watch. This morning blew away the cobwebs with a full salt water wash in the cockpit. Very invigorating’. 14

On day seven, December 30th, just as Laura got into her stride Helen began to wilt after her heroic efforts over the first few days. In the small hours of the morning she recorded in the log - ‘Feeling miserable. Have been trying to sit in the chart area. The only place vaguely comfortable with the awful motion. Can't feel human anywhere, The wind is not that strong. It did get up to 33 knots earlier, but the seas are lumpy’. @ By the next afternoon however she was recording that she had had a good sleep, been treated to breakfast in bed and was feeling human again. Laura continued to be in fine form and spent sometime working out how to use the hand held water-maker we had bought in the Canaries. As it entailed handing the filter over the side of the boat we eventually decided that it was an operation that should be tackled when conditions were calmer, especially as there was no immediate panic over water. Having said that, Helen and Laura both maintain that I had a fixation about water usage all the way across, the extent that they would be aware of me giving them the evil eye if they dared to pump water from the tap. By Friday 31st of December we had been at sea for exactly one week and had covered one thousand and fifty three miles giving an average days run of 150 miles plus, much better progress than we had dared hope for. After a slightly quieter day the wind got up again the evening. Our plans for a Millenium party became increasingly curtailed as the evening wore on the winds got stronger. It was a strange feeling moving in to the year two thousand as we surged and plunged into the blackness. vases to be continued in the next edition of Navigans.

Commodores Notes In the two months since the last Commodores Notes, the Club has run several excellent events and one consultation meeting, The consultation meeting related to the Five Year Plan. It was well attended and very lively discussion took place. It is difficult to summarise a two hour meeting, but I think its true to say the main thrust was that refurbishing the changing rooms was more important than building a veranda. By now you should have received my letter about our Opinion Poll on the Five Year Plan, together with a Recording Paper and a stamped addressed envelope. If you have not already recorded your opinion and returned it, please do so now. The Piers Race took place in late July, Race Day was windy with 5-6 forecast, but from a benign direction, north westerly, and the full race was run. There was once again a very good entry, and Xylonite made a great starting line boat, very evocative of Essex and the Blackwater. The Race was won by an Australian sailing an American cat (a Hobie Fox) registered in Holland. It seems to show what a truly international event our Race has become. Thanks to the good work by the ECPR Committee we had record sponsorship and we should be able to donate a record amount to the Cirdan Trust, who were again our chosen charity. Thanks and congratulations go to Lee Harrison who, after this year’s four de force, has decided to stand down after three years in the Race Chair. Well done Lee and thanks also to Davina as behind every great man is...... Grateful also thanks go to Charles Anderson, Chris Davies and all the ECPR Committee. The Glynns, the Toveys, Jenny Ball and Mick Richardson made an excellent job of making the site presentable and very special thanks go to Mike Turner who once again ably filled the role of Race Officer. Lastly, thanks to the cruiser sailors who carried out mother boat and matriarch duties. Its not pleasant spending the day at anchor in the good old east coast chop, but I can vouch that competitors are grateful and reassured by your presence out there. The Rescue boat crews were ever present and had some custom on in the lively conditions. The Cruisers made their annual pilgrimage to Shotley Woods over the Bank Holiday. After the now traditional meal on Sunday evening, the fleet made off in every direction possible, some are still on their travels. Sue and myself had the pleasure of attending the end of Cadet Week Prize Giving. I have never seen so many beaming young faces, they had obviously had a fantastic week. Peter Clayton, aided and abetted by Kevin Dowley and Steve Monks and together with a vast list of trainers and helpers, have obviously built on the traditions of Charles and Chris. About 85 cadets attended the week, anyone seeing their skill levels and enthusiasm will be certain of the long term future for our Club and our sport. I close with a second reminder, please return your Opinion Poll Recording Paper as soon as you can. The Main Committee really want to know how every member feels about the Five Year Plan. View from the Rear I can’t believe that we are in September already - (probably October by the time you are reading this) - and the sailing season is nearly over. Looking back though - we have had some superb sailing events this summer and at least the weather in August and September has been considerably better than May, June and July. I believe the main sailing events may be covered separately elsewhere in this magazine - but I just want to touch on the highlights. ECPR I think it was only a week or two before the Piers Race that I helped my Dad motor AmyJack back from Tollesbury - it was so cold, wet and windy that we were in full winter gear and it could not have been further from the kind of weather you would want in July. I remember fretting about how the Piers Race would turn out if this weather continued. Fortunately, the weather finally began to turn in time for the Piers Race and, although it wasn’t the hottest weekend we have had, it did bring an excellent sailing breeze. With a turn out of around 60 boats, the Piers Race proved it could still attract the key European cat sailors, (and one Australian who eventually won the event), and a superb weekend was had by all. I extend my thanks to the ECPR Committee and the army of helpers and volunteers who made all the arrangements - it takes a lot of hard work to bring off such an event. Cadet Week Words cannot express what Cadet Week means - and it goes from strength to strength. A staggering 85 cadets were catered for this year plus 20 adult cadets - these numbers only outstripped by the numbers of helpers on shore and on water who ensured that everyone could have a full week of sailing activities. Peter Clayton, Steve Monks and Kevin Dowley somehow managed to keep everything co- ordinated and under control (!) throughout the whole week and it never ceases to amaze me how many people will give up a weck’s vacation to be run ragged by 85 children!! On a serious note, although Cadet week is hard work and puts a tremendous strain on club facilities - the sheer activity and enthusiasm from those involved really shows the club at its best and is a credit to us all - long may it continue - (although I am busy training up the older cadets to take over running things so the rest of us can retire!). If you ever wonder about the future of our sailing club - come along to a Cadet Week prize giving and you will be very much re-assured. Summer Points The Summer Points series is now over and a vast improvement in turnout for all fleets compared to the Spring Points series. Although dinghy/cat racing is only one part of what the club does - it is good to see such strong turnouts and I hope this continues into the Autumn points - hopefully the weather will hold good through September and October. Thanks again to those people who have been manning the support boats and race box so that we can continue to get out on the water every Sunday. And Finally - Club Members Property It seems a shame to have to include a “moan” in all the good news above - but there is one matter of importance that I would like to bring to club members’ attention. Could I remind all members that if you need to move another members’ property on the club site - you must ensure that you contact the owner and ask their permission first. Apart from the fact that none of us would like to arrive at the site and find our belongings missing or moved - it also makes things very difficult for all concerned if anything is found to be missing or broken from the property that has been moved. If you need to move an item and cannot identify the owner - please gather as much information as you can about it and contact your Fleet Captain who will help you to track down who the owner might be. I would greatly appreciate your co-operation in this matter. 1 look forward to seeing you all on the water for rest of the season! Jenny Ball Rear Commodore and Bonfire Monitor

TOM PATTERSON- a friend and colleague remembered. Tom died in hospital on 5th August as he approached his 91st birthday. Few of present day members will remember Tom in his sailing days at Stansgate. Some, however, may have noticed in recent times a small figure sitting on a chair on the top of the sea wall, sometimes alone and sometimes accompanied by his daughter Jean and his grandchildren. He still drove his car to Stansgate at the age of 90 years, just to look out over the river and soak up the beauty of the estuary and to watch the boating activities of the club and other river users. I first met Tom when I transferred from Marconi New Street to the new Acrodynamic Manufacturing unit at Basildon in 1955. We soon became friends and shared a common interest in sailing, particularly the aerodynamics and hydrodynamics of multihull design. We became avid members of the Amateur Yacht Research Society, which did much to further catamaran and trimaran development. Tom purchased a small 2-man catamaran, not unlike the early Hobies in that it had seating for the helm and crew, together with a rigid floor between the hulls. It was great off wind but hopeless to windward and tacking usually entailed going into reverse! There was only one other catamaran in the club at the time, a Prout built Swift. Jack Bigden was Commodore, George Underdown was the Steward, ‘Petes Palace’ and the old clubhouse were the order of the day. At the age of 90 Tom was still toying with the idea of buying a cat and getting afloat again! His love of Stansgate and sailing is an example to us all. Ron Greygoose. Presidents Progress I am back home again some two stone lighter, can you imagine it! Someone suggested I switch to a Mirror or a Topper - some chance! I am glad to say that I am now putting on weight but am unlikely to be fit enough to sail again this season. Mary and I would like to thank all the Committee and members who have expressed their support and particularly those who have visited and stocked me up with Guinness and Mars bars during my period in hospital. Visitors are welcome to call at [redacted], Maldon. Telephone 0162 1-8[redacted], should they feel so inclined. Ron Greygoose

Adult Cadets 2000 During this year's cadet week, an Adult Cadet section was run. There were 22 cadets in this section all from a variety of backgrounds, cat sailing, cruiser sailing, limited dinghy helming and crewing and some with no sailing experience at all. The course was run in a relaxed and not-too structured way trying to provide for the cadets varied needs. However, every cadet carried out the capsize drill on the Monday after seeing a demonstration on land. Using a spinnaker was covered on Tuesday and general sailing on Tuesday afternoon. Wednesday was a general sailing day with some cadets putting into practice the capsize drill learnt on Monday. Thursday was meant to be a sail to Mill Beach in Heybridge followed by a picnic, but a severe thunderstorm knocked this on the head. When the storm cleared a good afternoons sailing resulted. Friday was an excellent sailing day with all cadets being on the water at the same time in Enterprises, Mirror 16, Wayfarer, 420, laser 2, Pico and some cats. After a quick sail around the marks by the club all of the cadets in the week sailed to Osea Island for a picnic on the beach. During the picnic a number of Adults borrowed the Toppers and Picos and had some fun sailing off the beach. The week culminated with a sail around the Island. During the week a number of club sailors stepped in to offer boats and instruction, this was greatly appreciated. The prize giving was held on Saturday with all Adult cadets receiving a certificate, also best Adult Cadet was awarded to Jane Muggs for her enthusiasm and improvement shown during the course. A special bravery award was also made to Iris Knights who suffered a bad capsize during the week and spent a morning on Osea beach sitting out a thunderstorm but a no point did she moan or complain but kept smiling. This year's E.C.P.R. has come and gone and I would like to thank those members of the fleet who gave their support to this event. It was a nice gesture of Chris Davies to offer a trot boat service in the Orkney at the end. Unfortunately, not many were able to take advantage of this since they had needed their dinghies earlier on to get out to their boats, but thanks for the thought. It was also a nice gesture by Charles Anderson to present a couple of ECPR Mugs to the Mother Boats and Matriarchs, shame we did not get one, never mind. Our flotilla cruise to Shotley showed a good turnout with 17 boats in the main party joined briefly by ANGEL 11, PEACE, SERUPIN 11 and BLUSTER each of which had alternative commitments but it was nice to meet up with them if only for a short while. Thirty four members including Frank Bennett who drove up especially, sat down to an excellent meal in the "Stour Suite” of the Shipwreck Bar with its panoramic view over the River Ore and Stour Estuaries. I think we were all very pleased to have made it especially in view of the weather on the Friday night and the general forecast. On Monday the fleet did a bomb burst with those needing to get back for work locking out carly whilst the remainder split into two groups with Trumpeter, Winkler and Aldebaran opting for the river Stour and Erwarton Ness whilst Happy Medium, Fantasea, Icarus, Fraise Du Boise, Tahiti, Serupin 11, Reflection and Sea Gem opted for the river Deben with a bar-b-que on Tuesday at the Tide Mill, Woodbridge. By Wednesday most of the fleet were back in the river Orwell with the Stour group on the pontoons at the Royal HarwichYacht Club, whilst those from the Deben, (less Sea Gem who had to return home and Reflection whose forestay broke on the way down the Deben and had to return to Woodbridge for repairs,) secured to moorings off Lavington. On Thursday morning we all met up again at Ipswich Haven Marina with yours truly giving a demonstration on how not to wire up an alternator! Thanks Roy, Bob and John for your technical support and help. On Friday Tahiti and Fraise Du Bois left for Wolverstone where they were mecting up with the family. The weather forecast was giving us all some concern but some positive action by Sue on Fantasea galvanised some of us into action resulting in Fantasea followed by Winkler, Seruptin 11 and Happy Medium leaving for the Blackwater for which we had a surprisingly good passage back with Winkler and Seruptin 11 returning to M.S.C. whilst Fantasea and Happy Medium went into Salcott Creek to round off the week. By Sunday those due to return did so, leaving Tahiti and Fraise Du Bois in the Walton Backwaters area and poor Mark and Peter with Reflection still up at Woodbridge. We all wish them the best of luck with their rigging and a safe passage home. By popular demand the WATER CRESS RUN is on this year. I have been able to book us into Heybridge Basin on weekend 23/24 September, unfortunately the previous weekend which had a better tide was already booked, so it means with high water at 0831 we will have to lock in about 0800 on Saturday morning, unless some of you wish to go up the night before (HW1943). There is a list on the notice board, would those wishing to go please enter their boat name on the list so I can advise the Lock Keeper. Remember to take your dinghies for the trip up the canal to Beeleigh Weir on Saturday. Locking out on Sunday will be between 0900 and 1000. I must at this stage draw your attention to the fact they we are getting close to laying up time. Please make sure your cars are not obstructing the road especially on the corners, remember quite a few boats are now using the Travel Hoist which needs a great deal of room to manoeuvre, also of course do not obstruct other members trailers. I will be putting up the "Haul Our List" also the "Cruiser Park Layout" lists shortly, remember only those members who have paid winter storage in advance will be allocated spaces - no space allocated - no storage - sorry. I cannot close this edition of Cruiser Comments without saying how sad we all are at the death of Ann Bates and our heartfelt sympathies go out to Murray and his family. Derek Kirby - Cruiser Fleet Captain. 10

Mona's Travels Continued New Year's morning we saw what was only our second ship since leaving the Canaries. | was going to call him up. Then when it became clear that he was going to pass well astern of us, 1 decided not to bother. As he steamed off I went down below to write it up in the log. When I went back on the deck I could hardly believe it when I saw another ship steaming straight for us. I called him. He wished us season's greetings and confirmed that he had seen us and that he would pass safely across our bows without us altering course. We spoke to a couple of French Yachts - both crews were very lively saying that they were drinking wine to celebrate the new millennium. As we were English they assumed that we were celebrating by drinking cups of tea! The Captain of the ship that was approaching us came on air to wish us his own greetings. He asked where we were from and was very interested in our trip. He then asked if there was anyone we would like to send an e mail to. All in all it proved to be a more sociable New Year's Day than we had anticipated. January 2nd brought with it a succession of stronger squalls many of which were accompanied by heavy downpours. These were eagerly awaited opportunities for one or other of us to have a freshwater shower in the cockpit. This activity seemed rather strange at first when we were rattling along in gale force winds with huge seas rolling up behind us, many of them breaking. That night Laura recorded - 'Had a great night watch. Spent a lot of time lying on the foredeck being at one with nature! Still gusty. During one were logging nine knots. Wind now steady 25 to 30 knots. Lots of flying fish, listening to world service’ After nine days at sea we were all experiencing highs and lows. At one point I went up into the cockpit to find Helen staring gloomily over the stern at the rolling waves that were racing after us. She made the following comment in the log book’ I spy with my little eye something beginning with 'S'. Conditions carried on much the same with only minor variations., although the weather was getting steadily warmer. Day 19 brought more squalls of 40 knots plus. Laura recorded - 'Our intended destination has officially been changed from Barbados to St. Lucia. Only 300 miles to go. Opened another fruit juice to celebrate and Dad even ' broke out' another container of fresh water!’ Day 21, January 13th dawned to reveal the distant outline of St. Lucia. After nearly three weeks out of sight of land it was a very special sight. At last confirmation that you have actually been getting somewhere. As we sailed round the north of St. Lucia Laura suddenly remarked that it was the time of the ARC net. This was a daily chat session that had started before the ARC crossing itself, when boats had been converging on the Canaries from various parts of Europe. The intention had been to carry on this daily chat net after the ARC itself. I switched on the SSB to be greeted by the unmistakable lilt of Pat from Aldebaran, chatting to another ARC boat. | was all set to call him up as soon as they had finished talking, when we heard him asking if they had an news of 'Muna'. We very quickly made contact and when he had established where we were he invited us to his son's wedding in St. Lucia two days later. As we sailed round the island it was time to take in the downwind rig twenty days and three thousand miles after we had put it up. I have long had something of a reputation for not doing any more sail changes than was absolutely necessary, but one sail change after three thousand miles was rather taking things to extremes even by my standards. Sailing under Yankee alone, closer to the wind than we had been all the way across we were suddenly aware just how strong the wind was. This was reinforced by secing large yachts exposing their keels as they plunged from wave to wave. Suddenly everything seemed to happen incredibly quickly. As Helen put it after days at sea we were suddenly sailing into a picture postcard as we rounded Pigeon Island and sailed into Rodney Bay. We started the engine and motored into the Marine in the lagoon, arriving twenty days and two hours after leaving La Gomera. In that time we had logged three thousand and forty seven miles. The Monitor had steered nearly all the way, and the downwind rig had really proved its worth. it overriding quality had been that we could reef it to whatever size suited the conditions. The other piece of gear that had been superb was the wind generator. Together with the solar panels it had kept the batteries up all the way to the extent that we had only had to min the engine for two hours out of gear for the entire trip when the batteries had lookeda little low. Having tied up in the marina we were suddenly inundated with locals offering to do our washing and clean our hull. We just looked at each other slightly bemused. We had arrived. Part Twelve - St. Lucia. Having arrived in St. Lucia it took us quite a long time to accept that we had actually arrived. Although crossing the Atlantic was something I had fantasised about for most of my life, as the actual event had drawn ever nearer I had found it increasingly difficult to imagine being at sea for that length of time. Even during the crossing, it was difficult to have a concept of sailing three thousand 12

miles. For that reason the halfway stage was particularly significant as by then you knew what sailing fifteen hundred miles was like and you only had the same distance to go. In the closing stages when we were within five hundred miles of making a landfall we could relate this to previous trips. We were much fresher when we arrived than we had expected to be. That first evening we caught up with the crews of several boats that we had last seen over two months earlier, before they had set off with the ARC. The ARC had once again suffered from, or been blessed with, mainly light variable winds with longest periods of flat calms. It was fascinating comparing our very different experiences, Back on the boat it was a strange experience lying in our bunks without being thrown around. We stayed in the marina at Rodney Bay for nearly two and a half weeks, far longer than we had initially anticipated. During that time however, the trades continued to blow extremely strongly and it was pleasant to be able to relax and sort things out on the boat, without having to worry about the safety of the boat. |We were also able to explore that part of St. Lucia at our leisure. Of particular interest was the remains of the British Garrison on Pigeon Island, now a national park. Just two days after our arrival we went to the wedding of Pat and Olivia's son. We had first met Pat and Olivia in Spain and had been bumping into them ever since. The wedding turned out to be a double one with friends of Pat and Olivia's son making up the second couple. The wedding was a superb day, quite a change from being at sca. We were relieved to discover on phoning my parents in Poole, that Jenny had arrived safely in England on Christmas Day and was intending to get a flight to join us for a few wecks. As we were in no particular hurry, we decided to stay on in St. Lucia for the time being in the hope that Jenny would be able to join us there before too long, In the meantime Pat and Olivia persuaded us to sail down the St. Lucian coast. This provided the push we (or I) needed to get out of the marina. We sailed down the coast to Marigot, a tiny enclosed bay where Admiral Rodney (a contemporary of Nelson) is reputed to have hidden his fleet disguised as palm trees while the French sailed by. From Marigot we moved onto Souffriere an area of incredible scenery protected as a National Park. The anchorage nestles against a palm tree lined beach between two amazing peaks known as Pitons. Their name has been taken over by the local beer, which is also very good. The authority running the Marine Park have laid buoys along the shore in an attempt to protect the coral. The system is that you pick up one of these buoys and tie your stern to a convenient palm tree. There are an abundance of boat boys competing for the chance of helping you complete this operation. It is big business with boats mecting you a couple of miles offshore to secure your custom. Once secured, or even before. other boat boys will appear attempting to sell you wares of all shapes and sizes. We stayed for the best part of the week in this Marine Park, taking the opportunity to explore further inland. One of the most energetic trips was a visit to the rain forests at the centre of the island) The recommended way of doing this was to take a tour, whereby a taxi would take you high into the hills from where you walked through the forest trail. We decided to do it the hard way, by local bus. A trip on the bus is always a fascinating experience. There is generally a ‘background! of very loud music, either country or reggae. The drivers are very trusting, never expecting to be paid until the end of the journey. The walk around the rainforest was an incredible experience, just seeing the variety and scale of the plant life. We spent several hours following the various paths that had been cut out. During our stay in St. Lucia we met some fascinating people. Helen was particularly taken by a boat/fruit vendor called Love who always seemed to give her a good deal, putting in extra fruit after the deal had been struck. Another local who made a good impression was Vision a charismatic character with perfect white teeth who kept wanting to take Laura and Helen to visit the banana plantations and sunsets over Marigot bay where he lived. The waterfront at Souffeire had been devastated by the recent Hurricane Lenny which had swept the island just two months earlier and had hit particularly hard by virtue of the fact that unlike other hurricanes it had tracked from west to east, attacking the soft western underbelly of the islands. Over the next few weeks we were to see more evidence of Hurricane Lenny on other islands. In Souffriere we saw many people still living in houses that had all but been demolished by the wave that had swept the shore. What struck us most forcibly was how happy and friendly they were in spite of the suffering they had been through. We were told by locals that although they had very little they were well fed due to the abundance of fresh fruit readily available. Eventually Jenny flew out to join us and we were reunited as a family for the first time in two years. Having given Jenny a brief taste of St. Lucia we set off North for the French Island of Martinique. Martinique Coming out from behind the shelter of St.Lucia we faced a stiff north easterly of 25 knots or so and some fairly heavy seas between the islands as we beat across to Martinique. Mona revelled in the conditions while Jenny enthusiastically settled back into sailing. Only I, I'm ashamed to admit, felt decidedly queasy and had to lie down for a while. We sailed into the shelter of Martinique in great style and anchored off Marin to check in at customs. Having landed we discovered that customs wouldn't be open until the morning. 13

We also immediately noted the contrast with St. Lucia. No boat boys, no locals clamoring to do jobs for you. The locals we came in contact with were generally very reserved. Prior to crossing over | had been almost totally ignorant as to the status of the various islands, apart from the fact that some had in the past been British colonies. It was only now that I discovered that Martinique was in fact a full department of France with the same status as any other department such as Brittany. Anyone living on the island was able to travel to France if they so wished and take advantage of any provision such as education and health care available to other French citizens. The marina at Martin was teeming with French charter boats. In the morning Helen and I went ashore in the dinghy to check in at customs. Meanwhile, unbeknown to us a large customs launch anchored just upwind of Mona. The crew then disappeared below decks. The launch then preceeded to draw down on Mona. In spite of the combined efforts of Jenny shouting from the foredeck and Laura calling them on the VHF, it was some considerable time before they managed to elicit any response. When the crew finally did emerge, just as the two boats made contact, they tried to make out that it was Mona that had dragged, upwind! Once Helen and I were back on board we made our way over to St. Annes where we anchored off the beach just as Pat and Olivia arrived from St. Lucia in Aldebaran. As soon as we had anchored we were all swimming off the boat. It was our 25th wedding anniversary and Laura and Jenny prepared us a special Anniversary lunch. We had a very pleasant time sitting in the cockpit opening cards and presents from home that Jenny had brought out with her. After lunch we went ashore where we met up with Pat and Olivia. We all walked along the bay as far as the Club Med set on a peninsula where we sat on the beach as the sun went down and drank a bottle of champagne that Jenny had bought us on the flight over. A very special moment. When we went back into St. Annes we tried to get a table at a restaurant we had liked the look of earlier, only to find that it was now fully booked. We eventually found somewhere else to eat that looked O.K. So far on our trip when we had eaten out we had been very lucky and had some lovely meals, On this day of all days things went badly wrong. Having ordered before a quarter to eight, it was nearly ten o'clock before we were served our first course, In the meantime I had made visits to the kitchen only to be told that we would be served very soon. When the food finally arrived it was almost uneatable. It all became something of a farce. Olivia complained that her vegetables were almost uncooked and cold. Her vegetables were taken away only to reappear two minutes later on my plate. In the end we cut our losses and brought the meal to a close. Not the anniversary meal we would have liked but we all managed to laugh about it. As Helen said, we'd had an unconventional wedding so it was only appropriate that we should have an unconventional anniversary. The next day was Pat and Olivia's anniversary so we had a barbeque on board Aldebaran as a joint celebration. We moved onto Anse l'Anne opposite the capital Fort de France. We crossed over to Fort de France where Helen and I had the memorable experience of watching a mass baptism off the local beach. From Anse I'Anne we made our way up the coast to St. Pierrre a town that had been almost totally destroyed by a volcanic eruption in 1902. Almost thirty thousand people were killed and fifty two ships sunk at anchor in the bay. There had been only two survivors, one of whom was being held on a charge of murder in the town goal. He had been saved by the thickness of the cell walls and door. After the event he hae been given his freedom and been exhibited in Barnham's Circus. We climbed the volcano, an expedition that became something of an epic as the local bus stopped some way short (about four miles) of the start of the climb itself. By the time that Jenny, Helen and I reached the café at the start of the climb we were already exhausted in the heat. Pat and Olivia had caught the bus before us and we later discovered that they had managed to hitch a lift up to the café. It turned out to be a very exciting walk/climb. Pat and I reached the summit with me some twenty minutes behind. As I got there the mist descended obliterating the view. Setting off from St. Pierre we had fickle winds until we came out of the lee of the island. Between the islands the winds steadied as they normally did and we had a good sail across to Dominica, another island that had once been a British colony. Part Fourteen - Dominica Dominica made another impressive landfall as we sailed in past Scotts Head and anchored off the Anchorage Hotel near Roseau, using the anchor off stern to a palm tree technique. We were helped in this manoeuvre by a couple of boat boys. As another ex British colony Dominica had a culture similar in some ways to that of St. Lucia but with it's own individual characteristics. The boat boys were again in evidence but not to the same degree as in St. Lucia. We had an interesting walk around Roseau in spite of the fact that it was dominated on the day we were there by the presence of an enormous cruise liner tied to the tiny town quay. We got rather tired of being mistaken for passengers off it. A shop where I enquired about having some films developed justified the highly inflated prices, by asking how much we were paying to travel on that ship. From Roseau we motored up the coast of Dominica in an almost flat calm. It was still a novelty to be able to stay in deep water just a little way offshore and have a really good view of the various settlements and changing scene as you went by. When we arrived at the large sheltered anchorage off Portsmouth at the north west tip of the island, we were besieged by boat boys before we had even 14

anchored. Harassment of visiting yachts has proved to be counter productive to the local economy in the past and in Portsmouth they have tried to address the problem by forming an association of official guides. We enlisted the services of one of these, Oscar, who early the next morning rowed us up the Indian River deep into the heavily wooded interior. We had an invigorating swim in cool fresh stream water. Later Oscar took Pat and I across the bay to the custom dock. For this trip he used the full power of his Yamaha outboard. The combination of traditional wooden long slim chined hull and modern powerful outboard (generally Yamaha) proved to be very common in the islands particularly St. Lucia and Dominica. On this occasion we traveled faster than I can remember going before on water. In the evening Oscar persuaded us to go with him to his home for a meal. He assured us that the fact that Laura was a vegan would not present a problem. In the event he was right because we all had a totally vegan meal, something that Pat was not to let Laura forget some time. It was a fascinating evening however and a rare opportunity to have a glimpse of the local lifestyle. All the houses we Saw were very simple affairs with corrugated iron roofs. On the second of March we set off for Iles des Saintes just twenty miles to the north. Part Fifteen - Guadeloupe The Iles des Saintes are a group of small islands that are politically part of Guadeloupe, another French Island with the same status as Martinique. We had a brisk sail from Dominica weaving our way between the off lying rocks and islets. Our first anchorage was in a sheltered bay called Anse Fiedelling on Terre D'en Bas, a small extremely quite island. The houses we saw there were notable for their solidity and comfort compared with the flimsy structures we had seen on Dominica. We had an enjoyable if rather hot walk the length and breadth of the island. Moving over to the main island in the group, Terre D'en Haut, we anchored off the main town of Bourge de Saintes. Ashore we saw several really large iguanas that had been taken over a tree right on the shore. We had a very pleasant walk across the island to Baie de Pointpierre, a lovely beach where after snorkeling we rested on the heavily shaded beach and Olivia was molested by several local goats, From Iles des Saintes we had another lively sail across to Basse Terre in the south of Guadeloupe. We had hoped to stop there to see something of the carnival that was due to start in the next couple of days. However, we didn't like the look of the anchorage so carried on up the coast to an anchorage near another Pigeon Island, where we were reunited with the crew of Johathon a French yacht we had last seen in Graciosa in the Canaries. We then stopped in the large sheltered anchorage of Deshaics on the north west corner of Guadeloupe. We stayed there for three nights, enjoying superb walks through the forest, one of which involved following a mountain stream and where we were able to have a wonderful swim in a natural freshwater pool. On the last day that we were there, Laura went off on one of her epic explorations, that involved getting lifts from various people and touring practically the length and breadth of the island. Her return well after dark unfortunately coincided with the arrival of a heavy swell which turned the previously idyllic anchorage into something of a nightmare. Having looked for Laura ashore earlier to no avail, I was reluctant to leave the boat again as we pitched and tossed dangerously close to other boats. A lack of wind meant that boats were swinging in all directions. Eventually Laura appeared from the blackness in a high powered rib accompanied by two husky Americans. The next morning we sailed the forty-five miles to Antigua in the company of Aldebaran and Vitamin Sea, another boat that we had been meeting up with since Portugal. Sailing into English Harbour was like sailing into a page out of a history book, with its restored Nelson's Dockyard. The landscape around the entirely natural harbour was sufficiently rugged to have staved off too much obvious signs of development. Part Sixteen - Antigua and Barbuda Antigua gained its independence from Britain in the early eighties, together with Barbuda, a sparsely populated reef fringed island lying some thirty miles to the north east of Antigua. Apparently the inhabitants of Barbuda were largely against independence and resent being lumped together with Antigua. 1 really enjoyed our time anchored in English Harbour with its combination of natural beauty and historic interest. However we found the locals working in and around the dockyard to be some of the surliest of anyone we had encountered on the trip so far. Helen put this down to the fact that they were coming into daily contact with crews, owners and charter guests of some of the biggest yachts in the world. In Falmouth Harbour, just next door to English Harbour we saw an amazing array of super yachts, both power and sail. These exotic craft dripping with opulence and ostentation seemed to dominate and take over the area in the same way that colonial powers like Britain had dominated the islands, in a heavy handed fashion, in years gone by. There were many occasions during our 15

time in these islands, especially when seeing evidence of the slave trade, when it was difficult not to feel a deep sense of shame at our countries involvement in many aspects of these islands’ history. We enjoyed some vigorous walks up to and around the headlands surrounding these bays, including an energetic climb up to Shirley Heights, the site of one of many British Forts, where, entertained by a steel bank, we watched the sun setting over the hills and saw Mona's anchor light burning in the bay far below. From English Harbour we sailed round the reefs to a marina at Jolly Harbour, where amongst other things we caught up with a number of jobs that needed doing on the boat. It was noteworthy that the locals we came across here were far friendlier than those we had come across near English Harbour. We had for sometime been keen to visit Monserrat, which had, suffered severe volcanic eruptions in 1995 and 1997. There had been predictions of further volcanic action for the last few weeks. Under the circumstances, a sensible alternative to sailing across was to visit by ferry. Pat and Olivia our Irish friends off Aldebaran had decided to do this on March 17th St. Patrick's Day. I hadn't realised previously that Monserrat had strong Irish connections dating from a time when Irish settlers had fled there after facing persecution in the neighbouring islands. To this day St. Patrick's Day is a national holiday on the island and is marked by festivities. As St. Patrick's Day is also my birthday it seemed like too good an opportunity to miss and we decided that we would all go over as well. In the end John and Margaret from Vitamin Sea and Michael from Edain also came across so we made up quite a party. Having hurtled over from St. John's Antigua, on the early morning high speed ferry to Little Bay in the north west corner of Monserrat we struck a deal with a taxi driver to give us a tour of the island. In marked contrast to other sightseeing trips we had done when | would spend half the time with my eyes shut as we hurtled round yet another impossible corner with a sheer drop on one side, this tour rarely exceeded walking pace. It is a beautiful island with a largely mountainous terrain in the north and a flat plain in the south in the shadow of the volcano. prior to the eruptions that started in 1995, the vast majority of the island's twelve thousand inhabitants lived in Plymouth on this southern plain. Now Plymouth is completely deserted. As we stood on the outskirts looking down into the town everything looked intact but simply covered in this thick layer of ash. Absolutely everything was grey. There were many larger houses on the hills overlooking the town that had been owned by Americans and Canadians. One of these had a carport with a jeep still parked in it. The ash was halfway up the jeep's radiator. Further from the town we passed the golf course that now lay under a thick layer of ash. We stopped at a hotel that overlooked this golf course and the bay that had previously been a good anchorage. The hotel had been repeatedly cleaned in the hope that it could eventually reopen. The whole visit was a sobering experience. Knowing the population had been reduced to just three thousand at its lowest ebb, it now stands at four thousand, you wonder how the island economy can recover. However the people we met were all incredibly friendly, positive and enthusiastic with wonderful senses of humour. Around the devastated town of Plymouth grass was beginning to grow on top of the ash. After the tour we arrived at the St. Patrick's Day Celebrations at the local school. It was an amazingly festive occasion. Pat had dressed himself in patriotic attire and many of the locals were similarly attired. Pat revels in getting to know the locals wherever he gocs. We had a feast of local food. Preparations were underway for a pageant depicting a slave uprising on St. Patrick's Day during the eighteenth century, but unfortunately we had to leave before it took place, to catch the ferry home. Three days after our visit, a much anticipated dome collapse took place, covering the entire island with ash. One yacht anchored in Little Bay reported seeing an incredible pyrotechnic display at night followed by ash covered decks the following morning. By this time we had sailed from Antigua the thirty or so miles to Barbuda. This island has something of an awesome reputation surrounded as it is almost totally by extensive reefs that are home to at least two hundred known shipwrecks. Still sailing with Aldebaran we temporarily parted company when Pat headed for a tiny anchorage almost totally enclosed by reefs. We opted for a slightly more straightforward anchorage where we met up with Vitamin Sea and Duchess, We walked along the beach in front of a very exclusive beach hotel, reputed to cost in the region of a thousand dollars a night. Visiting yachtsmen were not welcome apparently because they had no mechanism for charging for anything. As we walked along the beach a burly guard ambled over and politely informed us that he couldn't stop us using the beach but he would be grateful if we didn't try and walk through the premises. By the morning the previously calm anchorage had developed a rather unpleasant swell. Vitamin Sea and Duchess both decided to curtail their visit and head back to Antigua. The SSB was alive with Pat telling everybody about the wonderful anchorage he had discovered, deep among the reefs, where from a flat calm he could watch the masts of boats anchored off Cocoa Point, swaying about. That is of course where we were. While we were debating our options he called us up on the VHF suggesting we join them round the corner. We decided that that was our best option and motored cautiously through the off lying reefs to a point off the anchorage where Pat was waiting in his dinghy to guide us in. Once inside we anchored with barely six inches under our keel but with no motion at all. 16

Later I sounded out the anchorage with the dinghy and leadline and discovered that we were in a pool unmarked on the chart but alongside a deeper pool acknowledged in the pilot book and on the chart. In honour of this discovery I named the pool, ‘Murphy's Hole’, reached by means of ‘Paddy's Passage' and duly entered these details on my chart. That night we all had a barbecue on the beach together with Ted and Muriel from Acedia, a Freedom 38 that had followed Aldebaran into the anchorage the night before. After a couple of days in this idyllic spot we all set off on a rare overnight passage to sail the eighty-eight miles to St. Martin. In spite of a noticeable lack of wind, with little time constraints, we managed to sail nearly the whole way. It was a lovely sail on a clear moonlit night. Sailing by St. Barts in the dark the island stood out quite clearly. At one point | was dozing (all right sleeping) down below when Laura who was on watch at the time, suddenly shouted out. Leaping up on deck, or as near leaping up as I can manage these days I saw the shape of a fishing boat just off our bows. As we sailed by just in front of him we saw a very faint red light in the rigging. Apart from that there was absolutely no sign on life. I called out several times but there was no response. We still wonder whether we should have done more to check that everything was all right, but to be honest at the time the shock of a near miss was uppermost in our minds. In the morning the wind got up, but very unusually for the Caribbean, from the southwest. After a lively sail along the coast of St. Martin we arrived at the normally sheltered anchorage of Simpson's Bay to find it an absolute maelstrom. Fortunately the bridge was due to open and we were soon in the shelter of the inter lagoon. Part Seventeen - St. Martin. St. Martin is a rarity among Caribbean Islands in that it is part French and part Dutch. The French part is St. Martin whilst the Dutch part is Sint. Maarten. Simpson's lagoon is part French and part Dutch. Anchored as we were in the Dutch part we could have day trips to France in the dinghy. The lagoon has long had a name as a hurricane hole, but in recent years, hurricanes have tend to hit it rather hard, thereby rather denting it's reputation. St. Martin is a duty free island. Not surprisingly it boasted several large chandlers. Its amazing how wandering round large well stocked chandlers makes your realise how many things you need. Whilst anchored in English Harbour, Antigua, our Even dinghy with outboard attached had flipped. Five minutes later the Even dinghy and outboard of Acedia anchored just ahead suffered the same fate. No amount of tender loving care revived our aging Yamaha and we now decided to replace it with a Yamaha 3. Putting this engine on the Even caused me considerable anxiety, so we started looking at various rigid transom inflatables on offer. In the end after much deliberation we opted for a heavily built large tube Caribe, which in spite of being only 2.5 metres long proved to be an effective load carrier and surprisingly fast with just 3 hp on the back. After this spending spree we had to recuperate in the Soggy Dollar Bar where we met up with several more boats that we had got to know along the way. Helen celebrated her birthday during our stay in the lagoon. We had a memorable evening during which Helen insisted on having a T shirt as worn by the waitress in the restaurant. When she looked at it in the morning, she decided that her taste the night before might have been slightly suspect. After nearly a week in the lagoon and some pretty hefty restocking it was time to move on. On the 30th March we motored out of the lagoon during the 5.30pm bridge opening in company with Aldebaran and Acedia bound like us for the British Virgin Islands and Puffin bound for the USVI's. Motoring northwestwards we witnessed the green flash as the sun set. Another night passage started with little wind. Just before seven we turned off the engine to have our supper in peace. in five knots of wind we were barely moving but it was such a pleasant night we were loathed to restart the engine, so drified slowly on. The wind gradually increased overnight. By the morning it was blowing quite strongly and we sailed right into the BVI's arriving off Tortolla about half past one in the afternoon. Our progress had slowed again and we were enjoying a quict sail in when Laura discovered in the pilot book that you have to pay the Customs overtime after three thirty. It was time to start the engine and motor in. to be CONMINUEM. ....... -6sccevecsccers 17

Commodores Notes The central theme of this month has been the Opinion Poll and its result. Up until today about half of the forms that were sent out have been returned and a theme has been established. The majority of returns opted for Plan A, that did not favour a hike in subscriptions, but I was interested to see that the sum of two options that proposed large increases, when added together amounted to about 40% of the returns. I thank everyone that returned the Opinion Poll form. You will note that the notice for the AGM is included in this edition. The AGM will again be at Beehive Lane on Sunday 12" November 2000 starting at 1300hrs. The Autumn Prize Giving will take place after the AGM. - For the first time since I have been a member, the AGM is not the same weekend as the Last Fling Race and the Laying Up Supper. I hope this will enable you to have a clear head when you attend. In keeping with the wishes expressed in the Opinion Poll the Main Committee are only recommending subscription rises in line with inflation. Elsewhere, the Quiz Night, which was well attended on the last Friday of September, yielded a win for the same team as last year. Less than a week before this event Laura had so few advanced bookings that we were seriously thinking of canceling it, and yet seventy odd members attended. I ask members to plan ahead a little more on these occasions, let the Entertainment's Committee know your intentions a bit earlier and save the raised blood pressure. Perhaps we could all start by making early reservations for the Laying Up Supper on Saturday 18" November. Contact Steve & Debbie Glynn. Frank Bennett has now finally accounted for this year’s Piers Race which will raise £6,500 for the Cirdan Trust, another record amount, well done everyone that was involved. I look forward to seeing you at the Laying Up Supper, the AGM and Prize Giving. View from the Rear And so we reach the end of another sailing season and winter is upon us again. I know this to be the case, not only because the weather has turned, but also because we have already begun the process of planning next year's sailing season!! 1 would therefore like to take this opportunity to remind you of some key usual events that will take place over the winter and to encourage you to give them your full support: Dinghy Park Clearance Please could all owners of boats in the Dinghy Park (in front of the clubhouse) ensure that their boats are moved along the western hedge by 25th November 2000. The masts should be lowered and the boats should be staked down. Please park the boats close together to conserve space and do not leave your boat in the area designated for Windsurfer Rigging - (the area between the marked barrier and the tractor shed). If you are going to have any difficulty in this, please advice the Handicap Fleet Captain, David Ball on [redacted]. Any boat that is not moved from the Dinghy Park is liable to being removed by the sailing sub committee. Fleet AGM's Each Fleet Captain will organise an AGM for their fleet over the winter months. This gives you the opportunity to discuss matters, which are important to your particular type of fleet, and to stand for fleet captain if you so wish! Please keep an eye out in Navigans for your particular fleet's details. Sailing Club AGM Most of us dislike meetings - (very reminiscent of being at work for a start!) - but the AGM is one meeting that you should really try to attend. No matter how much or how little use you make of the club, everyone has an opinion about how they would or would not like it to be run. The best way for you to make that opinion heard is to come to the AGM. Full details of agenda and proposed resolutions / nominations for Club positions are included in this edition of Navigans (See Pages 19-25) please take time to read them and then come along and make your opinion known. (This year’s AGM will take place at the MASC, Beehive Lane, Chelmsford on 12th November at lpm). Working Parties As you will be aware, we pride ourselves on being a self-help club and one of the ways we are able to keep membership fees to a reasonable level is due to the voluntary hard work and commitment of members. One of the ways this is achieved is through the work Party events during the winter where the principle of 'many hands make light work' is applied to get some valuable site maintenance and other work done. I would again urge you to support these events in whatever way possible. Certain fleets were conspicuous by their absence last year and as a result, we were not able to get all the tasks done that we wanted to. If you are not able to participate at a Working Party but can contribute in another way - please do not hesitate to contact myself or another member of the committee. The autumn working party has been scheduled for Sunday 26th November. (See Page 5) Laying Up Supper And finally - just to prove that it is not all work over the winter - the premier social event of the year, the Laying Up Supper will again take place at the Three Rivers in Cold Norton on Saturday 18th November. (See Page 2) This is always a hugely successful event and thoroughly enjoyed by everyone. Tickets are available from Committee Members, Fleet Captains and the Glynn family. I look forward to secing you there! Finally, | would like to thank the Sailing Sub-Committee, all Support Boat Crews, Race Officers and Assistants and the many people who have contributed to making this year's Sailing Programme so busy and so successful. Jenny Ball Rear Commodore Support Boat Drivers VHF Radio-Telephones. A Reminder The radios fitted to Jack B, Orkney and the RIB are required by law to be capable of operating on all International channels including 16, They must, however, only transmit on M1 or M2 unless operated by, or supervised by, a licensed operator, or in the case of dire (life threatening) emergency. This is important for safety reasons and the continuance of our licences. F.C. Bennett.
