CRUISER RACING NEWS Overcast skies and brisk Northerly winds greeted the competitors for the Knoll Trophy Race. The Bench Head course was selected and the fleet reached away, led by a new comer to club cruiser racing David Onyon’s in his Sonata ‘Quiet Airs.’ Ian Wood single-handed in his Contest 25 ‘Jan’ showed tremendous speed holding second place until caught at Bradwell by a reluctant ‘Ocean Slipper’. Mark and Neil Burgess in the Eygthene 24 ‘Chicane,’ another newcomer to club racing, held off Dave Payne’s “Live Wire’. At the Bench Head ‘Quiet Airs’ led followed by’ Ocean Slipper’ and ‘Jan’ chased by ‘Chicane’ then ‘Live Wire’, ‘Bluster’ and ‘Four Two’. The return leg was a beat and a tussle developed between ‘Jan’ and Chicane’ all the way to the line with ‘Jan’ prevailing. However the tail end of the fleet was only 25 minutes behind, and once again Colin Leveridge’s persistence won through with Ian Wood a creditable second. Helm of the Year Final Series 2000 The Series this year was once again sailed in Picos kindly loaned by Club Members for the occasion. It was sailed on Saturday 7th October, and as usual Navigans sent along it’s roving reporter to marvel in this highlight of the MSC sailing season. Here is his report: - The Helm of the Year title has for years been competed for by the Champions of each major fleet and this year they comprised - Colin Leveridge (Cruiser); Tim Wallace (Fast Cat); Peter Tovey (Medium Cat); Jenny Ball (Dart 15); David Ball (Handicap); Steve Monks (Solo); and Anthony Monks (Cadet). A cool and rainy day was not ideal for the Final, but at least the SSW force 2 to 3 wind which slowly freshened to a 4 through the day, enabled the 5 race series to be completed without difficulty, and the enthusiastic spectators who turned up for the event were treated to a well sailed and exciting series. The boats were rotated between competitors after each race, and one discard was allowed, so that the competition was as fair as possible. The decommissioning of Jack B during the week before the event due to a malfunction, meant that race box starts had to be used and hence course setting was more limited than usual, but all courses still contained a reasonable windward leg and provided a true test for the challengers. In Race | Jenny established an early lead with Colin moving smoothly through the fleet to challenge her on the reach to the finish line. Jenny held on, and Anthony eased through to third place at the final windward mark, which was overstood by half the fleet. Peter held off Steve for fourth. Race 2 saw Steve and Anthony at the front racing side by side down the first leg of the course, but on the run Anthony generated enough speed to take him clear of the others, a lead which he was able to extend through to the finish. Behind him Tim relegated himself to the rear of the fleet with a spectacular dismount on the run, while Colin again showed good speed to work his way through to second, in front of Steve. Race 3 again saw Steve and Anthony side by side leading the first leg, with Anthony just in front at the start of the first beat, but his luck ran out soon afterwards when a capsize put him to the back, leaving Steve to win comfortably from David and Jenny. Race 4 saw David and Jenny lead the fleet away, Balls instead of Monks, and these two passed and repast each other around the course until David finally was able to establish a lead up the final beat which he maintained to the finish. A good beat by Steve lifted him up to second just in front of Jenny The final race was a classic with Steve, Jenny, and David all in with a chance of the title and all leading at some time during the race, and all three within feet of each other as they approached the end of the final beat with David just covering the other two. In a last desperate effort for victory Steve tacked early at the windward mark, diving under David’s transom to lead away onto the final reach, but in doing so he just touched David’s boat incurring a penalty which let David through for the win just in front of Jenny. This result enabled David to claim the overall title, a thrilling end to a great series, which provided 4 different winners in 5 races. All competitors performed with credit, especially Anthony who at 11 years old showed a formidable talent, which will make him a hard man to beat in years to come. Weekend 23/24 September proved to be a busy one with twelve boats taking part in the "Watercress Run" at Heybridge Basin whilst the racing fraternity were busy competing in the "Medusa Race", which is the last of this year's cruiser races. Twelve cruisers comprising Amyjack, Cornish Gold, Fantasea, Happy Medium, Icarus, Peace, Reflection, Rubicon, Suruca, Trumpeter, West Marie and Winkler, made the early morning start to Heybridge Basin locking in about 0900. At mid-day twelve dinghies and crews started the trip up the canal past Tesco's to Beeleigh Abbey in search of the now elusive watercress. The weather was great the only ones who did not seem amused were the anglers on the canal bank having coped with twelve dinghies first going up the canal then returning some two hours later. The day was rounded off with everyone enjoying an evening meal in the "Ship" pub where Murray, Mike, Joan, Derek and Margaret joined us. The return journey on Sunday morning was also very civalised - thank you to Sophie and Thomas for suggesting it. The winter lay up is now in full flight, the Haul Our List also Winter Storage Layout are both on the club notice board, if you have any queries please contact me. There has been a tremendous response to use the travel hoist, at present there are twenty-one boats being stored in the cat field. Surprisingly this has not created many spaces in the Cruiser Park, in fact nearly all these spaces have been allocated to other boats. One of the problems is that member's boats are getting larger and require more space. Whilst on the subject of winter storage, may I please draw your attention to the disposal of rubbish, The waste skip is for household type of rubbish only, it would be appreciated if you would observe the following: - Used engine oil - must be taken away and disposed of at a Council Recycling Centre. Metal parts - such as scrap from trailers, brake shoes, engine parts, mooring chain etc. must be taken off site. Timber - should be placed on the old mooring trailer at the eastern end of the cat field. Members then use this for bonfires during cadet/camping fortnight. It is in everyone's interest to keep the cruiser storage areas clean and tidy, please help by making sure your arca is, this should not be one of the tasks of a working party. This years Cruiser A.G.M. will be held in the Conference Lounge at M.A.S.C. on Thursday 16th November, commencing at 2000 hours. The agenda is as follows: - 1. Apologies 2: Review of this year's sailing/cruising programme. 3, Review of this year's racing programme and prize giving. 4. Review of haul our procedures and winter storage. 5. Election of Fleet Captain, Vice Captain and Race Co-Ordinator. 6. Working Party. i Paint orders for year 2001. 8. Mooring chain and shackle orders for 2001. 9 Proposals for next year's cruising and racing programmes. 10, Any other business. As we turn our minds to winter pursuits onc of the other bright spots of an otherwise dull November is the clubs Laying Up Supper (See Page 2). Those of you who attended last year will not need me to tell you what a great night it was, if you have not been, why not give it a try? Derek Kirby - Fleet Captain 15

Commodore's Report 2000 1.0 Introduction I will now like to give the meeting my report on the Club for my second year as Commodore. It has been a year of steady progress in many areas of the Club activity and I will attempt to summarize every aspect of the Club. I do intend to mention names of members where they have been of particular service to the Club. Inevitably in a Club where at least a quarter of the membership contribute to the running of the Club, I will not mention everyone and I apologize in advance for any omissions. 2.0 Sailing a Sailing is the raison d’etre of the Club. I do not wish to pre-empt the Sailing Secretary’s Report, but I see all the signs of robust good health in our Sailing Activities. The Club enjoys extremely good sailing facilities with acres of boat storage space on land, excellent 24-hour access to.wide but still relatively sheltered sailing waters, and good back up facilities. Our members make good use of these facilities in many divergent ways, which leads the Club to have a high usage, whatever the sailing conditions. The Sailing Sub Committee under the chairmanship of the Rear Commodore Jenny Ball and the hard working Sailing Secretary Dave Williams control sailing. Jenny and Dave, together with the fleet captains have arranged season long racing for all classes. This is no small exercise, each race requires seven members to man the Race Box and run Rescue. Our Cruiser Section ranged far and wide, and this year has also seen a rebirth of Cruiser Racing with Frank Burgess, Mike Turner, Derek Gardner, Dave Payne and the Ball family much involved. Two new kids on the block upset the natural order of things when Mick Richardson and Ian Caruth won some races with the Robbers they have just brought to the Club, The Board Sailors continue to use the Club when the rest of us are thinking of catching up with the gardening, ensuring full use of our facilities. 3.0 Safety It has been a year of consolidation and progress for Colin Kidner in his capacity as Safety Co-ordinator. I am sure he would wish me to thank our safety advisor, Malcolm Robertson, for continuing to give his time and professional expertise to the Club. The Safety Committee have continued to look at our systems for launching and recovery of cruisers. Peter Clayton & Murray Bates have been much to the fore in the development of safe working practices. Thanks Gentlemen. While the objective of this work is obviously to operate the Club in Safety, it has another important function. The Health and Safety Executive quite simply do not believe an organisation has Safe Systems of Operations unless the Procedures are fully documented. The work of the Safety Committee greatly reduces the chance of the HSE prosecuting the Club or Club Officer in the event of an accident. _ Eventually we intend to look at every aspect of the Club’s activities both to comply with the law, but primarily to set up systems to ensure that our funis not spoiled by avoidable accidents, 4.0 Rescue The Club continues to run three support boats, the Rib, Jack B and the Orkney. The Rib is our most effective rescue boat. However it has seen a lot of service and has needed heavy maintenance during the year. The launching trolley was remade professionally, and the trailer was extensively rebuilt by Mick Richardson. The RIB is currently at the Main Dealers having the engine serviced and repaired. The Committee will keep a close watch on such expenditure, and judge the time for replacement. Thanks also go to the Bosun Roy Hardwick for his week by week maintenance that has kept this valuable asset viable. The Jack B has served the Club well over many years and has many more years service left in her. Geoff Josey has serviced the engine and kept it sweet and I am sure I remember seeing Murray Bates one cold and windy winter Sunday changing the main shaft bearing. We were not able to do much work to the hull this season and the new Bosun, Eric Cockerton will have a busy year. Thanks for volunteering Eric.

The Orkney has performed reliably and well throughout the year and is especially useful during Cadet training sessions when its controllability make it possible to give close quarters support. Tim Sweet & Barry Glynn have looked after the Orkney this season. The system of rostering and notifying Support Boat crews was brought in last year and has been successfully managed this year by Tony Ferguson, Barry Hutt and Dennis Gilby. However we do need more drivers, particularly for the Jack B. I am sure the Sailing Secretary will say more. 5.0 Cruisers Cruisers make up almost half of the boats registered at the Club. Members who own cruisers enjoy good facilities at a fraction of the fees charged by professional boatyards elsewhere on the East Coast. This pricing structure is only made possible by the members themselves undertaking many jobs that are dirty, wet and physically hard. These self help efforts alone would not be enough without the leadership of the Fleet Captain, Derek Kirby, and the work of the Moorings Sub Committee under Peter Clayton and Murray Bates, which channels and manages the efforts of the members to achieve the objective. Tractors continue to be the most important single resource for handling boats on the shore. Our tractors are not new, but the hard work of the Tractor Coordinator Roger Gibson and the mechanical skills of Roger Camp, have maintained the tractors and even made modest improvements, at reasonable cost. Another tractor was added to the fleet during the year. This machine is some years old but in a well maintained condition. Although it was obtained by the Club at a bargain basement cost we are confident it will give many years good service. The travel hoist has been in service for about a year and is proving its worth. The moorings are laid and lifted each year by the members using the mooring barge. The investment made three or four years ago in this barge continues to deliver efficient and low cost service to our members. 6.0 The East Coast Piers Race Last Saturday I was privileged to present a BIG cheque to Nick Back of the Cirdan Trust in the sum of £8,000. Race Chairman Lee Harrison, together with Race Committee members Chris Davis, Charles Anderson, Marcus Wallace and Debbie Yorston attended. The event took place on the Cirdan Trust barge the Lady Galadriel at Maldon and was photographed for posterity by Geoff Baker. Compared with the other attendees I did little more than enter the Race and fill in when Charles ‘The Voice of the Piers Race’ Anderson needed a break from talking at the Prize Giving. Nevertheless I was proud to represent the whole of the Club at this ceremony, because the event can only be run with the full involvement of every section of the Club. Our Race continues to be the only Race of its type in the UK that is run in aid of Charity and all the membership can feel justifiably proud oftheir involvement. One section of the Club deserves special mention, the cruiser sailors who provide the mother and matriarch boats. This is an unpleasant job with little of the glory. Crews get up and leave the Club hours before the competitors are awake, and rarely arrive back at the Club until after the Prizes have been awarded. But we cannot run the Race without the safety and assurance that these ‘boats give. That is why I was particularly pleased that Frank Burgess joined us at the cheque presentation. He was there to represent the 18 cruiser sailors and their boats who all gave freely of their time for the good of the cause. Mike Turner again did his usual excellent job as Race Officer After three highly successful years, Lee Harrison has stepped down from the Race Chairman’s position but has agreed to stay on the Race Committee next year. Thanks for a job well done Lee. Chris Davies has already taken over as Chairman and arrangements for next year’s Race are underway. The provisional date for next year’s race is Sunday is July, so put it in your diaries.

7.0 Cadets When telling you of the presentation for the Piers Race, I spoke of being privileged to represent the Club, well I felt similarly privileged to present the prizes for Cadet Week. You will recall that a new committee of Peter Clayton, Steve Monks and Kevin Dowley took on the organization this year. They were aided and abetted by Steve and Debbie Glynn who never seem far away from the centre of Club events. Over 75 Cadets were given tuition during Cadet Week. It is probably not an exaggeration to say that twice that number would attend if we were not restricted by safety and hygiene considerations. The Prize Giving was a sea of young keen happy faces who had obviously enjoyed a great week. The prizes were almost endless and I was glad ofthe help of my wife Sue in presenting them. The medium and long-term future of any Club can be found in the enthusiasm of its Cadets. The future of Marconi Sailing Club therefore must be assured. Cadet Week constitutes but half of Camping Fortnight. I must thank Hilary Ashley for managing the applications once again. This job requires the strength and judgment of Solomon to fit the supply to the over demand. Thanks Hilary. 8.0 Entertainments The Social sub Committee comprising Laura Gill, Claire Davies, Chris Hutt, Fenella Thomas, Sally Ferguson and Hilary Ashley, organized events throughout the year. January saw the Barn Dance, April the Fitting Out Supper and September Quiz Night. In addition the new Century was seen in at the Clubhouse and the Summer Solstice was celebrated in style. All events most enjoyable and were well supported, even if the support did not materialize itself until the last minute. Thanks for all the ideas and hard work ladies. Laura is standing down from the Social Manager role after two years and I am pleased to welcome Fenella Thomas who has agreed to be co-opted onto the Main Committee to replace Laura. Thanks Laura and good luck Fenella. Steve and Debbie Glynn, have again arranged the Laying Up Supper this year. I look forward to the opportunity of seeing members next week clad in something other than sailing attire. Many thanks Steve and Debbie. When attending the club Please drive on the roads Do not drive across the grass

This is going to print prior to our Cruiser AGM due to be held on Thursday 16" November so the minutes of this will be printed in the next edition of Navigans. The weather these past few weeks has been diabolical and has no doubt influenced one or two in deciding when to haul out, there are at the time of writing a number of boats still on their moorings which will soon be under pressure to move as moorings are lifted. At the risk of being accused of “ teaching Grandmothers to suck eggs” some members decided to abort hauling out purely on the weather forecast when in fact conditions off the hard are quiet, it is worth coming down to see for yourself. On the same subject, if you do decide not to haul out or launch please make sure you advise the tractor driver/winch operator. For those of you who may have “PART 1 REGISTERED” boats I thought it may be worth reminding you of the timescale set by the Maritime & Coastguard Agency for re-registration which are: - Year of build Date for renewal 1971 — 1975 | Jan —31 Mar 2001 1976 — 1989 | Jan — 31 Mar 2002 1990 — 20 March 1994 1 Jan — 31 Mar 2003 Year of build unknown apply as soon as possible Lifting moorings is now under way the ‘A’ Team having done their bit on weekending 4/5 November. Members on ‘B’ & ‘C’ teams may be pleased to know Doreen together with some ladies from the fleet is running the galley during these weekends providing hot drinks & refreshments at nominal cost, so there is no need to spend the night before or very early morning making sandwiches & flasks of coffee. On the subject of moorings, these when lifted are where possible placed on pallets in front of the members boat in the cruiser park however, with the ground being so wet it is possible those in the Cat field may find their moorings together with those belonging to members who winter elsewhere and those moorings that cannot be identified, placed in the cruiser park along the sea wall. We will again be holding our series of winter meetings at MASC so whilst the details have yet to be confirmed you may wish to make a note of the dates which are all on Thursday evenings, 18 January, 15 February and 23 March. - Derek Kirby — Cruiser Fleet Captain. Mona's Travels /continued Part Eighteen - The British Virgin Islands Most of what we had read and heard about the BVI's failed to prepare us properly for them. We had got the distinct impression that they weren't really worth a visit. Consequently as we sailed through the protective ring of outer islands we were literally stunned at how beautiful they were and from a distance at least, how relatively unspoiled they were. The vegetation is so lush that many of the smaller islands are virtually unmarked roads. Small resorts have been established round individual bays with little intrusion on the rest of the island. Having said that there are large numbers of charter boats, but there is such a wealth of protected anchorages that it is never difficult to find somewhere to anchor. 11

Our arrival on Tortolla was slightly marred by an immigration officer, who, after comparing my experience with that of others, appears to delight in making life difficult for visiting yachtsmen. When confronted with a windowless door with a large sign saying knock and enter, most people do just that. If however on opening the door you discover someone already there then you are shouted at for coming in when she is dealing with someone. When I was there my customs clearance that I had brought with me from upstairs, completely disappeared while | was filling out forms for all the crew. Other people had come in whilst I was doing these forms and most of them had been shouted at as well. When I realised that the form was missing, she just kept telling me that it was my problem not hers and treated me like an extremely irksome and naughty schoolboy. When I eventually gave up and went back to the customs upstairs, they were extremely helpful and after contacting the lady in immigration decided that someone must have picked up my form by mistake and gave me a photocopy. To be fair, most of the customs and immigration officials that we have come into contact with, have been friendly and helpful, particularly considering that some of the rules they have to enforce are bizarre to say the least. Checking in and out is always an experience and sometimes a very lengthy one. The anchorage at Road Town where you check in is a very exposed rather lumpy one, so once back on board we upped anchor and moved across to Great Harbour on Peter Island which belying its name, was in fact a picturesque and sheltered little bay. We were able to snorkel straight from the boat. The great thing about the BVI's is the ease with which you can move from one anchorage to another. The next day we attempted to explore the heavily wooded island. There was very little development apart from a very exclusive resort in the next bay. In the afternoon we met up with Ian and Anne on Miss Chips, another boat that we had been meeting up with at various times on our travels. It had become something of a joke that they would first know that we were around by bumping into Laura in some obscure location. They were on their way to join in with a five day Virgin Island Rally that the Ocean Cruising Club were organising. Ian showed me some of the OCC cruising information he had been given and I was most impressed. He kindly offered to propose us as members and we decided to move over to Trellis Bay, the next day, for the start of the rally. On arrival, we were made extremely welcome by Mike Pocock, Commodore of OCC, on board Blackjack, the boat in which he and his wife Pat circumnavigated about ten years ago and are now doing an Atlantic Circuit. This circuit was forming thee basis of a whole series of OCC meetings and rallies. Some OCC boats were doing the whole circuit with Blackjack, others were just meeting up for particular rallies. On board Blackjack when we visited, was Mary Barton wife of the late Humphrey Baron. Helen was quite overawed when Mike having readily agreed to second my membership proposal, Mary insisted on seconding Helen's. At Trellis Bay we met up with John and Anders from Fanai that we had last seen in the Canaries. The next morning we sailed around the top of Tortolla, in company with Fanai, Astolata and Aldebaran, through some narrow reef lined passes down to Cane Garden Bay, an anchorage sheltered by an off lying reef with just one narrow pass through it. While the others managed to anchor in close proximity in the sheltered but crowded part of the bay, I incurred the wrath of the crew by doing my usual thing of circling the anchorage three times, then opting to anchor in the more exposed part of the bay where we had plenty of swinging room. On going ashore we all got involved in the rescue of a twenty-six footer that had come up on the beach. A combination of applied technology and gang ho got it refloated. The owners a Canadian couple who had lived on the island for about twenty years invited us all up to their house which had incredible views across the islands as far as St. Thomas in the USVI's. The next day we made our way to an isolated by on Little Jost Van Dyke. We had the place virtually to ourselves with just Aldebaran for company. We had a fascinating time sitting on the shore watching the pelicans diving for fish. The whole time that we were watching them, we never saw one fruitless, or fishless, dive. In the morning the anchorage soon filled up as Ocean Cruising Club boats arrived for a beach party. It turned out to be an extremely sociable day and a good opportunity for learning from other peoples experiences. From Little Jost Van Dyke we carried on our circumnavigation of Tortolla passing through a narrow pass at its southern tip and sailing up the Francis Drake Channel to Cooper Island where we anchored outside the buoys in at least seventeen metres. Some of the bays are almost totally filled by these mooring buoys, which you are free to pick up for the princely sum of twenty dollars. By the time darkness fell most of the buoys would generally have been taken. We had one of our best sails for a while close hauled up the coast of Virgin Gorda then motoring through a gap in the reef to the large expanse of enclosed water that is Virgin Gorda Sound. Anchoring off the Bitter End Yacht Club we were again in company with a number of OCC yachts for the last event of the rally, a dinner ashore for eighty-six. 12

Minutes of the October Main Committee Meeting Previous Minutes. The previous minutes were accepted with one amendment viz. The reference to gang mowers should have been to pasture mower. Executive Meeting. The executive met on the 4/10/00 when the following items were discussed. Opinion Poll; Correspondence; Channel 16 incident; Calor gas; AGM; MASC/MSC; Accident report. Safety. M Bates. A representative from Parasol has re-validated the various test certificates we require for our hardware. F-Bennett, enquired when the white lines are to be placed on the hard, M Bates said we have a quotation in hand but could not give a firm date. P Black tabled an accident report referring to the hazard presented by steel cables stretched over the hard. J Ball tabled an accident report concerning the RIB. East Coast Piers Race. Mr Chris Davies has replaced Lee Harrison as Chairman of the ECPR sub Committee, the Committee expressed their thanks to Lee for his hard work in this position. Post Meeting Note:- The 2000 Piers Race resulted in a BIG cheque for £8,000 being presented to the Cirdan Trust on Saturday 4" November. Finance. Statement of accounts tabled for 1999/2000. Clubhouse and Site. P Bloomfield. Repairs to urinals, quotation of £526 received from R Hardwick. Mr Hardwick’s estimated accepted, work to proceed. Calor gas installation to proceed, boiler replacement to be discussed between P Bloomfield and F Bennett for recommendation to the Committee. Sewage plant, F Bennett has requested a report from the Environmental Agency. The Agency requires all effluent to pass through the plant. During periods of overload it may be necessary to tanker the surplus away. D Kirby. The number of boats using the Travel Hoist this year has increased the need for storage space in the cat field. This is seen as a temporary solution, the Moorings Sub Committee to consider alternatives. Mr D Thomas requested that the Windsurf rigging area is kept clear of dinghies over the winter. The tractor shed and the race container both have severe roof leaks. Moorings Sub Committee. P Clayton. Mooring lifting programme commences on 4° November 2000. Tractor problems, one tractor with engine failure and one with PTO problems. .Clubhouse Secretary and Moorings Sub Committee to recommend way forward. A suitable pump is available to power the winches. Costings required. Sailing Sub Committee. Jenny Ball thanked M Bates and his helpers for the swift repairs to the Jack B. The Orkney has been returned to Tollesbury for repair. As a result of the channel 16 incident radio procedures and training are to be reviewed. Membership. There were no new members this month. Recruitment, Mrs Margaret Yeoman has accepted the task of increasing the membership level. Five Year Plan. The Opinion Poll yielded the following results, Option 1, 115 votes: Option 2, 64 votes: Option 3, 31 votes. Correspondence. Letter from Mrs D Glynn requesting that smoking is prohibited in the lounge whilst food is being served. The Committee thought this to be a reasonable request and a notice to this effect would be displayed. 13

The Cruising Association invites MSC members to attend their meetings at the MASC during the winter. Channel 16 incident. Letters received from two members. Any Other Business. P Bloomfield. Fire safety audit, fire extinguishers to be placed in the Dell Bar, the exit should have an illuminated sign. Fire Officer to be asked to give survey. F Bennett informed the Committee that Mr Tom Patterson a long-standing member of the club has died, the Committee offered their condolences to Mr Patterson’s family. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXAXXXAXXXXAXXAXNXXAXXXXXAXXXAXXXXAXXXXXAXXXXXXXXXXXAXAXXAXXAXXAXXAX Commodore's Report 2000 9.0 Membership Our Membership has remained stable through the year at around the 400 mark. Within this figure many members are family members whose membership permits partners and children to use the Club facilities which means at least 1000 people make a call on the Club services. The Main Committee feel that the Club has much to offer prospective members and believe the Club would benefit from a modest increase in membership. The added income would help the Club’s finances and new members often bring new ideas and enthusiasm. To this end the Executive has invited Margaret Yeoman to draw up a plan for increasing recruitment to the Club, She has already got together a sub committee to help her with the tasks, and you will see her name on the list of nominees to the Main Committee where she will be able to keep us in touch with her progress. 10.0 The Site and Clubhouse Two members have responsibilities for the Site. They are the Vice Commodore, Peter Bloomfield, and Clubhouse Secretary Mick Richardson. Steve Glynn, Frank Bennett and Pat Black have also contributed their time and expertise in many ways. If the gate opened, the shower worked, the grass was cut, a pint was pulled or a bacon sandwich consumed it was due to the organisation of one of these members. Darren is the sole employee of the Club. He has operated the dedicated grass-mowing tractor during the year. He has also undertaken regular cleaning duties. Tony and Wendy operated the Galley concession throughout the year, including the Winter Series. Judging from the feedback | have received, they are delivering the service most people want. In the Spring of this year Neil Pembleton took over the vacant position of Bar Manager. He reorganised the system of deliveries and thus reduced the work load of the Bar Manager. Also a new cellar chilling system was installed by Neil, Steve Monks and other members, this led to a full flow of cool drinks even at the busiest times. Neil made it clear that he would only undertake the role on a temporary basis, and the position of Bar Manager is again vacant. We need a volunteer, no Bar experience is necessary as Nei] will train the new recruit. The stark reality is, no Bar Manager, no bar, so if you think you could help please see me after this meeting. TM 11.0 The Five Year Plan The first, and most fundamental element of any Five-Year Plan must be that the Organisation should continue to exist at the end of the period of the plan. The Executive has closely monitored the health of our parent MASC, especially with regard to the future after the lease of Beehive Lane expires in October 2001. To this end the Executive has met with the MASC Committee on three occasions during the year. Some of the assurances we were seeking were not forthcoming and the Executive thought it prudent to set up a sub committee to prepare a plan that would ensure that the Club could survive should the parent expire. The sub committee has prepared a Business Plan which is ready to be put into action if necessary. | am extremely grateful to Chris Davies, David Thomas and John Bird who joined Frank Bennett, Pat Black and myself in many long and productive meetings during the year.

Several members joined me at the MASC AGM a week or so ago. Les Murray, the President of that Committee, relayed verbal assurances that he had received from the Head of Property Services in BAe, Dr. Malcolm Green. It seems that BAe have decided to grant MASCa further lease of five years on Beehive Lane ‘on condition that the Club remains solvent’. So it seems the threat may be receding. You may be sure the Executive will continue to monitor the position and will be ready to act quickly if necessary. I will keep the membership fully informed. In order to get early warning of outside influences that may affect the Club we have continued our policy of serving on local Committees that deal with the future of the Blackwater. Ron Greygoose and | have attended the quarterly BACSPA meetings. BACSPA is a local Committee of the RYA and is dedicated to protect our right to sail on the Blackwater. | believe that by attending such meetings we will be able to influence opinion and policy on matters which are of direct concern to the Club's future. During the year the Main Committee have spent much time discussing, pricing and prioritising the future spending plans of the Club over the next five years. I kept the membership informed via Navigans as each step was concluded. Two consultative meetings were held with the membership during the summer. The process of consultation culminated in an Opinion Poll wherein every member was given the opportunity to choose from three proposed Plans for expenditure. The majority of members returned their Ballot papers and a clear pattern emerged. Members did not wish the subscription rate to be substantially increased to finance expansion and improvement of Club facilities. Accordingly the subscription rise you will be asked to approve later is for inflation only, and work at the Club will be implemented in accordance with Plan A. 12.0 The Secretariat The Secretariat is made up of our Hon. Treasurer, Frank Bennett; our Hon. Secretary Pat Black and the Membership Secretary Linda Chaplain. The Club cannot operate without the day to day attention to detail of these members, who freely and willingly give up at least one day every week to their duties. Frank’s role is particularly time consuming, as well as constantly giving good financial advice he is a familiar figure at Beehive Lane where he ensures the Club’s position is safeguarded. Another important day to day task is that of Navigans Editor, and Kevin and Belinda Dowley have produced an extremely readable and informative publication which has grown in size as the enthusiasm of our members grows. To the members who tell me they don’t read it, I can only say ‘You don’t know what you are missing’ In response to my request at the lat AGM Mike & Maggie Boreham have taken over the distribution of the magazine. Navigans is a vital organ of the Club, building enthusiasm and informing members, and I thank Belinda, Kevin, Maggie and Mike for their dedication. 13.0 Main Committee I would like to end my Report by thanking those members who have served on the Main Committee during the year. | will not list them all by name as over twenty members serve on that Committee. The meetings have been well attended despite the fact they regularly last two and a half hours. The wide range of opinions expressed were most helpful to the Executive and to the running of the Club. Some Main Committee members stood down this year. I thank Rob Davies, Jon Yorston, Eric Cockerton, and Mike Smith for their contributions over the year or in many cases years. After this AGM I look forward to welcoming Margaret Yeoman, Steve Monks and Chris Davies, and look forward to working with you. The Executive have also met every month and have often sat late into the evening while discussing the Club’s business and future. The Rear Commodore Jenny Ball has kept the main business of the Club running most efficiently, aided and abetted by the Sailing Sub Committee. It is not widely known, but the Rear Commodore has a greater load of regular meetings than even the Commodore. Three a month. Jenny’s involvement with Cadets and Cadet Week pushes that number higher. It is a lot to fit in with a full time job and still get out sailing from time to time. Our two ‘Honoraries’ have given much time and no little skill in the conduct of Club affairs. You will recall that the term Honorary means ‘Unpaid’ which is very good for the Club as, if we were to employ professionals to do these jobs, we would need to double the subscriptions. No praise is too high for the dedication of Pat Black and Frank Bennett. One of the Executive comes to the end of his tenure at this AGM. He is Peter Bloomfield our Vice Commodore, Peter has worked hard for three years to keep all of the Club’s on-shore facilities in working order. It is a mark of Peter’s quiet but determined application that he did not wish to stand down. The Committee will not lose his expertise as he has indicated his willingness to serve as Vice President. Thanks Peter.

I could not finish this section on the Committee without mentioning our President of many years, Ron Greygoose. He has continued to promote the best interests of the Club throughout the year and in many ways. He suffered a spell of poor health during the year, but we are all very pleased to see him back at Committee meetings where his counsel is highly valued. 14.0 Closing Statements We have a difficult year ahead, but I am certain that, not only will the Club survive but it will come through stronger than ever. Welcome to the New Year! The time passed so quickly I forgot the last edition of Navigans would be the last before Christmas and I omitted to wish you all a very Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. 56 members including the Commodore and Rear Commodore attended the Cruiser AGM, held at MASC on Thursday 16" November. Apologies were received from Jack Goodie, Derek Hall, John Haywood, Russell Hadley, Maureen Ball, Margot and Keith Starkey. Derek Kirby reviewed the year 2000 sailing and social programme. Commencing with the Fitting Out Supper held in May, which was attended by 62 members who were entertained by Frank Burgess and members of Erith Sailing Club together with the ‘Marconi Buoys’. Fourteen boats made the trip to Brightlingsea, with 32 people joining up for an evening meal in the Colne Yacht Club, in honour of the retiring Harbourmaster Peter Copeland. Peter was presented with an engraved Marconi Sailing Club glass tankard. The Shakedown Cruise was wiped out by the weather, even so, 28 members arrived by road to enjoy an evening meal at the Royal Corinthian Yacht Club. The late Summer Bank Holiday attracted 16 boats to Shotley Marina, plus 3 part time, with 31 members enjoying an evening meal in the Shipwreck Bar. The last organised event was the Watercress run to Heybridge Basin in September which attracted 12 boats with an informal get together in the Ship. Frank Burgess reported on the fleets racing programme, which he felt, had been well supported with an average turnout of 11 boats. He thanked Dave Payne for his work in producing the results and Murray Bates for the trophies. These were presented by Rear Commodore Jenny Ball as follows: - EAGLE SHIELD I“ — Colin Leveridge 2 Jez Rowles 3 John Easton STEEPLE BAY TROPHY 1“ Nick Hillman 2 Colin Leveridge 3% Dave Payne DOCTOR SHIELD 1* John Easton 2 Colin Leveridge 3” John Burgoyne KNOLL SHIELD 1* — Colin Leveridge 2 lan Wood 3 Dave Onyons MEDUSA SHIELD I* John Easton 2TM Jez Rowles 3 Derek Gardner BARNACLE SHIELD i” Colin Leveridge 2TM John Easton 3° Jez Rowles The trophy for the best log went to Helen and Malcolm Shaft, currently sailing Mona in the Caribbean and therefore accepted on their behalf by Malcolm Yeoman. The Commodore Clive Shenton then presented the SEAMANSHIP trophy to Hilary and Derek Gardner of Kilara II for their part in the recent rescue of the Rib Crew under testing conditions. He then presented the “BIG COCK TROPHY’ plus awards to two other members , in what was described as a “conspiracy of silence”. However, in accordance with established protocol only those members attending the AGM know the recipients and circumstances. Peter Clayton and Murray Bates spoke of the need to be vigilant when hauling out and launching, drawing attention to the clubs Code Of Practice For Launching and Recovery of Cruisers, copies of which are circulated to all members of the cruiser fleet. There being no other nominations, the election of Captain, Vice Captain and Race Coordinator were re elected en bloc. Proposals for the 2001 sailing programme were discussed and it was agreed to generally follow last years format. Frank Burgess announced the intention to hold five races with new courses that will take in the yellow river buoys. Chris Davies revealed that £8,000 had been donated to the Cirdan Trust as a result of last years ECPR, thanking all for their support and was hopeful for similar support in 2001. Mona's Travels /continued We spent a couple of days taking it easy in Drakes’s anchorage behind the reef. While we were there | studied the charts and decided that Anegada a reef strewn island 4 miles to the north of Virgin Gorda would be well worth a visit. When Aldebaran joined us it turned out that they had been thinking much the same thing. We had by this time been cruising with Aldebaran for nearly two months. There had been very little forward planning to our cruising itinerary. It had simply evolved as we had gone along. Both boats would move on as they felt like it. Without any great arrangements, our plans just seemed to coincide. It had added to the fun and been an added ingredient in our cruising. The sail up to Anegada was another fast one and the arrival at the anchorage fairly uneventful with the entry through the extensive reefs being well buoyed. The most alarming bit was when the depths in the entrance suddenly shoaled. Thinking we were going to run aground at any second I chickened out and headed for one of the mooring buoys that had been laid there. In the afternoon we attempted to explore some of the interior of the island. We found a large lagoon, home to pink flamingos, that we managed to get fairly close to. Our attempts to penetrate further were thwarted by some extremely thick undergrowth that seemed to cover the island. An extremely low lying island the highest point was reputed to be twenty cight feet above sea level. The next day we had an exciting trip in an open truck that was called a taxi, across the island to a beach on the north side where the snorkelling was particularly good.

While we were in Anegade we heard someone just off Tortola asking for help because the steering on his charter boat had jammed. No one seemed able or prepared to help him and there must have been several boats in the area at the time. Tortola radio told him to call the US Coastguard, who failed to reply. After repeated calls for help on 16, someone came on telling him to switch to a working channel and not block 16 and then proceeded to book dinner for that night at one of the many shoreside restaurants! The next day we had another fast sail back to Virgin Gorda and an area known as the baths. Free short stay buoys are provided for where you dinghy into a bay. If, as on the day we went, there is a big swell running, you can tie your dinghy to a line between two buoys and swim or snorkel ashore. We were rather concerned as to whether we would manage to get ashore at all. When we finally got there we still weren’t entirely sure that we had come to the right place. I was therefore relieved to see a large kiosk with the word INFORMATION emblasooned above it. Approaching the rather bored looking individual who was positioned underneath this sign, listening to the radio, | asked whether this was in fact the place known as the Baths. Tearing himself away from his radio with great reluctance, he looked at me soulfully and with considerable effort replied ‘Yeah’. I failed to elicit any further response from him at all. We found our way into the Baths which turned out to be a whole series of partially flooded underground caverns, formed by virtue of a large number of enormous boulders resting on one another. It took about twenty minutes to scramble from one end of these walkways to the other through a variety of routes. The effect as the sea surged into these caveners with light streaming in through gaps in the ceiling of rocks above was electrifying. At one point | clambered over a rock to see Mona perfectly framed in a gap between the boulders. Seeing me looking an American couple coming up behind me stopped to look as well. ‘Don’t you just wish the view from home was as good as that?’ the man said. I was able to reply with some pride ‘that is my home’. Our next port of call was a return visit to Road Town with its very exposed anchorage. We needed to do some provisioning but the main reason for our visit was that Jenny need to book a flight back to England. She was committed to returning b the middle of May. All in all, this time as a reunited family had worked remarkably well. Clearly there were always going to be times when four adults living on a ten metre boat for an extended period, was going to be a bit of a squash. That things went as well as they did must be put down to a combination of the weather, which meant that there were very few times when we were all battened down below decks and the tolerance and understanding of the skipper. That last bit will probably be edited out by my censors. The main difficulty on board was not having a second sleeping cabin. This was not so much a problem at night when the girls were generally quite happy sleeping the comparatively airy saloon, but more so during the day when in the general business of living we would on occasions simply run out of space. We had always known that there was going to be limited space when there were more of us on board. Mona had in all fairness been designed for two people to live on. It was only at anchor that lack of space became a problem. At sea there were few complaints. On balance there would have been times when we all got on each others nerves even in a bigger boat. All in all it had been a good time for all of us and I think we were all genuinely surprised and pleased that it had all worked out as well as it had. Jenny got a flight booked from Puerto Rico for May the fifth. We had decided that it would be worth pressing on through the USVI’s and the Spanish VI’s, before beginning our journey south for the hurricane season. We had left home without obtaining US visas so we now had to take a day ferry trip the USVI’s which would give us a three month visa waiver in our passports. In the event we had quite an enjoyable high speed ferry trip from Sophers Hole in the south of Tortola to St. Thomas in the USVI’s, weaving our way through tiny rock strewn passes without any reduction in speed. We got the necessary stamps in our passports and the prized green cards and were now in a position to embark on an epic hour and a half long voyage in Mona to the states. Part Nineteen — The U.S. Virgin Islands Mona’s introduction to the USVI’s was a little bit fraught. Sailing downwind from Soper’s Hole in Tortola we had a pleasant genoa run between a number of islets including the negotiation of an extremely narrow reef lined pass. I am a notoriously bad delegator in situations such as this, so 1 was quite proud of the fact that I let Jenny steer us through and managed somehow or other to keep my hands off the tiller. I did however succumb to a severe bout of nervous behaviours. We very quickly arrived at Cruz Bay on St. John’s where we needed to check in. On taking the sails down and motoring in we discovered it to be a very small and extreemnly busy port. As we ventured in towards the custom dock, fast ferries seemed to be charging in and out at an alarming rate. Two buoys reserved for boats clearing customs were occupied. As we passed them in the narrow channel we could see the customs dock ahead. In the pilot it said that boats could tie up alongside for short period. With Helen telling me that it was too narrow and busy and that we should turn round and anchor outside the harbour, 1 headed for the customs dock and promptly ran hard aground. No amount of gunning the engine in reverse had any effect. Neither did the appearance of a customs officer who indicated where we should tie up alongside the dock. Eventually a couple went by in an inflatable. They valiantly attempted to push our bows back into deeper water with no success. While they were doing this an American in a powerful R.I.B. came over to us. “Got a problem’ he asked in a thick Texan drawl. Applying full power to our bows he was only successful in completely soaking himself. He then attempted to push our stern out as I put the engine hard astern, again without success. He then came up with the idea of pushing our bows onto the sandbank while I again went hard astern. It sounded crazy to me but this time I was willing to try anything. With both our engine and his roaring at full power and spray flying everywhere, we moved. We were off. Helen went below to get 10

our rescuer a cold beer. With a loud ‘Yahoo’ he spun the R.1.B. around at full revs gave us a wave and disappeared as quickly as he had come, in a cloud of spray. Helen appeared in the companionway clutching the beer ‘Where is he?’ Then after a pause watching the cloud of spray disappear into the distance, she said ‘Who was that?’ ‘That’ I said, narrowing my eyes for dramatic effect, “That was the Lone Ranger’. Making our way gingerly back through the outer harbour we passed Aldebaran anchored sensibly near the entrance. Our recent escapades had been hidden from their view by a steep promontory and they now assumed that we had successfully checked in. We decided to anchor as a couple of other boats had done, right outside the harbour. As we were about to do this, one of the boats that had been on a customs buoy, left the harbour indicating that the buoy was free. Heading back in we secured to the buoy with less that six inches under our kee] and made our way at long last to customs. After our experiences in the British Virgin Islands, the whole process of checking in was a revelation. The officials were professional but polite and friendly. On of the stranger stipulations was that while we were in the USVI’s under no circumstances were we to take any garbage ashore, even if we had bought the originai product there, as by being on the boat it would have become contaminated. When we asked what we should do with our rubbish, they asked where we were gong next. We replied that eventually we expected to move on to Puerto Rico. ‘Take it there then’ they replied. Our brief tour of the town was rewarded with happy smiling friendly faces, in marked contrast to the BVI’s. We could only stay for a limited time on the customs buoy so we returned to the boat and motored around to the next bay, Caneel Bay, was unlike Cruz Harbour there was plenty of space and an abundance of mooring buoys laid off a white sandy beach. A large part of the island was given to the National Park by the Rockefeller family. Recent bequests have allowed the National Park Authority to fulfil its aim of setting up mooring buoys in each of the bays overseen by the authority. The main aim of these buoys is to give people access to the Park at the same time as limiting the damage being done to coral by anchoring. For the time being these buoys were free which made another pleasant change after the BVI’s. In spite of the wonderful surroundings the stress of the earlier part of the day had got to both Helen and myself so Pat’s idea of going back into Curz by taxi to visit an Irish Pub ha had discovered earlier, turned out to be the light relief we needed, involving a lively meeting with a group of Puerto Ricans and an impromptu game of darts. We spent the next the days or so, circumnavigating St. John’ very slowly and loved all we saw of it. The National Park Authority have made such a difference by ensuring that any development is restricted and effectively controlled. In the Cinnamon Bay our second stop, a large campsite run by the Authority is masked by trees and completely invisible from the bay. This campsite proved to be very welcoming and gave us the unaccustomed luxury of plentiful freshwater showers. From Cinnamon Bay we tackled a fairly ambitious trek across the island to Reef Bay. The rough path cut deep through the dense forest and was mercifully shaded from the intense glare of the sun on the way out. On the way out we saw ancient rock carvings made by early Arowak settlers. By Reef Bay we explored the ruins of an old sugar mill factory with an intact stationary steam engine manufactured in England. The island is now so densely forested that it is hard to believe that a hundred years ago it was almost entirely cultivated. We swam in the surprisingly warm water of Reef Bay, then made our way back up the steep track, now much more exposed to the burning afternoon sun. During our time so far in the Caribbean we had acclimatised better than we had expected to. This was in no small part due to the fact that the early months of the year had been somewhat wetter and cooler than usual. Now as summer approached we were finding the heat increasingly hard to take, particularly on land. On the plus side the heat was proving very beneficial to aching bones. Back in Cinnamon Bay we attended a free open-air play illustrating the history of the island. From Cinnamon Bay we went to Waterlemon Bay where we snorkelled and explored the remains of another sugar mill factory. Part of these ruins was a stoutly built cell where reca Icitrant slave’s had been ensconced. Further round the island we anchored in Hurricane Hole, as its name implies, an extremely sheltered spot behind the Mangroves. From there we had to brave the exposed point of Ram Head, which came as something of a shock after the sheltered water we had just left behind. Keeping well into the rocky headland to avoid an off lying shoal, we bashed under engine into the head winds and seas. It was a great relief when we had rounded the headland sufficiently to bear away and bring the wind abeam. Its at times like that when you realise how dependant you are on the engine. It’s a situation that makes me distinctly uneasy and gives me intense respect for those brave souls who sail engineless, particularly in waters like these. Heading into the sheltered Great Lameshur Bay, it was a special pleasure to be once again greeted by a plentiful supply of free mooring buoys. As we secured to a buoy and began to take in our idyllic surroundings, I noticed a Maxi 1000 on another buoy. I was just debating with myself whether it could be Maximum that we had me in Graciosa and had last seen in Puerto Calero, when I 1]

saw Jack and Jeanette climbing onto their dinghy and coming over to see us. It was yet another of those chance encounters. They had been on the point of leaving when we came in. It was great fun sharing experiences and finding yet another potentially much faster boat, that by tackling the Atlantic crossing over a month before us, had taken considerably longer. This bay proved to be a superb snorkelling and simply enjoying the location,. We once again appreciated the existence of the National Park which was responsible for preserving this tranquillity by preventing the kind of untidy development that would undoubtedly have taken place. Ashore we were made extremely welcome at the environmental centre that functions as both research centre and education camp for, mainly American, students. It was fascinating to see more evidence of the natural reforestation of the island after years of cultivation. This was a place we could happily have stayed on a lot longer. However we had a deadline with Jenny’s flight on the 12" of May from Puerto Rico. It was now the 26" of April so we moved slowly down the coast following Aldebaran onto Rendezvous Bay, an anchorage that initially I wasn’t too keen on, as it felt rather exposed and windy. Helen and I explored the nearby beach while Pat, Olivia and Jenny went ashore at another more developed beach as they wanted to go back into Cruz Bay to use e-mail etc. On their return it transpired that they had been given a lift into town by an American couple staying in one of the holiday villas and that we had all been invited to have a barbeque with them that evening. The barbeque turned out to be a lavish meal. We all had a thoroughly enjoyable evening while we marvelled at the unaccustomed luxury of deep armchairs, sunken swimming pools and space. Early the next morning we said our farewells to Pat and Olivia and settled down for a lively and enjoyable genoa run to Charlotte Amalie on St. Thomas. As we approached we still had the VHF on 77 dual watch, the channel we had been using for inter boat chat. Now we realised it was being used rather more formally by a cruise ship monitoring the activities of it’s boats, transporting the passengers ashore. St. Thomas although part of the U.S., has been declared a duty free zone. It has therefore become a very popular stop with American tourists. As we approached the harbour it slowly dawned on us that the ship that we had been listening to was none other than the QE2. She made an impressive sight anchored just of the rocky harbour entrance. Once inside the harbour we anchoreda little way off the Cruise Ship Dock. Once ashore we had access to the biggest supermarkets we had seen in a long time and as in St. Johns a remarkably cheap phone service. The next morning we visited customs to discover that to move on to the Spanish Virgin Islands it was necessary to notify customs but not Immigration as we would be passing from one U.S. state to another. The Spanish Virgins Islands are part of Puerto Rico which is officially party of a U.S. Commonwealth. A 1993 referendum voted by a narrow majority to remain a Commonwealth, defeating those who wished the island to becomea full USS. state. After leaving customs we made our way to the fuel dock where we topped up on diesel, petrol for the outboard and water. By the time that we had done all this, time was pressing, so rather than head off for the island of Culebra, as we had originally intended, we stopped off at Water Island, just off the entrance to Charlotte Amalie Harbour. After investigating one or two possible stopovers we anchored in Flamingo Harbour. After investigating one or two possible stopovers we anchored in Flamingo Bay next to two or three ‘ being worked on’ type of boats. It turned out to be a fascinating island. Just inside our anchorage was a narrow cut to a shallow inner lagoon where some rickety pontoons served a collection on tatty but serviceable and powerful runabouts. By the lagoon a collection of rusty old cars minus things like bonnets and doors, gave the place the look of a scrap yard. While we were there, another powerful runabout roared in through the narrow pass. An affluent looking family unloaded their shopping, climbed into one of the doorless and rusty cars and calmly drove off. On walking around the island we found it to be a strange mixture of affluent properties and deserted ruins, some with optimistic for sale notices.

Minutes - November Meeting of Main Committee Executive Meeting. Ai their meeting on the 25'" October 2000 the Executive discussed the following: Urinal replacement, RIB replacement, MASC AGM, MSC AGM, membership. MASC AGM. The MSC was represented by C Shenton, MR & Mrs D Kirby, P Black, F Bennett, N Pembleton, Ron & Mary Greygoose. The revised MASC constitution is on hold. The Club Manager appealed for members to join the MASC Committee, during most meetings there are not sufficient members to form a quorum. The President, Mr L Murray said that there was a possible 5-year extension to the MASC Yease but this was not yet in writing and depended on the MASC remaining solvent. The Club Manager said that plans were being prepared to upgrade the Club and these were available for viewing. Safety. White lining on hold for better weather. RIB accident, Ms J Ball said that additional training is being scheduled on boat handling and VHF radio operating procedures. Mr R Greygoose advised the Committee that the public footpath passes in front of the Clubhouse and terminates at the boundary fence. East Coast Piers Race. Mr C Davis arranged for a presentation of the proceeds of the race to the Cirden Trust, £8000 was donated. The date for the next ECPR is 15th July 2001. Clubhouse and Site. Work commenced on urinals. Sewage plant, we have received a letter from the Environment Agency, the system was re-inspected on the 3'9 October, no real result. Clubhouse Window, progress contractor. A review of the Cruiser Park is to be conducted for 2001. Mr M Bates asked that a note be placed in Navigans re not driving on the grass during the winter. Mr R Greygoose, passed on a comment from the Solo AGM, that the eastern end of the clubhouse was untidy, notably the skip. Mr F Bennett said that the skip had to be in an accessible position for the collecting vehicle and also where the vehicle, which is large, would not cause any damage. Social. Mrs L Gill has retired from the position of Social Manager; the committee thanked her for her contribution during the year. The new Social Manager is Fenella Thomas. Moorings Sub Committee. Mr P Clayton said that a large triple hydraulic pump, (Acquired and refurbished by M Bates at no cost to the club) has been trialed and the results were good. Estimated costs, Valve £60; Tank £150; Filter £265; Interconnecting Hoses £20.00 All ex VAT. These costs could be offset against the purchase of a new snatch block £253.00, the existing block being condemned. F Bennett asked if the existing winch motor would be compatible with the proposed more powerful pump, M Bates said it would need to be replaced to realise the full potential of the large pump, cost £600. Post meeting note, the existing winch motor will be fitted to a second smaller winch. Mr F Bennett asked if the winch proposal was a departure from the five year plan, a general discussion ensued. The Executive to produce an expenditure management plan. The Jack B work plan is complete with names against various tasks. Mr Eric Cockerton has volunteered for the position of Jack B Bosun. Mooring recovery has commenced. Club trolleys are in need of major repair, costs to be provided at next meeting. Mast Rack, the interior is complete, exterior roof required, estimated cost £100. Mast derrick falls to be replaced. Tractors. One Fordson has run a main bearing loader is required, the small tractor is under offer £650. The 4WD is in good order and the latest Leyland is performing well. 13

Sailing Sub Committee. Ms J Ball; the Orkney has been collected from the repairers. The RIB has been sent for repairs. The 2001 programme is progressing. Next AGM start time and venue to be considered. A number of dinghy trailers have been removed from the site without the owner's permission. Navigans. K & B Dowley now on the Internet, mail to: [redacted].com Correspondence. Essex Magistrates, licensing sessions for 2001. Publicity handout, tobacco smoke extraction. Calor gas notice of price surcharge. Radio Communications Agency, survey. Any Other Business. Laying Up Supper, Mr R Greygoose suggested the venue should be decorated to compliment a sailing event. Mr P Black said that the owners of Dart 18 Top Cat had been in contact with a view to selling the boat. (They are no longer members). A person showing interest in the derelict Kestrel has been given permission to remove it from the site. Mr P Clayton said that scrap trailers were being disposed of. Commodore’s Notes My contribution to Navigans over the last two issues has been to publish my report to the AGM. I hope you found it informative. You will have read that a small sub committee has prepared a Business Plan in case the Club should need to go it alone from our parent, MASC. I am pleased to tell you that, following an announcement of an extension to the Beehive Lane lease at the MASC AGM, this threat appears to have receded. In the depths of January, as I write this, the new season seems months away, but several hardy and dedicated members are hard at work at the Club to ensure that our equipment is ready for the new season. Jack B is undergoing a thorough overhaul under the careful eye of the new bosun Eric Cockerton. Doubtless the old hands, Ray Ball and Geoff Josey are free with their advice and help. Mike Smith, Alan Clark and Roy Bellord complete the team that are ensuring this most valuable and flexible of the Clubs assets is ready for the new season. We have several more assets without which the Club would soon founder, our tractor fleet. They need constant attention, maintenance and care during the winter to ensure they keep going through the year. The band of members engaged in these tasks this year is Jack Goody, Jerry Champion and Howard Griffiths, and, as usual, Peter Clayton and Murray Bates are very much in evidence in both operations. Thank you gentlemen. Another gentlemen and good servant of the Club, Neil Pembleton, has been unwell. After a spell in Broomfield he is on the mend. We all wish you well Neil. At the risk of making this seem like an episode of Casualty I must tell you about the Glynns. We thought new grandson Daniel was too young to ski this Christmas so we gave “our” apartment in Tignes to the Glynns for the holidays. Debbie phoned to thank me on her return. They loved everything, the resort, the snow, the restaurants, the fireworks and the rescue services which Debbie had experienced when she broke her arm in three places after colliding with Michaela. Hope you heal soon Debs, the sailing season approaches. . I look forward to seeing you all at the working party later in late February, and at the Fitting Out Supper at the Club on March 24°. I wish you good sailing in the new season. Clive Shenton Membership Renewals Membership renewal forms should be with you by now. Please return them with the amended details by end of February. New Members Requi red Last year a sub committee was formed to find a way of attracting new members. The committee are as follows :- Julie Bloomfield, Cynthia Preston, Cathy Robertson, Joan Smith and Margaret Yeoman. See their action plan and what they require from you.................. See Page 5

Hello again from Jenny and Emma! We hope you are all welll We haven't much to report this month other than a small competition that I'm sure you will all enjoy. As you know, one of our main events of the year at Marconi’s is the ‘East Coast Piers Race’ (ECPR) and each year Tee-shirt and jumpers are available to buy. Well this year you cadets have been asked to come up with some Tee-shirt designs for the ECPR 2001.There is no particular size or any colours that you have to use, its all up to you, but we do ask that you would leave spaces for the sponsor names to be placed later on. I know what you're all thinking right now “What's in it for me?” Well think no more, there will be a reward for the cadet whose design is chosen with temporary membership of the start team aboard the committee boat for ECPR 2001, in other words you get to be on the boat that starts the races on the day and help in the sequences up to the start! So don't hesitate to start now on your designs and get them in to Chris Davies before the closing date, which is April 6TM 2001 GOOD LUCK! Jenny Miller Emma Knights Cadet Fleet Captain Assistant Fleet Captain [redacted] [redacted]

One idea we came up with was approved by the Main Committee and as every member of the MSC will be involved we thought it was best to let you all know early.
