Your Club Needs You!!!! and we can't do this without YOU. Regards to you all Margaret

Mona's Travels /continued Part Twenty - Puerto Rico and the Spanish Virgin Islands We made an early start the next morning, leaving Water Island for Culebra. Once again we just had our genoa set and made good progress past the well named Sail Rock, standing well out on it’s own and visible for miles around. Having negotiated the extensive reefs surrounding Culebra we motored through the narrow reef lined entrance to Ensanada Honda, a lagoon that stretches deep onto the island. Having made our way to the far end of the lagoon we anchored just off the town of Dewey. Jenny and I went ashore to clear in at customs. I To clear customs you had to go to the Airport, although airstrip might be a more accurate description. The customs official clearly had little to do because he seemed quite genuinely pleased to see us. We weren’t initially taken with the anchorage off Dewey, so in the morning after sitting out a torrential rain shower, we made our way out of the tye lagoon towards the little island of Culebrita. The wind was blowing in the mid twenties and kicking up a nasty chop in the channel. We were relieved to get in the lee of the island. We headed for an anchorage near to a path that led to the top of the island. One yacht was already anchored there and as we circled behind him we discovered that the anchorage was smaller than we expected and we slid across the top of a rock. Making our way further round the island we could see the bay that is the best anchorage on the island. However to get to it we would have to negotiate a narrow pass through a reef. In the current conditions the pass looked less than inviting. In addition being Sunday, the bay was full to overflowing with Puerto Ricon Navy, large fast white powerboats with enough elevated structures above to keep a stainless steel worker in business for years. We decided to anchor off the tip of the island in the shelter of the reef, from where we were able to dinghy ashore. The beach we landed on was a superb example of the best of Caribbean beaches. White sand lapped by turquoise water and no one else to be seen. The only drawback was that there were no paths allowing for us to explore the rest of the island, but we settled for a deserted beach. Later on that afternoon we made our way back in Mona to Culebra where we picked up a mooring buoy just behind the reef at the entrance to the lagoon. It was a wonderful spot. We were exposed to the full force of the wind, but sheltered behind the reef the water was flat calm. As in St. Johns the buoys were again free, in this case provided by the Government. I learned that the buoys were free after talking to John on a 29 foot S and S design on a neighboring buoy. Although he based hi s boat there, he was from Nantucket where he kept another boat. He divided his time between the two boats. This boat was now engineless and he sailed singlehanded, with just Lucy his dog for crew. Lucy was an obedient and loyal a crew as you could hope to find. John took great delight in restoring old dinghies and rigging them very simply for sail. While we were there he gave us a great deal of interesting local information. He told us that Water Island off St. Thomas was occupied by eccentric millionaires, many of whom had businesses on St. Thomas and who used Water Island as a recluse. When John need some extra cash he would go ashore with Lucy and put a sandwich board around his neck advertising day charters, apparently he never had trouble attracting custom. I was amazed that he could operate engineless from this lagoon, the narrow entrance was dead into the prevailing winds. Making the most of the quiet solitude of these islands, before we had to cope with what we felt would be the bustle of Puerto Rico, we went the short distance to the little island of Cayode Luis Pena, just to the west of Culebra. The bay we headed for had just two mooring buoys, one of which was occupied. The other boat turned out to be on a diving expedition and left shortly after we arrived. We then had the place all to ourselves. We rowed ashore to the secluded little beach from where we were able to walk across to a bay the other side of the headland. There we saw evidence of what looked like wartime military structures. We sailed off the buoy early the next morning and had another fast downwind sail. After studying the charts and pilot books we had concluded that the East Coast of Puerto Rico had very few sheltered anchorages and that we had little option but to make one of our increasingly rare visits to a marina. Heading into the coast towards Puerto Del Rey we were conscious of the number of reefs and rocky islets we were passing. It was akin to running merrily into the lion’s jaw. Puerto Del Rey Marina was something of a culture shock. An enormous complex consisting of a long wide concrete dock, complete with a three storey facility block halfway along its length and numerous smaller solid docks running off it. The normal mode of transport around the docks were golf buggies. The marina was absolutely full with row upon row of mainly white, powerboats. My introduction to this alien world consisted of being directed into an empty berth in a long line of smaller powerboats and then being whisked off in a golf buggy to the main office. After the peace and tranquility of the smaller islands it took a bit of getting used to.

We decided to hire a car for a couple of days to facilitate getting Jenny to the airport and also to see something of at least the eastern end of the island. We also needed to refill a couple of our gas cylinders and get a few supplies in. Most of these services seemed to be a fair distance away. We were definitely in a land of the car. My introduction to this aspect of the culture was a little fraught. Having been assigned a large immaculate vehicle I had a bit of trouble dealing with the automatic gearbox, having never used one before. The family hardly dared speak while I maneuvered with difficulty out of the marina car park and on to the highway proper. We then experienced difficulties in translating the scale of directions we had been given at the marina office into reality. Just a little way on your left turned out to be several miles. Consequently we turned off far too soon and instead of arriving at the propane gas works, that had been our intended first port of call, found ourselves instead arriving at the Roosevelt Roads U>S> Naval Base in the middle of a security clampdown, in response to anti American protests that were taking place at the time. Having successfully found the propane gas we needed wejoined the main highway to San Juan. This four and at times five lane route proved to be an even more severe test of my already shredded nerves. Whatever speed I was doing didn’t seem to be fast enough for the police behind me and whichever lane I happened to be in seemed to be the wrong one. After a brief beach stop where a row of near identical bars seemed to stretch for a least half a mile, we turned off the highway and escaped up a side road into the peace of the rain forest. Reputed to be the only tropical rainforest on United States Territory it proved to be a magical experience. Parking the car high up the mountain we walked through the lush and damp vegetation, realizing that for the first time for a very long time we were actually cool. We eventually arrived at an impressive waterfall cascading into a pool that were able to swim in. The next day we had to negotiate the main San Juan highway at morning rush hour. I was still finding great difficulty in coping with the speed and sheer volume of traffic. The situation wasn’t helped by the fact that the turn offs are only marked once, some distance prior to the turn off itself. The actual turnoff if simply marked Salida. It took me a while to realize that this meant exit. I initially wondered why so many places had the same name. Eventually after only two wrong turnings we arrived at the airport and saw Jenny safely on her way. After leaving the airport we attempted to make our way into San Juan itself. The roads were even busier and we ended up getting lost and heading of in totally the wrong direction. When we eventually got to the town we discovered that we had arrived in the middle of another Vieques demonstration. San Juan proved to be a beautiful and fascinating port. The heat however seemed to be gaining in intensity by the day and we were all rather wilted. Heading back to Culebra meant bashing straight into twenty-five knots of wind, an adverse current and a short sharp chop that the area is notorious for. We tried sailing but progress was painfully slow and our tacks took us worryingly near the many rocks and outlying reefs that enclose the area. Eventually bruised and battered we headed into the little island of Cayo Luis Pena that we had left the week earlier. Once again we had the bay to ourselves. It was a great relief to be able to swim straight from the boat again and havea totally relaxing afternoon wallowing in the solitude. As we picked up the buoy I had noticed a patch of yellow on the seabed, I took this to be sand among the coral. On diving in with her mask Laura made the alarming discovery that it was in fact a sunken yacht lying just a few feet below our keel. Heading back to Culebra we made contact with Pat and Olivia on Aldebaran . They had been in Culebra a few days having picked up friends in St. Thomas. The previous night they had taken part in a turtle watch and had put our names down with the warden as being interested. Having rendezvoused behind the reef we had a pleasant time meeting their friends Jim and Rita and catching up with each other’s experiences. The next day I met the warden Hobino. We arranged to accompany him that night but unfortunately heavy rainfall made the path down to the beach untenable and the expedition had to be cancelled. The following night we went ashore and met up with Hobino. We were luck in that that night Sam, an American professor who had studied turtles in general and leatherback turtles in particular was coming on the watch. He was a world authority on the subject. He was also the owner of a Hans Christian 43 with a strong desire to sail off into the wide blue yonder and was very interested in our activities. We were also joined by a group of high school students from Puerto Rico whose teacher was also very interested in our activities as his parents were liveaboards in the states. The group having assembled we made our way in Hobino’s four wheel drive accompanied by the school mini bus along a succession of narrow rutted tracks until we could go no further. We then walked down a rocky path to one end of the Brava beach. Sam told us that this beach had been a nesting ground for leatherback turtles since dinosaurs roamed the earth. They have few predators, their worst enemy being man, originally for his desire to hunt them but more recently for his tendency to develop resorts on their traditional nesting sites. Once this happens the turtles stop coming and are left to wander the oceans looking for alternative sites. The New York Institute that Sam represented had been in discussions with the owner of this beach for some years to persuade him not to develop the beach. So far they had been successful but they did not know how long this state of affairs would last.

When we got to the beach we walked in single file along the shoreline so as to cause minimal disruption to the sand. Too much disturbance and the turtle’s might be put off landing. Halfway along the beach we headed up to the vegetation and made camp. The plan was that two groups of two would walk in opposite directions the length of the beach. They would wait ten minutes and then return. If they spotted fresh turtle tracks they would flash a torch three times so that the rest of the group could join them. Laura went off with Sam as one of the first pairs. Time seemed to pass very slowly; we tried to make ourselves comfortable. Much to our surprise some of the students managed to go straight off to sleep. Suddenly we saw three flashes. Making our way as quietly as we could we met Sam who told us that as he and Laura came back along the beach a turtle had just come up. When we got there it was still digging an enormous hole with its flippers. These turtles are staggering large. With a shell over six feet long they make tracks up the beach over eight feet wide, their flippers are incredibly powerful. When they start digging sand is moved at a remarkable rate. Once the hole has been dug they start laying. At this stage the turtle goes into a trance and you can approach to watch proceedings and even touch them without disturbing them. Laura counted eggs as they were being laid. There were approximately eighty fertile eggs and twenty-four smaller infertile ones. All the eggs in one batch were the same sex. If the turtle laid in the cooler sand near the top of the beach they would be female. If they were laid in the cooler sand near the sea they would be male. Make of that what you will. It was an amazing experience watching this huge creature laying eggs, oblivious of the people crowded around it, holding its rear flippers apart so that the eggs could be counted. Once the laying was over the turtle reversed it previous action with its flipper filling in the hole until not a trace remained. It then turned itself around and made its way laboriously to the sea. The whole process had taken about forty-five minutes. When we got back to camp someone started pointing just beyond the surf line, a dark shape could be clearly seen in the moonlight just approaching the shore. A turtle reached the beach and lumbered up the sand straight towards us. Hardly daring to move we kept as still as we could until it finally stopped just a few feet away from just and started digging its nest. We had a ringside view of the whole fascinating process. Helen and I did one more patrol the length of the beach. It was then time to go. When we got back to our dinghy it was just getting light and we made our way back across the lagoon to Mona. We were now beginning to think seriously about heading back down south for the hurricane season. As we had visited a great many of the islands on the way up, I like the idea of heading straight back down. The problem was that to make a southeasterly course was to more or less head into the prevailing winds. The easiest thing would have been to head south to Venezuela or the Dutch ABC islands. However we had not ventured below St. Lucia and were now keen to visit the Grenadines and Grenada. We therefore decided to head for Bequia in the Grenadines. We now had to tear ourselves away from Culebra. Having been initially unimpressed with the little town of Dewey we had now become very fond of it and felt very comfortable and relaxed there. To be continued/...... STOWE MARINE PARTS Alan Williams of A. W. Marine, Marine Electronics. http://awmarine.com has purchased all spares and mainline produces of Stowe Marine. Minutes of December Meeting of the Management Committee New Committee Members Proposed by N Pembleton, seconded S Glynn that Mrs F Thomas and Mr S Ashley to be co-opted onto the Management Committee, agreed. The Commodore welcomed the new committee members. Previous Minutes. The previous minutes were accepted with one correction, Mrs M and Mr R Greygoose were in attendance at the MASC AGM. Executive Meeting. Mr P Bloomfield was invited to attend to the meeting on the 29/11/00 when the following was discussed:- Vice Commodore, Spending Plan, Project Manager for changing room update, Camping, Safety, RYA Affiliation, Maylandsea Bay SC rates reduction, the death of Lady Stansgate, RGG has sent letter of condolences, Gas container. MASC, The MASC has received a letter offering a further five years lease on the Beehive lane site followed by a second five- year term, on the condition that the MASC remains solvent. Mr N Pembleton announced that he had resigned from the MASC Main Committee. C Shenton asked for Sailing Section members to volunteer for the MASC Committee. Safety. Mr C Kidner tabled the minutes of the Safety Committee meeting and the Hazard Analysis Report dated November 2000. He reported two accidents, both as a result of tripping over cruiser recovery wires. It was suggested that more danger notices were required, N Pembleton suggested that this could imply that we have a legal liability to actively enforce the restriction. It was decided to seek professional advice. Mr F Bennett asked if any accidents were reported to the HSE, C Kidner said no. C Shenton volunteered to find out if we were obliged to report accidents. Post Meeting Note:- Both the RYA & safety professional advice is that no notification to HSE is required in respect of these incidents. C Kidner said the winches are to be rated for Safe Working Load. East Coast Piers Race. Mr C Davies said that the date for the next ECPR has been fixed for the 15" July 2001. The problems associated with safety cover and communications are being resolved. There is a requirement for someone to handle the sponsorship activities. The press release concerning the ECPR donation to the Cirden Trust will be released soon. Finance. Mr C Shenton tabled an expenditure statement for consideration by the committee. As some members had not received the accounts for 99/00 before the AGM, it was decided to reprint them in Navigans. N Pembleton asked if the Hon Treasurer had received a request from the MASC for section budgets, Mr F Bennett replied that he had. Clubhouse and Site. Mr P Bloomfield thanked all those who attended the working party, despite the poor conditions a great amount of work was completed. Sewage plant and the Environment Agency, Mr F Bennett has written to the EA, action closed. Concern was expressed about the generally unkempt appearance of the clubhouse. The catering agreement states that the galley must be kept in a clean condition. It has been reported that the caterers have not cleaned the galley. Post Meeting Note:- The Caterers returned and completed the necessary cleaning. Mr D Kirby suggested that the caterers should contribute to the club for their use of the galley. Mr Shenton said that the galley was run as a service and only a token rent was charged. Calor Gas, action continues. Mr R Greygoose said that the flagpole will be refurbished in the spring, the park bench on the hard could not be removed, who has the key? Mr S Glynn has generously agreed to act as the project manager for the changing room’s refurbishment scheme. The first step is to determine the schedule and costs. Mr M Bates said that quotations for the repair of the tractor shed roof are being requested. Mr P Bloomfield reported that the urinals would be operational soon.

Social. Mrs F Thomas. The Fitting Out and New Members Evening has been scheduled for the 24" March 2001, there will be a buffet. The theme for the summer barbecue scheduled for 26" May 2001 has yet to be determined. Laying Up Supper for next year has been provisionally set for 10" November. We have been advised that the Three Rivers Country Club is shutting down their function rooms. The Committee extended thanks to Steve and Debbie Glynn for once again organising a very successful LUS event. Moorings Sub Committee. Mr P Clayton. All moorings, race marks and club boats are now ashore. Last year it was decided to purchase epoxy paint for the Jack B hull. Before this can be applied the hull must be grit blasted at a cost of £170.00, spend approved. Replacement dinghy trolleys first quotation £131.00 +VAT other quotations being sought. The window frames in the tractor shed are decayed and need replacing, cost £60.00 for timber + glass. The mast derrick hauls are to be replaced, cost unknown. The Jack B battery is to be replaced, £100.00 spend approved. It was suggested that a two battery system is installed with one battery dedicated to engine starting, There was a general discussion concerning powered winches. P Black asked if the existing hydraulic motor would be able to take the power delivered by the new pump, M Bates replied that it would. Commodore’s Notes Its early February and the days are getting longer. I picked up my new Hyde sails last week, so I am looking forward to the season so | can try them. I hear that two members have upgraded into the fast cat fleet by the purchase of two Inter 18’s, so I will need all the speed I can get from the new Hydes. With the season nearly upon us | remind you of the Working Party on 25" February. I hope you will all turn out to help to get the Club ready for season which starts in March. Winter works, especially the Jack B, have been hampered by the weather and we may need to hire a barn so it can dry out before painting. While club life goes on, it is my sad duty to tell you of the sudden‘oss of one of our long standing and well liked members, Geoff Baker. Geoff was a professional photographer and took many pictures of Club activities. It was Geoff that recorded the handing over of the Piers Race ‘Big Cheque’ aboard the Lady Gadriel last autumn. His pictures were printed in local papers in January. He will be missed. Fenella Thomas is now our Social Manager and she has been hard at work arranging the year. The first event is the Fitting Out Supper which will be held at the Club this year on 24" March. I look forward to seeing you there. Please contact Fenella for tickets. She has also managed to book up for the Laying Up Supper. This has been a difficult task as our usual venue, Three Rivers, is being refurbished and is not available. The event will be at the Heybridge on 3TM November. This is not the date published in the Year Book, so I ask you to alter your copy as soon as it arrives. [ want to finish with a special plea to Marconi and BAe current employees who are Sailing Club members. You will see in the Minutes reproduced elsewhere in this issue, that Mike Worboys has resigned as Chairman of our parent organization MASC. Mike is a Sailing member and has put in a lot of work to ensure the future of MASC, but pressures of work has meant he cannot continue. I am not suggesting that you leap in as Chairman, but that Committee is urgently in need of members, both to represent the Sailing Club, and to help with deciding future policy. I ask any current employee (the Constitution precludes retired or non Company members) to consider volunteering. Just contact Ralph Coates at Beehive Lane. Good Luck with Fitting Out Clive Shenton Wha-haay- the sailing season is nearly upon us again and | for one am looking forward very much to getting out on the water again. At least, | am sitting indoors in the warm — possibly slightly less keen when | am outside in the cold wind and rain that we keep having this winter! — (and | will miss my Sunday lie-ins!). Anyway — the sailing (racing) programme officially commences on the 25" March which will only be a few weeks away by the time you read this. As ever, we have a very full programme this year — including the usual points, racing, cruiser racing, open events and the Dart 15 open has now been replaced with a Small Cat open event which we will open up to other small cat fleets — (further details to follow). The programme is published in the Club Year Book which will be sent to you shortly. We are already mobilising our team of volunteers to man the Race Box and Support Boats and as ever, I would appeal that you all check when you have been allocated a duty and do everything in your power to carry it out. If you can’t make it, please arrange a swap with another person on the rota — do not leave it to the Support Boat Co-Ordinators/Sailing Secretary to sort out and do not leave it to the night before to tell anyone you can’t make it. That’s the first nag of the season out the way, hopefully it will be the last. Our support boats have been undergoing a lot of work over the winter. The rib has been sent away and hopefully the engine problems are resolved — thanks to Mick Richardson for organising this. Eric Cockerton, Peter Clayton and Murray Bates have been leading a team of volunteers to carry out some major overhaul work on the Jack B this winter. Their efforts have been greatly hampered by the wet weather — but I am very grateful to the team for their hard work. 1 look forward to seeing you all shortly — and hope that you will kick off the season in style and join us at the fitting out party at the club on the 24" March (tickets available from Fenella Thomas — see order slip in Navigans). Happy Fitting Out! Jenny Ball — Rear Commodore 2

Several did brave the outdoors and either waited on the quay or took the walk along the river bank to keep the hard-working rowers in sight. The West Mersea Inshore Lifeboat visited the event to remind everyone of the good use that will be made of the funds raised. Over 40 boats took part in the race and the event's record total income is expected to top £10,000. The Basin Oars ladies won their usual prize for the most sponsorship attracted by one boat - over £4,000; and another boat wona prize for its single occupant whose sponsorship amounted to over £2,000 - over half the event's income coming from just two boats. Grateful thanks were expressed by the organisers at the prize-giving ceremony to all those who had contributed either through donations on the day or Sponsorship of a boat. Marconi Sailing Club made its presence felt again this year in the blue rowing boat kindly lent by Charles Anderson - thank you, Charles. Their fancy dress theme was Thunderbirds, with David Ball as Brains (‘making a spectacle of himself’ according to Malcolm Stuart); Lucy Boreham as Lady Penelope (Parker, having been given the day off, didn't appear); and Jenny Ball and Claire Davies as two of the International Rescue pilots. The Marconi entry won the prize for fancy dress and also for being the first to finish out of the mixed crew entrants. There were a couple of collecting buckets to receive donations for the Thunderbirds boat, and Sarah Davies collected most of the £51.70 that Club Members and other shivering spectators contributed - our thanks go to all of them. This money is in addition to sponsorship of over £75 raised by the Thunderbirds crew from Club Members, families, friends and work colleagues. Next year's event will apparently 'skip a year' and take place on New Year's Day in 2002 - you may want to mark your diaries now! Thank you to everyone concerned for your support of the Marconi boat. Mona's Travels /continued Part Twenty-One - Heading South for the Grenadines. Setting off early on Monday the fifteenth of May we cleared the outlying reefs and in a fresh easterly made good progress, holding a course to clear the eastern tip of Vieques and make for St. Croix. We had decided to make St. Croix an option as it is in the USVI'S. If we had cleared out of Culebra it would have meant surrendering our temporary green cards something | was not happy about doing with all the naval activity in the area. As it happened we reached St. Croix after dark. The main anchorage is heavily reefed so the decision was made for us and we kept going. After an uneventful night, the wind slowly dropped off the next day. We gradually settled into a slow but comfortable passage. Well clear of the main island chain this Part of the Caribbean is very quiet. We saw no ships or yachts for the whole of our passage. As we progressed southwards I became preoccupied with a small rocky islet that lay due south of us. The chart showed it as having a light but I had heard that it was now reputed to be unlit. As the wind shifted our course was taking us first one side of it, then the other. We eventually passed well to the east without ever seeing it. This rock is apparently part of Venezuela and I was- later to hear a fascinating story about it. A few years ago a group of scientists had set off from Venezuela to study the rock. This was before the advent of GPS and they took a little while to find it. When they eventually got there they landed and were astonished to be greeted by three yachtsmen who had been wrecked on the rock three weeks earlier. We had once again timed our passage to coincide with a full moon, which makes all the difference for night sailing. After a long rest the monitor self steering was put back into action and once again did everything that was asked of it. Our watch system of four hours on eight hours off once again ensured that we had plenty of rest. In the conditions our daily averages of between eighty and ninety miles weren't too bad, although at times progress felt painfully slow compared with some of our earlier passages. What little wind there was, was hard on the nose and as we had anticipate our problem was making enough easting. We became obsessive about our course competing with each other as to who could make the most easting and who lost precious easting when a wind shift went against them. The lack of wind made the heat even more noticeable. On one occasion the afternoon was enlivened by the sighting of an impressive looking Portugese Man of War swimming right by the boat. On the fifth night the wind dropped right away. | realised that the way we were going we would eventually miss the whole island chain completely. We started the engine and managed to motorsail and set a course directly for Bequia. During the night the wind increased until it was blowing between fifteen and eighteen knots. It seemed al] wrong to be motorsailing with a good wind blowing so I turned the engine off. Inevitably over the next few hours although we made good Progress our course sagged off. As the wind increased I realised that it was going to be a real struggle to reach Bequia. A few calculations quickly showed that Union Island would be an easier bet. Laura read up the Pilot and discovered that Chatkam on the Western side of the island was completely open to the west and would be easy to enter. Just what we needed. A little way Out from Union Island we started the engine and motorsailed under Autohelm straight into the bay. We anchored off the beach in the company of just two other boats five days and four hundred and fifty miles from Culebra. Part Twenty Two - Union Island and Carriacou. The Grenadines are a very popular and busy part of the Caribbean. It was therefore particularly pleasant to be in a large bay with just a couple of other yachts for company. We should have by rights checked in straightaway at a port of entry but we couldn't resist staying in this lovely, peaceful bay for at least a couple of days. I say peaceful, but there was in fact a wind effect that caused strong gusts to rush down between the hills. It was a beautiful bay for swimming and we enjoyed a fairly strenuous scramble up one of the surrounding hills giving us glorious view over the rest of Union and surrounding islands. From that height the reefs were particularly clear and showed up in glorious technicolour. Two days after arriving in Union, we attempted to move round the island to Clifton to check in. Having missed Bequia we had decided that after checking in we would make our way to the Tobago Cays, a spectacular reef lined anchorage. Motoring along the coast of Union, the trades had returned with a vengeance and we found ourselves bashing into it head on. Negotiating the narrow reef lined entrance to Clifton we, were suddenly in a crowded anchorage with boat boys coming alongside trying to gain our custom. After the solitude of the last few days it was all a bit much and having failed to find a sufficiently large space to anchor I turned Mona round and headed back out of the harbour. We headed through the reefs to Palm Island but the anchorage there was decidedly rolly. We did consider going over to Tobago Cays without checking in but at this stage my desire for a simple life held sway and we unfurled the jenny and set course south for Hillsborough in Carriacou. Carriacou is officially part of Grenada so once checked in we would be cleared for Grenada as a whole. We had a lovely sail inside the Jack A Dan a small off lyin islet and anchored in hillsborough just in time to clear customs before overtime rates came into play. I had a bit of a tustle with customs because I had failed to clear out of Culebra but eventually all was resolved and Laura and I got back to the 10

boat to find the two Chris’ from Globe Star that we had last seen in Portugal, on board talking to Helen. It was something of a surprise as they had originally planned to stay in Gibraltar and not come across until the following year. One of the fascinations of this life is not knowing who you are going to meet up with next. We stayed in Hillsborough a few days, which gave us time to explore the island. Helen and I caught the bus to Windward on the other side of the island where the Carriacou racing sloops are built on the shore. It was certainly a beautiful location for boat building. We were interested to see a modern yacht, being built among the trees using all kinds of epoxies and exotic materials. We wandered along the waterfront. Helen followed her ears and found someone hammering out a steel drum. We then followed a dirt track that led past a cemetery among the trees, and arrived at an absolutely deserted reef lined beach. This was the Caribbean | had dreamed about. We swam in complete seclusion and reveled in our surroundings with the view of Union Island, Petit St. Vincent and Petit Martinique. While we were anchored in Hillsborough we met up with Mike.and Mary on Meriva, a classic wooden holman Pye forty-one footer built at Tucker Browns in Burnham in 1967. As members of the Ocean Cruising Club they had been at the Virgin Islands Rally but we hadn't really got to know them there. Leaving hillsborough we anchored for a few hours at nearby Sandy Island, a genuine desert islandtwo hundred yards long with white sand, a clump of palm trees and an off lying reef. While we were there an American couple were brought out to the island by water taxi and deposited there presumably for a few hours of genuine ‘isolation’. It was quite rolly at Sandy Island so we motored round the headland to the calm of Tyrell Bay back on Carriacou proper. Tyrell Bay is a fascinating settlement where everything appears to move very slowly. We saw the contrast of a new lift out facility being built complete with travel hoist, right next to a fifty footer being built on the beach by traditional methods. We spent a pleasant couple of hours at the yacht club drinking cool fruit juices and working my way through a plentiful supply of yachting magazines. With the approach of the hurricane season the weather was becoming slightly more unsettled with tropical waves beginning to move through. Meriva moved on down to Grenada. The next day we had torrential rain and managed to catch enough water in our bimimi to refill our tanks. This was a great help to us and must have been a relief to the island as previously we had been unable to even buy water there, it was in such short supply. We took advantage of the next break in the weather to make our way south towards Grenada. We had a fair wind and a good sail past the rocky little island of Isle de Ronde. Slightly further on we passed, the underwater volcano Kick ‘em Jenny that lies about seventeen metres below the surface and reputed to be getting nearer the surface all the time. It, erupted in both 1988 and 1989, I worked out that we were close enough to peer down into the crater. I later learned that the local ferry running between Carriacou and Grenada, steers a course well clear of the volcano. As we reached the lee of Grenada the wind dropped and we were quickly engulfed in a torrential shower that for a few minutes completely obliterated the coastline Part Twenty Three - Grenada. The rain cleared as we made our way across St. George’s Bay. We decided to keep going round Saline Point to the south coast. As we rounded Saline Point we were taken aback by the strength of wind in our faces. We motorsailed in a heavy chop tacking out past a small island and then in towards Prickly Bay. Prickly Bay looked rather full so at the last moment we diverted to the neighbouring True Blue Bay where we anchored along - with just two other boats. Helen and | celebrated our arrival by having a meal at the exclusive True Blue resort restaurant, built over the water in a corner of the bay. We didn't know it was exclusive until we landed there. We had a superb meal particularly after Helen had asked for more rice. We were initially served with tiny little mounds of rice. I can never work out why haute cuisine has to be served in such meagre portions. After a couple of days in True Blue we went round the corner to Prickly Bay where we met up with Mike and Mary on Meriva and their friends Tim and Jean on Sassie. We spent just over two weeks in Prickly Bay. I realised then how much I had needed to stop. We did a guided group walk into the rain forest with Selwyn Maxwell a Grenadian who had an encyclopedic knowledge of the flora and fauna of the island. We again swam in the cool fresh water under a waterfall. We also had a tour of the island including visits to the nutmeg factory and a rum distillery. Both plants were using technology of a hundred years ago. The longer we spent in Grenada the more we realised that it was quickly becoming our favourite Caribbean island. The people were incredibly warm and friendly without being the slightest bit pushy. There were no boat boys as in other islands hanging round the boats at anchor. Once ashore you might be asked if you wanted a taxi but when you said no thanks they would just smile and wish you a nice day. The local buses were cheap and very regular. Consisting of small mini buses they would 11

invariably be filled to capacity and beyond, but nobody ever seemed to complain. When someone wanted to get out from the furthest corner of the bus everyone would pile out with little comment and wait patiently until they could get back in. After two weeks anchored in Prickly Bay we moved to Mt. Hartman Bay. This bay is protected by a reef that all but blocks the entrance. Consequently there tends to be a lot less swell there than in Prickly. By this time Meriva had moved round to the moorings marina in Mt. Hartman. Mike and Mary were leaving her there and flying back to England for several weeks, Lau:ra moved on board becoming an official boatsitter, and giving us all some much needed space, we couldn’t believe that we had all been together for a year. Mike and Mary flew back to England. The two Chris's from Globe Star hauled out at Prickly Bay and went back to England on the same flight as Mike and Mary. On the same Friday Tim and Jean on Sassie set off on an overnighter to Trinidad. Suddenly everything went quiet. However it was not to last. On the Sunday after everyone had moved on we decided to go by dinghy to the weekly barbecue at Hog Island. Just before we went, Pat on Aldebaran called up to say that they were on the way down to Grenada and would probably stop at St, George’s. We told them we were off to a barbecue. Later that afternoon we had just finished eating when we looked up and there was Pat and Olivia. Within a few days Graham and Joan on Karma, and Richard and Rebecca on Tutella had also anchored in Mt. Hartman Bay and we were back to happy hours and a hectic social life. Helen and I did an expedition up to the rainforest with Pat and Olivia. After an interesting bus ride up from St. George's, during which once again I spent a fair bit of time with my eyes shut, we arrived in the cool of the forest. We decided to tackle a fairly ambitious walk up to the top of Mount Qua Qua. Unfortunately we had failed to take into account the heavy rainfall we had been having lately. Some way along the path Olivia and Helen decided to walk around a volcanic lake instead. In the event their walk proved to be fairly arduous. The walk to Mt. Qua Qua turned out to be something of a mud bath, which was a bit worrying when you were walking along the top of a narrow ridge. The view from the top was well worth the effort, but coming back down proved to be even harder than going up. Pat and I competed for the number of times we fell over. At one point Pat was ahead of, me when I slipped and I went shooting past him landing in the bushes, Pat was so busy laughing he slipped over too. While we were anchored in Mt.Hartman Bay we had the strange experience of sitting in the Marina Bar under the shelter of the overhanging roof while the rain absolutely poured, watching tennis live from Wimbledon which was bathed in sunshine. When we had arrived in Grenada it had been our intention to haul out for a refit if that proved to be possible. If not we would move on to Trinidad. Initially the main haul out facility in Grenada, a new operation at St. Davids, further along the south coast was full, but because we liked Grenada so much, we decided to stay anyway. Now we found that we could be hauled out. Once again we had a parting of ways. Karma went off to Carriacou. Aldebaran and Tutella set off for the overnight trip to Trinidad. The next morning we motor sailed to St. David’s where Mona was hauled out of the water for the first time for nearly a year. Commodore's Notes As members wake up from hibernation and prepare for the new season, a cadre of members have been working hard to ensure that the Club and its equipment are ready for the season. The Jack B is being forcibly dried under a cocoon of plastic sheeting so it can accept its new coat of paint. The wet winter made natural drying out impossible. Jack B also has a new rudder courtesy of the skills of Brian Piggott. As many of you know, Brian worked as a boat builder and repairer before his retirement and has worked on many members boats including my own. His repairs are better than the original. This edition includes the application forms for Camping Fortnight. You will note that we have changed the pricing structure this year. Most of the costs, for example electricity, water, heating, rubbish disposal and particularly sewage disposal are in direct proportion to the number of people camping. It seemed logical to include a fee for each person using the facilities. Furthermore the direct and indirect costs of camping continue to rise steeply and consequently | perceived the need to increase the fees. Its not all bad news though, we have removed the charge for cadets camping in the cadet area, however such cadets will need to pay the ‘per person’ charge and this should be included in the application by their responsible adult. When it all washes through, the fees for camping will increase by an overall 30%. | must say that, in my opinion, even with the increases, Camping Fortnight is very good value for money and considerably better and less expensive than comparable holidays. This is only possible due to the hard work of the organisers and the small army of helpers led by Peter Clayton, Steve Monks and Kevin Dowley. Hilary Ashley is once again undertaking her role of camping co-ordinator and all applications will be dealt with in her usual impartial way. To avoid disappointment - book early - VERY EARLY. My thanks to all the members who braved the snow and Foot & Mouth to turn out for the Working Party jp of HAIY: They were rewarded with bright sunshine and much good work was done under the guidance of Peter Blue 4 On the subject of Foot & Mouth, the Club is still accessible but | must ask you to ensure that you do net anter surrounding farmland or footpaths nor allow your dogs to do so. a A We must ensure we do our bit to eradicate this awful disease. | look forward to seeing you at the Fitting Out Party on Saturday 24” March. Clive Shenton Hello Everyone, 1 hope you have all found a supply of flyers and a poster enclosed with this edition of Navigans. In February you were advised that 20 flyers and 2 posters would be supplied but due to printing costs we have had to reduce the amount supplied to each member. Please ensure the items are displayed by Good Friday the 13TM April as we are aiming for an advertising bomb’. The flyers can be attached to cars in any car park e.g. supermarket, multi storey, railway stations, places of work, any street or anywhere you see a car! The posters can be displayed in works canteens, libraries, police stations, leisure centers, schools, pubs, local newsagents or anywhere else you can think of! The above places of display are only suggestions and you may think of many more and far more imaginative than I have thought of! The important thing is that they are displayed and we attract a lot of attention and interest to our club. The advertising committee thanks everyone for their help with this campaign. Regards Margaret Yeoman

Despite the fog our meeting at MASC on Thursday 15" February was well attended, members were shown three videos illustrating ‘Scenes of Essex Life’ from 1909 up to the late 50°s. This was followed by archive film from the Imperial War Museum depicting life on Osea Island during its term as a Naval Base in the early 1900’s, also action relating to their Coastal Motor Boats which were capable of 37 knots, the forerunner to the M.T.B.’s. The last video was ‘Day Trips to the Sea’ featuring trips from London Bridge down the Thames to Southend, Herne Bay and Ramsgate and also the River Medway up to Chatham featuring the pleasure steamers Royal Sovereign, Queen of the South and the Waverley, of which only the Waverly pays the occasional visit to our waters. The last of this series of meetings will be held on Thursday 22 March when our guest speaker will be Roy Hart who will be talking about his sailing adventure from the River Crouch to the Antarctic in his yacht Barracuda. | am sure you will find his talk both informative and entertaining. Time is creeping on and hopefully the weather is getting better, before you know it panic will be setting in to make ready for launching with all those “I’ll get round to it” jobs suddenly becoming urgent! I am informed moorings are due to be laid on the following dates 31 March c2-6; | April 14-28’ 14 April b2-13, 15 April B14-24; 28 April A2-9: 29 April A10-16. Those of you who require chain etc. may | remind you that Don Holdsworth will be away on holiday from 27 March to 10 April. Telephone — [redacted] With regard to our Shakedown Cruise to Burnham, | am pleased to confirm we will be holding our dinner at The Swallowtail in Burnham Yacht Harbour on Sunday 27 May for which Doreen and I were able to negotiate an excellent meal for £14.00 per head. The usual reply slip is printed on page 8 and I would be grateful if this could be returned to me together with a cheque (meal only) by Sunday 20 May at the latest. | understand other clubs are interested in booking a meal there but we were in first i.e. | booked on 20 November 2000, so it pays to get in early. Likewise when booking with the Marina when booking our visit last November Harbourmaster Bill Cole was seriously considering limiting the number of club bookings for this weekend, don’t worry we are in. Please note the Launching List will be displayed on the club notice board towards the end of April. Derek Kirby Cruiser Fleet Captain

HOW _TO START THE WORKBOAT Several people have said that they are having trouble starting the workboat engine. The engine was marinised and fitted last Spring by three or four club members and is something that Heath Robinson would be proud of! It is easy to start if you go about it the right way. On boarding the boat (if it is your first time, it is easier to lift off the engine box for access) visually check that the gear lever is in neutral (in the middle). Do not wiggle it backwards and forwards as this will make the clutch cones stick and make it harder to turn the engine over. If you look on the port side of the engine where the throttle linkage joins the speed lever, you will find it marked "stop" in one direction and "run" in the other. Make sure that it is in the "run" position by moving the throttle lever by the gearbox in the appropriate direction. Move to the starboard front lower part of the engine and pull out the half-inch diameter knob painted red, a click should be heard. This is the cold start device and if it comes away in your hand then you have pulled the dip stick out so you might as well check the oil while you are about it. The next part is where most people go wrong. To set the auto decompressor which is found a the top of the engine at the front (also painted red), rotate it clockwise to the 12o'clock position. Place the starting handle in the hold at the front and rotate if clockwise until the handle is at the 8 o'clock position. Reset the decompressor again by rotating clockwise until it is pointing to 12 o'clock, you are now ready to start. Turn the starting handle briskly. On the fourth rotation as you pass 8 o'clock and can therefore use your should body strength, the decompressor will release and the engine will start. This last part is most important. If you start from any other position, as it hits compression your hand will fly off the starting handle and you will rap your knuckles on the engine beds and your chin on the exhaust. This may seem long-winded but takes about tend seconds to set up. To stop the engine, close the throttle. A new challenge will be introduced to the middle of the course and a ‘Race within the Race’ has been devised to create a single, fun coniest in which all crews in both fleets (full ECPR and Colne Point races) will be competing SHORTER COURSE OPTION — As ever, ECPR entrants have the option ofsailing the full 50 mile course or of choosing the shorter Colne Point course. With a separate start within the ECPR start sequence this race offers an exciting option for smaller craft or in more challenging weather conditions. THE CHARITY - East Coast Piers Race 2000, run by Marconi Sailing Club, raised £8000 for local sailing charity Cirdan Trust. Over twelve years the club has donated over £70000 to this and similar charities, all produced by ECPR competitors, sponsors and supporters. We are pleased to support Cirdan Trust again in 2001. INDIVIDUAL SPONSORSHIP — we will again promote and acknowledge individual sponsorship of boats in support of the Cirdan Trust charity. Get your friends, neighbours and workmates to support you and see just what a contribution you can make. Ask us for sponsorship forms if this will help your efforts. REGISTRATION - £30 in advance, using entrance form available from website or any committee member, or £35 on the day. Entrance fee per boat £50 to include up to three nights camping. Not only the best long-distance event but also the most reasonable! The whole ECPR Team look forward to welcoming you once again — and to your offers ofhelp in the many tasks involved in both welcoming our visitors and supporting our supporters, Chris Davies Chairman, ECPR Committee

ECPR —- Help is needed Charles Anderson Cruiser Help Well a change takes place this year when the event takes on the flavour of a cocktail with a twist. All will be revealed nearer the time but we will stil! need around 20+ cruiser owners to join the support fleet. The race itself is on the 15" July, so now is the time to get it in the diary and plan your summer sailing around it. Well it would be really nice if you could. For those that are not familiar with the ECPR, the club is unique in putting on this annual event. The race is the only one of its kind offering 2 man-cat sailors a water-borne version of the London Marathon. The charity we support is local to Essex and based in Maldon. Many of you I know will have seen their vessels moored in Maldon or you may well be more familiar with the Hartlepool Renaissence, Duet, The Queen Galadriel and the sailing barge, Xylonite all of which are often out on the Blackwater. The Cirdan Sailing Trust provides sailing breaks for the disabled, disadvantaged as well as their helpers (not necessarily together). The money we raise goes towards bursaries which help those less able to pay make use of the charity’s services. Again as usual, a copy of the weekend’s questionnaire is in this issue; please don’t forget that if you do respond, your offer will be taken up so keep an eye on Navigans news about the weekend and definitely please do turn up at the weekend. This year we will continue to use MII/ch80 for routine coms as we thought it made life much clearer last year. Don’t fret though if you don’t have it but pleas make it clear on the form. Dinghy Help We will also be entertaining some sponsors on the Saturday so if you are a dinghy sailor and able to help here as well please indicate accordingly on the questionnaire. There are other ways to assist as the endless jobs at the club and on the hard keep us all entertained over the weekend. So again if any of these look a possibility please mark them to help us with the planning. Unique race and unique support We are all justifiably proud of the contribution we make to Cirdan. It is unique in the sailing world and amongst sailing clubs. Other long distance events have sprung up since MSC established the Piers Race but we remain the only one with the charity link. We have made a big difference to disabled sailors through our purchasing of boats for the RYA’s charity Sailability, the RNLI and bursaries for Cirdan’s youngsters. Once again | thank all of you who have helped in the past and my deepest gratitude goes out to those able to make a genuine contribution by joining us this year.

Commodore’s Notas Normal service resumes this month after an email virus and other difficulties prevented my contribution reaching you last time. Most of my article was to thank Doug Eyles and his team of helpers, and most especially Steve Glynn for transforming the changing rooms. Maureen Ball did a good job thanking you, but this is thanks again lads, job well done. You will all have seen the sign ‘No Camping Until Further Notice’ and this does look a little stark, so I will try to flesh it out a bit. When the Foot & Mouth epidemic started, Pat Black contacted the local farmer, Spencer Klingsick, to see how it would affect the Club’s business. Spencer said that, as long as we kept ourselves and our dogs confined within our site boundaries, things would be fine. However in April one of our members crashed his vehicle through a gate and wrote off both the gate and the vehicle. This incident caused Spencer to worry that the vehicle may have transmitted disease to his land and he threatened some harsh action to protect his livestock. Pat began to negotiate, the upshot of which was the introduction of the disinfectant strip and the banning of camping until further notice. These actions must be seen as minor when one considers that many sailing clubs are closed by the disease and the much more onerous action Spencer was considering to protect his stock. | have had a few emails criticising the farmer, but you must see his point of view as well. His way of life is threatened; all we loose is a few days camping. | must thank Pat Black for his calm and mature handling of this very emotive situation. Now to a prediction. The F&M outbreak appears to be reaching its end. Essex has not had a case for some weeks and the restrictions are beginning to be lifted in the county. | would be very disappointed indeed if we could not lift our camping ban in time for the Piers Race and Camping Fortnight. When the Executive makes the decision I will give Hilary the nod to bank your cheques and notify you. Hilary tells me that everyone who applied for a camping slot will be allocated one, provided of course that the ban is lifted. Enjoy your sailing, Clive Shenton NEW WEBSITE ADDRESS The club website address has changed to: www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Steve Ash Solo Fleet Captain Solo News Spring Points 9/10 A steady force 2/3 s/westerly greeted the seven solo sailors for the first of two races on Sunday 22nd April. Mike Taylor was to lead for the first two laps much place changing for 2nd place between Ron Greygoose, John Salmon, Roger Smith and Steve Monks. The wind almost dropped off completely on the last lap, which resulted in some interesting wind shifts. Mike held on to the lead and finished 1st with Steve taking 2nd with the ever youthful Ron taking 3rd.It was good to see our newest solo member John Nisbet joining in the racing and enjoying himself. The wind picked up to a 4 after lunch with some strong gusts. Mike again was first of the line closely followed by John. This was to remain until the second lap when both Mike and Roger decided to go for some swimming practice on the long down wind leg from B to C mark. (rumour has it Roger was just checking the paint work on the hull of his boat before he sells it!) This let both John and Steve though to claim 1st and 2nd with Mike in 3rd and Roger in 4th. Steve Monks

Our Cruiser Fitting Out Supper was held at M.S.C. on Saturday 28" April and attended by a full house of 63 members. My apologies to those whose bookings we were unable to accept. Generally speaking everyone enjoyed their meal, although unfortunately one of the tables were short of vegetables and whilst the caterers tried to retrieve the situation with offers of double helpings of dessert, that part of the evening was spoilt for them, sorry. After the meal we were once again entertained by members of the Erith Yacht Club fronted by our own Frank Burgess ably assisted by Peter and Julie Bloomfield, Margaret Yeoman and Dick Papworth. Moorings have all been laid and boats are beginning to find their way afloat and it is at times like this we must impress upon members to park their cars in a manner that will not impede the movement of boats and trailers between the cruiser park/cat field and the hard. This is especially important where the travel hoist is concerned; recently we spent over an hour trying to trace members to move their cars at a time when we were launching three boats from the cat field resulting in one missing the tide and therefore having to abort launching. Whilst on the subject of launching, we still find there are a few members that once launched disappear up or down the river leaving the shore party to clear up and stow the gear. Once launched members are expected to pick up a nearby mooring if not their own and come ashore to assist with the clearing up before sailing off. [ am sorry I have had to mention this but I have been requested by shore party members to do so. Bookings for the “Shakedown Cruise to Burnham” are coming in, we have 14 to date with 26 members booked in for the meal at the Swallowtail on Sunday 27th May. This trip includes the “Eagle Trophy Race” scheduled to start at 09.30 on Saturday 26"; also remember you can come round by road for the meal if you are unable to make it by boat. This will probably be the last “Comments” | will be writing before Doreen and | sail off to Holland via Ramsgate and the French/Belgium coast in company with SURUCA and TAHITI and there seems to be a chance we will be meeting up with VARUNA II later. Anyone else wishing to come along will be welcome, we tend to coast hop in about 6 hour passages, rather than the long hauls of ten to sixteen hours. Since I will be away during June [ thought it worth mentioning our proposed trip to St. Katherines commencing Saturday 21" July. I have 13 boats listed at present for which I will allocate “Booking Slips” (nothing to pay) which | would like returned to me by Sunday 8” July. I am pleased to report we have a club concessionary rate discount of 20%. That’s all for now folks, happy sailing. DEREK KIRBY CRUISER FLEET CAPTAIN

Commocore’s Notes Last month | expressed my hope and expectation that we would be able to open the Club site for camping before the summer season. | am pleased to tell you that Pat Black has obtained Spencer Klingsick’s agreement to this, providing that there is no reoccurrence locally of Foot & Mouth before the events. Those who applied for a pitch for camping fortnight should have heard from Hilary Ashley by now, if not then give me or Hilary a call. You will see from the minutes published elsewhere in this issue that Linda Chaplin is in the process of passing her duties as Registrar to Nick Beavins & Jan. This is a planned change which is taking place at a time of year when the Registrar's work load is relatively light. My thanks to Linda for undertaking this vital but largely unsung role for the last two and a half years. | also thank Nick & Jan for coming forward and wish them good luck and, most of all, enjoyment in their new duties. By the time you read this the Piers Race will be only a matter of one or two weeks away. You have heard me speak about our Race many times, of its unique feature of donating all proceeds to sailing charities and my pride in the Club that aspires to such goals. | encourage all members to make this year’s Race memorable either by entering, taking part in the organisation of the event, or, perhaps, by sponsoring an entrant or buying a Tee shirt. Some members manage to do all of these things. The Race Committee, led by Chris Davies, has secured the services of Lord Faulkener to start the Race, and Charles Anderson has also been highly active on the sponsorship front. It would be great if we could equal last year’s donation of £8,000 to the Cirdan Trust. I wish you all good fortune and good sailing. Clive Shenton View from the Rear Having just come back from a glorious and dry Bank Holiday weekend — (I never thought I would get to write that!) — it finally feels like the season has properly started. It has been a bit of a blustery season so far — but the turnout at weekends has been good and seems to be increasing in direct proportion to the levels of sunshine! Unfortunately, we have not been able to camp at the two bank holiday weekends due to the Foot and Mouth but have been able to make other arrangements at the Star and Sun and Anchor instead without too much inconvenience. The only casualty so far is that we had to cancel the Small Cat Open to ensure that people did not bring motor homes onto the site — (usually the competitors only form of transport when they come to such an event). Hopefully, we did not upset the Catapault fleet too much who were due to bring down a fleet of boats and it was nice to see that a couple of Catapault sailors still made it down to visit us. Wednesday night racing has just started — (which definitely means that the season has started) and we also have the Solo Open, SeaVets visit and of course the East Coast Piers Race all coming up at an alarming rate. I would like to thank everyone who has been manning the Race Box and Support Boats so far this season — often the weather is quite demanding and appreciate your continued support in carrying out the required duties for the rest of the season. We ran familiarisation session on Sunday 3 June in place of the afternoon race and offered people the opportunity to learn about the RIB, Jack B, usage of VHF radio and Race Box/Race Management. We had around a dozen people take part in the training — but were disadvantaged by the weather, which put more people off. I still think this is the best forum to attract people to attend these sessions, we will fun more in the future. My thanks go to Colin Leveridge, Kate Williams, Dave Williams, John Easton and David Bal! who all kindly volunteered to be “trainers”! Hopefully the season will continue to bring good winds and sunshine and I look forward to seeing you all on the water! Jenny Ball Rear Commodore [redacted]

We have to date, 14 boats scheduled for the trip and as mentioned I have been able to secure a 20% discount on the berthing fees. The proposed programme is to leave MSC moorings early Saturday morning, stopping overnight at Queenborough and then leaving early Sunday morning for the passage up to St. Kathrine Dock. It is suggested Monday and Tuesday will be “lay days” locking out early on Wednesday morning. On the way back from St. Kathrine Dock on Wednesday we were considering going up the river Medway to the new Marina in Chatham Dockyard, having a couple of days there before leaving possibly on the Saturday for Brightlingsea, returning to MSC on Sunday. Derek Kirby Cruiser Fleet Captain EAST COAST WIND FARMS I have been reading in the press of the plans for Wind Farms to be built along the East Coast. I believe that there could be consequences for the ordinary pleasure sailor unless their interests are safe guarded. I therefore wrote the letter below to the Royal Yachting Association and have received the reply also below. I would like to encourage all members, whether dinghy or cruiser sailors, to write to the RYA expressing their views. Remember that we have a number of shallow banks at the entrance to our river which in time could be seen as suitable for such wind farms. N.T.Pembleton The Secretary Royal Yachting Association Dear Sir, I have been reading in the press about the proposals to site a number of Windfarms along the East Coast for the generation of electricity. As a yachtsman who enjoys this stretch of coast, particularly from the River Blackwater in Essex to Great Yarmouth, I am writing to express a number of concerns. Whilst appreciating that it is unlikely that these developments can be halted, I hope that the RYA will be making adequate representation to those concerned to ensure that: Free passage inshore (Shore to 2-3 miles say) is maintained during any construction phase. Similarly free passage inshore is available after any construction phase. Any safety zone created around such farms is as limited as is consistent with its purpose and adequately buoyed and lit. Such farms are constructed in a manner as to allow safe passage from the inshore channels to the offshore channels without requiring major and lengthy deviation.

> Responsibility for the maintenance and financing of all safety provisions including buoyage etc rests with the operators and does not call on general public funding or yachtsmen in particular. Responsibility for the safe removal and return of the seabed to its original state at the end of the working life of such farms rests with the operators. This must include the total removal of all underwater constructions. The operators have a legal responsibility to indemnify yachtsmen for any damage caused to the structures and all underwater services however caused by them. The operators have a legal responsibility to compensate yachtsmen for any damage however caused to them by the structures and all underwater services. The reply was:- We have been tracking the development of this subject for some time and have attended a number of 'stakeholder’ meetings and had informal discussions with organisations like the Crown Estates and some of the main potential site builders. If you haven't yet located it, the industry view can be found at www.offshorewindfarms.co.uk. You will also see there is a general article in the current issue of RYA Magazine that is both intended to inform and stimulate discussion. Your suggested criteria are very helpful as a contribution to this process. Generally, | agree with these, and they are consistent with the points we are putting to those involved in the development on the sites, although I doubt that the indemnification requirements you put forward are, legally, practicable in that form. We are hoping to use the RYA website as a means of keeping members up to date with this subject, and to gather views and experiences. Yours etc.. CRUISER RACING NEWS The morning of the Race to Burnham dawned fine but with very light winds and so the fleet motored out to the Swin Spitway, where with a favourable tide we began. The course became a close reach, and with the tide under us, progress was brisk up the Crouch to Burnham Marina, where we met all the other MSC members for the Club Rally and ‘Shakedown Cruise’ organised for us by Derek and Doreen. The weekend, complete with reserved berths, and an evening dinner on Sunday in the Swallow Tail Restaurant was a great success, with over 50 members attending. May I express our thanks to Derek and Doreen who are now cruising in Holland. Dave Payne’s ‘Petronella’ at last fulfilled the promise of the racing refrigeration, followed by a new addition to the fleet Chris Good’s Limbo 6.6, ‘Limbo Lady’, and Ray and Jackie’s ‘Hartley’.

Minutes of the Management Committee Meeting held on the 30" April 2001 Previous Minutes. The minutes were approved with the following amendments; 1 Clubhouse and Site, Calor Gas, the action is not closed, the compound surrounding container the has still to be erected. 2 Car parking, action erroneously allocated to C Shenton. Executive Meeting. The Executive met on the 25/04/01 when the following matters were discussed:- The foot and mouth problem and its impact on camping. Grass cutting and driver training. RYA publications, Managing Health, Safety and food Hygiene Ashore. Gunfleet Sand Wind Farm. Calor gas. Changing rooms. MCA GG66. Sewage plant. Club Registrar. Linda Chaplin has decided to resign from her position as Registrar, the Officers and Committee extended their thanks to Linda for her dedication to a vital and sometimes difficult task. Nick Beavins has volunteered to fill the position and the hand-over will take place within the next six weeks. Safety. Mr C Kidner. Advice on recovering persons from the water possibly suffering from spinal injury, awaiting response from Essex Ambulance. Burnham Fire Station have confirmed that they have a key to the clubhouse and site. The lounge fire doors have been serviced but the correct fitting of the fire blanket in the galley awaits. East Coast Piers Race. Mr C Davies advised the meeting that Lord Faulkener has agreed to start the Piers Race this year. In order to keep the lounge clear of race control personnel and equipment the ECPR Committee is considering using a double-decker bus which would be parked on the hard. Following a discussion it was decided that a firm detailed proposal was required before the idea could be considered. The TA is keen to participate in their usual communications role. More support boats are needed to cover the course. Clubhouse and Site. Mr S Glynn said that the mulching machine and a team of operators are ready to start work, we await dry conditions on site. Foot and Mouth. Mr S Glynn offered to erect notices at entrance to Stansgate Road in time for next open meeting stating “no caravans permitted”. Mr P Bloomfield. Grass cutting, the initial cut has been completed, we await dryer conditions before continuing with the club machinery. Repairs to cruiser road, action continues. Repairs to fascia board, action continues Rubber doormats have been purchased and are in position. The caterers have supplied their own refrigerator, the club refrigerator is unserviceable and is to be scrapped. Lamp in galley requires new tube and starter. Tractor shed roof leaks. Mr R Hardwick has prepared a quotation. Race Equipment Container roof sealed. Sewage Plant. Mr C Shenton set out the Executive proposal for management of the plant during periods of heavy use. Basically we would use a contractor to pump out and carry away the effluent on a daily basis, and there would be a person on site to handle any emergencies. There were objections to this viz. e Too much reliance on volunteers, there may not be any. Previous maintenance agreement was a failure, why not specify to a contractor the service we wanted. There was not sufficient data on site for the person “in charge” to deal with a crises. Persons could be trained in the functions of the plant but this would not be ideal. It would be better if the club entered into an agreement with a suitably qualified contractor who would be available on callout in the event of a difficulty. It was noted that the previous contractor declared the system to be functioning correctly but failed to confirm his findings in writing. No firm conclusions were reached and the action reverted to the Executive Committee.

Commocore’s Notes I expect you will be reading this in your tent at Camping Fortnight or on your boat during your summer cruise. I hope the weather is good and you are enjoying yourselves. While you have time for quiet reflection | ask you to think about the Club and whether you could devote some time to help with it’s organisation and running. The Club only has one part time employee, all other jobs are done by the members. Every three years our Rules require that Flag Officers stand down. This year is the end of one of those three year cycles. Normally junior members of the Management Committee aspire to Flag rank and I am not expecting this year to be any different, however this process does create vacancies on the Committee. | ask you to consider if you could give the Club one evening a month to attend meetings and give us the benefit of your opinions and expertise. Please don’t think that you do not have the necessary qualities, all the best Committees are made up of people with diverse qualities and experience. Please phone me on [redacted] if you would like to know more. By now the Piers Race will be but a memory and Chris Davies and his Committee will be thinking about next year. Two weeks before the Race sponsorship was going well despite the drop in Internet company stocks. | hope you had a good day as an entrant, helper or spectator. Have a good summer Clive Shenton View from the Rear With the fine weather hopefully upon us and here to stay , we look forward to some of the major events at the club this season. As I write we are only days away from the Solo Open, East Coast Piers Race and Camping Fortnight. The Summer Points are well under way and the dinghy racing turnout has been very high over the last few weeks. I would like to thank those volunteers who continue to man the support boats and race box each weekend so that we can continue sailing. In particular, I would like to thank those people who have had to stand in at the last minute because someone has not turned up to complete their duty. Can I remind you to check the support boat / race box rota for the dates you have been scheduled and make sure that you either can make it or that you have arranged someone to swap with you. The role of the support boat co-ordinators is not to cover unmanned support boats because someone has not turned up! Still on a slightly nagging note - I have noticed that the RIB is sometimes being driven at an unnecessarily high speed through the moorings. Clearly we must abide by the speed limits and we also need to show courtesy to our cruiser members when navigating through the moorings. If you are driving the RIB and need to get to an incident quickly - please get into the main channel before you open her up. Looking out of my office window across the sunny rooves of Dunton and Laindon - I can honestly say that I would rather be on the Blackwater at this moment in time! Hopefully this weather will continue through the 2001 season and we get some really good sailing in. See you on the water! Jenny Ball Rear Commodore

SOLOS AT MARCONI Marconi Sailing Club held it’s annual Solo Open Meeting as part of the Eastern Travellers Series on Sunday 8 July. 29 Solos, comprising 13 visitors and 16 club members, arrived at the club on the River Blackwater estuary in cool, showery and overcast conditions, this followed a successful Solo training day on the Saturday tutored by Jim Hunt and Steve Ede and attended by 15 keen to learn soloists! The race officer, John Weedon set some long courses in the tidal estuary, the wind at the start being North Westerly gusting to force 5. This strong breeze was maintained throughout the day with occasional lapses which posed questions to the competitors as to which course to take (o minimise the effect of the strong tide. The first race was won by Steve Ede, only just passing Godfrey Clark from King George on the finishing line. Mike Taylor of Marconi was third followed by the rest of the fleet enjoying the exciting conditions. There was a fair amount of place changing down the fleet as the locals exploited the tidal conditions. The second race, followed the same course as the first with a long fetch with the tide past Osea Island and back with a long run and reach against the tide. Steve Ede was unfortunately late for the start due to a gear breakage, but still made his way through the fleet to finish equal fourth. The lead changed hands a few times in the first lap with Godfrey Clark unlucky to lose a hard earned lead by over-standing the windward mark at the start of the second lap. This let Roger Smith through to gain a first place, followed by Ron Laure and Godfrey Clark. After a break the third race took place with the tide changing and a slightly lighter breeze. Steve Ede romped away with this race to finish first and win the event. The rest of the fleet had a job to work out the best route in the tidal conditions but Mike Taylor got it right to come in second followed by Steve Monks in third. Doug Eyles and Ron Greygoose of the home club read the conditions well to get good places in this last race.
