feo COMMODORE'S NOTES On behalf of all the members, I would like to thank all those who retired from the Main Committee and other positions within the Club at the Annual General Meeting. Without their unstinting efforts, the Club would not have functioned and prospered the way that it has. I would especially like to thank Clive Shenton for the vision that has led to the compiling of plans to safeguard the Club into the future. I would like to welcome all those elected to positions at the Annual General Meeting. As you will be aware there were a number of positions which were not filled at the Meeting. I am pleased to say that since then Dave Payne has been co-opted by the Main Committee as Vice Commodore, and Mike Smith with Malcolm Yeoman have been co-opted in the role of joint Bar Manager. The main remaining vacancy is that of Rear Commodore which in my opinion must be filled as soon as possible. I believe that the Rear Commodore should be a person from the Dinghy/Catamaran fleets as one of the main functions of the role relates to Club racing and the members of the Cruiser Fleet are neither close enough to dinghy racing rules etc and tend to be away from the Club most weekends during the summer. Another very important reason relates to the balance of the Executive Committee. This is comprised of the Commodore, Vice Commodore, Rear Commodore, Secretary, and Treasurer. Of these five roles, four are currently filled by members of the Cruiser Fleet. In my opinion it is essential that the Dinghy/Catamaran fleets have a strong voice in this Committee and that at least one, if not two or three of the positions, should be filled by representatives from them. Finally, unless this position is filled quickly, the Club will find it extremely difficult to continue with Dinghy/Catamaran racing as the members of the Executive would not be able to carry out this vital task along with their other duties. If you are willing to be co-opted into this position, please contact any member of the Executive Committee as soon as possible to ensure that Club Racing can continue next year. Finally may I wish you all a very happy Christmas and enjoyable sailing/racing in 2002. A Year in the Life of a Rear Commodore As you will be aware, my three year tenure as Rear Commodore has just come to an end. As such, one of you now needs to volunteer to take on this important and interesting position. The purpose of this article is to give you an idea of the type of things you can expect if you volunteer to be Rear-Commodore. Key Purpose of Rear Commodore: The role of Rear Commodore - whilst important, is not as arduous as you may think. This is due to the raft of other club volunteers who are in place to support you. Your primary function as a Rear Commodore is to oversee sailing activity for the club - your secondary function is to ensure that the views of all club fleets are fairly represented to the Exec Committee and the Main Committee. Benefits: = you get a very good insight into the workings of the club = you get to play a key role in determining its future direction = you get to work with some great people = you get the satisfaction of seeing club members enjoy a full programme of sailing as a result of your efforts The following is an overview of the role of the Rear Commodore: 1. Chair Sailing Sub-Committee >» Sailing Sub-Committee meets monthly and consists of sailing secretary, fleet captains and support boat co-ordinator. > This committee is the hub of organising sailing programmes - the role of the Rear Commodore is to ensure that all aspects are covered and that tasks are shared out amongst the Sub-Committee members. Member of Executive Committee &V V Exec Committee meets monthly and consists of Commodore, Vice and Rear Commodores, Treasurer and Secretary. This committee is the core team of the club and discusses all matters relating to MSC - both current and future. Your role as Rear Commodore is to input the views of the fleets and to keep the Exec informed on sailing matters. You may also be assigned specific tasks or projects from time to time. » Member of Main Committee > Your role on the Main Committee is to report out on the activities of the Sailing Sub Committee. It is also the opportunity for Committee members to raise any sailing queries or matters with you. 4. Moorings Sub Committee > Although the Rear Commodore technically oversees the activities of the Moorings Sub-Committee - the reality is that this group run themselves under the able leadership of Pete Clayton and Murray Bates. The Moorings Sub-Committee are responsible for all matters relating to the mooring, launching and recovery of cruisers and they complete a tremendous amount of work each year. However, the input required from the Rear Commodore has been absolutely minimal during my time. I should also add that, although I personally spend quite a lot of time on Cadet activities - this does not form part of the Rear Commodore role - Cadet activities are co-ordinated separately by the Cadet Fleet Captain and the Cadet Committee. I would encourage any of you to consider taking on the role of Rear Commodore. It is one of the less difficult positions within the club and also the position that receives the most support from other club officers / co-ordinators. I would be happy to discuss the role further with any of you who may be interested - so please feel free to call me to find out more. As a final plea - this role is essential if we want to continue to have the sailing facilities and programme that we all enjoy. I know the Exec Committee will take a very serious look at whether we can continue normal sailing activities next year if this role is not filled. Please consider whether you would be able to help out. Thanks, Jenny Ball [redacted]

Sailing Secretary's Report 2001 (from the AGM) The 2001 sailing season included the usual programme of club racing for the Dinghy and Catamaran Fleets. New racing rules of sailing were due out for the start of the season. Unfortunately these were late being published and so the Sailing Sub Committee decided to run our Spring Points series using the old rules. The new rules were introduced in time to be incorporated into our sailing instructions for the summer. I would like to thank Roger Smith for attending seminars and redrafting the club's standard sailing instructions for the new rules. With 82 different races organised for club members only 2 were cancelled due to adverse weather conditions. This must be a record for recent years. Do we see the onset of global climate change or are we all getting older but less wise? With 93 different helmsmen across the whole year it would appear that the club racing is in a strong position. Turnout in the Solo and Handicap fleets was similar to last season. There was some increase in numbers in the Fast cat fleet after a slow start to the season. Unfortunately there was a reduced turnout in Medium cats and the Dart 15's. A decision was taken early in the season to combine the Medium and Fast catamaran fleets, encouraging good competition for all competitors. The Cadet fleet numbers peaked in mid summer, as usual, but were somewhat lower as we neared the end of the season. However, one of the reasons for this was a number of cadets switching week by week from the Cadet fleet to race in the Dart 15, Handicap and Cat fleets all of whom will keep the rest of us on our toes next season. The now firmly established Cruiser racing fleet organised their usual series of races with a similar number of entrants to last year's record season. A similar series is already planned for next year in co-operation with the established BJRC cruiser racing that takes place on the estuary. August again brought with it another camping fortnight and another hugely successful Cadet week. For the second year, in addition to the Cadets, tuition was organised for the "Senior Service" group although on a slightly reduced scale compared to last year. As I am sure you all remember the season started under the cloud of Foot and Mouth disease. We were very fortunate that, unlike many of the other clubs in the country, we were able to start our club-racing season on time. Unfortunately the Small Cat. Open meeting planned for the Spring Bank holiday weekend had to be cancelled. This was to be the first running of this event, which had been planned to replace the Dart 15 open. Plans are already underway to ensure that this event will not be lost to our members. Easing of Foot and Mouth restrictions in the county allowed us to proceed with our other open events. The Solo open meeting was extended to two days by adding a training day on the Saturday. The event itself attracted a turnout of 29 competitors this being the best attended Eastern Area open meeting this season. | think congratulations should go to the fleet captain for his efforts in getting as many club boats out as possible and to his organising committee for attracting such a large visiting fleet. The Kestrel fleet visited us over the August Bank holiday weekend and a small fleet of visiting Hamble Stars threatened to join our club racing but found the lure of the bright lights of Maldon to much to resist. The East Coast Piers Race, saved from foot and mouth, attracted 60 entries. I am sure you will have heard about the funds raised from previous speakers. The next section I shall call 'Marconi Sailors Abroad’. Although ‘abroad’ will include such destinations as Thorpe Bay and Lawling Creek. A number of our Solo fleet members contested races in the Solo open circuit, with Roger Smith securing third place in the Solo Scottish National Championships. Our Catamaran sailors were out and about this season with Hurricanes and Formula 18's competing on the circuit. Highlights of the season were Tim Wallace following up his 2nd in the ECPR with a third place at the Thorpe Bay Open (part of the Hurricane GP circuit). While Phil Longhurst became Hurricane Spinnaker National champion with Lee Harrison runner up. Finally, with seven of the Sailing Sub Committee standing down this year I would like to thank them on your behalf for all their hard work, in some cases over many years Dave Williams. Last Working Party: Thank You to all who came on 2nd December and worked so hard in the Clubhouse, Galley, Bars and all over the site. Next Working Party: Sunday 30th December, 9am. The traditional Christmas Holiday Working Party has been revived this year for outdoor work to continue. Volunteers needed with gardening tools, including secateurs, pruners, strimmers, sickles, (petrol strimmers and, perhaps, chain saws?) to chop more vegetation for eventual feeding to the mulcher. Strong gloves (& wellies, Jenny!) are a necessity. Hot drinks and rolls from the Galley once again, free to the workers. Ed.

The post involves attending one meeting a month held at MASC, usually the first Monday, and receiving by various means the articles that members and committee members wish to publish. The Editor's work ends after producing one typed copy of Navigans and passing it on to other volunteers for copying and distribution - being done very ably by Maggie and Mike Boreham. It is more the responsibility of the articles' authors to get their copy to the Editor on time than for the Editor to chase them up for it. It's useful, of course, if you can be contacted on-line, but not essential, as Royal Mail and hand deliveries and a bit of telephone dictation are options still available to us all. Navigans does cost the Club something per page to print off and post each month, hence my narrow margins and as much information packed on a page as I can fit in. I occasionally hear the rumour that Navigans copies are passed on and may be more widely read by interested people outside MSC membership than within it! I would be happy to continue with producing the annual paint order, see at the end of this edition, (convinced I'm the only one apart from Gordon who understands it); typing Mona's Travels (too interesting to give up); and the 'For Sale Board' entry (so I can keep that notice board's paper anarchy in order.) Navigans to some extent can be what its Editor makes it and the magazine would certainly benefit from the Editorship periodically passing round diverse pairs of hands and various Fleets within the membership. An Editor will get some useful insights into the operations of the Club - far more than can be guessed at by simply visiting the site to sail and going home again. There are no tough decisions to make, the Editor simply conveys information within the Club. By seeing at closer hand the care and work put into the Club by very experienced, able and supportive fellow Committee members, an Editor can emerge much wiser at the end of his/her tour of duty. Los Roques are a collection of mainly small islands with reef-strewn anchorages, protected from prevailing winds by extensive reefs on the eastern side. Working your way through these reefs is like negotiating a maze. Our entry was in the SE corner at Sebastopol, where the entrance lies between a very low-lying spit of land, hardly visible from just a little way offshore, and a submerged reef. With a strong wind up our tail and a heavy swell it was all a bit nerve-racking, especially as the entrance was fairly shallow. Also our new Imray chart of the area was almost a quarter of a mile out, being based on surveys done well before GPS had been thought of. Once through the gap we identified an inner reef that we needed to follow. Though still fully exposed to the wind, the water was completely sheltered by the reef. We anchored behind a tiny island, and it was a fascinating experience walking along the outer reef with waves crashing on one side and a flat calm on the other. After a day of absolute solitude we followed a tortuous route through the reef to the northern area where the main islands of the group are situated. They are becoming quite a tourist centre for people from mainland Venezuela and we decided to give them a miss. Sailing westwards, where a number of islands lie in fairly clear water, we started a tour that was to last the best part of a week. As a cruising ground, this area would take some beating. Each island has its own individual character and lies within easy reach of the next, and on two or three occasions we had the anchorage and indeed the island to ourselves. Some of the islands had their own interesting entrances through the reefs. Laura adopted a reef-spotting position perched on the lower spreaders from where she had a much clearer view of the shallows. One anchorage in particular, between three tiny islands and an offlying reef, involved following a tortuous route to reach it. A bit stressful at times but the rewards were great. This island of Nonsqui Arriba was one of the anchorages that we had to ourselves and was a magical experience. Laura, snorkelling at dusk, became aware of a large dark shape very close to her and didn't hang about to investigate further, but next morning she came face to face with a large barracuda. We had heard from friends that the island of Cayo Agua was well worth a visit. When the Amerindians occupied the area this island had special significance as it had a freshwater well. Another horseshoe shaped bay, we found great difficulty in locating the passage through the reef. Eventually we anchored off and Helen and I went ashore in the dinghy to take a closer look and get more information from a boat already anchored there. Once in, we had a walk across the island. Next morning the calm anchorage had become a little swelly so we decided to move on 30 miles or so to the next group of islands, Isla de Aves. A fast downwind sail, but on approaching the islands the skies clouded over and there were ominous rumblings in the distance. The cloudy conditions made reef-spotting a bit difficult but we worked our way slowly into one of the easier anchorages. Then the sun emerged for long enough for us to push on further into an anchorage close in to the trees. Living up to the name of ‘The Islands of the Birds' the land adjoining the anchorage was heavily wooded and absolutely alive with birds, particularly boobies, which wheeled about and screeched above our heads and engaged in some very strange behaviour patterns. They seemed to spend most of their time fighting over bits of twig, and when Laura went swimming they seemed fascinated, hovering right over her. Next morning we met an American couple, Bob & Carol, on 'Sasparilla' and did a book swap - a vital part of cruising life. After years of not having enough time to read much, I had rapidly become an avid reader. I got a gem of a story of how Alain Bombard crossed the Atlantic in the 50s in a rubber dinghy to prove that you could live on fish and sea life, getting necessary water from certain parts of the fish. It was now 19th December and some lost fillings needed attention from a dentist before everywhere closed for Christmas. 'Aldebaran' had reached the Dutch island of Curacao and, on the radio, Pat and Olivia told us how nice it was and thought the teeth could be sorted there. So we abandoned the plan of day-hops along the island chain to the western part of Los Aves and the Dutch Island of Bonaire to do an overnighter to Curacao. We upped anchor late

afternoon and, once clear of the reefs, set up our twin rig. We shot out of the shelter of the islands like a cork out of a bottle. Our main concern overnight was whether we would reach Curacao before dawn. Part Twenty Eight - Christmas in Curacao We were closing the coast of Curacao fast just as it began to get light and were homing in for the very narrow and as yet unseen entrance to Spanish Water. A vessel heading straight for us proved to be a large coastguard vessel who called us up on the radio to ask us our intentions. When I told him we were heading for Spanish Water he said we would have to go to the capital Willemstad first to check in. I replied I had been told we could check in at Spanish Water and he told me to stand by while he verified this. To my relief he came back after a few minutes to say we could go into Spanish Water. We carried on towards shore with some trepidation and eventually spotted the inlet and entered very close to rocks on one side and a white sandy beach on the other. We entered a land-locked expanse of water that immediately reminded us of Holland, with the Dutch influence on the island very marked, particularly the style of housing in the capital, Willemstad. Another huge lagoon behind Willemstad is home to a giant oil refinery. The island was the most industrialised of any that we had visited. Less hilly than most of the Caribbean islands, the few hills had been eaten away by extensive quarrying. I reckoned the Dutch felt more at home without hills. Spanish Water was a lovely anchorage with good holding in shallow water. A strong wind blew almost constantly through the anchorage which made trips ashore rather wet. ‘Aldebaran' had moved on the day before to tackle a potentially difficult passage to Cartagena in Columbia, but we met up again with Peter and Angie on 'Dromina' whom we hadn't seen since La Gomera in the Canaries. They came over to brief us with all we needed to know including details of a dental appointment Pat had made for me for the Friday before Christmas. Helen and I took the dinghy ashore to catch the bus into Spanish Water to check in with customs and immigration. The buses were ex-trolley buses, built in the 19th century, and reminded me of Mississippi paddle boats. Arriving in Willemstad was like being transported to Amsterdam, the buildings all very Dutch in style, the only difference being that they were painted in bright Caribbean colours. After we had checked in with a very friendly official at customs we needed to get to Immigration, which was situated on the Crise Ship Lock, by way of the Floating Bridge. Well over 100 years old, this fascinating structure consists of a long series of floats or narrow barges with the roadway built on top, the whole structure pivoting on one bank. At the other end an engine powers the bridge into the bank when ships need to pass through (fairly often). At such times the bridge can be closed to traffic for some time and ferries then come into operation. After dealing with the very friendly Immigration official we had an enjoyable afternoon around the town. We couldn't get over the size of the ships that passed into the Inner Lagoon. The locals were all very friendly but difficult to understand as they speak a strange mixture of Dutch, Spanish and English. We were still contemplating moving on towards Panama and the San Blas Islands before Christmas, but once my teeth had been temporarily sorted out, Helen came down with some sort of bug and we decided to stay. A pig roast planned for Christmas Dinner at our anchorage proved tempting to stay for, and Sarafundy's Bar was a very friendly helpful place where we got various things done, like refilling gas cylinders and procuring some much-needed charts of the San Blas Islands. Christmas Eve was spent having a really good meal on board and playing our CD of Christmas Music. Christmas morning Helen and I went into Willemstad to check-out with Immigration as we had decided to move on on Boxing day. The buses were running a skeleton service but the drivers were in a very festive mood. When we got to town Helen and I made our way across The Floating Bridge just as it started opening so we were actually transported across on it! When we got to Immigration there was no sign of life even though they had assured us that they would be open right over Christmas. We eventually found a security guard who made a phone call on our behalf and assured us that someone would arrive soon. By this time we were worried about missing one of the few buses back to the boat so we made our way to the bus station only to find that the Bridge was again open and we had to wait for a ferry. We got to the bus station in time but I then decided that we really ought to get the checking-out over and done with. Leaving Helen to return with Peter and Angie to 'Muna' at the anchorage, I made my way back to Immigration. The official had turned up and I was able to get my papers stamped. I then had over an hour to wait for the next bus back, so I decided to try and phone my parents. This proved to be harder than I had anticipated. I had phoned a few days earlier at very reasonable cost from a special booth laid on mainly for cruise passengers. Today these were all closed. I tried a couple of phone lines which refused to accept my credit card number. I then tried in vain to find somewhere that sold phonecards. I eventually made the call from a hotel where the very helpful receptionist repeatedly told me it would be very expensive! By this time I was getting close to missing the next bus so I hurried back only to find that the Bridge was again open. The ferry seemed to take forever to go and I charged back to the bus station, arriving just as the bus was about to leave. As I breathlessly climbed aboard, the grinning driver said 'You upstairs sexy’. Not being used to being addressed in such fashion by middle-aged men (or anyone else for that matter) I was a little taken aback to say the least, particularly as the bus was a single decker and therefore had no upstairs. 'Sorry?' I replied rather confused, to which he repeated ‘You upstairs sixty?’ This time my confusion turned to indignation as I realised his true meaning. I was, after all,, only 52 in my socks. This cruising life must be more wearing than I had hitherto thought. 'No,'I responded. 'Ah, ' he nodded knowingly "You downstairs sixty?' "Yes Iam,'I said. 'Then you pay.' he said. It seemed that as it was Christmas Day the over-60s were being given free travel for that day only. Handing him a ten guilder note, I accepted a handful of coins as change. It was only when I had sat down and counted my change that I realised that he had given me 10 guilders 25 cents. By this time I was too exhausted to take it any further. Safely back at the anchorage we went ashore to Sarifundys for the Christmas Day celebrations. The pig roast

proved a great success. Everyone had brought dishes and the resulting meal was superb. A very different Christmas from anything we had experienced before. We made our departure as planned on Boxing Day at about two in the afternoon. Once clear of the entrance we set up the downwind rig and set off to clear the north of Aruba, the third of the Dutch ABC Islands. We had decided to head well offshore for more favourable currents and made really good progress overnight. By next afternoon we had covered 166 nautical miles in the first 24 hours. At times there was a fair bit of swell as we rolled downwind but it was nothing like as bad as we thought it might be. This stretch of water has a bad reputation as the strong trade winds blow straight into this corner of the Caribbean and the heavy seas that result have literally nowhere to go. They tend to be much shorter and steeper than seas out in the Atlantic, and we had heard many disconcerting accounts of yachts being overwhelmed in this area. Our intention was to head straight for the San Blas Islands, but Pat on 'Aldebaran' thought we should stop at Cartegena in Columbia where they now were. Eventually after much discussion we relented and headed along the Columbian coast to Cartegena, and it was quite a relief to take down the downwind rig and put up the main. We had a very pleasant beam reach along a largely unseen coast. We were destined to arrive off Cartagena in the dark and we prepared to anchor off the beach for the night, when Pat and Craig (an American we hadn't yet met) came out in Craig's dinghy to guide us through a very narrow entrance and into the anchorage in the heart of the city. It was a spectacular landfall with the floodlit ramparts of the old city. It was a calm anchorage and very pleasant not to be spending the night rolling off the beach. Part Twenty Nine - New Year in Cartagena Cartagena proved to be an absolutely fascinating city and on our first day there, Pat and Olivia took us on a walking tour of the old town. Bustling with life, people were constantly coming up to us to try and sell things. We wandered round a maze of narrow streets and then walked up on the ramparts of the old city walls. Next day was New Year's Eve. Last year we had spent both Christmas and New Year at sea, but this year we managed to be at anchor for both events having squeezed a 490- mile passage between them. We started off our New Year celebrations with a meal at the small marina that served as a base for the yacht anchorage, and as we went ashore we celebrated GMT New Year. After a very enjoyable meal we made our way into the old town for the celebrations. The centre was transformed from the day before. Very few of the locals were now in evidence, now in their stead, extremely elegant and obviously wealthy Columbians were sitting down to lavish meals in the various restaurants. Armed police were much in evidence. After people-watching for some time we made our way to the ramparts where we had a superb view of the elaborate firework display that started on the stroke of midnight. The large number of visitors in the town were mainly Columbians and everyone we spoke to was very friendly. Later on, wandering round the town, we got pulled in to impromptu street dancing. We eventually made our way back to the anchorage at about 3am while the celebrations carried on all night. All in all it was quite a contrast to our New Year celebrations last year. Whichever one marked the ‘true millennium’, both in their own way were pretty memorable. We spent just over a week in Cartagena and visited the old fort, an impressive structure that had been the focal point of a prolonged assault on the city by the British in 1741. The British under Vernon were so confident of victory that medals had been struck long before the battle took place. The leader of the Spanish forces, Don Blas had lost his left leg, his right eye and his right arm in previous battles but was portrayed on the medals complete as he knelt in surrender. Apparently the British felt that it was ungallant to conquer half aman. Half aman or not, Don Blas held on and eventually the British, having suffered substantial losses and becoming victim to dysentry, malaria and yellow fever, were forced to retreat. In spite of the heavy police presence we always felt safe walking around Cartagena and it was strange seeing security guards with machine guns at the supermarket. On our intended last night in the city a group of us went for another really enjoyable meal and we gave Pat and Olivia a lift back to 'Aldebaran'. We had considered re-anchoring earlier because the nearest boats to us had left that morning and we felt a little exposed on the edge of the anchorage, but had decided it wasn't worth moving for just one night. We went to bed having secured the dinghy close astern with both painters and wire security line. Laura got up at 2am and all was well, and again at 4am to discover the dinghy had gone. COMMODORE'S NOTES I would like to start by hoping that everyone had an enjoyable Christmas and happy New Year. During the break ( for those who did not have to work), about forty five members turned up at the Club on Sunday 30" December to continue the good work started at the earlier working party. Dave Payne managed to provide some crisp and dry although not very warm weather as well as the necessary gear to allow Pete Clayton and the rest of the wrecking squad to scrap the remaining trailers. In the meantime Dave Steward organised a very successful party in the depths of the hedge at the top of the Cat field. We all owe a tremendous vote of thanks to those who worked so hard at both working parties to clear the scrap and cut back the hedge. Following the Annual General Meeting, the committee has many new faces at all levels and it will take a couple of meetings for us to find our feet. I would like to thank Jenny Ball for her succinct description of the role of Rear Commodore in the last edition of Navigans. The Club needs to see this position filled by the end of February to ensure that the Executive and Sailing Sub Committee can function effectively. Please do not rely on Dave Williams to fulfil the role of Sailing Secretary and by default that of Rear Commodore; give him your support by stepping forward to fill the vacant position of Rear Commodore. The Committee has given its approval for safety recommendations to be implemented on the Travel Hoist involving the fitting of platforms to allow the adjustment of the lifting blocks. This follows an assessment of the dangers of using the ladder to move them, and one or two near but not dangerous situations during the last year. As with all operations in the Club we continue to learn from experience and thereby reduce the potential danger to members. I am pleased to say that Jenny Ball and her team are continuing to drive forward the project to identify a replacement for the RIB. Quite nghtly she is not only identifying the initial boat and engine to be purchased but also the ancillary equipment, as well as the best method of maintaining it. Whilst it is hoped that this exercise can be completed in time for the start of the season there will still be a number of hurdles to cross; obtaining the approval of MASC for the capital spend, negotiating any maintenance contracts, and finally obtaining and commissioning the boat. This will represent a large investment of members' money and it is essential that we get it right, even if this causes some delay in its entering service. I would like to thank Dave Payne for assisting Jenny with this task in the absence of a Rear Commodore. In addition to the RIB replacement we are also considering the provision of the veranda. This is another of the Five Year Plan items. I know that many members have given considerable thought to a number of schemes for this. The first task is to establish the different possibilities along with an estimated cost for each. Bernard Rogers Tel [redacted] [redacted] has agreed to co-ordinate this activity. Please do not assume that your ideas have reached him: contact him direct to give your input because if you do not, it will not be included in the schemes being considered. Also do not be surprised if he asks you to help providing initial outline plans and costs. We are also examining ways to replace Darren the caretaker who left last year. As usual with such an unsung person, it was not apparent until he left how much he did around the site in addition to the grass cutting. The last major item which will be occupying the Committee during the early part of the year is the state of the electrical supply to the Clubhouse, within it and around the site. Increasingly it is necessary for the Club to hold certificates of compliance and this is one such area. In order to obtain this we may need to spend a couple of hundred pounds or we may need to spend a number of thousands. B r & Duties 2002 é Long discussions have been held in connection with support boat duties for the coming season (2002). The club has always provided, for many years, 2 main support boats - the "Jack B" and the Rib, with the Orkney as a standby for the OOD/Race Officer. The club can only provide this level of support with the help of "volunteers" to man both boats. On each race day we need 5 people - 3 for "Jack B" and 2 for the Rib; and with 42 races to cover (excluding the Wednesday evening series of 12 races for which we have 2 people who have volunteered to cover all these) it can be seen that for each person to do only 1 rescue boat duty we need 210 people. Currently, using the 2001 list, we have only 109 who have said that they will do the support boat duties. There is also extreme concern that at this stage the majority of the cover is being provided by 2 fleets. One that is not normally active in racing, namely the cruiser fleet covering 38%, the dinghy fleet covering, 38% and the Cat fleet 24%. This needs to be addressed. If people wish to race and have the level of cover that needs to be in place, then they must be prepared to assist in support boat cover. The sailing sub committee has agreed that the target for the season 2003 is for each person to do one support boat duty a year, but for this to happen then we need to double the number of people who are willing to take part. For the coming season it is the sailing sub committee's aim to ensure that people will do no more than two duties during the year. Those that have been nominated as "Jack B" helms that have received no formal training in the operation of the Jack B will be invited to attend a training session early in the season. The following changes have been agreed: 1. The duty boat rota will be published prior to the start of the 2002 racing season in Navigans. 2. People will then have 4 weeks from the date of publication to request changes. 3. The final list will then be posted on the Race Notice Board with a copy to all fleet captains and a copy in the race box. 4. If for some unexpected reason the nominated person is unable to do their support boat duty, it will be up to them to arrange a swap and inform the duty co-ordinator, advising him of the changes. 5. If the nominated person for that day's duty fails to attend, then racing is to be cancelled through lack of support boat cover. If Jack B crew fails to attend, then monohull racing will be cancelled and if the Rib crew fails to attend, then cat racing will, likewise, be cancelled. As the sun sets on yet another year I find myself with a new role to play. Fleet Captain no less, quite an honour. I'd like to thank you for this chance to serve! and sincerely hope I can follow the good work all previous incumbents have put in and help reinforce the excellent reputation our section of the club is currently enjoying and of the club as a whole of course. I'm not sure exactly what has led to the new emergence of the Solo section as such a force to be reckoned with in recent times but over the last few years since I've been a member at Marconi there has been a gradual increase in Solo pilots joining and our numbers have increased significantly. (must be down to me then!) The attraction for me is close racing, which you can only get in a true class racing situation. (not as close as I'd like most of the time but I still live in hope) In addition we have excellent sailors amongst us who have competed and still do compete nationally (even internationally if you count the Scottish open!) with considerable success. Despite this all these people are approachable and friendly towards new members or less experienced sailors as I found out after joining from another club a few years ago. Another important aspect I think is of course the club racing. Marconi people work very hard to organise a fantastic racing programme throughout the year and although I find it hard to find time, when I do have time there is invariably an opportunity to race whereas before there was invariably no water in the creek! The boat itself must play a large part as it has been a perennial favourite since introduction back in the fifties. Interest waxes and wanes but people keep coming back to the Solo because it has great qualities of robustness, important when rounding ‘Marconi’, remaining competitive even after many years of abuse, there are a lot of them around with a selection of boats to suit all pockets, they can be adapted to suit different helm weights by choice of mast etc. and they sail nicely, looking good on the water. This could turn into a book if I'm not careful so I'll stop there! Lastly I'd like to sound a note of encouragement to anyone uncertain about joining the racing on Sunday or in the summer Wednesday evenings in their Solo. Please have a go! I know everyone says the same things but it's true, there is nothing to lose, no one will shout at you (much) and although it can seem a bit daunting when studying the rules it really is best just to have a go. In the end the importance of winning or losing is up to you, at best you will have a great sailing experience heightened by that element of competition which adds a new dimension and at worst you will have had a great sailing experience - so 'Go For It'

The cut painters and security line were just hanging from the stern with the metal towing eye still attached to the security line which had been cut off at the dinghy. We contacted the Harbour Authority on the VHF who promptly sent a coastguard boat to us to take details and conduct a search. In the morning Laura and I went to the police station to report the incident. There was very little else we could do so we decided we would move on the next day. Panama would probably be a better place to replace the dinghy and we still had our old Even on board, as well as our folding seahopper. It was all very annoying as the dinghy and outboard were less than a year old. We kicked ourselves for not lifting the dinghy every night as a lot of people did. A sad aspect of the affair was that we had gained such a positive feel for Cartagena and now this went against that. We tried to be philosophical about it, after all, nobody had been hurt. The next day, with an unusually clear foredeck, we made our way in company with 'Aldebaran' along the main channel that leads for some 7 miles behind the islands and out of Cartagena. Once out to sea the wind got up sufficiently for us to have a gentle sail across to the Rosario Islands that we had decided to use as a stepping off point for the San Blas Islands. We had very limited information on the Rosarios, only Pat had an electronic chart with very little detail. We had been given a waypoint for a reasonable anchorage and we homed in on this. The entrance to the anchorage througha reef proved to be quite straightforward, but the anchorage proved to be much shallower than we thought it would be, and the area of water deep enough for us to anchor was quite limited. Eventually we managed to anchor close to the reef and went for a very welcome swim. Next morning we crept out of the anchorage at first light hoping to cover the 200 miles to San Blas in two days and, unusually, we were met by a flat calm. 'Aldebaran' then discovered she had an oil leak and we passed over some spare oil and an oil filter. They carried on, keeping the engine revs down, and as the leak did not get any worse they decided to keep going. For the rest of the morning we motored on keeping our revs as low as possible. Ever since we had a new prop fitted during the refit at Tollesbury, our engine had been much more efficient, giving us 3'/2-4 knots at just 1000 revs. Eventually in the afternoon the wind finally arrived and we were able to sail, albeit slowly at first.

After that the sailing was good, though by this time we had reconciled ourselves to two nights, rather than one, at sea. The wind stayed fresh so by the second day we had an ETA of around midnight. Pat in 'Aldebaran' was pressing on as fast as he could in an attempt to get into the islands before dark. When it became clear that he wouldn't make it, Craig on 'Sangarris' offered to pilot Pat in to the islands, which he eventually did. After studying the chart and pilot book for some time I decided that if we went on and entered the island chain by the next pass several miles further on, our arrival would probably coincide with dawn. Overnight the wind increased and backed so we were now some 40 degrees off the wind. Our speed of around 6 knots was being knocked back by an adverse current so that our speed over the ground was barely 4'/, knots. As we closed our waypoint just off the entrance between the reefs it was still dark and I considered turning back, however it started getting light just in the nick of time and we sailed through the pass, having extended our passage to some 243 miles. Part Thirty - The San Blas Islands There are more than 360 islands (one for every day of the year) in San Blas, situated on the shallow continental shelf that skirts the Panamanian coast. Most are very small and very low, protected by their reefs and larger offlying reefs. Many are uninhabited, some have just a few inhabitants, while others are populated to the point where there is literally not an inch of space. We made our landfall at a group of islands known as the Hollandes Cays, anchoring in a sheltered lagoon next to the tiny island of Tiadup and joining 'Aldebaran’, 'Sangaras', 'Zephyrus' and 'Cap d'Or'. Tiadup is occupied by one or two Kuna families led by the local chief Snr Robinson. Kuna Indians are indigenous to these islands and have very strong traditions and lifestyle that they are very keen to preserve. Their main mode of transport are their dugout canoes which they sail and paddle with consummate skill, in marked contrast to other parts of the Caribbean where the locals now put their faith in the ubiquitous Yamaha. We did see some dugouts in San Blas with their ends sawn off and replaced with transoms to take an outboard, but these were still very much in the minority. We landed with some trepidation on Tiadup, such a small island that we felt we were arriving in someone's back garden, which in effect we were. Snr Robinson couldn't have made us feel more welcome, and spoke very good English which helped enormously. Even Spanish isn't universally spoken here. He told us all about the islands, all the visitors they had there, and showed us a scrap book of drawings, photos, etc. given to him by visitors. Pat had taken some balloons ashore which went down very well with the children. The women on the islands spend much of their time making molas, traditional and intricate examples of reverse applique. Incredibly labour intensive to make, but they have proved to be a profitable source of income. Mola selling can be quite an intensive exercise, with mola sellers touring an anchorage in their dugout canoes, and some of the older women have become masters of the hard sell. However we never felt intimidated by these approaches. The Kuna Indians are incredibly friendly. We tried to buy coconuts on Tiadup, but Snr Robinson preferred to barter for foodstuffs that they could not readily get hold of. This suited us fine and we acquired several coconuts and bunches of plantain in return for flour and rice. Just off the island, straddling the reef, was the remains of a Hallberg Rassey 42 that had attempted to enter the pass the previous year at night, using GPS. Now that GPS is almost totally accurate, the inaccuracies of the charts we are using have become painfully obvious. I had read about this particular incident soon after we arrived in the Caribbean without really being aware of where the San Blas Islands were. The owners of the boat were an experienced couple, having already completed a circumnavigation. In the year since the boat landed on the reef, tearing the hull open, it had been stripped clean. Rather sadly, I thought, part of the foredeck, complete with teak covering, had been cut away and was in use as a picnic table at a nearby uninhabited island popular with yachties as a venue for barbecues. We stayed almost a week in this superb, wind-blown anchorage. The water was crystal clear and the most beautiful colour. The islands were classic ‘desert islands' crammed with palm trees and the deserted islands proved to be the perfect venue for group Happy Hours at the end of a long hot day. A short sail across to Green Island, an even more sheltered anchorage where there was a freshwater well and we were able to enjoy the luxury of freshwater showers with as much water as you wanted. Another short passage to Ria Diablo where the anchorage was formed by two islands just off the mouth of the river. They are inter-connected by means of a bridge and, unlike the islands we had seen up to then, were completely built up, with houses built out over the water, a convenient place to site the toilet, we discovered. We walked the island and were astounded at the friendliness of everyone we met, Everyone wanted to talk to us but nobody asked for anything from us. The next day we went on a trip up the river Diablo in Pat's dinghy in company with the crews of 'Aldebaran' and 'Zephyrus'. (We hadn't yet been able to replace our stolen Caribe.) After we had negotiated the rather tricky entrance we followed the river deep into the rich vegetation. Locals in their dugout canoes were paddling their way upriver to collect fresh river water or to do their washing. We followed to where they collected water and found a wonderful place to swim, where you could walk over a sandbank and, getting into deep water, be swept at high speed by the strong current round a bend in the river. On the way back downstream we stopped at a cemetery sited in a small clearing in the jungle. Quite elaborately built-up tombs had been constructed and most had food neatly laid on them to ensure that the dead did not go hungry. We had a pleasant but slightly worrying sail across to the beautiful island of Cangombia, in water littered with hidden reefs, and with the help of inaccurate charts. Sailing in company with 'Aldebaran' we were all confused by trying to identify ‘lighthouse rock' that we eventually concluded must have all but disappeared. Meanwhile we had wrongly identified another small island as ‘lighthouse rock' a situation that came close to putting us ona reef. In Cangombia was just a small group of inhabitants, including the almost inevitable mola makers, one of whom was clearly a transvestite, not uncommon among the Kuna Indians. We were told that sometimes boys are deliberately brought up as girls to add to the ranks of mola makers.

Our next anchorage was a mainland one at Gaiga, situated near to the tiny island of Mormake Tupu, another island that has literally wall to wall housing. Well laid out, incredibly clean and tidy, there is not an inch of wasted space, with alleyways barely wide enough for two people to pass. We had no sooner anchored than a fleet of dugout canoes arrived from the village, and we and 'Aldebaran' followed Pam and Roger on 'Cap d'Or's' example by making arrangements to take a trip in a dugout canoe up the Rio Esadi. Early the next morning two dugout sailing canoes duly arrived alongside. The canoes have a simple spritsail rig vaguely reminiscent of a Thames Barge in miniature. I was later to read that the spritsil rig had been developed in the past from European rigs that the Kunas saw on visiting ships. It is extremely well adapted to the dugout canoes and we had a superb sail into the river. Once inside the river mouth and sheltered from the wind, the crew, an extremely able lad who can have been no more than 8 or 9, took the rig down, including the mast, and proceeded to paddle vigorously upstream. Leaving the canoes, we had an intriguing walk through the woodland, seeing monkeys on the way. We met a chief from one of the islands collecting 'medicine' from the bark of a certain tree. We also saw areas where Kunas were harvesting various crops. The return trip was a hard paddle out of the river into the prevailing wind, and this time we all joined in with the paddling. The helmsman carefully steered the canoe into the lee of some mangroves where the lad put up the mast. The stay for the mast was one line which he held in his hand. We were then treated to a rare display of seamanship as the canoe, keel-less, was tacked up towards the island. It was a thrilling sail in a brisk wind. Landing on the island there was barely room to stand as Idelfonso, who had organised the trip, ushered us into his family's communal hut where his brother, a Master Mola Maker was hard at work. They had both visited us on Mona the day before and Helen had bought yet more molas. We couldn't believe how happy everybody seemed to be in such cramped surroundings, and we still can't work out how they kept themselves and their surroundings so clean when all fresh water had to be brought from the mainland by dugout canoe. From Gaiga we had a brisk sail across to Punta Playita, a mainland inlet where crocodiles had reputedly been seen. Anchoring in this completely sheltered bay, alongside 'Aldebaran' and 'Cap d'Or’, we had been there barely an hour before Laura spotted what she at first took to be a log until she realised it was going into the current. We watched as it made its way across the entrance to the inlet and then disappeared into the mangroves. At least an hour went by before it reappeared with a large pelican firmly clamped in its jaws and made its way past us to a corner of the bay where it obviously had its lair. Not surprisingly after this, our swims were fairly brief affairs. Our next trip was a rare beat into the strong prevailing wind to get up to Chichime Cays, a picturesque anchorage behind a reef straddling two small islands. This was another lovely setting for a get-together on the beach. It was now time to leave the San Blas, and the next day we tackled the 45 mile passage along the coast to Isla Linton. This passage involved keeping well inshore, well inside some nasty reefs to avoid an offshore counter-current. We were poodling along at about 3 or so knots ina 10 knot beam breeze when 'Cap d'Or steamed past us with his mizzen staysail set. Once clear of us they set about hoisting their cruising chute. Thus shamed, we decided that it was about time that we started using our chute, which hadn't seen the light of day this side of the Atlantic. Once it was up the whole boat was transformed. Soon we were making a healthy 5'/> knots and enjoying ourselves. When we reached the headland we had to decide between rounding it with contrary currents or ducking inside the inner passage that turned the headland into the island of Isla Grande. We elected for the inner passage but were soon to question our decision as we were faced with towering cliffs, submerged rocks and a swirling maelstrom of eddies. Once through, we anchored in the calm of Isla Linton. The next day, after a lumpy start, we had a pleasant run down the coast to Portobelo which is set in a wide, deep bay that makes a superb natural anchorage. It is a fascinating place with an intriguing past. In the 16th century, Portobelo was a major trading centre with warehouses so full of treasure that silver ingots could be pick up in the streets, Not surprisingly the place got the attention of pirates like Henry Morgan and semi-legitimised adventurers like Francis Drake who, on his final visit to Portobelo, contracted yellow fever and was buried at sea, four miles offshore. The major buildings from this time have survived intact as have the forts that guarded the bay. The ones on the north bank of the estuary have been rescued from the vegetation that once engulfed them, cleared and maintained. Artefacts like the numerous cannon that have survived have been restored to their proper positions, if they were ever moved, but otherwise there has been no restoration or prettyfying that often spoils historic sites. We had an energetic walk up a steep hill to the highest fort that looked just like a toy fort, from where we had a wonderful view over the entire bay. During our brief stay in Portobelo we witnessed our first live baseball match and we visited the church of the Black Christ. The origins of this tradition are in some doubt. One version is that the beautifully carved statue (made from very dark wood) was washed up on the beach in a packing case and considered by the locals to be a present from God. Another version was that two statues had been commissioned, one by the people of Portobelo and one by the island of Taboga in the Pacific, and the two shipments had been muddled up in transit. When the people of Portobelo saw the Black Christ, they were so taken with it they refused to exchange it. Either way the Black Christ has become the focal point of a major annual festival, with elaborate costumes made each year for the statue which is then carried through the streets. Costumes from past years are displayed in the museum. Devoted followers make the pilgrimage on foot to the church, many dressed in similar robes to that worn by the Black Christ. From Portobelo we made the short day-sail to Colon at the entrance to the Panama Canal. Sailing again in company with ‘Aldebaran', Pat & I had similar thoughts about the significance of this stage of the voyage. We were about to leave the Atlantic. to be continued Malcolm Shaft

COMMODORE’S NOTES You will have seen in the last edition of Navigans that the Club has a new editor, Bob Collins. In a strange way this, along with the distribution team, is one of the most important roles in the Club. Without Navigans we would find it very hard to communicate to all the membership and for people to express their views. In order to ensure its smooth running could I ask everyone to ensure that their copy is with Bob by the published deadline, generally the FIRST WEDNESDAY of each MONTH. In the past there has been a natural distinction between a dinghy (generally considered upto Wayfarer size and capable of hand launch/recovery) and cruisers (anything over 18ft), which have launched and lived on moorings. In recent years with the growing popularity of "Trailer Sailers" this has become blurred. We have therefore asked the safety Committee to look at the associated problems and make recommendations to minimise the attendant risks. Our Bar Management, Mike Smith and Malcolm Yeoman, are continuing to examine new ways of stocking and running the Bar. Kate Williams EAST COAST PIERS RACE 2002 — supporting Cirdan Trust Most readers will be aware that ECPR 2001 raised over £7000 for the Cirdan Trust sailing charity and that over the years the event has raised in excess of £70000 for Cirdan and other worthwhile sailing- related causes. We continue to support Cirdan with the 2002 Race meeting, to be held over the weekend of 29/30" June. Sponsorship has always played a big part in creating the funds that we pass over to the charity of our choice. All of the profits from ECPR go to the charity. Corporate sponsors provide the financial underwriting to allow us to make advance spending commitments as we plan the event and the more of them there are — and the more generous they are — the greater the likely excess. Corporate sponsors come and go - helping as and when they are able. We are fortunate to have a core of supporting companies, which help year after year. Ernst and Young have been an important supporter over the last few years and we have been tremendously grateful to them. However, we always knew that such support was only available for a limited period and that period has now come to an end. New Corporate Sponsors We are always looking for new sponsors for ECPR and would ask members to support us in our search. Such sponsorship can take a number of forms, ranging from an anonymous donation, through advertising in the ECPR Programme right up to a corporate hospitality event on the site and on the barges on Race Day. Another approach might be the free provision of essential supplies. Sponsors can benefit from local and national media coverage, advertising in our programme and on our website and direct exposure to a discerning band of competitors and their supporters. If you know of a company or individual who may wish to support a worthwhile charity and/or obtain publicity through association with our event please let me know. Personal Sponsorship — competitors There is huge potential for financial support for the Charity through personal sponsorship of competitors. Last year one MSC member raised in excess of £800 from relatives, workmates and friends — and yet he was almost alone on this activity. If each of, say, 80 competitors raised just a quarter of the amount above we would break all records for our fund-raising in 2002. Sponsorship forms will be available in Navigans and on the web site and will be posted to non- MSC members on our ECPR database. There will be a reduced entry fee for competitors with minimum £100 sponsorship. Competitors — start planning your sponsorship campaign now! If you are too shy why not appoint a campaign manager? I would welcome any ideas and offers of help and look forward hearing from you.... Chris Davies [redacted] [redacted]

Bob Collins Mona's Travels (Edited slightly) Part Thirty One - The Panama Canal in February 2001 Approaching Panama, the first thing you notice are the number of ships anchored offshore. We sailed through the newer of the two entrances through the outer wall. Once inside, we made our way through the small ship anchorage, round the Cruise Liner Dock to the Flats, the designated anchorage for yachts. Anchoring in this wind- blown, exposed and, as it turned out, rather dirty area, our first impression was actually that the whole place wasn't as bad we thought it would be. After anchoring we were preparing to go ashore (Pat had been doing sterling service these past weeks as our official ferryman since our dinghy had been stolen) when we were approached by Peter from 'La Boatique'. He was trying to upgrade his Caribe RIB for a larger model, had a provisional order in with the local Caribe dealer but wasn't going ahead with it unless he sold the old one. In the intervening weeks since our dinghy had been stolen we had given considerable thought to its replacement. The problem in a way was that we had been very pleased with our stolen dinghy and wouldn't willingly have exchanged it. However being forced into that position it was sensible to see if it could be improved upon. A Caribe 2.5 metre with a folding fibreglass floor, it had proved to be extremely dry and stable and an extremely good

10 load carrier. it also fitted fully inflated on the foredeck with its sponsons straddling the mast (something our old Even had been unable to do). Its main drawback was that it was very heavy for its size, something we noticed particularly when trying to pull it up a beach. The options were to replace it for a similar type; go for a full inflatable with inflatable floor; or opt for a small RIB. We were tempted by a full inflatable for is lower weight and stowability. This would mean an Even or Zodiac, which though very well built and much improved on earlier models, still have smaller tubes and tend to be wetter than the equivalent Caribe. A small RIB was a serious contender as they are very robust for pulling up beaches etc, but the main drawback was that it would always have to be carried as deck cargo. Peter's dinghy was therefore a tempting proposition. We hadn't really expected to find a secondhand dinghy that would fulfil our needs but having paid out for a new dinghy less than a year before, the chance to get a secondhand one only a year old itself was a welcome one. Next day Peter loaned us the dinghy to try it out on deck and it fitted perfectly and was almost exactly the same weight as the old one. We struck a deal that night. The Caribe dealer had a 2 year old Yamaha outboard for sale and within 3 days of arriving in Colon we had become the owners of a Caribe RIB with a Yamaha 8 outboard. Before we left England the prospect of owning such a combination would have struck me as bordering on the ridiculous, but living on board full time, it's amazing how much of a workhorse the dinghy becomes. In many places the best anchorages are some distance from convenient landing places and a dinghy that will take you considerable distances with reasonable ease is a major asset. When you rarely visit marinas you have to transport a considerable amount of stuff by dinghy. One thing we did right away with the new dinghy was to devise a convenient way of hoisting it out of the water at night. Once sorted, it became a daily routine a bit like putting the car away in the garage. This anchorage was a good example of being a good dinghy ride from the dock. Going ashore meant crossing the harbour to the Panama Yacht Club, situated in part of the old French canal workings. A friendly establishment that served large pitchers of beer for $3 and excellent food at reasonable cost, it was the hub of yachtie life. Taxi drivers were on hand to help out with what could be a very tedious checking-in process. Everything we had previously read or heard about Colon had led us to believe that it was one of the most dangerous cities in the world and that under no account should you venture out of the yacht club on foot. Like any big city you need to be careful and there are areas where it's better not to go but in general we found everyone to be extremely friendly and helpful. In fact when I went out to get petrol and managed to get lost, I ended up walking down one of the poorer streets. Seeing my petrol can everyone kept pointing unasked in the direction of the garage. The supermarkets were quite an experience with their guards armed with sub-machine guns. I couldn't help wondering what that would do for discouraging shopliftingin England. Panama Canal. Not surprisingly the most popular topic of conversation at the Yacht Club was the transit itself. For what is basically a fairly straightforward setup of 3 up-locks, a 31 mile man-made lake in the middle, and 3 down-locks at the other end, an awful lot of myth and mystique has grown up about it. I had recently read the both tragic and fascinating story of the building of the canal. The loss of life incurred during the building almost defies belief. An American yachtie who had recently gone through the canal as a line handler took it upon herself to give a briefing on the transit. One of the stipulations of the canal company is that each boat must have at least four line handlers, apart from the skipper. This means either hiring local handlers or recruiting fellow yachties to help, which is what generally happens. Apart from anything else it is very helpful to experience a transit on someone else's boat before you take your own boat through. In the course of her briefing she wanted to emphasise her point that you needed to be strong to be a line handler. For some reason she decided to address her remarks to Laura who was standing quietly at the side of the room "For example, I wouldn't count on you being a line handler" she declared, jabbing her finger in Laura's direction. I think she must have been taken aback by the obvious reaction of people in the room who knew Laura. As Laura will testify I am not renowned for leaping to her defence, but on this occasion I found myself responding that she'd picked the wrong one there. In the event Laura went on to do no fewer than five transits including our own within a two-week period and, not surprisingly, was much sought after as a line handler. There are basically three ways in which a yacht can pass through the locks, These are: 1) alongside a wall; 2) centre lock, either alone , in pairs or a raft of three - either way, lines are taken to both sides of the lock; or 3) rafted alongside a tug. Each method has its advantages and disadvantages. When you are measured for the transit you have the chance to state your preference, but in the event it doesn't seem to make much difference what you say. Pat and I had elected to transit together as we would at least know the other boat we were in the lock with. The admeasurer who came out to the Flats to measure the boats turned out to be a delightful Panamanian girl called Jaz who made what could have been and extremely longwinded process much more palatable by acknowledging that most of the paperwork was a formality and emphasising the important bits. The charge for transiting the canal was US $500 for yachts up to 50' and US $750 over that size. People with boatsin the mid to upper 40s were

1] carefully removing any overhanging bits. I didn't need to worry and Mona actually came out as 38', not bad for a 33 footer. In addition you are required to pay an $800 deposit which is returnable in full if you transit the canal without incident. A problem in the past has been that this deposit has had to be paid in cash, but is returned by cheque to your home address several months later. Fortunately they had recently changed the rule to allow VISA instead of cash. No other credit card was allowed. As part of the paperwork you sign a declaration to the effect that if any canal property is damaged in the course of your transit, it is your responsibility. If your property is damaged, it is also your fault no matter what the cause. Every yacht that transits has to have an advisor on board, generally tug boat Captains training to be Canal Pilots. As skipper you are responsible for the safety of your vessel, but must listen to advice given to you by the advisor. If you ignore this advice and there is a problem it is your fault. However if you take the advice and there is a problem, it is still your fault. Having paid our dues at the bank we contacted the Canal Office for a transit date. We were offered the following Friday. By this time Helen and I had both transited on different boats and found the experience both useful and enjoyable. Mine had been a one-day transit while Helen's had taken two. Getting through in a day was down to making an early start from Colon over which you had no control; the type of ships that were going through on that day; and the advisor you were allocated. Going up the locks, yachts went behind the ships; coming down, they went in front. there were only certain categories of ships that yachts could lock through with. Obviously, really large ships, or Panamax as they are known, need the whole lock, and ships with flammable cargo have to lock through alone. Advisors varied in how much effort they made to get you through quickly. By this time Laura was getting to know the advisors quite well. One in particular, Jimmy, took special delight in getting as many of his yachts through in one day as he could. Another advisor, popularly known as 'Sleepy Tony' brought his pillow on board and literally slept through the locks. One bonus of doing a two day transit was that you anchored overnight at Gamboa at the end of the lake in an anchorage reputedly frequented by crocodiles. However, you than had the problem of accommodating your line handlers for the night. Even bigger boats, if well stocked for the Pacific, could find this a problem. Helen and Laura had both taken two days going through with Joy and Richard on 'Fair Hippolyta' and had had a great time. Having been set to transit 'Muna' on Friday I decided I couldn't spare the time to transit on 'Windsong' on Wednesday as I had planned to do. Laura decided that she would still go on 'Windsong' and luckily Jim was able to find someone to replace me. Their transit turned out to be an interesting one. 'Windsong' is a British 28 footer and they were scheduled to transit with 'Sangaras' an Amel Santori 46, and 'Cap D'Or a Roberts 44. Both were boats that we had been meeting up with for somt time. There was much speculation as to how they would go through. In the event the advisor, Jimmy, chose to go on 'windsong'. They didn't start until just before 8am but Jimmy pushed things on all the way. The three boats went through in separate lockings, each rafted to a tug and Jimmy got "Windsong' into the first locking. Once up on the lake he urged Jim on 'Windsong' to push the 9hp diesel for all it would give and somehow or other they got right through the canal in a day, while the potentially much faster ‘Sangoris' and 'Cap D'Or' anchored overnight in the lake. It was a bonus for us as it meant Laura came back from Panama on the bus with a day in hand before our transit, complete with long lines that we were borrowing from ‘Fair Hippolyta' and which "Windsong' had also used. While Laura was away Helen and I had been trying to ensure that we would have enough line handlers for our transit. We were lucky to get the services of a young Swedish couple form 'Manana’, a Hallberg Rassey 31. Adrian from 'Steadfast' also agreed to come, and his wife Gabby and their two sons were transiting on 'Aldebaran' along with Tony and Martin from 'Diva' who had just arrived in Colon. It was the first time we had met up with Tony and Martin, although I'd remembered 'Diva' from Heybridge Basin, and Martin was in fact a Maldon man. Tony co-owned a small but successful company and had a mutually beneficial arrangement whereby he and his partner each managed the company for 6 months at a time. They had started the latest part of their trip in Trinidad and were on a pretty tight schedule to get to New Zealand by July. We were scheduled to start our transit at around 8am on Friday 16th February. In the event the advisors didn't arrive until 9.20am. Our advisor jumped over from the pilot launch complete with an enormous bag of ice. He informed us almost straight away that we would be taking two days over the transit which at least took some of the pressure off. After motoring up to Gatun Locks we rafted up alongside 'Aldebaran' outside the lock and hovered about until the ship that we were locking through with had passed us and entered the lock. We followed him in and secured alongside a tug that was against the wall. There was considerable turbulence as the lock filled. Being alongside a tug we didn't have to worry about adjusting shore lines. When the ship started to move into the next lock the prop wash was unbelievable. Our advisor radioed through and after that the ship kept its propwash to a minimum. When the ship was secured in the next lock, 'Aldebaran' cast off from the tug and, still rafted together, we hovered while the tug moved on into the lock and we were able to tie up against him again. In this fashion we got through the three locks. Once clear of the lock we unrafted and headed out across Gatun Lake. This lake is man made, flooded by diverting the waters of the River Chagres which service the locks at both ends of the canal

12 without any need for artificial pumping. Before actually seeing it I had never realised how picturesque the whole area was. In addition to the main channel there are smaller cuts that yachts can take and passing through a narrow section of Banana Cut we saw several monkeys in the trees staring down at us. In spite of the fact tat there was no chance of us getting through in a day, our advisor wanted us to proceed as fast as possible to the anchorage 23 miles across the lake. With our genny set, I had the engine on as high revs as I dared go, with the stern sinking alarmingly in the freshwater. Already heavily loaded with four extra bodies in the cockpit, the cockpit sole was awash. When we reached the anchorage at Gamboa the advisor went off on the launch and we rafted alongside 'Aldebaran'. We went for a very welcome swim. Adrian and his family and Martin and Tony went off in Pat's dinghy to explore the resort hidden away round the comer. We had a very pleasant lazy afternoon. I had picked up some sort of bug in Colon as a lot of people seemed to do and had developed an annoying cough and sore throat. Much fortified by a medicinal couple of hot Jamesons and lemon I went on to enjoy the rest of a very sociable day with a superb evening meal and wine. Just before it got dark a large crocodile glided by across our sterns. We had been told our advisors would return at about 9 the next morning but as time went by there was no sign of them and no-one was answering our calls on the VHF. then at about midday we saw 'Peace' and ‘Aloha’, a large American yacht, come steaming around the corner. As they had left Colon that morning, Pat and I were getting a bit agitated to say the least. Fortunately our advisors arrived soon after and we got underway. Our advisor, Alex, was very friendly and helpful and explained a lot about the working of the canal. Soon after leaving the anchorage Alex told me to throttle back. A large crocodile was making its way right across the canal. We made our way through the Culebra or Gaillard Cut, that part of the canal that had given the most difficulty during the construction. The hills on either side were very unstable and as they were cut back, landslides occurred. many times during the construction the work site complete with railway lines and machinery had been completely obliterated by fresh slides. When we arrived at Pedro Miguel Lock we tied up at the pilot station. 'Aldebaran' was already tied up alongside ‘Peace’ and ‘Aloha’, and it transpired that they were going through the next locks together and we would be going with 'Zephyrus' who was just a little way back and had olso left Colon that morning. Once rafted up we make our way to the lock where we tied up alongside a low wall just outside the lock to allow the tug to bring the ship into the finger extending from the lock. Once secured, the ship's lines were taken by the 'mules', electric engines that act as moving bollards. The tug then passed us and secured at the head of the lock where to moved to lie alongside. Coming out of the Pedro Miguel Lock we stayed rafted up with 'Zephyrus' to cross the 1'/, mile long lake to reach the Miraflores Lock. By this time we had a following wind of 20-25 knots. This time we were going into the left- hand of the two locks and it was the turn of 'Zephyrus' to tie up alongside the low wall. Just as we were entering the lock their advisor told us to turn as water was breaking over the wall. Turning into the wind it was surprisingly rough and water was breaking over our decks. We then had to wait while the ship secured to the finger with a tug pushing him in. We then had to make our way round the ship and the tug, with the propwash from the tug adding interest to the proceedings. We had to squeeze the two boats through a narrow gap between the ship and the side of the lock with the wind up our tails doing its best to throw us off course. Luckily 'Muna' and 'Zephyrus' proved to be well-matched and made a stable raft. It was all a bit hairy and we then had to tie up to a higher wall on our side of the lock. Fortunately our line handlers were doing a superb job and everything went well. It was now the turn of 'Zephyrus' to tie up against the tug. I was a bit nervous about the next move into the last of the two Miraflores Locks. When I had previously come through as line handler we had hovered while the tug changed locks and we had been caught by the strong current that can run at up to 5 knots, and the boat had been slammed into the lock side but fortunately was well protected by its tyres that most boats equip themselves with for the transit. This time on 'Muna' we reversed off and held steady while the tug moved into the last lock and we could come alongside again. All went well except that, as we came alongside the tug, one of the line handlers on 'Zephyrus' threw the line too early and it fell short. Fortunately we were able to reverse into the current while the line was secured. At this point Harold the skipper of 'Zephyrus' beckoned to me and leant confidentially across his guardrail. "Malcolm," he said in his thick Texan drawl, "Before I go to bed tonight, I'm going to kiss my Perkins". I knew how he felt. We had been placing complete reliance on our engines and any problem could not only have meant a disaster in the lock but also instant loss of your deposit if any delay in your passage resulted. Then the last gates were opening and we were coming into the Pacific. Passing under the impressive Bridge of the Americas we said grateful thanks to our advisor and made our way to pick up a buoy at the Balboa Yacht Club. Malcolm Shaft to be continued
