COMMODORES NOTES The two Daves, Payne and Steward, are continuing to tackle a number of items around the Clubhouse including : repairs to the fascia board, obtaining quotes to replace the fire doors in the lounge, fixing the leaking water overflow pipe, amongst others. The sub committee looking at the replacement of the electrical supply continues to make progress and has received an input from Roger Camp regarding the requirements in the Cruiser Park. They have also considered the need for outlets on the exterior of the Clubhouse, amongst other items. Work is continuing to reclaim the area between the Cruiser Park and Cat field with the intention of using it for cruiser owner car parking during the summer, and laying up cruisers using the travel hoist during the winter. This will reduce the number of boats that need to be stored in the Cat field. The Valentines party at the Club was very enjoyable and my thanks to Belinda and her team for the excellent meal that they provided. Just a reminder that we have the Club Fitting Out Party on 6" April at the Club, contact Fenella for tickets. Also, new members will shortly receive invites to meet the Committee, Fleet Captains and other organisers within the Club on 27" April, again at the Club. The sailing Sub Committee continues to beaver away at planning the season ahead. You should all have seen the Support Boat Duty Rosta in the last Navigans. Please ensure that you are available for your duty or have arranged to change with someone and informed those concerned. Now the really good news. The MASC has approved the purchase of the new support RIB and the order is being placed. Delivery is expected to take about ten weeks so we will need to nurse the existing boat through this period until the replacement arrives. As part of the purchase, Jenny Ball has also negotiated an ongoing contract with the suppliers to maintain the engine and hull, which includes a guaranteed engine repair service during the week. The Committee has therefore decided that if the engine is not running properly, it must be left for the supplier to resolve and club members MUST NOT attempt to fix the problem. Finally the form to apply for camping is included elsewhere in this issue of Navigans. Please remember that there is a limit on the number of pitches and that it is strictly "First Come, First Served". Those wishing their children to attend Cadet Week would be well advised to get their camping applications in early. This will also ensure that Hilary Ashley can confirm your application before Pete Clayton needs to know for whom he is catering during Cadet Week. Neil Pembleton Special Cruiser Fleet Meeting While visiting my son and his family in North Narrabeen near Sydney in February I was supprised to learn that a trip had been arranged for me by Margaret and others to fly us from Sydney to Auckland NZ and then onward by car to Opua Marina in The Bay of Islands (North Island) where Malcolm and Helen Shaft's boat Mona was currently berthed. Because of other commitments we could only stay with them for five days but each day was used to the full with numerous activities undertaken including sailing of course. During our stay Malcolm informed me that they would be flying back to the UK at the beginning of May to visit their parents and attend to some business.As there has been a healthy interest in Mona's Travels not only within the cruiser fleet but in other fleets also, I took the opportunity of asking Malcolm if he would be willing to give MSC members a talk about Mona's Travels to date if it could be arranged. He said that he would willing. So the talk by Malcolm Shaft ably supported by Helen no doubt on Mona's Travels is to be held at the M.A.S.C. Beehive Lane, Chelmsford on Tuesday May 28th. Arrive usual time 07.30 - 08.00 p.m. and all are very welcome. Malcolm Yeoman (Suruca)

BACSPA BULLETIN Last December, Neil approached me to enquire whether I would be prepared to take over from Ron Greygoose as the club’s representative on the Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association. As most of you know, this was supposed to be my year off, but you know how persuasive Neil can be, so I agreed. I’m not sure how many years Ron has been our rep. and I know that until recently he was secretary of the association, however I am sure you would like me to record a vote of thanks here for all his efforts. These meetings are held quarterly and as a sort of hand over we both attended the last meeting held on 6" December 2001 at the Maldon Little Ship Club. There are 29 clubs represented in the association, plus the secretary of the RYA Eastern Region, so you can imagine there is a wide range of topics covered at these meetings. I will try to report on those that have special significance to us. NAVIGATION — a) Looking at the minutes of the meeting held on 13" September 2001, reference was made to the, “proposed removal of the buoyage in the North Edinburgh Channel”. I do not have a copy of BACSPA’s response to this, however it was pointed out that “Fisherman’s Gat” is now buoyed. At the last meeting it was reported that additional buoyage might be provided in the “South Edinburgh Channel”. However, since it is further west it may be of little use to BACSPA members. b) A lattice tower will be established in position 51’ 43 55N, 01’ 11 84E, painted yellow and will exhibit an all round yellow light 12 metres above High Water Springs, flashing Morse “U” .._ every 15 seconds. This is a meteorological mast in connection with the proposed wind farm on the Gunfleet Sands off Clacton. The structure will remain in place for up to 3 years. The next meeting is due to be held on Thursday 21% March 2002. Derek Kirby - BACSPA Rep. FROM THE SOCIAL COMMITTEE The year has started off very well with the Valentines Fancy Dress disco on the 16th February. A big thank you goes to Belinda Dowley and Jenny Mead for organising it and to Belinda for providing the gorgeous food - well done Ladies! Everybody that went had a super time and those of us hardy enough to camp had a wonderful breakfast together the following morning before tidying up. It was a bit cold and uncomfortable for some (especially those who slept in their cars) but the morning turned out to be a beautifully sunny and calm one to make up for the hangovers and sore backs! We look forward to seeing more people at the next event, which is the Fitting Out Party on 6th April, where Belinda will again be providing an excellent meal, and Andrew and Tim will be providing the Disco. They are turning out to be fantastic DJ's as well as good sailors - a multi-talented pair! See you all soon down at the Sailing Club, Regards, Fenella Thomas, on behalf of the Social Committee

Mona's Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Two - In the Pacific - The Las Perles Islands On Tuesday 27th March 2001 we made our first tentative foray into the Pacific, heading off for the 30-odd miles to the Las Perles Islands, in a flat calm. It was strangely eerie motoring between the ranks of anchored ships, waiting their turn to transit the canal. After a few hours of motoring over a glassy sea, trailing a fishing line to absolutely no effect, we reached the islands. We had for a long time been complaining about our inability to catch fish, but it took Laura, a committed vegan, to point out that you won't catch fish if you don't trail a line. We had only recently taken this advice seriously and had stocked up on the necessary items in Panama. This was, quite amazingly, our first serious attempt at fishing. Anchoring to the south of the island of Contadora, I realised that I had overshot my intended target of the nudist beach and had anchored instead off the main beach. We had a refreshing swim off the boat. Our autohelm ST50 instruments give us, among other things, the water temperature. Throughout the Caribbean it had tended to register consistently around the 27°C level. It had come as a bit of a shock when taking our first swim in the Pacific that the water temperature was 17°C. We were now relieved to discover that it had crept back up to around 23°C. That evening we had a pleasant walk around Contradora with Pat and Olivia from Aldebaran who had set out into the Pacific at the same time as us. Our walk included a quick detour to the nudist beach where a large sign declared, in Spanish and English: 'No clothes are allowed on this beach.' Contradora is, apparently, used as a conference centre for meetings of South American Heads of State, as it can be made secure fairly easily. In the morning we made a trip ashore to top up our fuel and water. We had seen a garage on our walk the previous night and we weren't sure how often we would be able to get diesel. Having got my diesel, I set off to fill my water container that I had decanted that morning into our main tanks. This proved to be a bit more difficult. It is a very dry island and water is in short supply. Having been directed to a hotel that I failed to find, I found a large building where I could hear voices. Calling out ‘Ola’ in my best Spanish, a woman's voice answered and I entered a room to be confronted by a dozen curious faces. The girl in charge of this 'creche', who turned out to be a yachtie from Belgium who had moved ashore for a while, was very sympathetic. She led me to the ladies toilet where she told me I could get good water from the sink tap. With the help of an old dried milk container purloined from the nursery, I spent the next few minutes ladling water into my container, watched by a succession of young visitors. Having restocked our tanks we had a gentle, sail, drift, motor between the islands to a dramatic anchorage off the island of Pedro Gonzales, just inside a tiny island with a cross on top. All these islands were rugged and craggy and in marked contrast to the low, sandy, ‘desert! islands of San Blas. We had a good walk along the long, deserted beach. In the morning there was enough wind to allow us a gentle sail to the island of San Hose. Anchoring in a wide bay off a long sandy beach we ventured ashore with Pat and Olivia in our dinghy. Just as we reached the beach, as I struggled to tilt the outboard, a large wave caught us and we scrambled ashore rather wet with a fair amount of water in the dinghy. Pat in particular was rather miffed, as he had taken off his shirt to keep it dry. We had an interesting walk ashore and a game of boules on the beach, only marred by the sand flies. As darkness fell we relaunched the dinghy. This time we were prepared. Pat manned the oars while I handled the outboard. Having held the boat steady to the incoming waves, we judged our moment, scrambled into the Caribe dinghy as best we could, while Pat rowed into the swell as manfully as he could with the rather inadequate oars that Caribe supply. As I lowered the outboard and went to start it, we were engulfed by an enormous wave that broke right over the top of us. We emerged the other side of it with the dinghy literally half full of water. The outboard started first pull, and somehow or other the dinghy carried the five uf us and goodness knows how many gallons of water, back to the boats with Pat attempting to bail out with an empty beer can. We stayed in this anchorage for another three days but did not attempt to go ashore again. The next day 'Fair Hyppolyta' and 'Cap D'Or' arrived. That night we had Happy Hour on ‘Aldebaran'. For the next couple of days we ruminated on the best time to set off for the Galapagos. This 850-mile passage across the Equator has a reputation for its inconsistent and generally light and fluky winds, and takes anything from one to three weeks, depending on your willingness or ability to motor. We were hearing on the radio of boats motoring the whole way, something we just would not be able to do. While these ruminations were continuing, Pat, and Richard from 'Fair Hippolyta' , together with Carl from the American ‘Silver Fin' we had just met up with, laboured to get our pactor working, which in conjunction with the SSb and the laptop that we had bought in Panama, should allow us to send and receive Emails from the boat. We all seemed to get restless at about the same time and, quite independently, decided to leave the next day. Part Thirty Three - Onward to the Galapagos On the morning of Monday 5th March five boats left San Hose bound for the Galapagos; ‘Fair Hippolyta' , 'Cap D'Or’, 'Silver Fin' and 'Aldebaran’, with us taking up our rightful position at the back of the fleet after finally sorting out our mass of fresh veg. After non-existent winds the day before, we were favoured with 10 knots of wind out of the North East. By this time I had realised that if we were to get anywhere in the Pacific, we would have to start taking light weather sailing seriously. We were one of the smaller boats sailing the Pacific, and very much a heavyweight (by now overweight heavyweight). So it was that within an hour of leaving the anchorage we had the cruising chute up and flying. By early afternoon 'Fair Hippolyta' , ‘Cap D'Or' and 'Silver Fin' had all caught fish. The only ones who hadn't were 'Aldebaran' and us. We seemed to have a favourable current at this stage. I say 'seemed' because our log had been playing up for some time and we only had the GPS giving us speed over the ground to go by. We were sailing well, making 6 knots over the ground so, as night fell, we decided to keep the cruising chute up. Later in the evening ‘Silver Fin' radioed to say they were getting 18 knots and 'Cap d'Or' reported 25 knots. We took the chute down but never got more than 18 knots and then only for a short period. Overnight we saw a couple of ships pass us on a parallel course. We sailed most of the night at about 5'/, knotsin 10-14 knots of wind with just the main up.

10 The next day the wind dropped and we tried setting the chute. After a few hours it kept on collapsing. As the wind had come more directly astern we sailed goosewinged with the boomed-out genny. The wind increased again overnight and at one point we were doing 7 knots over the ground. It wasn't to last, however, and the wind dropped to well below ten knots. By this time we were heading for a point to the east of the tiny island of Malpella. This course was slightly off the direct course for the Galapagos, but was reputed to offer a greater possibility of wind. Close to Panama there tend to be overspill winds from the Caribbean, further out, it all becomes a bit of a lottery and three weeks to cover the 900 miles to the Galapagos are not uncommon. Conditions were very pleasant and we were making between 5 and 6 knots over a smooth and calm sea. We were able to shelter from the sun under our bimini cover that we had had modified back in Grenada, and it was now very effective. The motion of the boat was so steady that I managed to type out a fair bit of my ongoing log. The huge supplies of fresh fruit and vegetables that Helen and Laura had stoked up with in Panama were now put to good use. One day we had carrot soup for lunch, carrot cake for afternoon tea and carrot stew for supper. They were all superb. For some reason I never get tired of carrots. Helen also made rum pudding and cristophene pie which was very much like apple pie. With 3 of us standing watches we were getting plenty of rest. All in all this was passage making like we'd never known it before. Four days out the wind came round from the NE to the SE and dropped. We set the cruising chute and were going very nicely when Helen suddenly spotted a black flag some way off on our starboard beam. A little while later we saw a small white buoy to port. Helen was keeping a very careful lookout up in the bow when she sawa green line crossing our bow dead ahead and some two or three feet below the surface. It was too late to take evasive action but, luckily with our long keel and integral rudder we slid over it without incident. After that we spotted another 6 flags spread out over several square miles. We had just got clear when the cruising chute wrapped itself into a ball, which was eventually sorted and reset and normal service was resumed. Five days out the wind died away. We ran the engine for 2 or 3 hours to charge the batteries but after that just drifted. We drifted overnight ina NW direction at between % and 1% knots. We managed to sail with the chute for a while, then the wind died away completely again. We went for a swim off the stern - amazing feeling. Then the wind got up to 7 or 8 knots, just enough to get us moving at some 34 knots over the ground. Monday 12th March saw us one week out of Los Perles and making a heady 3 knots towards the Equator. This was to be our first time in the southern hemisphere for both Helen and myself so the occasion couldn't go by unmarked. Fortunately we had a visitation from a splendidly attired King Neptune complete with specially written ode. Laura contented herself by swimming across the line. That afternoon, in a flat calm, we motored for 3 hours and then settled back into a gentle drift. Later that night we motored some more. In the morning we set the chute and moved on at a steady 3 knots. By this time the Galapagos were a day or so away. I sorted out my island charts and started doing some serious navigating while Helen and Laura were inspired to have a spring clean. That evening the wind died again, but it was too early to motor in. We had no desire to arrive before dawn. We celebrated what would probably be our last night at sea by having yet another superb evening meal, sitting in the cockpit in a flat calm with absolutely no motion at all. We had sighted land late afternoon and, overnight, we motored slowly round Cristobal, homing in on Wreck Bay just after dawn. In the way these things tend to happen we were greeted by a sudden 25 knot headwind and a downpour which for a short time obliterated the bay. Mercifully it didn't last and we headed into the anchorage, meeting up with the boats that we had left Los Perles with, they having arrived a couple of days earlier. to be continued, Malcolm Shaft Support Boat Duties 2002 (Important Reading) Attached to this issue of Navigans is the Support Boat Duty Rota for this season, please note that no one has been allocated more then 2 duties, as already stated in Navigans. 13 Bits and Pieces I have quickly discovered that one of the problems of being the editor of Navigans is when you suddenly realise that you have a blank page to fill and nothing to put in it! This is where all those stories and anecdotes that I asked for last month would come in useful, so don’t be shy, put pen to paper and help make Navigans a more interesting read and not just a list of dates and notices. The new editor is also given a list of topics to go in Navigans each month of the year. This month it is adders. Parents should remind their children visiting the Club that adders are sometimes seen on site. They are harmless if not disturbed but you should take care in long grass. If you are bitten, the advice is to get to hospital within 2 hours, don’t apply ice or a tourniquet, don’t try to suck out venom. For those of you who live out of the district, the nearest hospitals with a casualty department are at Broomfield, in Chelmsford, or Basildon. Boat Jumble Over the Bank Holiday weekend of 4-6" May, there will be a boat jumble sale at the club in support of the RNLI. This gives you plenty of time to sort out your garage (or wherever you keep all your boating gear) and get any unwanted items down to the club. Think of the benefits, the RNLI is a good cause, buying secondhand is a good way of recycling and you may be able to get your car in the garage! Working Party There was a good turnout for the working party on the 17" March, the sun shone, it was mild and there was a good breeze. In fact the weather was just right to go sailing and there were one or two boats on the river, but not from Marconi as everyone was busy. The hedge was trimmed and the space between the cruiser park and the cat field cleared, so that in due course boats can be stored there. The hard was swept and gravel was collected and used for filling in potholes in the roads. Every where you looked there were people busy preparing the club for the season, the hoses are back on the taps in the cruiser park, the mast derrick is in working order and the dinghy field marked out and cut. These were just some of the jobs that I could see being done, no doubt there were people working away on tasks that are essential to the running of the club but which most of us are unaware of. At lunchtime there were over 50 people in the clubhouse where soup and rolls as well as cups of tea and coffee were provided by Maureen Ball and her helpers - Thanks Ladies. Being there was a reminder that the club is run on a self-help basis, which is what keeps the costs down, and that a lot can be achieved when people band together for a common cause. Marconi Web Site If you have access to the Internet why not take a look at the Marconi Sailing Club web site? It looks very professional and has details about the club, the various fleets and lots of information about the East Coast Piers Race as well as photographs of the club and boats sailed. Well worth a visit next time you are online, at www.marconi- sc.org.uk Bob

COMMODORES NOTES First of all, I would like to welcome John Salmon who has joined the Committee as Rear Commodore. John has been an active Solo sailor for a considerable number of years and has served on the Committee in the past as Sailing Secretary. I am certain that John will have much to contribute and I am pleased that we have now filled all the posts. Thank you to all those who helped at the working party to trim back the hedges and to those who generated the dust when the Mulcher finally arrived. In addition the Solo fleet did their usual thing of getting the racebox ready and I know that many other small but not insignificant tasks were completed. Once again Maureen and her band of helpers kept us properly fed and watered for which many thanks. While Murray was away in sunny New Zealand, his able stalwarts, Gerry, Jack, Harold and Eric continued to service all the tractors and madea start on the grass cutting equipment. As you will have seen over the Easter weekend this has paid off and Murray was able to start cutting the grass. I would like to thank this small, dedicated team who work throughout the winter regardless of the weather so that we can all enjoy the benefit. The concrete gang, otherwise known as the Windsurfers, have repaired the path beside the Clubhouse. I know that I have missed many other unsung heroes who have carried out tasks over the winter and offer my thanks to them as well. In these modern times the Committee have to deal with the red tape of legislation and attempt to avoid the Club being involved in litigation in the courts. One result of this is the current closure of the galley brought about by the need to renew the Environmental Health Certificate. This has brought to light a number of problems which we are in the process of resolving. On current plans we are expecting the galley service to reopen on Sunday 21“ April. The donation of a new cooker by Peter Tovey has greatly assisted in resolving one of the problems at minimal cost, for which we are grateful. l understand from Chris Davies that the East Coast Piers Committee are close to finalising details with a sponsor which will replace about 50% of the sponsorship that Ernst and Young have given in the last few years. They still need your help to find the other 50%. Over the Easter weekend it was pleasing to see the site busy with people sailing and preparing their cruisers for the coming season. It was also very pleasant to enjoy a pint at lunchtime from the Bar and my thanks go to the OODs who opened it, as well as Mike Smith and Malcolm Yeoman for the innovation of bottled Bass and Speckled Hen which saves the problems of setting up and cleaning the pipes etc. I hope that all OODs will find the new system much easier and that we will see the bar open more often. Unfortunately, we still have the hurdle of keeping the old RIB running until the new one arrives. If you encounter any problems with it, please ensure that Roy Hardwick [redacted] is informed as soon as possible. At the same time please listen to any advice he has to offer. Over the next few weekends we will need to juggle the resources of the Orkney, RIB and Jack B particularly on those occasions when moorings are being laid. I hope that all concerned will co-operate to ensure that the safety of those sailing is protected while the moorings are laid in a safe manner. Please bear with Race Officers who may set courses using the closer marks during this period. On the social scene, Mike Smith and Murray Bates organised a marvellous quiz for the final Cruiser meeting of the winter series. It was nice to see some dinghy members taking part. Congratulations to Fenella and her team for a superb meal and disco at the Club Fitting Out party on Saturday 6" April. It was nice to see so many people at the event. Elsewhere in this issue, you will see a letter that the Club has received from the Licensing authorities related to a number of matters including the consumption of alcohol by underage persons. Please remember that the Clubhouse is licensed premises and that the authorities may not distinguish between alcohol bought from the Club or privately if they visited the clubhouse. Neil Pembleton

CRUISER NOTES By the time you read this, the moorings will have started to be laid. Despite a few hitches on ‘C’ row caused by weather and the Jack B breaking down, they are going well. The cruiser launching list is now on the club notice board. When filling in your boat name, please remember to contact the tractor driver for that day and also tell him if you are on the travel hoist or not. Roger Camp NOTICE TO OWNERS OF DRYING MOORINGS A recent check on drying moorings has shown that scouring has uncovered some sinkers, especially at the clubhouse end, to the point where they are a potential hazard to dinghies (as well as to the boat on the mooring). Would all owners please ensure these are dug well in as soon as possible. The standard of moorings themselves leaves a lot to be desired in some cases, with: e Un-marked, or incorrectly marked, buoys. Un-wired and/or severely corroded shackles. Inadequately buried sinkers. e Seized or ineffective swivels leading to twisted chain with a few cases of rather dodgy chain. In some cases old chain has been abandoned near moorings, and would be better buried or removed to avoid additional electrolytic action and confusion. Please ensure that your mooring is in good condition before launching, or by the 1* June deadline if earlier, so we can avoid last year’s crop of boats breaking free from drying moorings. ECPR — A call for support - 29'"/30" June - Charles Anderson Last year Once again, we are at the point when we galvanise support for the Piers Race weekend. Chris Davis is in the chair again, although while staying on in another capacity next year, he has mentioned that he feels this will be his last in the hot-seat. So probably the first question to pose to all you budding organisers is, is it you? The charity Possibly one of the most significant differences the Piers Race has over other sailing events, is the generation of funds for our own locally based sailing charity “The Cirdan Trust”. You may be familiar with their Thames Barge ‘Xylonite’ which operates out of the Blackwater for most of the season and has for many years had a globe on her topsail, this year she sports a Snipe. In addition, their other boats include the Robert Clark designed ‘Hartlepool Renaissence’, a classic Edwardian yacht called ‘Duet’ and The Queen Galadriel a fine old Baltic Trader. While Maldon remains their base, they ply the waters of the north east/Scotland, the south coast and the south west/Channel Islands and Scilly Isles respectably. The Cirdan Sailing Trust provides sailing breaks for the disabled, disadvantaged as well as their helpers (not necessarily together). The money we raise goes towards bursaries, which help those less able to pay make use of the charity’s services. You may recall some of the letters of appreciation published in a previous edition of Navigans and the impact of what we were able to do for some of the youngsters involved. While in previous years we have supported the RNLI, Sailability (the RYA charity for disabled sailors) we have provided over £70,000 for charities in total. No mean feat for a sailing club and something we all should be proud of. Backbone Again as usual, a copy of the weekend’s questionnaire is in this issue; please don’t forget that if you do respond, your offer will be taken up so keep an eye on Navigans news about the weekend and definitely please do turn up at the weekend. For cruiser owners, we will continue to use M2 for routine comms although we can accommodate those of you stillon M1. If you do have a cruiser and would like to do a bit more with the weekend I would love to hear from you. While cruisers provide the backbone for the weekend’s support we always need additional help with running the bar, reception, runners, spotters, trolleys, rescue crews and so on. There is input from across the club so don’t feel bashful about lending a hand. Special race with special support We are all justifiably proud of the contribution we make to Cirdan and as mentioned, it is unique in the sailing world. Other long distance events have sprung up since MSC established the Piers Race 15 years ago but we remain the only one with the charity link as well as establishing standards that other events wish to emulate. We have made a big difference to disabled sailors over the years and we really appreciate the help and support we receive from you all. Once again I thank all of you who have helped in the past and my deepest gratitude goes out to those able to make a contribution this year.

11 LETTER TO LICENSEES Dear Licensee Re: Recent Legislation Affecting Licensing Laws I write to advise to you of forthcoming changes to the licensing laws which will be brought about by the Criminal Justice and Police Act 2001: Section 30 — Under age sales (expected 1* Dec 2001) Section 31 — Enforcement of under age sales (expected 1° Dec 2001) Section 32 — Permitting drunkenness & disorder (expected 1° Dec 2001) Section 38 — Permitting controlled drugs (expected early 2002) The purpose of this letter is merely to draw your attention to the relevant changes. If you are in any doubt as to how these changes may affect you then you should seek your own independent legal advice. Under Age Sales Section 30 of the Act amends the defences available to persons charged with offences under Section 169A of the Licensing Act 1964, involving the sale of alcohol to person under eighteen years of age. A defendant will now be required to prove that he believed that the customer was not under eighteen and that he took all reasonable steps to establish the customer’s age or that nobody could reasonably have suspected from the customers appearance that he was under eighteen. The intention of this amendment is to ensure that licensees and their staff seek proof of age before making sales of alcohol. As you will be aware accepted forms of proof of age are available through a variety of proof of age cards, photo-driving licences and passports. Enforcement of Under Age Sales Section 31 of the Act provides for the use of test purchasing operations to be carried out by the Police and Trading Standards Services using persons under the age of eighteen to purchase or attempt to purchase alcohol from licensed premises. Test purchasing will be used in order to combat the illegal sale of alcohol to underage persons and in general will be used only as a last resort where for instance a previous warning has not resolved the situation. Generally test purchasing will only be used on those premises where it is known that a problem exists with sales of alcohol to underage persons. Permitting Drunkenness & Disorder Section 32 of the Act increases the maximum penalty for the offences under Section 172 of the Licensing Act 1964 to a fine not exceeding level 3 (currently £1000). In addition Section 32 inserts a new Section 172A in the Licensing Act 1964, which makes it an offence for anyone (defined as “relevant person”) who works in licensed premises to permit drunkenness or any violent, quarrelsome or riotous conduct to take place on the premises. For the avoidance of doubt a “relevant person” is defined as any person, other than the licence holder, who works in a capacity (whether paid or unpaid) which gives him or her the authority to prevent the relevant drunkenness or disorder or the sale of alcohol. Permitting Controlled Drugs Section 38 of the Act extends the offence under Section 8(d) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 for an occupier or person concerned with the management of any premises (i.e., including licensed premises) to knowingly permit or suffer the administration or use of any controlled drug, unlawfully in a person’s possession at or immediately before the time when it is administered or used.

COMMODORES NOTES v-a The Club was founded fifty years ago and Fenella is organising a Fun Day and Barbecue for SATURDAY 15" JUNE. She has asked each Fleet to take on a specific role or task for the day to spread the load as widely as possible. I hope that all members will try to come to the party to celebrate FIFTY YEARS OF THE MARCONI SAILING CLUB. It was on 18" April 1952 that the inaugural meeting of the Club was held. In those days it existed in a shed at Heybridge and built its own Fleetwinds in a shed at Great Baddow. Since than it has progressed through its home on the barge Mamgu and the allotments at Heybridge, to its present site and Clubhouse at Steeple. Its present success is founded on the vision of those early members; the spirit of self-help within the Club and the tireless contribution made the membership. This has varied from those who have, and do sit, on one of the committees through to the person who anonymously and quietly performs some task which we all take for granted and never actually realise has happened. Another major contributor to the Club, as we know it today, is the diversity of sailing that it provides. There can be few clubs who cater for the out and out racer, to the potter about on the water sailor (indeed some might even include the “I’m fitting out and might get to the water one day” person); from the single handed Mirror/Optimist etc. dinghy, through catamarans to the fully crewed cruiser. It is this culture of self-help, reliance on and co-operation between the members, which makes the Club unique. Having said all of this, occasionally we do experience some problems. Generally these tend to be around the way we perceive others contribution, generally there tends to be a degree of truth behind such differences but many people work hard to overcome and correct such impressions and the Club benefits in the longer term. SOLO MATTERS (This month more than most!) Fellow Soloists and anyone else, who might be interested: I'm sure you all know by now that we have an Open meeting on the Sunday 9th June. There's no such thing as bad publicity however, so here it is again! Last year's event was very successful with a high turnout from our own fleet and a good number of visitors from a variety of clubs. This was due in large part to all the hard work behind the scenes put in by a small (but perfectly formed) group of our guy's efforts. This year we have taken stock of last year's strengths and weaknesses and hope in turn to improve an already excellent weekend's sailing. So what do we have planned for you? Well we kick off with Saturday morning pitching camp for any of those who wish to stay over for the weekend. Then we havea training day starting at around 11.00am on Saturday 8th June. Steve Ash has signed up Gordon Barclay, one of the Solo fraternity's 'Top Guns' whom I met this year at the Dinghy Show, Ally Pally. He is a very friendly and enthusiastic exponent of the art of Solo sailing as well as being a top competition sailor and we are lucky to get him. He is also The Class Association's chief measurer and so we had better all watch our step - No cheating! Last year, anyone who joined the training session with Jim Hunt did, I'm sure, enjoy it almost as much as the Open event itself. I would urge all of you to try and take the time to join in with this training event, as it really is well worthwhile, being both informative and great fun. It is rare that you get this kind of opportunity to watch, listen, ask questions etc. of someone who has so much knowledge to impart and we can all learn from the experience. So please do try to join in - even if you have no intention of sailing in the open itself as I'm sure there is something here for us all. Saturday evening we plan to light the barbeque and maybe even to cook something on it! Bring along your favourite cuts and char them to a cinder in the traditional fashion. Hopefully, Belinda Dowley will be around with a reserve sausage or two in case of total loss. We will open the bar and try to make a bit of a social gathering of the post training evening. Sunday morning our core team of organisers will be around from 8.30 or so. If you are sailing, as most of you will want to be, then it will be worth getting there in good time say 09.00, a) to grab one of Belinda's now legendary bacon rolls and b) to be around to welcome and assist any of the huge number of visiting competitors we are expecting to turn up. The rest of the day will follow the usual formula. See Poster in this issue for your information. One change from last year, we think for the bette,r will be that we can order our lunches from Belinda at the point of signing on, so that come lunchtime all will be ready and waiting for us with hopefully, the minimum delay. Anyone who has tried out the new catering arrangements at the club over the past few weekends will I'm sure agree that the improvement in fare and in the general club house environment as a whole has been commendable, unless of course you live on soggy chips and deep fried Mars Bars, in which case good luck.... After the great event of course, comes the prize giving. This year we are hoping that our famous neighbour, none other than Mr Tony Benn himself, will be on hand to present the prizes and say a few words. Whatever you may think of his politics nobody can deny that he has ever been anything but entertaining and I for one will be very interested in hearing from him. Finally, Please ask not what your club can do for you but rather what can you do for your club! e Ifyou are not sailing but would be willing to make your vessel available to another please contact me so we can start matching people to craft. e Ifyou don't have a Solo but would like to join the training or the open or both then please contact me and we will try to find a boat for you. (Don't worry about not being a member of the Class Assoc. it just means that your first place position can't be counted, shame!)

10 Membership Registrars Occasional Report I hope it is of interest to MSC members to receive this brief overview of the annual membership renewal process. Background I took over from the previous postholder, Linda Chaplin, in September 2001 after making it known to the Honorary Secretary that I wished to provide some input to the club. I am very ably assisted by my partner Jan. We use an MSC owned Sony Vaio laptop to store membership information. The MSC Membership database is in MS Access and features input forms to load its tables and a variety of reports and queries that produce everything from fleet lists to ‘Navigans’ labels. This years renewals In January 2002, 388 membership forms were produced via a report. The printer was fed batches of 100 forms (400 sheets) as we had to watch over it to deal with the frequent paper jams. The acquisition of a new printer is in progress. Membership renewals came back to us at an average of 6 per day with the inevitable rush towards the end of February with 21 and 24 received on those last two days. (Three members dropped renewals off by hand on the evening of the 28th to avoid the late payment fee!) We found that the form error rate was about 1 in 29 due to information errors that have now been identified. Thanks to the 167 members who adjusted other information on membership forms. We are continuously honing the database to be more accurate, please do not hesitate to let us know of any further changes as they occur. Thanks also to the 123 members who gave us e-mail addresses which have been recorded for future use. We did two or three sessions a week to deal with the returned forms and put membership packs together at the same time as updating the database. 347 members renewed in January and February (with only one cheque having a date in 2001!). Cheques are passed on to the Honorary Treasurer, Frank Bennett for processing. Frank also checks that each member has a current MASC membership before sending the packs out. There are currently 41 members from last year that have not renewed as I write this on the 16th March As we are new to this process, we have been a little flexible the over the renewal closing date as stated in rule 8e. Next year the rules will be applied as they are stated in the yearbook. Thus far I can only thank one late paying member for adding to club funds but no thanks for extending an already lengthy task for Jan and I! Prompt payment will always be appreciated. Several things occurred to Jan and I since we took up this post: 1/ MSC club fees are a total bargain when one weighs up the facilities and site available. 2/ The total amount of ‘behind the scenes’ work by volunteer club officers is colossal 3/ Just what nice people our members are. I had only pleasant converse with all members that I had to contact to sort out renewal problems - bearing in mind that I was often asking for more money! Nik Beavins Membership Registrar

If anyone wants me to forward the Newsletter to them by email then let me know) Tragic Drowning Some of you may have heard the story of the death of a pensioner at Hullbridge on the River Crouch recently. He was in a tender with a friend going out to a boat moored on the river when, according to the _ local news, the outboard motor stopped so the men rowed to a nearby buoy. On trying to grab the buoy the tender capsized and both men ended up in the water. One of the men was able to swim to nearby boat and was rescued while the other was swept away and later found drowned. Apart from feeling sorry for his family and friends this news story set me thinking, as I, along witha number of club members, go out to my cruiser on its mooring and seldom think about the dangers. It is a tragic reminder that sailing, in whatever shape or form, is potentially dangerous and we owe it to ourselves, our families and our friends, to take all sensible precautions. After all, if you can get into difficulties on the sheltered River Crouch at Hullbridge, you can get into difficulties anywhere and The Blackwater can kick up a chop when it wants to, which can make getting on or off your cruiser a difficult business. “Whatever boat you sail, wherever you sail this summer, have fun and enjoy yourselves but most of all, take care, and come back safe and sound.

15 Tail-piece Firstly, I should introduce myself. My name is John Salmon and I have recently taken up the duties of Rear Commodore at the invitation of Neil Pembleton. . I have been a Club member for about 22 years, sailing the Solo class dinghy which some of you may have noticed around the place, and sailed here as crew for Geoff Josey’s Enterprise for some years before that, going back to the time before our present clubhouse was built, so I have seen the Club grow and develop in that time. I have also served on Main Committee and Sailing Sub-Committee in various capacities. I presently sail a red Solo 4005, so if you do not already know me, come and say hello, and tell me how the sailing activities of the Club might be further improved. I have included my phone number and e-mail address below so that you can also reach me with those media, but face to face is best. As you probably know, this position has been vacant now for some months, which cannot be good for the Club since it places extra burdens on the Sailing Secretary and the other Officers, who should be focussed on their own responsibilities. I have therefore taken the position on a stop-gap basis, in anticipation that a suitable candidate for the longer term will emerge. It is important that these changes in responsibilities are planned in advance to avoid “holes” such as the one just experienced. So if you feel you would be able to take on this responsibility at some time in the future, perhaps with some coaching along the way, please mention it to Neil or myself now so that plans can be put in place. The Rear Com. responsibilities are centred around the sailing activities of the Club — the good bits which most of us joined up for — so it has many pleasurable aspects as well as being of real and obvious relevance to the membership. The previous incumbent, Jenny Ball, wrote an excellent description of the responsibilities in Navigans last year. In mentioning Jenny, it is appropriate here to record, on behalf of the Club, appreciation for a job well done. The style and energy, which she brought to the position, really made a difference, and we are all in her debt. Another post which needs a volunteer, is that of Support Boat Co-ordinator which Dave Payne took on before filling the Vice Commodore position. Dave has done a great job in setting up the Duty Rosta for the season, so the task will only involve managing any required changes as we move through the season. Please let me know if you can take this on. Meantime any queries relating to the Rosta can be addressed to myself or Dave. By the time you read this, we hope to have the new RIB commissioned. All drivers should take care to read the revised operating instructions carefully before using for the first time, and it is intended to provide a short hands-on briefing for each driver before his first stint with this precious piece of equipment. What of the sailing itself? Well the turn out for racing has been modest, and with racing cancelled on a couple of very windy days, it cannot be claimed that the program has been a great success to date. However, with warmer and sunnier weather on the way (I hope!), and the cruiser moorings successfully laid, the sailing activities will no doubt rapidly increase, and I hope you all have a memorable season. COMMODORES NOTES As many of you will have seen by now, the new RIB has arrived at the Club. I would like to thank Jenny Ball for all the work that she put into defining the specification, obtaining the quotations, and then progressing the final order. As with any new piece of equipment we are experiencing a number of teething problems and faults requiring correction. John Salmon is actively pursuing these as well as arranging the necessary training of drivers in its use. It is to be hoped that it will provide many years of useful life to the Club. In order to help achieve this it is important that any problems are recorded in the log book and reported by phone to the Boatswain (Roy Hardwicke) or the Rear Commodore (John Salmon) immediately they occur. Please do not rely on the fact that someone else has or will report faults. The sailing season is now well underway and although I have not been down to the Club as often as I would like, it always seems well attended when I am there, even if the weather is not always co- operating. It was back in the early Eighties that I had the honour of presenting the funds raised from East Coast Piers race to Princess Anne for the charity "Sailing for the Disabled" which we supported then. At the time I felt immensely proud that the Club was able to manage the race and of the tremendous support given by all sections of the Club to its running. Today I still take great pride in the fact that the Club can run the event and raise such large sums for charity and the benefit of others not so lucky as ourselves. I would urge all members to come to the Club on Saturday or Sunday 29/30 June to help make this year's race a resounding success, even if it is only for an hour Or SO. By the time that this reaches you, we will have had the Summer Madness Day to celebrate Fifty Years of the Club and I hope that the weather has been kind to us. Many thanks to Fenella for organising the event, those who assisted her and all who supported it. Neil Pembleton MARCONI ATHLETIC AND SOCIAL CLUB - MAIN COMMITTEE The future and the success of the Sailing Club are closely linked to that of the MASC. At last the MASC is in the process of amending its rules to allow non Marconi personnel to fully participate in the running of the Club and, as the first step, an Extraordinary Meeting approved a rule change to allow any member to serve on the its Main Committee. Currently David Thomas has been co-opted by the MASC Main Committee and we are entitled to have TWO more representatives. I hope that somewhere in our 400 members there are two (willing) volunteers to join David on the MASC Main Committee to help manage the MASC and thereby safeguard the interests of the Sailing Club. Please talk to David Thomas (Tel: [redacted] or myself if you are prepared to support the Sailing Club by serving on the MASC Main Committee. The Sailing Club made similar changes to its rules about 15 years ago and has benefited from the experience and expertise brought to it by the inclusion of all members in its running. Indeed many of our committees would not function without the support of non - Marconi employees. Where the Sailing Club leads - others follow.

Solo Open With Force 5 winds for most of the day, the 25 Solo sailors who entered this round of the Eastern Area Championship on June 9" faced challenging conditions, but were provided with some exhilarating sailing on the River Blackwater, including some long gusty reaches. Race 1 saw some carnage at the start as competitors struggled for control in the tricky conditions, but the main contenders got away cleanly with Keith Videlo gradually building a good lead on the long first beat, from Steve Ede and Gordon Barclay, positions which these 3 maintained through to the finish. Race 2 over the same course presented entirely different conditions as the tide had turned, and local sailors used their river knowledge to advantage, but eventually the same front 3 emerged to take the leading positions, with Steve Monks of the home club claiming a creditable fourth. Race 3 saw Barclay build a big lead on the first beat against the tide by judicious use of the Osea shore. On the second lap Videlo broke clear of a group of 4 boats disputing second place and gradually hauled in the leader to finally pass him on the last tack just yards from the finish line, thus emphatically taking the event. These 2 were followed home by Ede, Monks, and Roger Smith, after a close race. Overall results: 1° Keith Videlo (Frensham Pond S.C.) 2° Steve Ede (Ardleigh S.C.) om Gordon Barclay (Chichester S.C.) 7 Steve Monks (Marconi S.C.) 5 Roger Smith (Marconi S.C.) 6" — Godfrey Clark (King George S.C.) Cruiser Notes The shakedown cruise to Burnham went well with 16 boats going round to Burnham and 11 going on to Brightlingsea afterwards. We had 36 sitting down to a meal in the Swallow Tail and it was one of those rare cruises with favourable winds each day. The next trip is to Brightlingsea on 22" and 23" June and if people could let me know if they are going, I'll ring the harbourmaster on the Friday night before we go as he does like an indication of how many boats to expect. This works to our advantage as last time he reserved one section of the pontoon for 10 Marconi boats. If anyone hasn’t been before and wants to talk to me, I can be reached on [redacted]. The Piers Race is on 30" June and more volunteers are needed. The next major cruise is to Ramsgate on 27" July to 4" August. We will decide exactly what we are going to do nearer the time, maybe we could have a look in at Chatham on the way back. If you have any suggestions, don’t keep them to yourselves. The list will be on the board shortly. We have had an accident in the cruiser park when the travel hoist struck a boat whilst manoeuvring around a parked vehicle so, as said last month, only have your car in the cruiser park if you are working on your boat and be prepared to move it if boats and trailers are being moved around. With a few tons of boat and steel, you do not have a minor bump. The tender trolley storage area has been moved to the grass between the concrete pad and the gap in the sea wall and not at the end of the dingy rack as the people on the end were having trouble getting their dinghies out. BACSPA — Blackwater Estuary Consultation Workshop As part of the DEFRA (Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs) programme for flood and coastal defence, Posford Haskoning have been commissioned to carry out a dissemination project. The aim of the project is to provide training and best practice guidance to those with an interest, or a management function, in the estuary on the choice of approach and data for assessing dynamic change in the estuarine systems. The first phase involved a consultation exercise, which involved a half-day workshop meeting held on Tuesday 9" April, which I attended as your BACSPA representative. The meeting was organised by Posford Haskoning, DEFRA and the Environment Agency. I am sure members will appreciate it is difficult to condense a half-day meeting into a few lines for Navigans and as one would expect these days many buzz words and phrases were used but in essence the points to be covered were the physical properties of estuaries; long term effects; environment and human interfaces. There will be dissemination of the project data acquired at the meeting followed by training and best practice guidance to end users. This would be undertaken in the following stages: 1. Consultation (Posford) 2. Method selection (Project Team) 3. Data collection (Associated British Ports) 4. Data distribution (Associated British Ports) 5. Demonstration projects (HR Wallingford/Royal Haskoning) 6. Training programme (Posford) 7. Data Management best practice, to be decided Application of the uptake project to the Blackwater was given, which will consider — fresh water discharge by the Environment Agency, also surge data as well and Government Studies as in the case of Tollesbury. The impact on Estuary Dynamics was discussed and the undermentioned each gave short presentations: Graham Downing Chairman, Essex Joint Council of Wildfowling Clubs Iden Wickings Secretary, Maldon Barge Operators Group Roger Lankester BACSPA Representative These impacts included, erosion of the outer estuary, situation in the upper estuary and channel migration coupled with the effects of dumping dredging from Harwich and the extraction of fresh water from the Chelmer. As already explained, this was a consultation workshop, we now await the results and I’ll do my best to keep you informed Derek Kirby BACSPA Representative

Ed. ‘Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Four - The Galapagos We arrived in the Galapagos on the morning of 14th March. Since the 60s, large parts of the islands have been a National Park. In the past the Equadorian authorities have beer very reluctant to allow yachts to stay in the islands. In our pilot, published as recently as 1998, it states that the maximum length of stay in total is 72 hours. We had also heard that anyone entering the Park area had to pay a fee of $100 a person. In the event we were pleased to discover that the attitude of the authorities had become much more relaxed. We were officially allowed 3 weeks in the islands, in fact, we could easily have stayed longer if we wanted to. The issue of fees was still a bit unclear. We paid a total of $100 in entry fees for the boat but were not asked to pay the Park fees, although some people were. In many ways we were quite willing to contribute towards the Park but a fee of $100 a person was steep to say the least, especially as the official line was that you needed an official guide on board your boat for the length of your stay, and he didn't come cheap! Just accommodating him would have been interesting. All in all it was a great relief when the Port Captain was really friendly and no mention was made of Park fees. Wreck Bay was an amazing experience in itself. We had been greeted on arrival by a spectacular display of aerobatics by a group of dolphins. The anchorage was home to an enormous number of sealions. They were to be seen sunning themselves on every available rock and lying on the many small fishing boats that filled the harbour. At night you would often hear them grunting and snorting just by the boat. Helen often thought it was me. One large catamaran that had obviously been left for some time had been colonised by a group of sealions that shuffled up the sugar scoops at the stern and slept in the sun on the foredeck. One night as the sun was going down, we decided that they had obviously been people- watching. They had gathered in the cockpit and were having their own 'Happy Hour'. As it got dark we could see their silhouetted shapes moving about sociably together and engaging in what sounded just like

cocktail party conversations. In spite of the fact that we had to re-anchor at least four times before we were properly secure and clear of the many rocks that covered the seabed here, we quickly became very fond of Wreck Bay and the island of Cristobal. The wildlife was incredible. Apart from the sealions, a short walk along the shore and you were confronted by enormous iguanos. On the day we arrived Laura went off with Ron from 'Lazyjacks' and Pat on a diving trip to Kicker Rock. Although she did not have time to organise diving gear, she went snorkelling off the dive boat and was rewarded with a face-to-face confrontation with a hammerhead shark, a school of Galapagos sharks, and a couple of turtles. We had a week in Wreck Bay having a very sociable time with a birthday and St Patrick's Day celebration at one of the seafront bars. The day had been spent on a lovely beach on the other side of the island swimming with sealions. The town at Wreck Bay was fairly small and quiet but surprisingly well equipped with internet centres and an international telephone office that gave us the cheapest calls back to England since Puerto Rico. A short walk out of the town there was an Interpretation Centre that graphically illustrated the history of the islands and the work of the National Park. It had been funded by the Spanish Government and was one of the best displays of its type that I had ever seen. From Cristobal we motored the 45 miles to Academy Bay in Santa Cruz. Academy Bay was a bit of a surprise. Much more developed than Wreck Bay, landing there was a bit like suddenly arriving on the Costa Brava. The anchorage was also rather rolly and full of commercial tour boats. However we had an interesting tour inland to see giant tortoises in the natural environment. We were also able to see them at the Darwin Centre just along the coast. After a week in Academy Bay when we were able to stock up with propane gas and fill our tanks with excellent Galapagos water, we set off for Santa Maria and the infamous Post Office Bay. This is where the old ships would drop off their post in the hope that ships travelling in the opposite direction would pick it up and deliver it. It is a tradition that has been carried on to the present day, although these days it is perpetuated mainly by people on cruise ships. When we got there and anchored, a guide from one of the tour boats called us up on the radio and told us that, while we were perfectly entitled to anchor there, we could not visit the post box as it was in the National Park. This was the first time that we had any problems with officialdom in the islands. In the end, Pat from ‘Aldebaran' and I did a brief trip ashore in the morning to post our cards. I was satisfied that we had been able to uphold the tradition. We later heard that one of Pat's cards had been picked up by an American tourist who had taken it home to the States and given it to her husband who was going on a business trip to Ireland. He had also been doing some kind of charity work and had hand-delivered the card to the address in Dublin with the press in attendance for maximum publicity. From Post Office Bay we had another motor across to Isabela, by far the largest island in the group but one of the least developed. The anchorage at Vilamil is surrounded by an extensive reef which made it one of the most protected anchorages in all the islands. Isabela quickly became our favourite island of the group. The settlement at Vilamil was somehow what I had expected the Galapagos to be like. An incredibly peaceful place with a few well-spread-out shops and bars, sandy streets and an air of timelessness. Getting ashore involved a choice between skirting the rocks that surrounded the anchorage to reach the fishing boat quay, or braving the surf and offlying shallows to land on the beach. Initially we opted for the quay to find on returning to the dinghy that the fuel line to the remote petrol tank for the outboard was missing. What was most upsetting was that without the fuel line the outboard was useless. Luckily Pat on 'Aldebaran' had a Yamaha 5 which is the only one of the range to have both an integral tank and a remote tank facility. We were therefore able to borrow the fuel line. The Port Captain was very sympathetic. Before we knew what was happening Helen and I were being packed into a pickup truck and taken on a tour of the town in search of a replacement line. At one point we arrived at a rundown barn surrounded by pigeon lofts where outboards in every stage of repair or disrepair were in evidence. A hefty looking character from this establishment then joined me in the back of the truck while we continued our tour. We stopped at a bar where, after much musing, someone disappeared and reappeared with a cable minus one end fitting. Eventually our guide admitted defeat, but they certainly couldn't have tried harder. The few roads in and around Vilamil only lead a very short way northwards into the island. A few miles into the island there is a large volcanic crater some 10 km in diameter. “The only practical way to reach

9 this crater was by horseback. A group of us duly arranged an expedition at very reasonable cost. Helen opted out of this trip in deference to her back. I think was against Laura's principles to ride a horse (I did suggest that she carried the horse) but because it was the only way to see the volcano she decided to go along with it. In the event she was very useful, having been working hard at her Spanish she was able to communicate remarkably well with the totally non-English-speaking guide. Others in the group were Pat & Olivia from 'Aldebaran', Richard and Joy from 'Fair Hippolyta' and also Raul and Cindy from 'Manana' who had line-handled for us through the Panama Canal. (They had only then made the decision to come on through themselves, one of their concerns being their parrot, which might not get a warm welcome if they got to Australia.) After a bumpy truck ride we finally reached our horses, and my apprehension was slightly diminished by the fact that the guide seemed at least to be trying to match horse with rider. As I mounted and began to relax into the saddle I noticed that the manes on the other horses were lying flat while the mane on mine was sticking straight up, punk style. Pat and Richard then commented that my horse had an evil glint in its eye. I began to worry that once again I had been matched with the maladjusted member of the species, something I seem to have been fated in. My main aim at this stage was to remain mounted, so when the guide started encouraging the horses to start walking up the path, I made no effort to get mine moving. I was quite content to let him go in his own time. He waited while the others moved off, then he suddenly twigged what was happening and barged and shouldered his way to the front. Once there he was content to amble along, but as soon as he became aware that any of the other horses were attempting to get by, he would prick his ears up and break into a trot with me hanging on as best I could. This continued for the next 2 hours. I spent most of the time completely on my own while all sorts of altercations were taking place between the horses behind me. The volcanic crater was a spectacular sight. A little further we left the horses and walked on to where the fissures in the ground were still steaming. At one point you could clearly see a line between lava that came from an eruption in the 50s and one in the 70s. Back on the horses, Raul's mount decided to lead off at a pace. Much to my relief mine seemed content to let him go. But then as the others came up behind, he again determined that none would pass. At one stage he was engaged in a fast trot when he missed his footing and went down on his forelegs. I was suddenly aware that there was nothing ahead of me. I had taken as my riding style the advice to emulate a sack of potatoes which seemed to be pretty effective and I had started to see myself as some kind of lonesome cowboy riding across the prairie. Now as I headed earthwardsI rolled into a ball and, I'm told, did a perfect landing. My immediate reaction was concern for the horse, as was everyone else's but in the event, both of us came through unharmed. For some reason my confidence, once back in the saddle, was increased rather than diminished. I did think the incident might have calmed my horse downa bit, but this was not to be and he carried on in much the same manner all the way back. A couple of days later, Helen and I, with Pat and Olivia, undertook a long hot dusty walk to the site of a post-war prison camp, where for want of any more useful employment for the prisoners, the commandant had set them to work quarrying rocks and carrying them to the site of a totally purposeless wall. After several years and many deaths the wall ended up some 10 metres high, 10 metres wide and 100 metres long. Not surprisingly the wall became known as the Wall of Tears. We were now beginning to get preoccupied with the long Pacific crossing that lay ahead. It was now fast approaching April and this is generally recognised as the earliest time to consider going, as the Trades don’t usually settle before then. Some boats had already set off in an attempt to maximise their time in the South Pacific, but were reporting little or no wind, interspersed with fierce squalls. Of particular concern was the whereabouts of the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone, or ITCZ, which moves around the Equator and separates the North Easterly trades in the north from the South Easterly trades in the south. This separation zone, which can vary enormously in size and sometimes disappears altogether, generally features little wind, overcast skies and occasional brief squalls. By the beginning of April we were getting reports that the ITCZ was moving north. It seemed to be a good time to go. to be continued Malcolm Shaft

10 Tail-piece Well the new RIB was delivered as promised and has seen some service already. Most of you will have seen it on the water by now. You could hardly miss it in its brilliant orange livery. Early reports from the crews who have used it are very favourable, and if we take good care of it I have no doubt that it will be an excellent support boat for our racing activities in the years to come, particularly for the cat fleet who are the primary justification for this boat. Would drivers please remember to report any concerns promptly to the RIB Bosun — Roy Hardwicke. Thanks are due to all who put their thought, time, and effort into the specification, procurement and commissioning of this craft. As I write, the windy days are still with us, there does seem to have been a lot of them in the early part of the season, but I am pleased to report some improved turn-outs for racing recently, and looking at the Spring Points results the other day it was pleasing to see that 14 different boats took part in the Handicap fleet series. The Club hosted it’s annual Open Meeting for the Solo Class on June 9 with an excellent training day on the preceding Saturday. The event was windy (again!) but provided some very exciting sailing for those who could cope. We had 25 entries and the day was generally regarded as a success, which has further enhanced the Marconi S.C. reputation. So thanks to all who helped to organise and run this event. The next big one from a sailing viewpoint is of course the ECPR, which will probably be history by the time you read this. Preparations are nearly complete I am told, and the ECPR committee will no doubt deliver another well run event. e+1m COMMODORES NOTES My thanks to you all for your help and support to Fennella, Chris and Charles. (I know they are the front persons and that many are involved but there isn't room to mention everyone) Wow! What a month for showing the Club's ability to work together and achieve fantastic results. First we had the Club's Fiftieth Anniversary Fun Afternoon and Barbecue and we were fortunate that the rain held off until the end. Then we had the East Coast Piers Race where the weather was kind to us and allowed all the catamarans to return to the Club before the conditions really piped up. Many of the mother boats were not so lucky and had somewhat uncomfortable conditions to cope with and deserve much heartfelt thanks for their role. Both of these events clearly demonstrated the way in which all the members come together to make such events a success. It is nice to know that Fenella, Chris and Charles received such wholehearted support from you all. Well done to all who helped make both of these events such a success. The maintenance of the basic infra structure of the Clubhouse and site and the need to comply with the increasingly complex legislation regarding health and safety, certification etc. is just as important to the future well being of the Club as the more visible assets of support boats, race marks etc. As you are all aware from my previous notes, we have been addressing the problems raised by the need to certificate the electrical supply around the Club. It was clear that obtaining such certification was going to ' require major work and upgrades to parts of the system, and we decided that a sub committee should be appointed to establish a solution that would provide a system to take the club through the next ten to twenty years, making provision for increased demand and facilities. This sub-committee, under Clive Shenton's chairmanship, produced a plan with a number of improvements, such as external power points on the Clubhouse and portacabins, to allow easier access to power for people working on their dinghies, which should meet our requirements. They have put these plans out to tender and obtained a number of quotations for the work, which have ranged from £44,000 to £21,000 (although this lowest did not cover the full specification and excluded all the civil work such as trench digging etc). On the recommendation of the sub-committee and with the backing of the Executive, the Main Committee has given its approval for the work to proceed at a cost of £34,000 using a company called ACL. Meanwhile the sub-committee have continued negotiating with ACL and already achieved some cost reduction in the region of £2,000 without compromising the overall scheme. Subject to approval from the MASC to spend the money, it is intended to carry out the work in two phases. . The first phase will be to replace the underground cable from the edge of the site, across the dinghy park to the Clubhouse, carry out all the improvements and remedial work within the Clubhouse, Race container and tractor shed area. It is planned to do this during this winter to minimise disruption to the Dinghy Park during the sailing season. The second will cover the work required from the Clubhouse, through the Cruiser Park to the Race box, Race Reception and Cadet portacabins. This is planned for the summer next year. Whilst we pride ourselves on being a self help club, the scale of the work required, the need to obtain certification and the problems associated with managing such a project using our self help resources, lead us to believe that we are taking the right action by contracting out the project in this case. Neil Pembleton

EAST COAST PIERS RACE 2002 — ‘... the most hospitable event’. From Chris Davies and Charles Anderson After the summer we had enjoyed to date, it was no surprise that the morning of East Coast Piers Race 2002 dawned grey and windy. Your bleary-eyed correspondent attended the post-dawn Management Team meeting with a tricky forecast rattling round his brain and questions about whether the full course was possible. After proper deliberation the decision was made to run the full event, with the proviso that the course could be shortened if conditions up the coast deteriorated. As the intending competitors were roused from their beds to the strains of ‘ Also Sprach Zarathustra’ and Kate’s Kitchen prepared the first batch of forty bacon and egg butties, the Cruiser Fleet moved out from their overnight berths at Brightlingsea, or from their home moorings, to their pre-determined positions on the course. Rescue cover crews readied their boats and equipment, the Race Officer and his team guided the committee boat into position and the scrutineers and trolley marshals made ready to quickly and efficiently check competitors on to the slipway. Meanwhile, those on duty in Race Reception processed some last-minute entries, checked handicap details and sold another matching pair of his and hers commemorative rugby shirts. And deep in the bowels of the clubhouse a couple of poor volunteers were tidying-and re-stocking the bar following the previous evenings revels. On the big red bus all this activity was noted, as was the growing flow of information coming in over the Marine VHF, the private VHF, the TA net and over mobile ‘phones. And then something wonderful happened — the sun appeared! Before we knew it, the Race was under way and the fast boats were screaming up the course — through Bradwell, round The Twist, through the Colne Gate and on up to Clacton and Walton. For many the Race was completed in record time and for most the event was one to savour. A fast, exciting and challenging sai, with proper support and safety cover. The ones who were less euphoric about their involvement this year were the very few who had cause to call upon that safety support and thereby failed to complete the course. Of course, a good race for the competitors — and many said this was the best in years — almost by definition means an uncomfortable day for the Cruiser Fleet. This fact was fulsomely acknowledged by the ultimate winner, Richard Allen, in an impromptu vote of thanks at the awards ceremony. Other comments from competitors are shown below. Increased competitor numbers and some smart housekeeping means that, despite a lower level of corporate sponsorship this year, we will be able to remit a considerable sum to Cirdan Trust once again. We will announce the final figure as soon as the accounts are finalised and all the individual sponsorship is collected in. Charlie and I have endeavoured, as usual, to give individual thanks to all concerned in putting on this very demanding event; if we have missed you, we apologise. There were a lot of people involved. If we just look at the fleets we see that the Handicap and Solo fleets provided race officers, boat scrutineering and results processing; the catamaran fleets manned the bar, prepared and laid the marks of the course and provided a trot boat service for the cruisers; the cruisers themselves provided the time-honoured chain of comfort and communication up the course which makes ECPR the much- admired event that it has come to be. And all fleets contributed to the operation of the all-important

rescue and support fleet — and numerous other essential tasks and duties, large and small which are essential to an event of this kind. Thank you, everybody. And finally, a few words from our customers..................... Congrats on the event, thoroughly enjoyed it and was impressed with the slick organisation. Thanks to all involved. (Nigel Brown, Oxford Magnet Technology Ltd) Thank you for a great weekend. Really enjoyed it. And thanks again to the crew of the rescue boat (we broke a mast). Thanks. (Hein Behrens). I was out on one of the spotter boats not too far from Bradwell all day for the race and would like to thank everyone involved for letting me have the opportunity to be involved. (lan Dack) Good to see you all at the weekend, good to come Sth in the short race and even better to win the holiday! :-) I had heard that you were the most hospitable event for a long, long way and can now agree. (Colin Bennett) Many thanks for an excellent ECPR weekend (and especially for sorting out the wheelchair accessible PortaLoo!!!). Thanks especially to the folks sat out in the mother. boats - I didn't envy them at all. Cheers. ( Alan Grace Spitfire no:17) Thanks for an excellent race... Marconi Sailing Club ... ran a very well organised race ... it is always reassuring to see anchored along the course the club members in their yachts... ensuring that all the yachts are checked out and in. I look forward to returning next year and hope we have the same conditions as 2002 rather than 2001 when the race took some 7 and a half hours. (Richard Allen — winner ECPR 2002) I appreciate the balls of the organisers in letting a paraplegic enter such a race. This is best form of integrated sailing, where everyone looks out for each other and aims to have a great time. Roll on next year. ( Alan Grace ) There is a lot more where this came from. See the Marconi website for race reports and pictures. Chris Davies and Charles Anderson KITE SURFING AT THE MARCONI SAILING CLUB. An area of sailing development has seen the introduction of the sport of Kite Surfing where the person uses a kite for propulsion whilst standing on a surfboard. This involves the use of large kites attached to the user by long lengths of rope and has considerable safety implications in confined waters. The Main Committee has considered the implications within the Club particularly in the use of such equipment launched from the Hard and sailed within the moorings. After extensive debate examining a number of options, the Main Committee has decided to introduce a ban on the use of such equipment by launching from the Club or sailing within the Moorings.
