The Support Boat Roster — How it works! As you are all aware, the club racing programme is very dependent on an army of volunteers who helm and crew the support boats. On the whole, this process runs smoothly but like the swan, an awful lot of frantic paddling goes on under the surface! I thought it would be worthwhile just explaining the process that we use and the responsibilities of the various people involved so that the machine continues to run as smoothly as we would all want. At the beginning of the sailing season a Roster of support boat cover is published in Navigans. This identifies the crews and helms for Jack B and the RIB against dates and events. The Roster will have the names of those club members who have agreed to help with support boat duty. I will use this and previous rosters to assign names to duties. Obviously, the Roster will only work effectively IF EVERYONE CHECKS THE LIST TO MAKE SURE THEY ARE OK FOR THE DATE ASSIGNED TO THEM. Changes are inevitable but need to be locally agreed between individuals on the list. I cannot take on the task of finding replacements, but when changes are made between individuals, the details need to be passed to me so I can amend the master list. In addition to this, one week before the duty, Dave Williams will send out a letter to the Race Officer who is asked to contact the helms of Jack B and the Rib. The helms in tum are asked to contact their crews. This cascade method should ensure we have adequate cover for the race day. On the race day, the helms and crews should arrive at the sailing club in plenty of time to prepare the boats and begin racing at 11:00. This may mean laying buoys and generally making sure that the sailing details, courses etc. are understood. Clearly without the right level of support cover the racing programme would be jeopardised and a whole lot of people disappointed! So please do check the Navigans for your name so that we can continue to enjoy a full sailing programme. Les Hurrell-Smith Support Boat Duty Co-ordinator, Telephone [redacted] Commodore's AGM Report. Welcome to what I believe is the 50th Annual General Meeting of our Club. Since its founding in 1952 the Club has come a long from its beginnings in a hut on the allotments at Heybridge via the barge Mamgu to its present home here at Stansgate. This could not have been achieved without the vision and foresight of numerous members who have served on committees, undertaken projects to acquire, and I use that term in its loosest sense, equipment and buildings for the site and all those who have turned out at numerous working parties over these fifty years. We also need to remember the very real assistance given by the MASC during this time. Without the backing of its main committee and its considerable financial facility at that time, the site could not have been purchased and subsequently the clubhouse built. I believe that the greatest asset that the club has acquired over the fifty years is not this site but the members' willingness to recognise that we are all wanting the best for the club whilst each having a different needs from the club. It is this spirit of co-operation that has enabled us to build a club able to provide one of the most diverse sailing sites on the East Coast. This has not always been achieved without considerable debate and intelligent discussion along the way but the committees over the years have been able to move the club forward with the full support of the members after such debate. One of the luxuries we have on our site is space. However this does bring its own problems. It is often easier to allow unwanted items to accumulate than tackle the problems of disposing of them. Last winter committee decided that the time had come to tackle this particular area. A start was made by cutting up and removing a vast amount of

trailers and other metal from the site. At the same time Jenny Ball has been attempting to identify the owners of a number of dinghies that appear to be abandoned on the site. It is now intended to dispose of these in the next few months. Once this has been done, the committee will be enforcing the rules relating to the payment of fees or in the last resort the recovery of fees by the sale of such items. In the case of the cruiser fleet, this is already starting with the charging of members to scrap old trailers. By the way, the money raised does not go to the people who provide the labour but to the considerable cost of hiring equipment and more importantly the skips and subsequent disposal of the scrap. Increasingly we are faced with not only higher costs for disposal of waste from the site but greater legislation regarding the method. For example the skip provided throughout the year must not be used for the disposal of metal and garden waste, this has to be separated out. One of the main topics that the committee has had to deal with related to the electrical system. Again it is the requirements of today's legislation that highlighted the problem. The club needs to have its system certified as safe, however, when tested it did not meet today's definition - please do not get the impression that we are using a dangerous system. We were faced then with a number of options; should we do the minimum needed to obtain a certificate, replace like for like, or take a longer term view of replacing the entire system and allow for growth over the next ten, fifteen, or twenty years? I would like to thank Clive Shenton, Frank Bennett, Dave Payne, Dave Steward and all those they consulted for the time and effort freely given on the project to date. As a result of their efforts it was apparent that the most cost-effective long-term solution was its total replacement and expansion. Next they addressed the problem of how to do it. We pride ourselves on being a self help club but sometimes it is right to act as project managers and let the professionals do the work. We decided this was such a case. The latest major infra structure problem has again been highlighted by legislation. I refer to the Galley where the hygiene certificate has not been renewed - again please do not get the impression that we are all about to get food poisoning. So we need to totally refurbish this over the winter. In this case the project can be handled using the club's self help philosophy. Dave Payne has consulted with Belinda Dowley and the certifying authority, he has spoken to various people to acquire the necessary equipment, not necessarily for free but at very reduced cost, and he assures me that he has a team of very willing volunteers to carry out the work. Once this has been done, we are going to have to keep the Galley locked to comply with the legislation. We are currently looking at methods of providing facilities for making hot drinks in another area. Before leaving the subject of the galley, I am sure that you all would like me to thank Belinda and her team for the excellent fare this year. We have continued to invest in replacement of facilities at the club during the year. The most significant being the new RIB, which I understand, is most successful. Jenny Ball carried out much of the initial research and negotiation, and then John salmon and Roy Hardwicke took up the mantle. All of them and the drivers are to be congratulated on the smooth introduction of the boat. As [ have already said in Navigans, we can only apologise for the lack of cleaning during Camping Fortnight. This was due to a lack of communication within the Executive. Having examined all the methods available to us to make the refund, it has been decided to do this as part of the renewal process in January. On the sailing side I will only make a passing comment on the East Coast Piers Race and leave the sailing Secretary to report on this later in the meeting. This year's race must rank as one of the fastest ever sailed. Chris Davies and his team did a splendid job but as always some areas for improvement were identified and are being worked on. On occasions I hear the odd comment that the race is run only for the benefit of a few cat sailors from our club. Just to put the record straight, the entry this year comprised 55 boats from outside the club and 17 from within. I believe this reflects well on the ability of the entire club to stage the event and the commitment of all areas of the club to help each other. I would like to see us aiming for 15 to 20% growth in the numbers sailing the race for each of the next three years. Mike Smith and Malcolm Yeoman introduced a major innovation this year when they dispensed with keg beer and went to bottled in the bar. I believe that this has been a successful move although not without some problems, which they are looking at. MASC AGM [am lucky with our AGM in that a large proportion of the membership attends, it does ask questions and express views, which, whilst it can be uncomfortable at times, does allow the Executive and Main Committee to understand the feelings you have. Unfortunately the MASC suffers from a lack of attendance of members at its AGM. This is in part to due to their failure to publicise the date. This year's Annual General Meeting is on Wednesday 13 November starting at 7:30 at Beehive Lane. As I said earlier the MASC has in the past been very supportive in the development of our site. I would urge as many of you as possible to attend their

meeting and ask any questions you want to. The other area we need to address is representation on their Main Committee; we need at least one but preferably two persons to serve on it. It is only by having this that our views can be expressed and heard, and just as importantly we can know what is being planned for the future. I hope that some of you will contact one of the executive to volunteer to represent us on that committee. As you all are aware the first phase of the replacement of the electrical supply will start in November with the work being carried out in the area of the Dinghy Park, Clubhouse and Tractor shed. The second phase is scheduled to start in May next year mainly affecting the Cruiser Park, Race Reception areas. This work will require our co-operation to clear areas as required and we will inevitably need to carry out some reinstatement work afterwards. Please check in Navigans for advance warning and the need to help with moving of boats etc. Last year a considerable number of people retired from the committee and other positions within the Club so there has been quite a learning curve for many of the replacements and we apologise for any problems experienced as a result. This year we have a much more stable situation but there are some significant gaps to fill. Bob Collins took on the role of Navigans Editor last year, and then unfortunately for us was promoted within the education system and has had to move out of the area. Camping: Hilary Ashley a number of years ago decided that a better method of allocating pitches was required than the First Come First Pitched approach. Quietly and single handedly at that time she set about devising and implementing the system that we see today. After all this time, she has decided to retire from this self-created position and I ask you all to show your appreciation for the time and effort that she and her helpers have put in. Last and most significant is the retirement of Frank Bennett. Subject to your approval later in the meeting John Bird will succeed him . Frank has served as Treasurer for fourteen years and during that time the Club has improved its facilities, the reserve account has grown to a healthy balance to allow major capital expenditure year on year whilst the increase in fees has largely matched inflation. Aside from this, Frank has beena true friend to all who have served with him on the Club's committees over the years. I wish him a long and happy retirement and hope that we will see him around the Club for many years to come. Finally I would like to congratulate Fenella on the programme of social] events she has organised this year. One of my first memories when I joined the club was the Mid Summer Barbecue. Fenella suggested celebrating fifty years of the club by reviving it. She along with members from all sections of the club made a resounding success of the day and evening. All are to be congratulated and I hope that we may see it repeated next year. As I said at the start of my report, the Club has a long tradition of co-operation and friendship between individuals, groups, and fleets. It is also proud of its ability to improve itself by self-help. I firmly believe that these have been paramount to its success in the last fifty years and, if continued, will see its continuing success for at least another fifty years. That ends my report for this year. Commodore's thanks to Frank Bennett, retiring Treasurer. Finally before I close the meeting, I must return to Frank Bennett. It was just over fourteen years ago that I stood down from the post of Treasurer and was introduced to a young lad wearing shorts, quite obviously fresh out of school. In the last fourteen years this lad has blossomed into the fine figure that we know today. I cannot believe that there is an area of the club which has not received his magic touch, be it from chucking lighted paper into the hole we dug to replace the water main to check that we had not punctured the gas pipe, designing and building the gate and clubhouse locking system, maintaining the sewage system and many other jobs. At the same time there cannot be many members who have not benefited from Frank's knowledge and experience. I personally, and I am sure that all other previous Commodores, members of the Executive and main committees, have welcomed his calm, careful analysis and advice over the fourteen years. In addition to this he also found time to carry out the duties of treasurer, a role mainly in the background but most essential to the well being of the club. Without his careful husbanding of the club's finances we would either be paying very much higher fees or be unable to renew and develop the facilities the way that we have. The fact that we are able to move forward with the replacement of the electrical system, whilst reducing our reserve for the next two or three years, and not had to take the alternative route of closing the site is largely due to his skill in making every pound that we pay, stretch and work for all our benefit.

On behalf of those people who have worked with you on the committees over the years, I would ask you to accept this gift. John Salmon Rear Commodore [redacted] [redacted].fsnet.co.uk ‘Mona's Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Six - The Marquesas (French Polynesia) Having sailed engineless into Nuka Hiva we very quickly became enamoured with this first part of French Polynesia. The first morning we were there we visited the Gendarme and were pleased to discover that entry was straightforward and stress-free. Everyone we met was friendly and extremely helpful Taiohae Bay is the main settlement on the island. there is a bank, a hospital and several shops, but the little town is so spread out that at first sight there appears to be very little there and it took us several days to discover all the shops. There was a bit of a swell in the bay but we found it quite relaxing. After rolling down the trades on the milk-shake run, a total lack of motion would have come as a bit of a shock! Nuku Hiva was a very

12 relaxing place to arrive but it wasn't all rest as we had the most amazing mess to clear off the hull. Round the waterline we had been colonised with goose barnacles. These are basically stowaways, and fortunately once you stop moving they tend to jump ship! Above the waterline, however, where the topsides had dipped with the rhythmic rolling, the hull was a glorious yellowy green with patches of weed as extra decoration. Getting all this off turned out to be a major operation that we managed to make last for several weeks. We stayed in Taiohae Bay for 10 days. It was a week before the trawler yacht 'Atlas' arrived with our replacement pump for the engine. The story of our pump had become quite a saga. When he had heard about our problem, Jim had e-mailed his crew Ian who was still in Australia at the time. Ian had got the high-up in Perkins Australia who located the part at a dealer's several hundred miles away and had it flown in to Ian just a few hours before he was due to leave. Within a few days Rauol, a French yachtsman who had been in the Marquesas for a year, managed the far from easy task of fitting the pump. In fact, fitting the pump was easy, it was getting to it in the first place that was the difficult part. As soon as we started the engine again we realised that the bearing on the pump must have been failing for several months. Helen had been saying for a long time that the engine was noisier than it had been. Now we realised why. We were now free to move on. However, our time in Taiohae Bay had been far from wasted. We had done several walks into the hills and discovered our first Tiki Sites. Tikis are old stone carvings. They tend to have goggle-eyed expressions which have a look of aliens about them. An archaeologist we met said that the expressions probably originated from the fact that the statues were modelled on the victims of ritual sacrifice. The Tikis also featured large erect phalluses - however, most of these had been removed on the instructions of the early missionaries that had arrived on the islands in the 18th and 19th centuries. Some of these missionaries had not survived long. It was fascinating to discover that cannibalism had been perpetuated here until less than a hundred years ago. On one occasion we were treated to an impressive display of tribal dancing, one of these being a form of greeting. It featured a lot of chanting and repetition of your name along with chest banging and elbow gesturing. Entertaining though it was, if I had been greeted like that a couple of hundred years ago I think I would have beaten a hasty retreat. After we had been in Taiohae Bay about a week we had been joined by Pat and Olivia on 'Aldebaran'. We set off together on a circumnavigation of the island. Our first stop was Controller Bay where we had the anchorage to ourselves, nestled deep between dark forbidding cliffs. Going ashore we walked through the tiny village, almost buried amid the typically lush surroundings. All the vegetation seemed larger than life. I asked a girl if there was anywhere we could buy bananas. She took us to her home where her family entertained us and showed us round their extensive garden. As well as a hand of bananas they loaded us down with pamplemousse, breadfruit and various other fruit and veg. Before arriving in French Polynesia I had never encountered pamplemousse, a type of grapefruit which quickly became one of my favourite fruit. When we came to leave we tried to pay for these but they refused to accept anything. This was the sort of generosity that we were to experience time and time again in the Marquesas. The next morning we came ashore to attend a service in the local church. The main purpose being to experience the superb Polynesian singing that characterises church services here. Unfortunately the surf was running higher in the morning and by the time we had all got ashore in our dinghy we were all absolutely drenched. When we got to the tiny church it was already pretty full and Pat and I ended up squeezed into a pew near the back. After a while I was aware of a dripping noise and realised that we were making rather a mess on the floor. Pat had taken his socks and sandals off and was attempting to mop the floor with his sock under his bare foot. After a while he bent down and picked his sock up and wrung it out of the window. While this bizarre behaviour was going on the small congregation gave us the benefit of some glorious singing. The whole service was conducted in Polynesian. At the end of the service everyone was really friendly, totally ignoring the fact that we had invaded their service like drowned rats and had proceeded to exhibit some very odd behaviour. We were shown carved wooden tikis and exquisite jewellery . We also had the chance to give some small presents to the children of the family that had been so kind to us the day before. We then moved round to the middle of three inlets that, together, make up Controller Bay. From there we were able to make our way through some dense vegetation to one of the most spectacular tiki ceremonial sites we were to see. On the way we saw a great deal of evidence of earlier Polynesian dwellings. A few hundred years ago the population of these islands was far higher than it is today. Descending from the site we were engulfed in torrential rain which did nothing to dampen our spirits. In fact in this climate it was quite refreshing. The one thing that is cold round here is the rain. On returning to the boats we were cool enough to enjoy hot toddies. The next day we set off round the east coast of the island while Laura for some reason chose to cross the island on foot. As we sailed up the impressive coast about half a mile offshore our GPS plotted on the chart put us at least halfa mile inland! The north coast of the island presented even more deep bays. The one we were headed for, Anaho Bay, provided one of the best anchorages we had ever seen, sheltered as it was by an inner headland, making the anchorage invisible from seaward. A resort nestled behind the beach, but it was so low-key that we only ever saw two guests. There were only one or two locals living in the bay, one of whom insisted on heaping gifts of fruit on Laura. The only thing he wanted in exchange was her promise to marry him. I never could understand why Laura was so much more successful in being given fruit than me. This also applied when it came to getting lifts. On her walk across the island Laura had turned down lifts from every vehicle that passed her. From this bay we undertook an epic walk with Pat across the headland to the next bay to visit yet another tiki site. Olivia, wisely as it turned out, had elected to stay behind on the boat. In our enthusiasm to find it we overshot our target and ended up miles out of our way, but in the process managed to see three more bays. The problem was that the coast road was very open and we were fully exposed to the midday sun. Eventually I met a beer delivery truck coming the other way. They told me I was all wrong and told me to get in. On the way back they picked up Pat and Helen and very

~ kindly took us right up to the tiki site, which turned out to be a very elaborate one. I blamed Pat for taking us so far in the 13 wrong direction and Pat and Helen blamed me - so much for loyalty. The next day we motored 'Muna' round to the bay and returned to the Tiki site where an archaeologist was giving a very interesting talk that answered a lot of the questions we had been asking about the Polynesian civilisation. We carried on our anti-clockwise circumnavigation of Nuku Hiva, having a cracking sail round to Daniel's Bay where Daniels has been entertaining yachties for the past 28 years. From there we had a fascinating walk through dense vegetation up to a waterfall. We swam in the pool, having negotiated the path under several fallen boulders. The route up to the waterfall was littered with overgrown pai pai's or platforms made of large boulders as evidence of what had once been a teeming metropolis. We completed our circumnavigation of the island by returning to Taiohae Bay from where we sailed 25 miles to the island of Ua Pou, anchoring behind the breakwater in the main harbour in Baie D'Hakahau. This was another lovely island with an incredible skyline. The phallus shaped peaks only rarely appeared from behind the clouds. It was here that Laura left us temporarily. Henry on Maritime Express' a Canadian yacht had broken his wrist while climbing to the waterfall in Daniel's Bay. He had had to have pins put in and was therefore somewhat disadvantaged. Laura offered to help out. Our time in this anchorage was enlivened by the fact that the local boat club had a team entered in the Round Moorea outrigger canoe race, due to take place in Tahiti in July. This was a six-man event but for the marathon 80 km race, each canoe has a support boat with a relief crew. Once the race has got under way the crews can change as often as they like. We watched the Ua Pou team practising this changeover. The support boat would drop the relief crew in line in front of the canoe. The canoe would then go alongside the six in the water so they were between the canoe and the outrigger. The ones in the canoe would then leap out the other side, while the new crew clambered in. The Sunday before we moved on, the boat club put ona traditional pig roast, which turned out to be a very sociable occasion and an opportunity to experience traditional Polynesian food. Part Thirty Seven - Marquesas to the Tuamotus We now had 500 miles to cover to reach the Tuamotus. This was the first significant passage that Helen and I had been on on our own for some time. We set off with 'Aldebaran' and rounded the island. As we passed a bay further round we were joined by 'Cap d'Or' and 'Silver Fin’. So it was that four of the five boat that had set off from Los Perles together, were reunited. it was very pleasant on these passages to be able to communicate with other boats via the radio. Once out of VHF range, we normally set up a schedule for an informal 'net' on the SSB. After a quiet start the wind built up enough to give us good progress and pleasant sailing. We settled down to a comfortable beam reach as we were now heading almost south westerly. The second day out we were startled to see what we reckoned to be a sperm whale a good 45' long, placidly swimming alongside us no more than 100' away, blowing merrily. Fascinating though it was, it was quite a relief when it decided to leave us. The first two or three days were generally fairly pleasant. On the fourth day when we had been out of 3 nights, the winds went light onus. We drifted along all day with just a couple of brief squalls to liven things up. By this time 'Cap d'Or' and ‘Aldebaran' were far enough ahead to press on for landfall that day. 'Silver Fin' and ourselves were committed to another night at sea. The Tuamotus are not a place you would choose to arrive at night. That day there were rather ominous reports of bad weather on the French Polynesian forecast. After nightfall there was still very little wind. About 10 o'clock the little wind there was died away completely. I reluctantly started the engine as the motion was so uncomfortable. Within minutes we had, out of nowhere, 35 knots of wind well ahead of the beam. This was to continue, slightly abated, all night and all the next day. After wallowing about with all sail up we set off like a scalded cat. Initially thinking it was just another short-lived squall I hung on to full sail for a while. The auto helm which, up to then, had been doing the steering on this trip, was overwhelmed so we were now committed to hand steering. As the night wore on I put first one, then two reefs in the main. With the headsails partially furled we found that, left to her own devices, 'Muna' could steer herself. This is the sort of weather when we are really grateful for 'Muna's' weight and full-bodied design and we had a remarkably comfortable night, all things considered. As it got light I realised that at our current rate of progress we would have a job reaching our destination by nightfall. I therefore reassessed the rig, put up more sail and started hand steering. We started powering along at 6-7 knots through large seas, just holding our course. It turned out to be a cracking sail and after minimal sleep overnight I really began to enjoy myself. By cracking on we reached the pass at Makemo at dead slack water and had a tranquil passage through, in contrast to ‘Cap d'Or' and 'Aldebaran' who had had quite a bash the day before, entering on the ebb. Once through the pass we headed across the lagoon to an anchorage on the far side. The water in the lagoon was surprisingly rough and we had to be on the alert for isolated coral heads that rose vertically from the 20-30 metre depths. All the atolls in the Tuamotus are basically reef-lined lagoons with small islands, or Motus , scattered about the reefs. These atolls were originally volcanic islands that attracted a fringe of coral reefs. The islands eroded away leaving the coral reef behind. to be continued Malcolm Shaft

Club Notes Commodores notes. On behalf of all those who attended the Laying Up Supper, I would like to thank Fenella for organising a splendid evening in a pleasant location; also the other members of the Club who undertook various functions on the night. I would like to thank the Club and Mavis Weedon for the bouquet of flowers presented to my wife; without her patience and support the job of Commodore would be far more onerous. The Committee and I have been supported by many other members without whose help the Club cannot function. In saying Thank You to them on your behalf, I would like to include the many other partners who tolerate the time that we devote to running the Club. Finally, thanks to all those who come to the Club and enjoy its facilities and the sailing. Without you the Blackwater would lose its friendliest and most diverse club. As some of you may be aware, a suggestion was put forward that there should be some method by which members who were Time but not Cash restrained could make some form of payment in lieu of helping at working parties or in other ways. Earlier this year the Committee asked Clive Shenton and Steve Glynn to explore the possibility and present a proposal to it for consideration. At the last Committee meeting, Clive reported that whilst the idea had a number of benefits to members and the Club, they could not devise a simple and practical method of implementing such a scheme. As a result the Committee has had to abandon the idea for the foreseeable future. We are still looking for someone to join David Thomas on the MASC Main Committee. As many of you are aware the members of the MASC own the Sailing Club site, it is the only asset that they own. It is therefore very much in our interests to ensure that the MASC is well managed and run to ensure that we can continue to enjoy the use of the site. This extends beyond simply paying our fees etc to the MASC to include being actively involved in its management. Any member of the MASC can serve on its Main Committee and I am sure that there must be someone in the Club not actively involved in its management/running at present who can help David one, or very occasionally two evenings, a month to look after our interests. Please do not assume that someone else has stepped forward but contact myself, any other member of the Committee or David if you can spare the time. On 20" February Icom will give a talk about DSC Radio and on 20" March there will be a light hearted quiz as last year. 10 May the Cruiser Fitting out supper will be held at the Sailing Club. 24" May, a Bank holiday cruise to Burnham with a meal at the Swallowtail. 14" to 15" June there will be a trip to Brightlingsea. 6" July ECPR. Neil on behalf of Chris Davies thanked everyone for last year and hopes for support this year. 12" July Watercress Run to Heybridge, followed by barbeque. 2" August for one week, cruiser to St Katherine’s and Medway. 23" August, Bank Holiday cruise up the East Coast. There was a discussion on Shotley versus Ipswich. 11. Cock Up Trophy. There were various contenders but the winner couldn’t have made a more public cock up, his crew mutinied and the resulting spectacle was widely discussed in the yachting press. 12. Mooring Parties. Thanks to Derek and Doreen for providing hot drinks and snacks for the mooring teams. 13. Any Other Business. Victory Marina in the Medway was recommended as a possible club stop over. Colin Leveridge proposed thanks for the tractor and winch teams. Malcolm Yeoman concerned about access road re electrics. Dave Payne assured him it would be reinstated. Neil, on behalf of the fleet, thanked Roger. Meeting closed at 21.15.

If anybody has lost a set of tractor keys, please contact me. We still have a number of homeless dinghies to be claimed behind the mast container. Please avoid driving in the cat field as it is very boggy at the moment. The next event will be a talk by Gordon Dickens, Harbourmaster of the tidal Thames, on pleasure boating on the river Thames from sea reach to Tower Bridge. This will be on Thursday 23" January at 19:30 at the MASC in Beehive Lane. I would like to wish everybody a merry Christmas and a happy New Year. Roger Camp News RNLI Rowing Race, Wednesday 1st January 2003, the Hythe Quay, Maldon, organised by the Maldon Little Ship Club. Time of race, about 10.30am, is earlier this year, as is the daytime high tide at Maldon. I'm not sure if the usual Marconi Boat will be there this year. Perhaps a new boat and occupants might like to join the fun. If the weather is half reasonable this can be a very enjoyable event for the crowd of spectators who watch on the quay and we usually see many familiar MSC faces going by. If you have any cash left after Christmas please take it with you, there will be plenty of collecting boxes for the RNLI. As well as the couple of adjacent hostelries there is food, drink and shelter in the Maldon Little Ship Club. Maureen Ball Reminder that Chain and Shackles of decent quality at very reasonable prices are available as usual by contacting Don Holdsworth on [redacted] Maureen Ball My thanks to the members of the Committee who subscribed to the splendid barometer and watch presented to me at the AGM on my retirement as Hon. Treasurer. It has been a satisfying task over the 14 years, and I am grateful for the help and co-operation of the many Members with whom I have interacted. I'm sure that you will give the same support to John Bird, who will do an excellent and professional job. Frank Bennett An Oil disposal tank is being delivered to the club in the next month, ready for winter use. It will be situated in the cruiser park. Ed Our very own Rear Commodore doing his stuff at the Solo Nationals in Paignton this summer. John is clearly concentrating hard. Roger Smith

One or two members who cannot get enough of it, are tackling Winter Series at other clubs, notably Kate and Dave Williams. I am told they are going great guns at Maylandsea Bay. Most of you will no doubt be servicing boats and equipment, and making your plans for next season. Good for you. Much better than waiting till the last minute isn’t it! The Club programme for 2003 is now finalised, and it will not be long before we can get started. The Sailing Sub Committee continues to meet over the winter, with one or two new Fleet Captains emerging to add new ideas and energy to the process. There is now a new Medium Cat Fleet established which takes the place of the diminishing Dart 15 fleet, while still offering D15 and others of the smaller sized catamarans in the Club, a fleet to race in. Club Notes Commodore My apologies for not attending the working party due to ill health and very many thanks to all those who turned out on a very wet day. Iam amazed by all the work that was done, the hedge in the dinghy field cut back, the fence for the dinghy park moved, and further progress on the Galley refurbishment. These are the high visibility signs of what was done, I am sure that many small items were also dealt with. Looking to the future, many of you will have been contacted by your Fleet Captains and press ganged into helping with a number of projects over the winter. Obviously we need to complete these by the start of the sailing season. One of these is the disposal of a number of dinghies/catamarans where the owners cannot be identified. In next months Navigans you will find a full list of these either by the name of the boat or a description. If you own one of these, or know who does, please contact Kevin Kirby urgently. THIS WILL BE YOUR LAST CHANCE BEFORE THE DISPOSAL STARTS. It has been pointed out to me that a number of members have received renewal forms for their MASC membership which imply that you need to pay the Section Fee, £16.00 plus VAT, to them. This is not the case as it is included in your fees to the Sailing Club and will be paid by the Sailing Club to the MASC. DO NOT PAY THE SECTION FEE TO THE MASC when paying your MASC subscription. The days are lengthening and the start of the season is approaching. Lets all hope for some good sailing this year. Neil Pembleton Cat Fleet I hope you all had a good Christmas and are enjoying a good New Year so far. The new season is approaching fast; sailing commences 23rd March, prior to that we have the cat-fleet working party which comprises of two specific tasks and with as many hands as possible should not take too long. The date is Sunday 9th March starting at 9:30am. The jobs are to clean and paint the race marks and to clear the cat-field of all abandoned cats and trailers. They will be identified and a description posted in the next issue of Navigans, after which if not claimed they will be disposed of accordingly. It will be too wet to cut the grass but strimmers, scythes and bow saws (scrapers, wire brushes and old paint brushes for the race marks.)etc. will come in handy. Please try to attend, I appreciate that your leisure time is in demand. A couple of dates for your diary Sailboat and Windsurf show at Alexandra Palace- London. Saturday/Sunday 1st/2nd March: 10am-Spm. This is well worth a visit if you have never been. East Coat Piers Race- Sunday 6th July. Please cemenibes we are still looking for extra sponsorship and over the weekend looking for people to help on "Race Reception", Bar, trot boat (taking/collecting crew to and from Mother Boats). If you have time available however little and would like to help over the weekend, please give me a call or catch me at the club most weekends. Thank You Kevin Kirby Cat Fleet Captain [redacted]

Cruiser Fleet Not much to say at this time of year but I would like to thank Roy Bellord for being the prime mover in obtaining a waste oil tank. When this is up and running it is for waste oil only, no paint, antifouling, spirit or water. At the cruiser AGM both Shotley and Ipswich were discussed as a destination for the August cruise. A number of current issues were brought up, most of which will be fed back to the Sailing Sub-Committee for consideration. Club Notes eePw Commodore THIS IS IMPORTANT — IT CONCERNS YOUR SUBSCRIPTIONS Occasionally the Executive and Management Committees of the Sailing Club find themselves sitting on the ‘Horns of a Dilemma’. This is just such a time and I need to explain the difficulties we are dealing with. This problem concerns our relationship with Marconi Athletic and Social Club (MASC). Firstly, we must recognise that, as a section of MASC we have an obligation to operate within that structure. We also clearly have an obligation to do all that we can to protect the interests of our own members within the Sailing Club. We now find that these twin requirements are in conflict. Accounts published by MASC at the recent AGM in November 2002 showed that it incurred a trading loss in 2001/2002. Previous discussions and pronouncements had led us to understand that actions had been taken to address the underlying problems; the new subscription structure and the new gym were intended to ensure that the situation was reversed. It had been said that the deficit would be reduced and even suggested that a small profit could be produced for 2002/2003. Clear indications now are that MASC will create an even larger trading loss in that period and, more significantly, that the loss-making trend continues unchecked. When we look back at the MASC Main Committee minutes for December 2002 (after the AGM) we find two items that only serve to add to our concern: I quote from the minutes: "Financial Situation Le The General Manager, after making Les Murray (MASC President) aware of the financial situation, has set up a meeting with himself, President, Trustee and MASC Treasurerfor Friday 1 3 December. A committee member stated that it’s very clear that the income of the Club does not meet with expenditure and that the Management must take steps to rectify this situation. Proposals to be presented. Treasurers Report ms The Treasurer presented the accounts for September, who pointed out the increasing trading deficit. All areas of Club activities are down on previous years in particular catering which is now showing a £5000.00 deficit. There will be no further capital expenditure for the Club or Sections until the position improves." Our discomfort arises from the fact that, as a Section of MASC, we are obliged to hold all our funds within MASC. This means that the cash to meet our week by week expenses and the Reserve Fund which is used to cover our major expenditure is with MASC; we are not allowed to have an independent bank account under the constitution as it stands. Our Reserve Fund is projected to be £30000 at the end of the present financial year and a substantial portion of that is earmarked for the major overhaul of the electricity system, which is ongoing. We need to be satisfied that our funds are not threatened by the apparent financial weakness of our parent. As soon as the above facts became clear to our Executive I was tasked with writing to the senior managers of MASC to seek an explanation and assurance that matters were being properly dealt with. Informal discussions with officers of MASC had not produced the answers we need. I wrote a letter to the MASC Trustee, President, Chairman and General Manager on 28" January 2003. To date, and in spite of prompting, I have received neither acknowledgement nor reply from any of these people. The Executive Committee is clear in the view that, although we would not wish to do anything to harm MASC or our relationship with them, our first duty is to protect as far as possible the interests of our own members. The Management Committee fully supports this view and has decided that it will be sensible to stage Sailing Club subscription payments for 2003. This approach will afford some measure of protection and underline our serious concerns. We plan to collect half the subscription value at the normal time and the balance during June 2003. Those members who have already sent a renewal payment to the Membership Secretary will have their cheques returned with a request that they re-issue two cheques of equal value. One of these cheques should be post-dated

30" June 2003. Those who have yet to renew (and the normal deadline applies) should split their payments in the same way. We obviously regret the need for this sort of action and very much hope that we can quickly restore normal relationships with MASC. We are confident, however, that members will support the view that this is a situation that could not go unchallenged. This action is designed to be both protective and remedial; we will, however, continue to review the situation and be prepared to act appropriately in the event that we do not receive the required response from MASC. Solo Fleet Well it now seems like a lifetime since Christmas and the February blues are well and truly here but don't fret we have the excitement of many social events to look forward to. Dennis Dear has been working hard to organise two events; bowling at The Edwardian Club in Billericay and the traditional pre season meal in the club house. This latter event has been under some question due to the fact that one of its staunchest supporter’s in recent times has put his house on the market and may be leaving our ranks although at this stage we don't know quite what will happen. Doug Eyles if he does leave us will be sorely missed in many ways but hopefully everything will fall through and Doug will be forced to sign up for another year! Another problem with the meal has been the catering arrangements - at least the use of club facilities which because of new health regulations has called into question our use of the galley. We all hope something will be sorted out on this front soon. As I'm sure you are all aware we have a work party pending on the 9th of March and I'm sure we can rely on the usual high turn out from our fleet. I will be contacting key people to delegate tasks nearer to the day so try and contain your enthusiasm until then - if by any chance you don't hear from me please don't assume that you are off the hook - just bring yourself, a pair of stout boots, gloves and any useful looking cutting, screwing scraping and painting implements you can find and get down there. Final bit and on a more serious note please be aware that the new power cable to the club has been laid straight across the dinghy park running at an angle in a straight line between the main entrance and the supply pole over in the hedge where the boats are stored for winter. Just to make matters more interesting it has been buried about fourteen inches down and although armoured will not withstand a direct hit with a piece of 2 inch angle iron. YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED. The use of our usual 18inch long ground anchors is now verboten and Barry Hutt and Claire Davies are busy sorting out a new system. In fact there may well be another piece in this issue explaining the plans and execution of the new system. If not and you are taking your boat down to the club early then please use some sense and keep clear of the cable. (I hate the smell of frying flesh or is that flying fish!) Dave Steward A Message of Limited Appeal This will only be of interest to that select but misunderstood band of folk who are the Camping Fortnight Crowd. I need the help of just one or two of you to ensure the smooth running of this important two-week event.

Preparations for the fortnight are already in hand in some quarters and we can be confident that, when the time arrives, the bar will have been stocked, skip movements will have been arranged, sludge gulpers will have been booked and cleaning rotas will have been finalised. All of this activity is in the hands of various club officers - but none of them are campers. We need a couple of volunteers to share OOD-type responsibility for the on-shore aspects of the fortnight. They would need to take responsibility for knowing who should be doing what and when they should be doing it — and then have the information to enable them to co-ordinate a proper response if things do not go quite according to plan. We are quite definitely not looking for someone to undertake cleaning or bar work or rubbish removal - just someone with the means and the will to make sure those things happen as they should. I don't expect to hear from anyone who is heavily involved with Cadet Week and it might not be reasonable to rope in a member who already has extensive responsibilities elsewhere within the club ... but that does actually leave us with quite a few suitable candidates. Please think seriously about taking on an important role in support of an important event in our calendar. You can make a significant contribution to the success of the event without seriously affecting your own involvement or enjoyment - job sharing and mobile phones should minimise any potential inconvenience. Please call for an informal chat about this exciting opportunity (without obligation). Bill Broad who at the time was the Vicar of Steeple and the surrounding Parish. His aim, in founding The Trust, was to provide sailing adventures for disadvantaged young people; an aim The Trust continues to this day. Nick Back Chief Executive Ships Log Woody and Frank, to the Caribbean. For ‘Woody’ and I, our journey to the Caribbean started at 5am in a snowstorm on a dark M25, to Gatwick, to catch a JMC Airbus A330 charter flight. 8 hours later we landed at Port Salines on Grenada, and on reaching the open door of the plane we descended the steps in a blast of heat and bright sunshine. Customs in Grenada are typical in taking their time with much questioning, and rubber-stamping of documents, but we waited our turn, they let us in, so we left the airport building before they changed their mind, and found a ramshackle taxi to Spice Island Marina, Prickly Bay. Our boat for the holiday was ‘Essex Girl’ a C&C 30 built in Ontario Canada and owned by Graham from Blackwater Sailing Club. An evening meal in the marina restaurant followed by sleep, and on Sunday morning we motored round to ‘Hog Island’ a sheltered anchorage favoured by ‘live aboards’. ‘Hog’ is famous for ‘Roger’s Rum Shack’ set amongst the trees on a beach of white sand, and on Sundays there is always a barbecue, fortified by strong rum and cokes and the local ‘Carib’ beer. Our friend ‘Thilo’ the Mad German joined us. Thilo lives aboard a 40ft Wharram catamaran during long holidays from Cologne. I afraid we all got steadily merrier. Late that night we went to bed soon to be awakened by a splash. ‘Woody’, sleeping in the cockpit had got up to take a leak and had fallen in! Graham and I scrambled to the cockpit to find Woody appearing over the stern dripping but none the worse for his dip. The Grenadines are split into different countries and so on Monday we called at Prickly Bay Customs to officially book out. We then continued to St Georges the main town of Grenada to visit the supermarket, fill up with water and diesel, and change some money at the Bank. The Grenadines currency is the Eastern Caribbean Dollar, which is unobtainable in the UK so we took Sterling plus a small amount of US Dollars (which are accepted). A visit to the market for fresh fruit and the Grenada Yacht Club for showers, then back to ‘Essex Girl’ for a short passage up to ‘Halifax Bay’ where we anchored, dined, and watched the locals fishing, accompanied by a huge elegant yacht with a paid crew waiting on the guests. We left at 9am in the morning for a 6-hour beat North to Tyrell Bay on Carriacou passing over ‘Kick em Jenny’ the site of a volcano. Tyrell is a good sheltered anchorage and features a mangrove swamp where we explored 2 abandoned yachts. Then we visited the Carriacou YC for showers and dinner. Woody found a cockroach in his shower and chased it round the bathroom bashing it with a broom. The next day we sailed round to ’Sandy Island’, about 100 yards long the archetypal island with azure blue water, white sand, palm trees, and a reef for snorkelling. In the evening we were invited aboard a Sigma 41 from BSC Maldon, which had completed the Atlantic Rally for Cruisers. That night it rained and ‘Woody’ was forced to leave his cockpit berth and sleep with me! Next day, up anchor, and off to Clifton Town on Union Island where you run the gauntlet of boat boys selling moorings, fish, etc, to book in with Customs and Immigration for this group of islands, then over to Mayreau, Saltwhistle Bay...more swimming and dinner under the moon. Morning came, up anchor, and off to Tobago Cays, a paradise, of islands and reefs protecting the anchorage from 3000 miles of ocean. Woody and I paddled the dinghy onto the reef and tied it a mooring provided. Then over the side for the best snorkelling ever. Evening came, a fish dinner, with the sound of the waves breaking on the reef, the Trade winds blowing strongly, and Woody in the cockpit again, playing spinnakers with his bed sheet! In the mooring we re-anchored in the lee of ‘Petit Bateau Island’ where passengers from the cruise liner ‘Club Med 2’ were landed for swimming. Woody found a lobster in the reef and set of in pursuit for our lunch.... After a lunch of egg butties, we sailed North to Charles Bay, Canouan, the most northerly point of our cruise. More swimming,

and in the evening ashore, past an empty luxury hotel, and on to Annie’s the local bar. Here we met 2 guys from Poole who had sailed across in their 29 ft Albin Ballad. We then drank too much and on returning to our now deflated engineless dinghy we blagged a tow from the crew of a J boat Jeau d’Espirit, which had also done the ARC. We were a bit slow to get up in the morning........ but we upped anchor and sailed fast back to Union Island for Customs check out, more shopping and a conch roti, a sort of curried pasty made from conch a huge welk, very good! Away from Union and over to Hillsborough town on Carriacou to clear in with Customs and Immigration for Grenada. During the night Woody got rained out of the cockpit and morning found him asleep on the saloon floor. Up anchor, then off to Petit Martinique, where skip served up mangos, followed by avocado, and tomato. Woody and I went ashore and climbed the hill for a magnificent view of Tobago Cays Union, Canouan, Mayreau, and Petit St Vincent and further North the distant St Vincent and Bequia. Woody comments in the log here that, ‘we were in bed by 7.45pm ....’Essex Girl’ is becoming like an old peoples home!’ We left Petit Martinique early en route for Grenada, and sailing fast arrived off another Sandy Island, this one being where the ‘Bounty’ adverts are filmed. However it was too dodgy to anchor, so we sailed on towards the NE of Grenada. Ever since leaving Grenada, we had been towing a fishing lure with no luck, but suddenly the line was running and the reel screeching. Skipper Graham grabbed the rod, yelled at us to; ‘stop the ****** boat and get the HEHE oaff ..’ a lot of heaving and grunting and over the side came a beautiful Tuna. ‘Get the rum! What for? ...Give it a drink’, I shoved the bottle down it’s mouth....that’s how they do it....stuns the fish so you don’t have to bash it with the winch handle! ......... Ok, calm down, get underway, ...half an hour later the reel’s going again....more panic, more rum and this time it is a very big ‘King Fish’ nearly 4 ft long! Well that was the end of fishing for that day and by evening we had entered Clarkes Court Bay on Grenada, and anchored for the night off Woburn village. Graham called up ‘Little Dipper’ a Rasta restaurant...’Can you cook our fish?...No problem man bring him along’. Suddenly there was ‘Thilo’...remember him? ....the Mad German...’come and have dinner Thilo...OK Man’. Now Thilo needed to go back over the reef to his Wharram, so we waited for him. Eventually he returned, with a cut over his eye and a large bump on his head. ‘What happened to you?’ .......... *Well.... (in a German/South African accent)...I missed my way in the dark...the engine hit the reef, and I fell over the bow and head butted the TOOL ccscewew exe >Oh deary deary me’....we said... “you’d better have a drink!’ And so we went ashore, climbed the hill to Little Dipper and had the best meal of my life....for 3 quid!...then the trouble started, because Woburn is noted for Nimrod’s Bar. Now old man Nimrod had died just 3 weeks before, but his son had continued the tradition of serving yachtsmen. The bar is just a concrete shack, which sells groceries rum and beer. Behind the bar there are several visitor books signed by a generation of yachtsmen from all over the world. However you must ’cross the bridge’ which entails drinking a shot of 140% proof rum followed by a drink of water. If you survive this you can continue with the other local customs, which I had better not mention here! Next day we sailed round to Prickly Bay to anchor alongside ‘Jo’ a 26 year old from Norway. He had come via Caledonian Canal, Belfast, Isle of Man and Cork in a 31 footer. I must admit to feeling somewhat humble, as this quiet man casually mentioned the cockpit filling with water during the Atlantic crossing! For our last day we visited St Georges for souvenirs, followed by beers in the Nutmeg restaurant on the harbour side. We visited the Grenada YC on our return, and could not resist going over an old Westerly Conway for sale. The rest of the day we pondered the pro’s and con’s of boat ownership in the West Indies, and for our last night at the marina, we drank beer, listened to the Steel Band and the Reggae Band till 2 am, with Jo, and I think we invited him to visit MSC, on his back to Norway.....I think.....you see, we were very tired, and very Frank Burgess

BACSPA Last December I attended a meeting of the BLACKWATER & COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION and as on previous occasions I am reporting on matters raised which I feel may be of interest to you. Under the Eastern Region RYA Committee Report, reference was made to the McKinsey RYA Organisation & Governance Recommendations which in essence proposes the streaminlining of the Council and that Regional Chairmen are always to be Council Members. It proposes changes to RYA Central Committee that include a general reduction in size and less frequent meetings. The Chairman of BACSPA is not convinced of the efficacy of this and fears it reduces the input of the Clubs and Members and strengthens that of the staff,and has written an appraisal expressing these concerns i.e. the idea that it is necessary to reduce the influence of the clubs on Council as against the personal membership seems to be based entirely on the perceived mismatch in numbers and hoped the Council will recognise the weaknesses in this report and the danger of creating a more centrist arrangement that does not make best use of the people with experience based in the Regions. Asked whether there would be any opportunity to object to the proposals, the Chairman answered no ! It was pointed out by me that people joined clubs so that their voices could be heard. Peter Woods BIRC Cruiser Group announced he had resigned from his post on the Cruising Committee in protest at these changes. No one at the meeting had seen a copy of the RYA Briefing. It was pointed out the RYA Eastern Newsletter was available on the Internet. r PLANNING APPLICATIONS & DEVELOPMENTS :- MALDON - removal of fixed jetties and replaced with floating pontoons and new piling (near the chandlery) WALTON BACKWATER - planning application for coastal protection works to create new land wall and protect saltmarsh. BRIGHTLINGSEA - it is understood that James & Stone site with planning permission is now up for sale. ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES : - The Chairman signed up to the aims of the Colne Estuary Strategy as it was not at variance with BACSPA's aims. WINDFARMS : - A meeting was held with the Gunfleet developer in London on 5 November to examin concerns about yacht mast clearance in worst conditions as tower heights have been reduced by 5m. This battle continues through RYA Central. Also the developers are reverting to the Trinity House minimum for marking and the chairman is pressing RYA Central to tackle this issue. An Environmental Impact Study is being prepared. BRADWELL NUCLEAR POWER STATION :

In a letter to the RYA the Chairmans stated that Environmental Inpact Statement on De-Commissioning does not appear to give any consideration to the impact on either commercial or leisure boats in the estuary, visability of the buildings is such that they are said to be used a navigational aid for sailing boats in the estuary both day & night.Cessation of lighting on the building means it would be lost as a navigational aid. The Baffle Wall will be removed but not for several years however, once removed there could be a hazard to anchoring in the form of radioactive contamination of the sediment resulting from routine discharges over the years, It is perhaps possible such contamination may be experienced when recovering anchors, NAVIGATION : - Harwich Harbour Approaches/River Stour/River Orwell - Turbidity & Wave Measurement Buoys have been established. Description - ODAS Special Mark with yellow cross topmark. Light Characteristics - Each buoy is fitted with a yellow flashing light group flash (5) every 20 seconds. Each buoy has an instrument package suspended underneath and should be given a wide berth, mariners are requested to report any defects to Harwich VTS. Two yellow toroidal buoys established in the following WGS84 positions :- Site 5 Lat, 51 57' 1784N: Long. O01 15' 8990E Site 6 Lat. 51 59' O344N: Long. O01 16' 6938E Harwich Approaches - wreck of a yacht is located 7 cables SSW of the Rough Buoy WGS 84 position Lat.51 54'6980 N: Long. 01 30'2141 E 0. B. A. Chris Edwards - Tollesbury C.C. and Chairman of BACSPA has been elected Vice Chairman of the Eastern Region RYA also Chairman of the Training Panel for Eastern Region. There was no further news on the Piling at West Mersea. To date none had been removed or replacedand they were not being used. The question of whether they were dangerous in any way is being investigated. Derek Kirbby — BACSPA Representative

[redacted] Tail-Piece March is here already, and with it the start of the new sailing season. In case you have not noticed — Spring Points racing starts on Sunday 23 March. I hope we can start with a good turn out from all fleets as a suitable reward for all the work that has been put in by committee and working parties to enable this to happen. It may be tempting fate to say it, but the weather is often excellent for the opening day. After much deliberation, the plan for protection of the new electricity cables beneath the dinghy park has been decided. This consists of paving over the cable routes to prevent inadvertent damage from dinghy securing stakes. It is not anticipated that this will prevent any dinghies from being adequately secured, but care must be taken not to move or damage any of the paving slabs after they have been put in place. Thanks are due to the anne Fleet who have devised this plan and agreed to lead a working party to carry out the work. I know that Barry Hutt is working on a new layout for the dinghy park, so when you bring your boats down to the club at the start of the season, please be careful to comply with instructions for their location, to ensure that the new layout is adopted with the minimum of hassle. If in doubt, consult with Barry. It is quite a long time since the MSC Race Officers last got together to debate concerns and issues, and discuss possible improvements to the way in which we run our races. For this reason Dave Williams has issued an invitation to all R.O.s for a meeting at MASC, Beehive Lane, at 19.45 on Thurs 13 March. This type of event has proved to be very useful, informative and good fun in the past, so I would like to encourage all R.O.s, assistant R.O.s, and indeed anyone who is interested in the way that our racing is administered, to attend. All the best for a great sailing season! John Salmon Rear Commodore [redacted] [redacted].fsnet.co.uk 10

The Trust works principally with groups of young people, upwards of 10 years oldin particular those young people who are socially, mentally or physically disadvantaged. We aim to provide an opportunity for the groups to experience the adventure and challenge of life at sea by taking an active rolein running and sailing the vessel. Few other environments can match a large sailing vessel for providing young people with the opportunity to develop life skills and stretch personal boundaries. To assist with the fund raising activities for our Queen Galadriel Refit project Charles and Rupert Anderson have very kindly offered to run in The London Marathon on behalf of The Trust. Club Notes eare Commodore Over the winter period, a great deal of work has been carried out at Stansgate to maintain and improve the Clubhouse and site. This has included the installation of the new power cable to the Clubhouse and the provision of power sockets around the exterior of the building. This left the problem of protecting it across the dinghy park at which moment Claire Davies came forward with the idea of laying the slabs, much more cost effective than any ideas from the Executive Committee and providing a permanent mark. The Handicap and Windsurfer Fleets then held their own working party the week before the main one and carried out the work. In the meantime David Payne decided that he and a small band of very willing helpers (he assures me although I am told otherwise) decided to destroy the Galley and then rebuild it. As we can all see the result is a tremendous improvement and we have been able to renew the necessary certificate from Maldon Council so that Belinda Dowley and her team can continue to keep us fed and watered. At this point Fenella Thomas decided that she would set about improving the saloon. From somewhere she found a team to tackle the project. They stripped the area, prepared and washed all the walls before redecorating and making new curtains. Last Sunday, we were all able to see the results at the working party. This was one of the best attended that I have seen for many a year. All the fleets were well represented and it was just as well that the Handicap and Windsurfers had their go the week before. We could not have accommodated everyone in the Clubhouse. On a glorious day the Cat Fleet set about a major clearance of the cat field, the Cruiser Fleet destroyed a few old trailers, the Solo Fleet put the Race Box together along with moving all the outside furniture into position. In addition a wealth of other tasks were completed. While all this activity at Stansgate has been going on the Executive and Main Committee were debating the best way to protect our members fees which we have to pay to the MASC. The response by you, the members, to our request for you to send us two cheques has been overwhelming. We had anticipated that some members would have considerable doubts and might not renew, in the event Nick and Jan had the major problem of emptying their over full letter box each day and almost everyone had supplied the replacement cheques within ten days of the letter going out. As your Commodore, I feel very privileged to be a member of a Club which wholeheartedly supports its ethos of self help and which has demonstrated such overwhelming support for the decisions taken by the Main Committee. Given this support, I am convinced that we will weather the current problems at the MASC and that the Club will continue to flourish and grow into the future. Finally the time is rapidly approaching to dig out those sailing clothes and get back on the water. I hope that we all have a successful and enjoyable season. THANKS TO YOU ALL This list does not pretend to include everyone who has put time in at the Club over the winter but I would particularly like to thank those who worked on the Galley, Saloon and Dinghy Park which included: Jenny Ball, Jenny Miller, Nick Miller, Michael Miller, Malcolm Thomas, Les Hurrell-Smith, Dave Williams, Kate Williams, Dave Steward, John Weedon, Glenis Monks, Steve Monks, Steve Ash, Christina Hutt, Belinda Dowley, Kevin Dowley, Tim Dowley, Dave Payne, Maggie Boreham, Dave Ball, Mike Boreham , Jane Townsend, Gordon Flemons, Barry Hutt, Tristan Hutt, Nick Miller, Richard Dixon, Richard Jones, Roy Debney, Mr & Mrs R Wilson, Phil Dowsett, Dave Thomas, Barry Merke, Ian Edgeway, Dougie (surname unknown at time of writing, but he's quite unique!), Larry Walters, John Littlewood, Jon Smith, Frank Burgess, Tim Dowley, James Tovey, Peter Tovey, Steve Glynn, Debbie Glynn. Apologies if I have missed anyone out but I am working from lists supplied by Fenella, Claire and David who deserve thanks for organising it all. I also thank every one else who has helped in any way over the winter and I suspect that the full list would include virtually all our members. Many thanks to you all. Neil Pembleton

Pat Black Membership Registrars Annual Report In December 2002, 388 membership forms were produced via a report and sent out to members. As of this date (14/3/2003) we have 340 members who have renewed with 12 of those still owing the two cheques as requested in the Commodores letter dated 15 Feb 2003. In general, members response to that letter was very positive and on behalf of the Commodore and the Main Committee I would like to thank you all. We now have the e-mail addresses of 144 members, more than 40% of the total membership. There are currently 48 members from last year who have not renewed. I will be writing to these ex-members. Last year we were new to the process and were a little flexible over the renewal closing date as stated in rule 8e. We had intended to stick rigidly to the rules this year but the late changes to the payment requirements meant that it made sense to be flexible. Several letters have now been sent to members who have not come back with the two cheques. One issue that I would like to remind members of is the requirement to keep us up to date with address and boat details. Several membership forms went to the wrong address and some members only notified us of additional or changed boat details that had occurred during the previous year on their renewal forms. Renewal forms were therefore produced with the wrong information that caused extra work in levying the adjusted fees. We will try again next year to apply the rules as they are stated in the yearbook. Thus far I can only offer thanks to late paying members for adding to club funds but no thanks for extending an already lengthy task for Jan and I. If any member has any problems with their membership pack please do not hesitate to contact me. Nik and Jan Membership Registrars [redacted]

ECPR - A call for support — 5" /6" July Last year Once again, we are at the point when we galvanise support for the Piers Race weekend. Chris Davis is in the chair again ably assisted by the Piers Race Committee. The Race The race, a long distance catamaran event starting from Osea Pier and sailing to Walton-on-the-Naze Pier and then back, is once again expected to attract top catamaran sailors from across Britain and Europe. This year the race will be started by Reg White OBE, Tornado Olympic Gold medallist. The Charity Possibly one of the most significant differences the Piers Race has over other sailing events, is the generation of funds for our own locally based sailing charity “The Cirdan Trust”. You may be familiar with their Thames Barge ‘Xylonite’ which operates out of the Blackwater for most of the season. In addition, their other boats include the Robert Clark designed ‘Hartlepool Renaissence’, a classic Edwardian yacht called ‘Duet’ and The Queen Galadriel a fine old Baltic Trader. While Maldon remains their base, they ply the waters of the north east/Scotland, the south coast and the south west/Channel Islands and Scilly Isles respectably. The Cirdan Sailing Trust provides sailing breaks for the disabled, disadvantaged as well as their helpers (not necessarily together). The money we raise goes towards bursaries which help those less able to pay make use of the charity’s services. You may recall some of the letters of appreciation published in a previous edition of Navigans and the impact of what we were able to do for some of the youngsters involved. While in previous years we have supported the RNLI, Sailability (the RYA charity for disabled sailors) we have provided over £70,000 for charities in total. No mean feat for a sailing club and something we all should be proud of. Backbone Again as usual, a copy of the weekend’s questionnaire is in this issue; please don’t forget that if you do respond, your offer will be taken up so keep an eye on Navigans news about the weekend and definitely please do turn up at the weekend. For cruiser owners, we will continue to use MII/ch80 for routine comms although we can accommodate those of you still on MI. If you do have a cruiser and would like to do a bit more with the weekend I would love to hear from you. While cruisers provide the backbone for the weekend’s support we always need additional help with running the bar, reception, runners, spotters, trolleys, rescue crews and so on. There is input from across the club so don’t feel bashful about lending a hand. Special race with special support We are all justifiably proud of the contribution we make to Cirdan and as mentioned, it is unique in the sailing world. Other long distance events have sprung up since MSC established the Piers Race 17 years ago but we remain the only one with the charity link as well as establishing standards that other events wish to emulate. We have made a big difference to disabled sailors over the years and we really appreciate the help and support we receive from you all. Once again I thank all of you who have helped in the past and my deepest gratitude goes out to those able to make a contribution this year. Charles Anderson

Tail-Piece By the time this is published many of you will have had your first sample of sailing for the year, and for many others plans and preparations will be well advanced. I hope all is going well and that 2003 provides you with some really enjoyable sailing. I know we keep banging on about checking to see when your name appears on the duty roster for Race Office or Support Boat duties, and that there are probably other reminders in this edition, but I hope you will forgive one more reminder from me because it is so vital for the effective delivery of our race programme. The people who plan and co-ordinate these duties put in a lot of time and effort to making them as workable as possible for the Club and its members, and it is a huge help to them if you can use the duty lists to negotiate swaps for any day when you are unable to fulfil your assigned duty. If you have volunteered for duties this year (or would like to!), but your name does not appear on any of the rosters, please let Dave Williams, Les Hurrell-Smith or myself know, as we still have some personnel shortages on both Race Office and Support Boat Rosters. I will shortly be setting up the first of our Club sponsored First Aid Courses which are aimed specifically at support boat crews with RYA recommended content. I would still like to have a few more names on a reserve list to cover the situation where some individuals can not attend on the prescribed day, so if you would like to take advantage of this training opportunity please let me know. There was a good turn out for the Race Officers Seminar at MASC in March, and I hope attendees benefited from the discussions and information exchange which included latest changes to Guidelines, Sailing Instructions, and Codes of Practice. We also have some new ideas to follow up. Anyone who missed the meeting but would like a briefing on current practice can get copies of the relevant documents from Dave Williams or myself. Happy sailing. John Salmon Rear Commodore [redacted] [redacted].fsnet.co.uk Ld

Thanks Rog.” I'm sure you all know by now that we have an Open meeting on the Sunday Ist of June. There's no such thing as bad publicity however, so here it is again! Last year's event was very successful with a high turnout from our own fleet and a good number of visitors from a variety of clubs. This was due in large part to all the hard work behind the scenes put in by a small (but perfectly formed) group of our guy's efforts. This year we have taken stock of last year's strengths and weaknesses and hope in tum to improve an already excellent weekend's sailing. So what do we have planned for you? This is a good limber up for the Sunday, unfortunately I need about a week of this to do any good but there you are! Saturday evening we can light the barbeque and maybe even to cook something on it! Bring along your favourite cuts and char them to a cinder in the traditional fashion. Or join me down at the local for some decent cooking... Sunday morning our core team of organisers will be around from 8.30 or so. If you are sailing, as most of you wall want to be, then it will be worth getting there in good time say 09.00, a) to grab one of Belinda's now legendary bacon rolls and b) to be around to welcome and assist any of the huge number of visiting competitors we are expecting to turn up. (Don't worry about not being a member of the Class Assoc. it just means that your first place position can't be counted, shame!) e We need some helpers on the hard to man handle and marshal trolleys etc. and assist the O.0.D. with looking after any retirees etc. during the day. I look forward to seeing you, please support if you can as we are trying hard to make this year’s event a memorable one. If you want any further information please get in touch and I will try to help. Best Regards and best of luck on the day. News WIN A WILDWIND SAILING HOLIDAY IN ECPR SUPER RAFFLE. Enclosed with this issue of Navigans are two books of tickets for an exciting new, enlarged ECPR Raffle. First Prize is a holiday for two with Wildwind at their Mediterranean base. Second Prize winner will enjoy a two night Getaway Break in a Best Western hotel of their choice and the Third Prize winner can stay at home and view their brand new DVD player. There will be the usual extensive list of further quality prizes available ranging from designer label clothing to supermarket label wine; all prizes have been donated by sponsors (listed in the programme), whose support we gratefully acknowledge. All proceeds will go to the charity supported by East Coast Piers Race — the Cirdan Trust. Cirdan provides sailing adventure breaks and holidays for disadvantaged young people aboard their small fleet of traditional sailing craft — Xylonite, Queen Galadriel, Duet and Hartlepool Renaissance. Last year’s ECPR donation of £6500 provided bursaries for 101 young people in 8 separate groups. Watch out for the display in the clubhouse of reports and letters of thanks from the participants. Tickets are £1 each - £5 per book. Two books are enclosed and tickets can be sold to members or non-members. Please complete all counterfoils with name and phone number (address optional). Cheques should be payable to Cirdan Sailing Trust. Please return counterfoils and payment to: East Coast Piers Race Office 25 [redacted], Southminster, Essex. CMO [redacted] Reminder: Cheques payable to Cirdan Sailing Trust Please call me on [redacted] should you require more tickets. Many thanks in advance for your valuable support — and good luck! Caister Lifeboat Appeal Caister Lifeboat Station in Norfolk, which has run as an independent rescue service since the RNLI closed it in 1969, is appealing for funds to replace their old boat. Overhauling their existing boat could cost up to £200,000 so they are aiming instead to buy a Dutch Valentihn class vessel which uses steer able water jets instead of propellers and rudders. The design is ideal for use amongst the sandbanks. More details on their Website if you Search for Caister Lifeboat, and donations can be sent to: Treasurer, Caister Lifeboat Appeal, The Lifeboat Station, Tan Lane > Caister on Sea, Norfolk, NR30 5DJ.
