N Tail-Piece The racing season has started with some beautiful sailing days of sunshine and moderate breezes. Just the thing for easing ourselves back into the sailing activity, without it becoming too much of a shock to the system. It has been very encouraging to see that most fleet turn-outs have been good, and no doubt this will improve further as we get into the warmer weather. The cruiser moorings teams have been doing their usual efficient job, and most are now laid, so from now on there will be many cruiser launches to manage and the Club will soon be back in its summer operating mode. Remember to give launching operations as much room as possible and keep clear unless you are directly involved, in order to make these operations as safe as possible for everyone. Our first Open Meeting of the season has already been successfully completed — the 2 day Dart 15 Open which drew about 15 competitors. Excellent sailing conditions made this an enjoyable event, and thanks are due to the many that supported it by efficiently performing various duties. Unfortunately the home club did not provide the winner — but perhaps next year ... ..! One of the support boats used extensively during the Open, was the Orkney, which is a very useful general purpose craft, also used frequently by the windsurfing community. I still need someone to take over the job of bosun for this boat from Tim Sweet, and this is now a matter of some urgency, so please consider again whether you could contribute to the Club’s well-being in this way, and let me know if you can. The job does not require specialist knowledge or skills beyond those of a general handyman. You will have been reading about the turmoil and uncertainties surrounding the future of the Club elsewhere in this issue, and with all that going on it has been difficult to even think about sailing related matters. However, I have been most impressed by the energy and determination with which your Executive Team and its co-opted “Lifeboat Committee” experts has gone about the difficult task of attempting to protect the future of our Club, and hope that in the next few weeks a successful outcome can be reported. John Salmon Rear Commodore [redacted] [redacted].fsnet.co.uk

Bookingforms for the “Fun Day and Barbeque” and Cadet Week are in this edition. 2 Club Notes Commodore By now, you will have received the letter from Nik Beavins asking you to apply to join Thirslet Sailing Club. Please send these into him as soon as possible so that we do not have any delay in purchasing the site. Before we hold the AGM in November we still have to complete the purchase of the site, the writing of the bye laws and define the sub committee structure; and these are just some of the more important tasks. Looking towards the future, acquiring the site and creating the company, will have an effect on the way that we operate. Whilst we will no longer have to seek MASC approval for our spending plans, we will need to plan much further into the future. I would suggest that in the area of capital spend such as expansion of the clubhouse, replacement of boats, tractors and other major items, we will need to create and update a rolling twenty year plan. We will need this both to ensure that the Treasurer can have the money available and that we do not build something one day only to need to knock it down a couple of years later. Our new freedom may also mean that we will qualify more easily for grants to assist us with major projects. Two areas where the Committee would like help in this new era are people with the skills or contacts who can help publicise the Club and locate grant money. Obviously it is essential that the Committee concentrates on getting the new structures and the basic planning in place so that we can continue the development of the Club into the future. In my opinion it is essential that we continue to develop the Club and the site. This can only be successful with the backing of all the members and by evolution not revolution. Neil Pembleton Cruiser Fleet All the moorings are now down. There have been minor problems with boats being blocked in by cars, would people please therefore not park in the cruiser park unless they are within shouting distance of their car. The fitting out supper went very well, thank you to all the people who manned the bar throughout the evening. By the time that you read this the Burnham trip will have passed. The next trip planned is the cruise to Brightlingsea, please note the new dates of 7" and 8" June as on the original date there are 70 old gaffers going into Brightlingsea. The list for this trip is on the notice board. Note also that the Medusa Cruiser Race will be finishing in Brightlingsea on Saturday the 7". See Frank Burgess for race details. If anyone hasn’t been to Brightlingsea before, this is an excellent opportunity to find out about this small port. Contact me for details. Looking ahead, we have the club fun day on Saturday 14 June and the East Coast Piers Race on 6" July. Without the mother boats dotted along the course, this event cannot take place. I am sure that any help will be welcomed by Chris Davis and Charles Anderson so if you can assist in any way either contact them direct or alternatively you could return the questionnaire in the last Navigans and they will contact you. Also coming up in July on the weekend of the 12" and 13" we have the Watercress Run to Heybridge Basin. Traditionally we take our dinghies with us and go for a chug down the river on the Saturday afternoon looking for the watercress, followed by a barbeque Saturday evening, locking out to return to the club on Sunday. I have booked the barbeques at Heybridge for the evening which will be on a bring and cook your own food basis as last year. Lastly, it is the intention to have the Dell Bar open each Friday evening throughout the season. To this end Malcolm Yeoman is setting up a bar rota, so if anyone can volunteer to man the bar on one Friday evening during the season please contact him direct. Roger Camp, Cruiser Fleet Captain Tel: [redacted] or email: [redacted].co.uk

I am sure you will appreciate that to maintain a full race programme we must have adequate support cover which in effect means the Jack B and RIB need to be deployed each race day. Just lately we have had a number of “No Shows” which if it were not for the help of some last minute volunteers races the Race Office would have little alternative but to cancel the racing, and disappoint quite a few people. Please check the roster and if you do need to swap a duty please arrange this yourself and let me know either by phone or e-mail, I can then amend the roster. As ever your continued help in making sure we have adequate cover for race days means that we can complete a busy programme, and have happy sailors. Once again, this year’s event will be in the hands of Peter Clayton, Kevin Dowley and Steve Monks, ably assisted by the Cadet Committee who will endeavour to maintain the standards set in previous years. The committee’s work started sometime ago and a lot has been achieved. We now need you to complete the attached form and return it asap with your money, to assist us with the final planning stage. We have endeavoured to keep the cost to a minimum but fuel, prizes etc. all cost money. We will also attempt to hold a few fund raising events during the week — your support would be appreciated. Preventing the mad rush ! By now those who applied for camping plots should know whether they were successful and can now make a commitment. In an attempt to prevent the mad rush and duplication of our work on registration day we will adopt the same system as last year: Non-returnable deposit of £5 per person will be paid in advance with your entry forms. Cheques payable to MSC. This will assist us to identify and monitor the cadet numbers and restrict them if necessary, also those wishing to volunteer their services. Without your support it can’t happen, remember we are all volunteers allegedly on holiday. More volunteers less work. Senior Service Once again by popular request we will attempt to form an additional group — those who miss out on the cadet age bracket who wish to learn / brush up on their sailing skills. It was run again last year with some entertaining results, so if you fit into this category and fancy taking the challenge please complete the attached form. We hope to keep you well away from the Cadets, so that their concentration is not disturbed taking the micky out of Mum or Dad etc. Wanted Do we have any members who are in a position to offer the services of larger dinghies (Enterprise, GP, Wanderer etc) for use by the Senior Service group? To facilitate the marking of the camping pitches can I request that members do NOT PARK in either the car park or the Catamaran field (south side of the parked boats) in the week running up to the Camping fortnight. Many thanks for your help. Les Hurrell-Smith, Camping Co-ordinator. News Bilge Water Alarm Many Cruisers do not have automatic bilge water pumps fitted. Why not fit an automatic bilge water alarm, using an inexpensive home smoke detector. Use a “DICON” (Wickes) smoke alarm with internal metal sensor enclosure, solder a 2 core flexible cord to the test arm/contact and sensor enclosure with a T.V. co-axial plug at the bilge water end. The alarm sounds when the bilge water bridges the plug contacts. Sometime a “wet” boat can upset the electronics after a seasons use. Simply remove and put the detector in the airing cupboard for a couple of days. This same smoke detector can also be used for a simple intruder alarm using a two part magnetic reed contact fixed to the hatch cover with a concealed “Off” switch/latching relay in series. -———-* —L_ "Dicon" smoke alarm Concealed "Off" switch or latching relay Connectors ~, e+ e @ + Q s— “Intruder Alarm" Magnetic reed switch on hatch cover Co-Axial Plug "Bilge Alarm" Bob Jephson

"Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Seven - Marquesas to the Tuamotus continued.... “ The Tuamotus. Arriving at the anchorage on the far side of the lagoon we were sheltered by the reef and a beautiful little desert island. We were reunited with several boats that we had met on the way, including "Maritime Express' with Laura on board. In accounts that I'd read of round-the-world rallies I'd always been amused by the idea of a floating village moving on from one place to another. Even through we were travelling independently, the same thing seemed to be happening to us. Every place we arrived at we seemed to knowa large proportion of the boats there. As new boats arrived they would invariably be ones we already knew. It shouldn't have been surprising really. On a trade wind route, nearly everyone was heading west within a seasonal time frame and there were only so many route options to choose from. This was certainly a lovely place to stop. We had impromptu barbecues and sing-songs under the palm trees of the tiny island or motu. After a few days of peace and tranquility we moved back across the lagoon to the village by the pass. At least we did once we had got our anchor up. Nearly every boat that left the anchorage had had a fouled anchor and we were no exception. Richard from 'Fair Hippolyta' came over and, with the snorkel, directed us around the coral heads that we were neatly wrapped around. This was to prove to be a feature of the Tuamotus. Although we eangtionced some beautiful anchorages, none of them was free of coral and some were almost entirely coral. The village of Pouheva was a strange mixture of impressive buildings like a town hall, two churches, several shops and a collection of simple houses. One of the shops was staffed by three transvestites, who were obviously very proud of their dress sense. One was doing a passable impression of Tina Turner while the other posed over the freezer cabinet. When the third particularly masculine one appeared, complete with cigarette hanging out of mouth, sweeping up, it was like something out of an old 'Queen' video. We had already noticed in French Polynesia a particularly liberal attitude towards sexual diversity. The local papers regularly featured mahu or raerae (transvestite)-of-the-year competitions. From Pouheva we motored in company with 'Aldebaran' and 'Cap d'Or' along the lagoon. The lagoon was generally at least 20 metres deep but was dotted with near vertical coral heads that stopped either just below or just above the surface. Depending on the light conditions, they were not always easy to spot and it could get quite tiring hanging over the bow peering at the water, or so Helen kept telling me. By going as a group we were able to take turns as lead boat which made the whole operation a lot pleasanter. We headed towards an idyllic, almost coral-free, anchorage half way up the atoll. Sheltered from the prevailing winds by a heavily wooded motu we were just off a deserted white sandy beach. Traversing the narrow motu to the ocean side proved to be an adventure in itself so thick was the vegetation. The contrast between the ocean and lagoon side was amazing. It was hard to believe they were only a few hundred yards apart. The lee shore proved to be a treasure trove. Between us we found anchor buoys, a snorkel, one fin, and a wetsuit in excellent condition that later proved to fit Laura perfectly. Moving on to Passe Tapuhiria, the western pass of Makemo, we anchored off the abandoned village. This was another place where avoiding coral was virtually impossible. Our anchor ended up lodged over the edge of a coral bank. It held, but made for an anxious night when the wind blew up. At least Helen told me it made for an anxious night, I managed to sleep through it as I often did. In the morning the wind had come round, making the anchorage a rather uncomfortable lee shore. The lagoon was So wide that quite a sizeable sea could build up within it. Our anchor came up alright but 'Aldebaran' had quite a struggle with theirs. Once clear of the pass we hoisted sail and had quite a pleasant run until the evening when the wind went very light and fickle. It eventually picked up overnight and we had a good sail, arriving off the eastern pass at Fakerava in the morning. Anchoring just inside the pass once again, we met up with several boats that we knew, including Jim and Jo the Australian couple on 'Atlas', a Nordhaven 65 Trawler Yacht, who had been so helpful in getting the water pump for the engine. They hosted a party that night for everyone in the anchorage. Before that we went ashore to a small Pension run for the past 18 years by a Tahitian called Manahee. Basically a collection of straw huts that he had built himself on what was little more than a sand bank, it was in idyllic situation. Under the guidance of his partner Tilla, we had a go at weaving palm leaves. A couple of days later we returned and Pat and I helped Manahee roof one of his new huts. The main island next to the pass had been inhabited until the early 20th century when the entire population had left. In the last few years a hotel consisting of huts right on the water's edge has developed and a few people have moved back into the village. It was fascinating walking round the remains of the old school. We did a drift snorkel with Pat and Olivia through the pass on the incoming tide. It was an incredible experience floating by the almost sheer side to the pass. As we drifted we saw sharks and an amazing creature that turned out to be a Napoleon fish. As we passed the hotel we gained speed and literally shot by the fish traps that lay to the side of the channel. We took the dinghy across the entrance where there were a whole series of uninhabited motus. On one of these we discovered a collection of human skulls. We met a young Italian couple that had been dropped off on one of the motus for the morning as part of the 'Desert Island' experience. By now we were getting to the time when we needed to get to Tahiti to renew our 3-month visas. This had to be done a month before their expiry. The problem was that we had had several days with little or no wind. We decided to do the short trip across to the smaller atoll of Faaite. After extricating our anchor with some difficulty we motored the 12 miles across to Passe Teporiaha in Faaite. We entered on the ebb and had quite a struggle overcoming the current in the narrow channel. Eventually we managed it, but finding the anchorage behind the pass proved difficult. 'Aldebaran', who was ahead of us, ran firmly aground on the coral,. Luckily it was calm but Pat had to launch his dinghy to push 'Aldebaran' off. With no boats in the anchorage and no locals to ask, we finally gave up and headed back out of the pass to start the 250 mile trip to Tahiti. Stopping outside long enough to get our dinghies on deck and after Pat passed over some Tuna that a charter skipper had given us the night before, we motored off long enough to get clear of the island. Determined not to motor all night we waited until there was just enough wind to fill the sails and turned the engine off. Pat elected to motor on in the hope of keeping the trip down to two nights. We sailed on at a

stately one knot, which increased slowly overnight. By morning the wind had increased to 9 or 10 knots giving us 4 knots in the calm sea. Later that day we were talking to 'Aldebaran' on the radio when it transpired that 'Cap d'Or' and 'Green Ghost' a Canadian boat we had also got to know, had both left Fakarava that morning. 'Fair Hippolyta' left Tahanea that evening and we had another informal net again with 3 of the 4 boats we had left the Los Perles Island with. The next day the winds were even lighter but with the spinoa up we managed to make reasonable progress. That evening just after we'd taken the spinoa down the wind got up. Progress was good until just after midnight when the wind died away completely. We resorted to the engine. Unfortunately at about the same time the autohelm played up. We carried two rams but the other one had already given up on the way to the Marquesas so we were now committed to hand steering under engine. By the morning what little wind there was died away completely and we decided to keep motoring rather than spend yet another night at sea. At least it was a flat calm. From dawn we could see the twin islands of Tahiti. It was hard to believe that we were actually there. This was an island that we had been aware of for as long as we could remember. Beyond it we could already see the dramatic outline of Moorea. After an overcast, wet night and morning, the skies cleared and we arrived in Tahiti in blazing sunshine. Arriving at the pass off Papeete we called up Harbour Control who answered immediately and gave us clearance to enter. Having passed inside the reef we turned away from the main harbour and followed the channel for several miles inside the reef, to the extensive anchorage off Maeve Beach where we anchored near ‘Maritime Express' and 'Aldebaran’. ‘Muna's' Travels Part Thirty Eight - Tahiti and the Society Islands. We had heard so many reports about Tahiti being over-touristy, expensive, etc. that we had not allowed our expectations to ride too high. Consequently, perhaps, we were pleasantly surprised. The anchorage, though extremely busy was very pleaant and well protected by the outlying reef. Remember the Anthony Hopkins-Mel Gibson version of Mutiny on the Bounty , I did feel that there was a distinct shortage of bare-breasted females paddling their canoes out to meet us. There were two dinghy docks to choose from, one at the Sofitel Hotel and one at the marina. The main culture shock in going ashore was the amount of traffic in evidence. We hadn't really experienced more than one car at a time since leaving Panama. Our first task in the morning was to get into Papeete to check in. Nearly every place we had visited so far had had its own unique transport system and Tahiti was no exception. Here it was Le Truck. These as the name implies were lorry chassis with wooden structures built on the back. Some of these looked as if they had been a weekend project in someone's back garden, but they offered a regular if erratic and cheap service. Their long term future was apparently in some doubt as a Government Minister had decided that they didn't fit in with the sophisticated image he thought the island should be portraying. Checking in was a fairly lengthy but painless experience. Once again horror stories of just a couple of years ago proved thankfully to be incorrect. There seems to have been a definite softening of official attitudes towards yachts. Papeete is a real cosmopolitan city, where prices although not cheap, it is not nearly as expensive as we had been led to believe. Provisions in the well-stocked supermarkets were generally at a level with English prices. During our stay we witnessed the start and finish of the Round Moorea six-man canoe race that we had seen the Ua Pou team practising for back in the Marquesas. It was an impressive sight. The top teams came from Shell and Mobil, and were extremely professional. They didn't even allow themselves much self-congratulation when they finished. It was quite a relief to see the third team in clearly overjoyed with their performance. We also saw the opening night of the Polynesian Dance Festival. It was quite spectacular seeing 40 pairs of hips wiggling in complete synchronisation. The knee wobbling performed by the male dancers looked distinctly painful A few nights later we went to the Friday night entertainment at the Beachcomber Hotel. For the price of a beer we sawa really lively display with fire eaters, one of whom was spotlit, jumping from a rocky outcrop into the landscaped swimming pool. Papeete was the first place since Panama to have a chandler's and we were able to get one or two things we had been short of. I even found water filters that I hadn't managed to find since we'd left England. I was unable to find spares for the autohelm rams but was able to get one of them working again. Richard and Joy from ‘Fair Hippolyta' came over and Richard fitted a spare sender for my temperature gauge on the engine. A Belgian called Luke who had lived on his boat in Tahiti for the last year, working as a tour guide, arranged a special cut-price tour for yachties. It was a really good day, and gave us a chance to see more of the Island. We saw where Captain Cook first landed. After nearly two weeks in Tahiti we were ready to move on and had a short sail across to Moorea with Laura back on board. The short sail was not without incident as the gear part of the single lever control suddenly refused to engage. I had no choice but to climb down through the cockpit locker to the rear of the engine to disconnect the cable and change gear by hand. In this fashion we entered the pass into Cook's Bay and anchored behind the reef with help from Pete from ‘La Boatique' from whom we had bought our dinghy in Panama. Having helped us anchor, Pete came on board to look at the engine controls, but even he had no joy. He did help me set it up so that we could operate the gear change with a pair of mole grips in the cockpit. We had a comfortable night but in the morning the wind got up and we started dragging, a rare event for us. Our anchor had been on the edge of a ledge and had pulled over the edge into deeper water. We got the chain in and motored into the bay where we anchored just off the small settlement. We were now able to appreciate the grandeur of our surroundings. Moorea has an impressive and unmistakable skyline. I was able to catch the fast ferry back to Papeete where I bought a new single lever control and the next day I had it fitted. The failed one had been fitted in the Canaries and was only 18 months old. On the day I went back to Papeete, Helen and Laura did a long walk up to a Belvedere where they had a superb view. That evening one of the residents of the time-share apartments nearby organised a yachtie's barbecue for which he provided chicken, beer and rum. It turned out to be a really good night and was much appreciated. Cook's Bay proved to be a very convenient anchorage.

Ne, There was a water supply on bank where you could take the dinghy to fill up with water, have a shower, or do your washing. A jetty was conveniently sited near a supermarket that was well stocked and much more to our liking than the huge affairs in Tahiti. Moorea was an extremely lush island. I was amazed to see fields of pineapples. I don't think I had ever realised that they grew straight out of the ground. From Moorea we had an overnight sail to Huahine. It was a trip of about 85 miles which is a difficult distance to plan for. However it worked out all right leaving as we did just before sunset. The main problem is that you don't have time to settle down into anything of a routine before it gets dark. There was quite a sea running which made things a bit uncomfortable at first. However there was a good wind and progress was good. We left at the same time as a cruise ship and several other yachts and I was amazed at how many lights I could see around us. I just wasn't used to this. We had a good overnight sail and arrived off Huahine soon after dawn. Sailing round the northern end of the island we entered the reef by the main town of Fare and negotiated the 7-mile-long channel inside the reef to a lovely secure anchorage in the south of the island. It was a fascinating introduction to a new island. That afternoon we went ashore and walked along one of the loveliest beaches that we had seen in the Pacific. We spent several days in this anchorage and it quickly became one of our favourite spots. The island of Huahine is really two islands joined by a road bridge encased within the common reef. Helen and I spent a day doing a walking/hitching tour of the island. In the absence of any form of public transport, hitching is one of the few options for seeing the island and we reckoned our success rate was about 50%. Over one 2-hour period, making our way down the east side of the island we got two lifts from the only two vehicles that passed us. In the north of the island we saw a marae, or sacred site. Unlike the ones we had seen in the Marquesas, this one was built out over the water. A number of boats that we had been seeing on the way gathered in the anchorage and regular happy hours developed on the beach near a small bar. Laura did some snorkelling and diving with martin from 'Rover'. All in all it was a particularly relaxed time. When we finally decided to move back along the island we unfortunately chose a day when a slow-moving front was starting to make conditions rather unsettled. Motoring inside the reef in light rain that I had predicted would soon clear up, but instead developed into a torrential downpour, we were reduced to peering into the haze searching out the marks. Helen hadn't wanted to move, and stayed down below out of the rain. 'Aldebaran' had moved the previous afternoon to the anchorage off the town of Fare and had had an uncomfortable night, so we eventually anchored in the deep but narrow Baie Haavai where, in spite of strong gusts from the west blowing straight in, we had a reasonable night. We woke in the morning to more driving rain, all undecided as to whether to move on or not. In the end both 'Aldebaran' and ourselves decided to take a chance and tackle the 20 mile trip to the next island of Raiatea. We were rewarded with a brightening sky and a fresh northwesterly which gave us a good sail. Then, about half way across, our cockpit GPS started giving out strange information. Just minutes later the nav station GPS also reported 'no fix'. Both GPSs are Furuno and neither had previously given us any problems whatsoever. The real mystery was that both systems are completely independent of each other apart from having the same battery source. This sudden loss of information quickly reduced me to a gibbering wreck and made me realise how dependent I had become these electronics. The confusion was added to by the fact that we had had three passes through the reef to choose from. We had originally been headed for the southernmost of the passes but Pat had heard that the middle pass was easier. I had replied that the southern pass looked OK. We had both taken up each other's suggestions with Pat heading for the southern pass while we headed for the middle one. These passes are very difficult to identify so when... ee sorry reader - some text missing from here!) ...cccscsccsseeererees position we were able to push while Helen put the engine into reverse and we slid off. Fortunately there didn't appear to be any real harm done apart from scrapes on the side of the keel. We were very lucky that there was no wind or swell. Meanwhile Pat and Olivia had no luck in extricating their anchor. We rafted alongside them and Pat got out his diving gear so that he and Laura could dive down. Having got it clear, we motored round to Baie Faaroa. By the time we got there it was well after five and less than an hour before dark. We discovered that there was a Stardust Charter Base with a number of moorings. Calling up on the VHF they told us that we were more than welcome to pick up a mooring which was a great relief. We all had a much needed sundowner. That night the rain started again and carried on pretty much unabated for the next day. It didn't take us long to top up our tanks and fill every available receptacle. By the afternoon the wind got up and we were getting gusts of well over 30 knots. Visibility throughout the day was minimal and we were very glad to be where we were. All sorts of debris started to come down from the mountains, and we got advance warning of the worst of it from Harold on 'Zephyrus' who was anchored further in to the bay. The next day the weather cleared and we ventured ashore for a pleasant walk ashore. Later in the day Pat, Laura and I took his dinghy for an interesting trip up the river. From Faaroa we managed to sail slowly up the coast inside the reef to the town of Uturoa where we managed to get fresh fruit and veg. In the morning we indulged in cafe society, watching the world go by. We then motored north, still inside the reef, to the neighbouring island of Ta Haa. We met up with 'Cap d'Or' and ‘Fair Hippolyta' when we picked up a buoy to investigate an entertainment scheduled for that evening. While we were securing to the buoy, Martin from 'Rover' came by and took Laura off snorkelling. The hotel owner was very friendly but the price put us off so we headed back out to the reef where we anchored on sand in about 6 metres of crystal clear water, just behind a motu. John and Gail brought Laura back to us in their fast RIB from 'Rover' and in the morning we went snorkelling in the pass. It was here that we had a long overdue reunion with Martin on 'Ragtime' whom we had spent a lot of time with in Tobago and who was due to fly back to the Channel Islands for a cataract operation. We had a tremendous barbecue on the motu with a number of boats.. We sailed right round the north end of Ta Haa, inside the reef before enjoying a lively 20-mile sail across to

Bora Bora. As we rounded the outer reef we hardened up on the wind and 'Muna' revelled in it. The lagoon surrounding Bora t Bora is nothing less than spectacular. We spent the first couple of nights in a lovely shallow anchorage behind a small island i just to the south of the pass. We then went north around Bora Bora. At times we had just inches under our keel. Then we would be negotiating tortuous gaps in the coral. It was pretty exciting to say the least, but the anchorages were almost perfect. For the next few days we moved from one anchorage to another, each one giving us a different perspective on the infamous skyline. On a couple of occasions we snorkelled with giant manta rays, some having a span of 10-15". We had been following on the radio the fortunes of two boats who, within two days of each other, had lost their rudders while on passage to Suvorov, the atoll made famous by Tom Neale who lived alone there for many years. The first boat was an Italian 30 footer,'Amour', that we had first met in the Canaries, and had seen several times since. 'Amour' was a very light boat with a skegless rudder. They lost their rudder in fairly heavy seas and had great difficulty establishing any control. They eventually reached Suvorov where they were towed in to await the arrival of spare parts on another boat. The second boat with a lost rudder was a Grand Soleil 43, also with a skegless rudder. They managed to fabricate some sort of temporary rudder and carried on sailing to Samoa where they hoped to effect repairs. While we were on the east side of Bora Bora we tackled some sail repairs on the yankee where the stitching had worn through. On a blustery Sunday we sailed back round to the west of the island. We had the engine on, out of gear, to charge the batteries and ready in case we needed it as we negotiated the, at times, tortuous course between the reefs. As we passed the Bora Bora Yacht Club, Helen noticed that there were several free buoys. Heading in we suddenly smelt burning. Opening the starboard cockpit locker which leads to the engine, we were confronted with dense acrid smoke. Helen steered for the nearest available buoy which Laura secured us to, while I attempted to remove lines and other items from the locker. With the engine off we cleared the locker and the smoke slowly dispersed. Back in the Tuamotus I had discovered that some of the lagging of the dry section of the exhaust had started to disintegrate. To protect items in the locker I had wedged a piece of wood outside the pipe. This had completely burnt through and was the cause of the acrid smoke. I tried to get some new lagging on shore but without success. Then I discovered that Barry on 'Cherokee' had some fibreglass lagging that he kindly let me have. Meanwhile I had run the engine with the bad section of lagging removed and detected leakage. I had some exhaust pipe repair paste on board which I liberally applied. This seemed to work. I then covered this section of pipe with Barry's tape. We were now ready to move on. We were facing a passage of some 1400 miles to Tonga with the widely dispersed Cook Islands in between. We had heard very favourable reports of these islands. Their main problem is a lack of protected anchorages. Every time we selected a possible route we would read up on the anchorages and be instantly put off. Raratonga in the south is the main island but has a small, generally overcrowded, harbour. Penryn has a good lagoon anchorage but is a long way to the north. Suvorov, where Tom Neale lived for many years, sounded really nice but was also fairly far north. In the end we opted for a direct route to Tonga which would take us fairly near to Aitutaki and Palmerston where we could stop if conditions allowed, but which would not be too much off the direct route if we carried on. By the time we were ready to move, several boats had been waiting for more settled conditions. On the morning of Wednesday 15th August, while I was still working on the exhaust pipe, 'Orplid', ‘Cherokee’, 'La Boatique' and 'Maritime Express' all set off in the direction of Aitutaki, some 480 miles away. 'Aldebaran' set off just before noon and we followed mid afternoon. As we motored out of the pass, there still seemed to be fumes in the engine room. We considered turning back but decided to press on and were soon sailing. to be continued, Malcolm Shaft

Club Notes Commodore Once again we need to say "Thank You" to Fenella for organising such a splendid Fun Day. I would like to know her secret of predicting many months ahead when the sun will shine, a warm wind will blow and the evening although chilly is dry. In addition to my thanks to Fenella, I would like to thank all the others who supported her to make it such an enjoyable day. The stalwarts from the Cruiser Fleet who have cooked at the barbecue for many years congratulate the members of the Handicap Fleet on the work and sympathise with the streaming eyes and smoke filled clothes. Very many thanks to you all. As many of you will know, on Sunday 8" June the wind increased quite violently which caused many problems in the river. These were not confined to the dinghy fleet but included incidents with cruisers, particularly those racing and members coming ashore from cruisers. Our support boats and crews did an excellent job that day and as afar as I am aware no one was injured. The situation that afternoon acts as a timely reminder to us all that forecasts are not always accurate and that each of us MUST be responsible for ourselves when sailing. I know of at least one cruiser who left Brightlingsea, decided that it looked ominous and went back in, to return to the Club on the Monday. Even if you are racing, it is YOUR decision whether to continue, not the Race Officer's. Over recent weeks there have been a number of cruisers which have suffered damage whilst on the moorings. Although the damage may seem superficial, a mark down the side, a gentle bump to a tender, even these are time consuming to the owner to fix. In some cases damage can be much more substantial and costly. I. along with all the other cruiser owners, am well aware that such damage may not have been caused by other club members as many other amateur and professional sailors use the river. Indeed I doubt whether there is one of us who has never had a similar accident. However I do ask that anyone who thinks they may have toucheda cruiser to have the courtesy to contact the owner; it saves accusations being made and ill will generated. Iam pleased to say that the response to the loan note scheme is very encouraging. Although we have a little way to go to meet our target to fund the difference between the purchase cost and the bank loan, we appear to be on target to complete the purchase late June or early July. Please note that we are not banking the cheques until the sale / purchase contracts have been exchanged. Elsewhere in this issue the form for existing Marconi Sailing Club members to apply to join Thirslet and the form to apply for Members Loans are reprinted. By the time that this issue lands on your doorstep, we will have held the East Coast Piers Race on 6" July and I would like thank all those mother boat crews, shore side helpers and backroom people who support Chris Davies and the East Coast Piers Race Committee both throughout the year and on the day. Without you all, the Cirdan Trust would not be able to help the same number of people who are not so fortunate as ourselves. Neil Pembleton Cruiser Fleet We have now had our cruises to Burnham and Brightlingsea. We had 16 boats to Burnham with 44 sitting down for a meal and 13 boats to Brightlingsea and although there was no meal planned, we had 28 for a carvery in the Colne Yacht Club. Both cruises went very well with favourable winds on both trips although those who were late back from Brightlingsea had rather more wind than was comfortable. Looking ahead, we have the Piers Race on the 6" July which may or may not have passed by the time that you receive this and the trip to Heybridge Basin, known as the Watercress Run, on the 12" and 13" July. The plan is to lock in to Heybridge at approximately 11am on Saturday (high water 1200 hours) taking our tenders with us, then during the afternoon have a trip up the river to Beeleigh in the tenders, returning for a barbeque in the evening. To this end I have booked the barbeques on the lock side. You can either bring your own food or buy it at Tescos on the way back from Beeleigh. There is a list on the Club notice board so if you could add your name to it, I can inform the lock keeper of the numbers to expect. The other forthcoming trips are St. Katharines on the week beginning 2" August and Shotley the week beginning 23" August.

BLACKWATER & COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION On 20th March this year I attended the BACSPA meeting held at the Maldon Little Ship Club and as on previous occasions I am reporting on the matters which I feel may be of interest to you. WINDFARMS - The key issues resulting from the Environmental Impact Statement for the GUNFLEET remain i.e. marking/lighting, rotor tip clearance and exclusion zones. The rotor tip clearance issue has deteriorated further in that the tower height has been reduced to 80 mtrs above LAT giving clearances of less than 20 mtrs in. all but good conditions. Furthermore an application for an order under the Transport andWorks Act seeks to be able to reduce the clearance to as little as 14 mtrs above MHWS. - A yacht of 10.5 mtrs LOA with normal rig would have an air height of some 16 mtrs to innclude the VHF aerial. The RYA/BACSPA are waiting a response from the Developer's in which they say they will offer some mitigation to this problem. The Chairman of BACSPA had a useful meeting with the Navigation Manager at Trinity House on the issue of marking and lighting of wind-farms, with particular reference to the Gunfleet Project. A plot of the farm aray on the chart shows the SE corner to intrude on the direct line between the GUNFLEET SPIT and SWIN SPITWAY buoys which mark the extent of the Gunfleet sands by the East Swin/Kings' Channel. The Chairman received a letter from Trinity House accepting this point and they will be asking the Developer to install & maintain an additional starboard hand buoy some 600 mtrs SW of the mid point of the southern boundary of the array. Trinity House will also move the SWIN SPITWAY buoy some 330 meters SE of its present position. These changes will shift the East Swin clear route away from the farm array. HAMFORD WATER - Hutchison Ports (UK) Ltd on their scoping report on the proposed managed relignment in Hamford Water, which is intended to provide compensatory habitat for the Bathside Bay port development. The principal concern is the possible silting of the already shallowing PYE CHANNEL which could seriously restrict access to the WALTON BACKWATERS. WEYMARKS - The proposed managed realignment of the sea wall between Bradwell Nuclear Power Station & the Roman fort on the north coast of the Dengie Peninsula should have no measurable impact on the navigable area in the Blackwater Estuary. NOTICE TO MARINERS - Harwich Haven Authority : I mentioned in my last bulletin the inclusion of two turbidity & wave measurement buoys at sites 5&6, there are now two additional buoys site 9 & 10 at WGS 84 positions Site 9 Lat 51 52' 986182N; Long 01 13' 869072E Site 10 Lat 51 53' 766186N Long 01 15' 563255E Again these are Yellow ODAS Special Mark with yellow cross topmark with light characteristics yellow flashing group (5) every 20 seconds. WOODBRIDGE HAVEN - Approaches to the River Deben. following a survey of the entrance to the river Deben on 24 January 2003, the follwoing changes were made.

WOODBRIDGE BAR BUOY moved to Lat 51 58' 870N Long 001 23' 500E and renamed MID KNOLLS. MARTELLO SPIT BURY moved to Lat 51 58' 70OON Long 001 23' 725E and renamed EAST KNOLLS WOODBRIDGE HAVEN BUOY Moved to Lat 51 58' 545N Long 001 24' 250E name remains unchanged. It is currently planned to resurvey the area after four months to verify the positions of the channel - SO BEWARE THESE MAY HAVE BEEN MOOVED AGAIN. HALFPENNY PIER — HARWICH - facility for visiting yachts is available from 29 March to 19 October for a maximum stay of 72 hours. No reservation can be made and yachts must be prepared for others to moor alongside. Yachts may moor without charge from 0900 hrs until 1600 hrs. yachts mooring outside these hours will be charged. £5 up to 5 mtrs: over 5 mtrs £10.00 over 10 mtrs £15.00, 15 - 20 mtrs £20.00, over 20 mtrs £30. A.0O.B. - Brightlingsea Harbour have completed the extension to the pontoons. Next meeting due to be held at Stone Watersports Club Ltd., on 26 June 2003 Derek Kirby - BACSPA - Representative

"Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Nine - To Palmerston in the Cook Islands. Setting off from Bora Bora the winds were light but favourable. progress was slow but conditions were pleasant and it was good to be on the move again. When the winds were below 14 knots or so the difference between our performance and that of the boats that we were with was at its most marked, and it was no surprise when they all pulled even further ahead. By the Sunday, 4 days out, boats were beginning to arrive at Aitutaki. There is a very narrow, shallow, pass through the reef to a small but sheltered anchorage, but there was continuing debate as to how deep the pass was. 'Stella' had got in scraping the bottom and she drew 5'6". 'Capers' had been in for some time. In fact they had almost taken up residence. The only alternative was an anchorage outside the pass that was deep with a lot of coral and which was prone to a heavy swell depending on current conditions. 'Cherokee' decided to keep on going and head for Beveridge Reef. 'Orplid' anchored but decided only to stay one night. 'La Boatique' arrived and were talking of leaving quite soon. Pat and Olivia on 'Aldebaran' didn't even anchor. they took one look and decided to keep going for Palmerston. ‘Maritime Express' anchored and seemed reasonably happy. We were undecided as to what to do. We were set to arrive at around midnight and would therefore have to heave-to to wait until morning. In the end we kept going. The wind gradually increased and, after another couple of days, we were charging towards Palmerston at 7 knots. Having been concerned that we would be arriving at night and once again having to decide between standing off or not stopping, the strengthening wind ensured that we got in with just over an hour to spare. As we came round the island, one of the locals came out in his small aluminium runabout to guide us into the anchorage. Palmerston is an atoll much like those we had seen in the Tuamotus, with a large lagoon surrounded by a reef on which were situated a number of small islands or motus. The largest of these was Palmerston Island itself. There are a number of passes into the lagoon but none is deeper than 4'. The pass nearest the anchorage is incredibly narrow and twisting, with very strong cross currents. It would be extremely dangerous to attempt it in a dinghy, but the locals whizzed in and out in their aluminium runabouts day and night. When a yacht arrives at the island, it is a matter of honour for each family to claim it as theirs. Simon, who had guided us in, turned out to be the head of his particular family. Having shown us in he asked whether we were happy to be checked in in the morning. When we told him that we were, he said he would be back first thing with the appropriate officials. These turned out to be the Agricultural Officer and the Medical Officer. After a sociable checking in, in the cockpit, conducted over a beer, Simon asked whether we were ready to go ashore. Soon we were having our first experience of racing through the pass with coral heads and surging water all around. Once ashore Simon led us to his family home in a pleasant clearing in the heavily wooded island. Over coffee and cakes we started to learn the history of the island. Palmerston was settled in the mid-19th century by an Englishman, William Masters, who had run away from his native Lancashire. Having deserted his ship he acquired two Polynesian wives from Penryn, another of the Cook Islands. Having taken them to Palmerston along with a boatload of coconut seedlings, he then gained a third Polynesian wife from another Englishman who, having previously settled on Palmerston, refused to help pay for the coconut seedlings. After some level of disagreement he was then seen off. William Masters divided the island and the smaller surrounding motus between the three families. These three families are still in residence today. The whole setup is fascinating. As a rule, everything is shared. it is a bit like one of those social experiments that were popular a few years ago, except this one has survived for 150 years. When we had finished our coffee, Simon asked us if we would like a tour of the island. It will take an hour or so he said, then we will come back here for lunch. This turned out to be a regular feature of the week we were to spend on the island. Every day we were ashore on the island, it was taken as read that we would stay for lunch. The hospitality was staggering. Everywhere we went on the island, one of the 50 inhabitants would offer us coffee and biscuits or one of the ever-present coconuts. I had never previously realised how much of the coconut could be eaten. A delicacy that was completely new to us was the inside of a coconut that had started sprouting, where the milk had turned into a delicious substance reminiscent of marshmallow. 'Aldebaran' had arrived on the day before us and a couple of days after us 'Arganauta' and 'Maritume Express' arrived. They had both come from Aitutaki. As this was another of the Cook Islands they had been able to bring fresh fruit and veg which were very much appreciated by the islanders. Henry on 'Maritime Express' was also able to repair Simon's refrigeration unit. On the Saturday night a show was staged for the benefit of the visitors. It was a memorable experience sitting on a wooden bench in a clearing right on the edge of the beach, watching a display of Polynesian dancing accompanied by local musicians on a variety of instruments. The whole performance was lit by a single light bulb strung between two coconut trees. The dancing was excellent, but one of the highlights for me was when two-year-old John, who was clearly a musician/dancer in the making, followed his mum out onto the stage and copied her entire routine, taking the whole thing extremely seriously. John was very wary of me the whole time that we were there. He only started talking to me when it was time to say goodbye when he repeated ‘bye bye' several times with great gusto and obvious relief! The evening finished with the yachties being invited to join in the dancing. According to Helen, my version of Polynesian dancing was more akin to a Marquesan war dance, and could have started in international incident. Luckily it seemed to cause great amusement, but little offence. Sundays are a very special day on the island. No work is done and Sunday lunch is a very special event. It is the only day of the week when the staple diet is not fish and we were treated to a veritable feast of chicken, lamb and Basin birds that had been collected the day before. The supply ship had arrived early that Sunday but, in spite of wanting many of the supplies urgently, they would not start unloading the ship until sundown. Even that was a special concession to allow the ship to get away that night. The week that we spent on Palmerston was a very special experience that we won't forget in a hurry. We had become used to friendly islanders but these were exceptional. Everyone from the children up to the oldest inhabitants all seemed genuinely thrilled to have someone new to talk to.

‘Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Forty - Beveridge Reef and Niue. Our stay in Palmerston had fortunately coincided with sustained easterlies. The wind at this time of year and in this area is prone to coming round to the west every few days. Such an occurrence would make the anchorage at Palmerston untenable. When we left Palmerston the winds were light but fairly steady and from the east. It took us 2 days and 2 nights to reach Beveridge Reef some 290 miles away. As we approached the reef at dawn, the wind slowly headed us and settled into the west. It was good timing as the reef gives good protection from all directions. Until the advent of GPS Beveridge Reef was considered simply as a deadly hazard lying on the route between Bora Bora and Tonga. Its position as marked on charts was inaccurate and yachts would give it a wide berth. Now with accurate waypoints available, thanks to one or two pioneering yachts, it is fast becoming a rather special destination. Its fascination lies in the fact that none of the reef surrounding the 3 mile long lagoon is ever above sea level. Once through the single pass, the lagoon anywhere else in the Pacific would be considered a superb anchorage. Ten metres deep with only the occasional coral head to worry about, as an anchorage it is only surpassed by the fact that all round the lagoon there is a 100 metre wide band of pure sand just 4 metres deep. We joined ‘Aldebaran' and 'Stella' who had arrived the day before and our anchor bit deep into the sand. The water was so clear that you could see the chain disappear into the sand. The only landmarks as we looked around us were the different colours of the water and a solitary wrecked fishing boat lying on the reef. It was an amazing feeling knowing you were in the middle of the Pacific with no land for hundreds of miles in any direction. Several other boats arrived in the reef and in this desolate and isolated spot we actually had a very sociable time. In this location we were able to converse freely on Channel 16. At times we felt like of lot of naughty schoolboys. I kept expecting a stern reprimand from Thames Coastguard. On the last passage, Laura had kept herself amused by compiling a list of words that end in -ship. This became an interboat contest. Our list reached well over two hundred. After a few days the wind showed signs of returning to the east, and in spite of very light winds we struck out on the 130 mile trip to Niue. The light airs gradually developed into a steady breeze and we made reasonable progress overnight. By the morning the wind was steadily increasing and we had a fast run into the island with an enjoyable beat round the back of the island in calm seas. We picked up a buoy a couple of hours before sunset. neue is one of the smallest independent states in the world but is the largest coral island. Anchoring of Niue can easily result in your anchor being permanently lost in a deep chasm in the coral. We hired a car for the day with Pat and Olivia. Travelling around the island is very different from other islands we had visited in that, being flat and very heavily wooded, there are virtually no views. However, Mary and Walley, two friendly New Zealanders, who run the car hire as well as the Niue Yacht Club which is responsible for maintaining the 14 mooring buoys, had told us the best places to visit. With this information we did a number of short walks to some amazing sights. Being an island made almost entirely from coral, the caves were cathedral-like and spectacular in the extreme. While we were in Niue we realised how lucky we had been with the weather we had had since Bora Bora. We had generally had lightish winds but enough to keep sailing. We had been aware at the time of other boats, not that far away, having to motor for days on end. Now boats were coming into Niue, just a day or two behind us, with tales of horrendous weather. One had been rolled by a wave, causing mayhem below decks. After we had been there a few days we became aware of a developing situation on the Australian steel yacht 'Bifrost', on passage from Bora Bora to Tonga. We had first met Greg and Leonie and their two sons Ben and Jessie aged 4 and 6, at Christmas on the Dutch island of Curacao. On this passage Greg had been taken ill and, on advice over the radio from a New Zealand doctor, had taken medication for suspected malaria. It appears now that Greg may have had Dengie Fever. He is also diabetic. In any event he reacted badly to the medication and became seriously incapacitated. Leonie didn't know at the time what was wrong and had the boat to handle on her own, two young boys to look after and Greg to both look after and worry about. The weather was also deteriorating. Leonie was coming up on the daily net and after the situation had been developing from some time, Pat on 'Aldebaran' asked if she would like assistance. When she said that she would, he considered setting off back from Niue to meet them. At this stage 'Bifrost' was some 400 miles from Niue. Pat then realised that there were boats in Beveridge Reef who could intercept 'Bifrost' without heading back into the prevailing winds. 'Beacon' and 'Four Winds' immediately offered to go and Pat with the aid of his chart plotter worked out courses whereby they could meet up with 'Bifrost' without 'Bifrost' having to change course or slow down. 'Bifrost' by this time was heading for Niue as the nearest place where Greg could be given medical attention. ‘Beacon' reached 'Bifrost' in the middle of the night and, by means of some skilful manoeuvring, David was able to transfer some additional medication to ‘Bifrost’. Because of the conditions, it was decided not to attempt to transfer Alex from 'Beacon' which had been one of the options. 'Four Winds' joined the group and the 3 boats continued to Niue. Leonie said that it was a great relief having the other boats there. Pat continued to monitor the situation. It became clear that the boats would arrive in Niue sometime on Friday night. Pat co-ordinated plans for their arrival. There were 14 buoys at Nuie and at this stage there were just 3 left. Pat arranged for these to be reserved. When the boats arrived everyone did what they could to assist. I took Laura, and Ian from ‘Arganauta' to intercept 'Bifrost' on their way into the Bay. It was the furthest I had taken the dinghy offshore and had visions of making and early departure for Tonga. Once on board we could relieve Leonie from the helm. It was the first time that she had been able to talk to Greg for several hours as they have no autohelm and under power they have to handsteer. Other dinghies guided the boats on to their respective buoys and Julius from 'Arganauta', who is a pharmacist and who had been giving advice on medication, brought the doctor out to 'Bifrost' even before she had tied to the buoy. After he had given Greg an initial check, the local dive boat came out with a stretcher to take Greg ashore and up to the hospital. Thanks to excellent co-ordination the whole operation had gone extremely well. After a few days Greg felt well enough to carry on to Tonga. Laura joined them for the trip as Greg was still not strong enough to do anything physical. In the event we sailed with them in the company of 'Arganauta' and after 2 nights arrived in Vavau, the northern island group of Tonga. We had a bit of excitement on the way as, during a squall, several of our sail slides disintegrated due to ultra violet deterioration. After some difficulty, we got the main down and set the downwind rig which gave us an easy ride in quite breezy condition for the rest of

the way. In Vavau, Greg flew on to Australia for a full medical. Fortunately there appeared to be no lasting damage, just a bad reaction to the medication taken for suspected malaria. He was soon able to return to Tonga and continue their voyage home to Brisbane via Fiji. 'Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Forty One - Tonga Until we were well out into the Pacific I had always thought of Tonga as one island and was quite surprised to discover that it was in fact a widely-spaced island group. Although the most southerly island of Tongatapu is the main island and home of the King, the Vavau Group, about 150 miles to the north, is the more popular cruising ground and it was here that we made landfall. The group consists of one largish island of Vavau on which the main town of Niafu is situated and a number of much smaller islands, all in quite close proximity to each other and all protected from the prevailing winds by an extensive system of reefs to the east. The result is a sheltered cruising ground that has been taken full advantage of by the likes of Moorings and Sunsail. There are countless anchorages within easy reach of each other. Because of the complexity of the local names, Moorings have numbered the anchorages and this rather sterile system has even been taken over by the locals. As we arrived on a Sunday and checking-in is limited to weekdays, we made our way to anchorage No. 7 or Port Meurelle, historically believed to be the first anchorage for a European ship. A beautiful if rather crowded anchorage, we were immediately invited on board 'Beacon', who had arrived just before us, for a breakfast very tasty pancakes. After a quick doze back on board we were invited onboard 'Aldebaran' for lunch. They had a mooring in Niafu but had come down for the afternoon! In the evening we had a Happy Hour on the beach with the crews of 'Beacon' and 'Arganauta’. In the morning we reluctantly upped anchor so as to head up to Naifu and check in. Even in these sheltered waters we were registering winds up to 30 knots. Pat came out in his dinghy and helped us tie up to the wharf to await customs. They have quite strict rules here as to the importation of foodstuffs but the implementation of these rules appears to be somewhat arbitrary. Our coconuts we had been given in Niue were confiscated but the official decided that we could keep our tomatoes as they were a bit bruised. Nick on 'Force Eight', a South African boat, was asked what a particular vegetable was. When Nick told him it was an aubergine, the official said, "I like them, I'd better confiscate it!" Having checked in we moved to a buoy that Pat had managed to procure for us. We were quickly introduced to the rather strange mixture of cultures that is in evidence here. On the one hand the foreshore is a yachtie culture with Sunsail and Moorings bases and a number of waterside bars with dinghy docks and Happy Hours. Up the steps of the low cliff and you step into traditional Tonga with the men wearing skirts adorned with woven mats. We saw local girls swimming, dressed from head to foot in black. Just outside the town we came across some very basic homes with pigs running free everywhere you looked. We had a number of jobs to attend to on the boat and we ended up staying on the buoy for 3 weeks. There was a cruiser race every Friday and Helen and I crewed on 'Aldebaran' the first week. With Pat's dinghy racing expertise, we made a superb, if to me nerve racking start but were gradually overhauled. The next week I crewed on 'Arganauta'. For both weeks Laura crewed on 'Fair Hippolyta'. Helen had a number of fascinating treks around the island. Laura took advantage of low prices and excellent facilities to do a Rescue Diver's course on top of her advanced certificate. One night we went with Pat and Olivia to a Tongan feast on the other side of the island. It was organised by the inhabitants of a small village and was held in a very basic straw hut on the shore. The evening started with local dancing followed by the feast which was a fascinating mixture of local foods. We then sat cross- legged on the floor of the hut drinking karva while local musicians entertained us. Karva is made from the root of Karva, a local plant, and drinking it is steeped in tradition. Very much a male preserve, taking part in the ceremony is quite an experience. The liquid, served in a huge communal wooden bowl, looks like dirty washing-up water, tastes much the same, but has a calming effect. Some people hated it but I found it strangely compulsive. The musicians played on into the night. Outside, the wind howled and inside the Karva flowed. Pat managed to fall asleep sitting up and I felt at peace with the world. A truly memorable evening. We then spent an enjoyable couple of weeks sailing round the islands experiencing a number of magical anchorages. Going ashore on the tiny but thickly wooded island of Lappa we initially assumed it to be uninhabited, only to discover that there were in fact 20 people living there. We came across one family collecting coconuts. They were very friendly. The mother turned out to be the Headteacher of the local school. She invited us to supper which was served on the floor. The next morning we visited the school which had 4 pupils. We were amazed at how isolated the inhabitants of these small islands were. To our way of thinking the islands were so close together that communication between should have been fairly straightforward. In fact the few local boats there were were generally outboard powered and therefore expensive to run. I was surprised that there was no evidence of any local sailing craft. The Headteacher and her family hardly ever saw their relations on the main island. It was interesting to hear how, in spite of the fact that they had been so welcoming, they are in fact at times quite concerned about who might be coming ashore from the yachts. They had heard about some yachtsmen being armed. They had also heard about the September 11th attacks on the United States and when they sawa cruise ship stop off the island and start disgorging its passengers into zodiacs were seriously concerned that it might be an Afghan Troop Ship. There were 2 caves only accessible from the water that we managed to visit. The first, Swallows Cave, involved hovering off the entrance in Mona and going in in the dinghy. Once inside we landed and went through to an inner cave where once Tongan Kings had enjoyed feasts, lowered down through a hole in the roof. The other cave, Mariners Cave, also involved hovering off. This time several of us went in 'Aldebaran'. Here it was a case of snorkelling through an underwater pass into the cave. We had read that it should be possible if you could snorkel under the keel of your boat from about 10' either side. I had practised just that, that very morning and in the event had no problem. Laura of course was in an out like a mermaid. On

my way in I was swimming just below to the rock face at the very top of the entrance, feeling very pleased with myself, when I looked down and there she was way below me, effortlessly gliding through the water. Once in, it was fascinating to be in this dome-like cavern, only lit by the light coming up through the water. As the water outside surged the pressure inside the cave built up and a greenish mist would form and you would have to unblock your ears. While we were in Vavau we had been pondering our next moves. We had had extremely positive reports of the Happi Group of islands but the charts indicated that the area had large areas of reefs. The distance to the nearest islands of the group were an awkward 70 miles or so. In the end we went overnight, with 'Aldebaran' and 'Arganauta' leavinga little while after us. it proved to be a really good sail. The fresh south easterly just allowed us to hold our course. As dawn broke, 'Arganauta’ and ‘Aldebaran' were just coming up behind us. Just ahead we could see the island of Haano, the most northerly of the Happi Group. We followed 'Arganauta' through off-lying reefs into a large shallow bay. Later in the day we took the dinghy ashore and had an interesting walk with Pat and Olivia through the village, where once again the locals were eager to talk. Helen, Olivia and Laura spent some time exploring the beach down to the low water mark for shells. The next day we had a short genoa run to Foa Island where, having sailed through a pass in the reef, we anchored in shallow water over a sandy bottom off the town of Lotofoa where we checked in with a very friendly official who was very interested in our travels. We had an interesting walk across the island to the windward side where we saw a cemetery with elaborately decorated graves. Some even had large embroidered sheets suspended over them. The next day was Olivia's birthday and we sailed further along the island chain to the smaller island of Voleva. Like most of the islands in this group, Voleva is low and heavily wooded with long wide sandy beaches. This was the third time ina row that we had been with Pat and Olivia on Olivia's birthday. We all went ashore for a walk and Olivia found a tiny locally-run resort, catering for no more than 10 people at a time, who said that we could eat there that night. After a Happy Hour on 'Aldebaran' with 'Arganauta' and 'Cap d'Or’, the four of us went back to the resort for a meal and a wonderful evening around a log fire on the beach. The next day we went ashore again. Helen and Olivia walked across to a beach on the other side of the island while Pat, Laura and I were shown the sight of ancient ceremonial pigeon traps, where pigeons were caught for the edification of Tongan Kings. We then set off towards the far beach and ended up doing a route march round the entire island. By the time we met up with Helen and Olivia, Pat and I were exhausted. We then set off for the island of Ha'Afeva. The wind was on the nose and it was a slow sail that turned into a motor. Pat and Olivia decided to press on a bit further to the island of Oua. Julius and Sally on 'Arganauta' followed us into the beautiful lagoon at Ha'Afeva only to have engine failure just before they got there. They managed to sail into the lagoon. It turned out to be a fuel problem. (Julius had unwittingly run one of his tanks dry) and was soon resolved. We explored the island with Julius and Sally and were once again treated to the most amazing hospitality. A young mother called Star took us into her home where her father fed us on a shark dish. They then gave us bananas and took us into the forest where they picked fresh coconuts for us. Heading for the island of Nomuka to the south we had to weave between all kinds of hazards. We had thought that places like the Tuamotus were treacherous, but in fact the coral there was quite well behaved., most of it confined to the lagoons at the centre of the atolls, and between the atolls it was generally clear of dangers. Here the coral spread haphazardly across otherwise open water. Arriving at Nomuka Iki Island we were reunited briefly with 'Aldebaran' who, having arrived just before us, had decided to press on that night to Nuku Alofa. We went ashore and walked right across the beautiful deserted island that had once housed a tiny prison. The next evening we set off overnight for Nuku Alofa in company with 'Keyta' an American 30 footer that we had got to know. We had a good beam reach and actually made better progress than we had intended, arriving off the entrance channel to Juku Alofa well before dawn. In the meantime we had almost lost the blade to our self steering when the pivot pin came loose. Arriving in the port of Nukalofa we anchored off the wall with our stern tied to the shore. We spent nearly a week there and found it to be far nicer than we had been led to believe it would be. We managed to repair the self steering and the autohelm and get stocked up for the passage to New Zealand. We witnessed the ceremonies marking the opening of Parliament and had a brief glimpse of the King of Tonga. After we had checked out we moved out to an outlying island for the night where we met up with 'Arganauta'. We had a very pleasant evening together at the small island resort. The next afternoon we set off together for New Zealand.

Club Notes Commodore Hopefully the Club grapevine, notices around the Clubhouse and email sent out will have ensured that everyone has heard the great news that CONTRACTS HAVE BEEN EXCHANGED AND THE COMPLETION DATE IS 01 SEPTEMBER 2003. From that date we, the members, truly own the site and can manage the Club without reference to MASC. There are many people I would like to thank for their support and effort since we embarked on buying the Club. First, Clive Shenton and the team that produced the initial business plan when he was Commodore. This needed very little change apart from the updating of the numbers. Then there was the team who earlier this year delved into the intricacies of company law and the banking system to define the structure of the new company and select a supportive bank. During the last two to three months, which has seemed like a lifetime to me, the work has fallen almost entirely on the shoulders of John Bird dealing with the finance and Julian Royle sorting out the legal deal. Both have had to deal with the MASC, surveyors who had no idea of the urgency, and finally with me badgering them during their annual holiday; without their efforts we would still be feeling our way through the maze. During all this time the running of the Club on a day to day basis has been shouldered by the members of the Management and Sub Committees. I know that I speak on behalf of the entire Executive in thanking them. Finally, and most importantly, are you, the members of the Club. You have supported us right from the start when we presented the future at the special meeting, you have raised at least £128,000 in members’ loans (and it is still arriving with John), you have tolerated my evasive answers when asking how it was progressing, and ensured that the spirit of the Club will continue into the future. Navigans is the lifeblood of communication within the Club but it does represent a large controllable expenditure. We are therefore experimenting over the next few issues with sending it electronically to those members who have email addresses in addition to sending the normal paper copy. If those receiving it electronically have any comments, good or bad, please email them to Matt (the editor). If the project is successful, we aim to drop the paper copy for those with email from January 2004. Again THANK YOU FOR THE SUPPORT and HERES TO THE FUTURE OF THE CLUB. Neil Pembleton Vice President What’s in a Name? When you read this in early September there is good reason to hope that Thirslet Sailing Club Ltd. will own the Sailing Club Site. You will recall that the name Thirslet Sailing Club was chosen in haste when it was important to act quickly to react to the rapidly deteriorating situation with our parent the MASC. We can now allow ourselves time to reflect on the name that we wish to be known by for the next 50 years. I ask you all to think about this matter and when you have formed your views, please contact me on [redacted].co.uk or [redacted]. I will correlate all the suggestions and produce a short list for further consultation. No decision will be taken until the AGM but we must have a short list for consideration at that meeting, so please contact me with your suggestions by early October. I now wish to give you my views on our future name and ask you to take these into consideration when forming your opinions. Many of you will have a loyalty to the name “Marconi”. There is no doubt that we have a good reputation within the sailing circles using that name, and, if you are like me, part of you says “Why not keep to the old name?” If that is your view then I need to give you the downside of such a decision.

Although many members stay for many years, others do not, and we need to attract new members every year. Indeed our Business Plan requires that we increase membership. My experience is that “Marconi” causes difficulties with prospective members. They automatically think that they have to be a Company employee to join. Recently, the name Marconi has been associated with a failing telecoms Company and that leads people to wonder if the Club will sink with the Company. Also we may get some trouble from Marconi about the use of their name. Lastly, if we continue to be associated with Marconi, even if that association is only in name, it may affect our chances of a loan from the Sports Council when we come to improve our facilities. In conversations I have with members, they talk of Stansgate Sailing Club giving the letters SSC — the same as our near neighbour Stone Sailing Club. If members favour use of Stansgate, I would advocate the name Stansgate Abbey SC giving SASC as our shorthand. Not too bad you may think, the SAS are a legendary Regiment of the British Army, but is it right for our new Club? You may wish to consider a name without a geographical reference — there is a Club called “Castaways” that has been around for years, although I have no idea where they are based. After thought you may think that Thirslet SC is not such a bad name after all. In the title I asked the question, ““What’s in a name?” My answer is “Quite a lot actually” Please let me have your ideas. Let’s get a dialogue going. Please think hard. Clive Shenton Solo Fleet SOLOS AT MARCONI: 157 June 2003. 26 Solos took to the water at Marconi Sailing Club on the River Blackwater on 1° June. The event was part of the Solo Eastern Area Championships and also a Sea Series event. Fifteen visitors complemented the eleven club members. Following a superb training day on the Saturday with bright sunshine and force 3 — 4 wind the weather on Sunday was disappointing with thundery clouds, no wind initially and a light breeze which never picked up above a 2. Nevertheless the Race Officer John Weedon set a course and the first race started in a light Southerly wind on a course using the full width of the river. Andy Davis from Bartley set an early lead which was never challenged and it was left for others to scrap for the places. Steve Ede was second, Jerry Garner third followed by Dave Nixson and John Salmon. Race 2 followed very much the same pattern although the beats were more interesting in the strong tide which changed during the race. Andy Davis first followed by Jerry Garner and Steve Ede. With the tide now ebbing, the fleet was being swept across the line at the start of race 3 resulting in a general recall. At the restart, Andy Davis was over the line and had to return round the end but made impressive speed to overtake all but three of the fleet by the end of the rather long race. Steve Ede won this race with Steve Denison second and Jerry Garner third. Results: ih. Andy Davis Bartley S. C. a Steve Ede. Ardleigh S. C. a" Jerry Garner Papercourt S. Cruiser Fleet In the two months since the last Navigans we have had the Watercress Run to Heybridge, the Piers Race, anda cruise to St. Katharines. Nineteen boats locked into Heybridge with a dozen going to Beeleigh in the tenders with about fifty people having a BBQ in the evening on the lock side. Light winds caused the Piers Race to be shortened at Clacton pier but for the cruisers it was very pleasant to be anchored in the sun with calm conditions. Thank you to all the cruisers who helped on this major club event. The St. Katharines cruise was carefully arranged to coincide with a heat wave and although not much sailing was done it was an excellent holiday, with eighteen boats locking into St. Katharines and going on to Chatham later on in the week. The Shotley cruise will have probably taken place by the time you receive this, likewise the working party to clear the cruiser park. Just to re-cap, we shall get ten power points down the centre of the cruiser park from the engine room to the gate by the pill box, four on the north side of the hedge, two on the south side of the hedge, and one by the mast derrick. The waste oil tank is now in use, this is for waste oil only. It is emptied free of charge but if it is contaminated by water paint or spirit, they will not empty it, so only waste engine oil please.
