BLACKWATER & COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION On Thursday 4th September I attended a meeting of the above association held at the Marconi (Thirslett) Sailing Club, Stansgate. I am reporting below on those matters which I consider of interest to you PLANNING APPLICATIONS & DEVELOPEMENTS Maldon District Council has granted the building of a counter wall across Tollesbury Wick. Objections had been raised as the proposal was based on the premis that the main sea wall could fail and could be allowed to. It was felt such a breech could seriously affect all sailing activity (including Marina, etc) in the Tollesbury Channels. CLACTON MARTELLO TOWER C - Change of use to incorporate a new National Coast Watch Tower. MALDON - Floating Mooring for a 32m barge off Northey Island. ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES : BLACKWATER & COLNE EEEMS - A further (undated) draft of the Estuary Scheme -of Management has been received for formal comment which has been made. The Chairman expressed concern that although the key issues we have raised have been incorporated, the document has been changed to omit the specific categary of 'other interested parties' (eg the users). The document does refer in a number of places !o the importance and need for the inclusion of ‘users' but the omission in this version of the previously included 'user' category is worrying and raises fears that users will not be involved in the consideration of measures which could adversly affect them. WINDFARMS - GE Wind Energy have stated they are prepared to remove the exclusion zone clause also provide a legal undertaking fixing the minimum rotor tip clearance height at 20m above MHWS. This is still 2m less than was being sought and on the basis that this will not be allowed to set a precedence, the RYA will probably accept this. WEYMARKS - WETLAND RESTORATION : DEFRA stated they had 4 points in support and 19 in opposition including our concern re potential siltation. A final decision is expected at the end of 2003. ANY OTHER BUSINESS : Dabchicks S.C. have complained in the past about the excessive use of M2 by other clubs and in particular Stone S.C. that they now have thier own VHF Channel. It is pointed out that transmitting on 1 watt should suffice for most club activities. WEST MERSEA - there is a proposal to remove the dinghy landing pads because they are dangerous. MARCONI S.C. At the request of a member, I drew attention to the problem and potential hazard experienced at the club by the excessive wash caused by fast motor cruisers especially during launching & recovery of cruisers, (ro.

the same can also be experienced by dinghy fleet members. The Chairmans comments and those of members of the Association have been passed on to Marconi/Thirstlett SC main committee for action. Derek Gardner [redacted] or e-mail [redacted] Some Notes on the Club Security System. (Gate Cards) Our club members have the unusual privilege of access to the site and clubhouse at any time they wish. This is achieved by means of access cards, which have a magnetic strip that may be programmed. Some cards provide access to the first floor bar and the cellar. Access to these will depend on the responsibilities of the member. Each card has a serial number associated with the member so that each card is unique. If a member leaves the club the card will be cancelled so that it will no longer provide access. Every time a card is used the reader consults a list to see if the card holder has the right of access. Ordinary cards are normally issued by the Club Registrar. (Membership Secretary). Occasionally a member will lose ‘their’ card and will then seek a replacement. After a new card is issued the original card is cancelled. If the member subsequently rediscovers ‘their’ lost card it will be useless and should be returned to the club. The cards have nothing visibly written on them except for the serial number. There is nothing to associate the card with the sailing club so that our security is not significantly jeopardised in the interval before the card is cancelled. It is inevitable that other members when they have forgotten to bring ‘their’ own card or when they have temporarily mislaid it will borrow a card from another member. If you borrowa card it is essential to return the card you borrowed and not the mislaid card. If you subsequently leave the club ‘your’ card will be cancelled. If this has earlier been swapped with another members card, that member will be denied access to the club. Unfortunately the serial numbers on the cards wear off with time. This makes the recognition of swapped cards impossible without a card reader. In the future the serial number will be marked on the card using a more permanent method. There are times when the card readers fail. The degradation is usually due to wear and is progressive resulting in some cards being recognised whilst others are rejected. In this situation we endeavour to repair the card reader as soon as possible. We can only apologise to those members who have been inconvenienced. Misalignment of the gate or door is another recurring fault. The relative position of the mechanism is critical and changes in temperature and humidity can cause misalignment. Rough usage will also cause misalignment. Frank Bennett created the security system some 10 years ago and for a large proportion of the time it performs satisfactorily. The alternative was to purchase a proprietary system with a maintenance contract at considerable expense to the club. We hope you find these notes helpful in explaining the background to the operation of the security system together with some of its limitations. Perhaps it is worth making the following points. 1. Treat ‘your’ card with the same respect as your bank card. Keep it clear of magnets.(Car radio speakers). 2. Operate the gate to the site and the door to the clubhouse with care. 3. Ensure that you keep the card that was issued to you and make a note of the serial number. This is particularly important if you have more than one card.

6 4. Ifyou are likely to be leaving the site when few other members are around use ‘your’ own card to check its operation. Don’t just follow another member in. 5. If ‘your’ card is worn or damaged please ask for a replacement. 6. All cards remain the property of the Club. Frank Bennett and David Steward Tail-piece As I will be standing down from the position of Rear Commodore at the AGM, this will be my last “Tail-piece”. It is an appropriate time to thank all those who have helped me to plan, organise and execute the sailing programme this last couple of years. The principal players in this have of course been the members of the Sailing Sub- Committee so my thanks to them all for the excellent teamwork which has made my job so pleasant and straightforward. I must make special mention of Dave Williams who has been an absolute stalwart as Sailing Secretary. It remains then for me to wish my successors the same levels of enjoyment which I have derived from the job. Iam sure you will all give them your support. to Club Notes Commodore’s Comments It is with some surprise that | find myself writing this piece. My expectation, like yours, was that Neil would carry on in post for some time yet. He was very much the right Commodore at the right time; he steered us magnificently through the minefield that was the purchase of the Club and we all owe him a debt of gratitude. The Executive team has seen some changes of personnel and is enlarged; we now have two Vice Commodores and two Rear Commodores. This increase was designed to enable us to better deal with the additional administrative and management loads placed on us as a result of our new-found independence. | am delighted that Pat Black and John Bird have agreed to stay on as Secretary and Treasurer respectively. The two Vice Commodores are Ray Ball and Peter Clayton; Claire Davies and Clive Shenton take on the two Rear Commodore roles. Ray will major on matters concerning the Clubhouse and site; Peter will take responsibility for issues concerning equipment and moorings, camping and Cadet training; Claire will look after all sailing matters and Clive takes over responsibility for ECPR and social activities. | think this makes a very strong team; | am grateful for their support and confident that in turn they will get full support from Club members. | won’t name the Management Committee individually here. Their names will appear in the new Handbook and the roles they take on are broadly understood. They contribute significantly to the smooth running of the club; their commitment is widely appreciated. | do not overlook the efforts of a much larger band of members who, working within the Club's self-help ethos, do so much - sometimes on a regular basis, sometimes on an occasional basis - to assist with the running of the Club. This involvement is a major contributor to the character of the Club. We all go through periods where work, family or personal circumstances prevent us from being as involved as we might wish - but all contributions are welcome, no matter how small or irregular. Management Committee provides the focus for that effort - to discuss doing more or any ideas, make contact with someone on that list. Now a few words about our intended focus for the coming year. Recent concern has been for the purchase of the site and the creation of a financial plan to support that activity - with some valuable work being done to maintain the site. Now we need to carefully take stock of what we have bought and how we use it, so that we have the information to develop from our strong financial plan. However, this does not imply a period of introspection and no activity - there is a lot to be done to ensure that the site is maintained in safe, practical and presentable order. There is also a case for reviewing the most important aspect of our existence as a Club - our sailing!. So three initiatives are born: e Knowledge Fund will pull together all the information we can gather about the site, site facilities and how members use the site and all it contains. This information will aid our decisions in managing and developing the site. e _ Foresail will re-examine all sailing activity with a view to identifying anything that we could do better or more often and to consider new ways in which we might improve what we offer to members and potential members. e Homepride will address the need to maintain the site in good order and to present the Club facilities in such a way that they are pleasing to existing members and attractive to potential members. Everyone will have an opportunity to be involved. A lot of the information-gathering will be done through the Fleet structure. So please be prepared to be involved in a series of activities that are important to our future as an independent club. | hope you all had a Happy Christmas; have an Excellent New Year! Chris Davies Retiring Commodore - A few final notes Many thanks to all who attended the Annual General Meeting and contributed to the discussion. As you will be aware the vote to select a new name for the Club resulted in the decision to retain the name "Marconi Sailing Club". This was selected by an overall majority over the other two names which had emerged as "front runners". Subject to Chris Davies and the new executive establishing that there is no legal problem, this will be the name. One of the duties of the Commodore each year is to decide who will receive three of the Club Trophies. Firstly there is the Mamgu which is awarded for the best log submitted by 1*' October each year. | received two entries and the award went to Les Hurrell-Smith for his log entitled "Three men and a boat - the tale of a yacht delivery" which | found informative, amusing and educational. The next is the Seamanship Trophy which is awarded to a person who has performed an act of outstanding seamanship. Again there were two entries and it went to Nick Miller and Rob Mead jointly following the dismasting of Rob's Pico and the retrieval of him and his dinghy by Nick in another Pico. Although this happened locally to the Club during Camping fortnight when the safety boats were available, both of them dealt with the situation using their own resources and skills rather than assuming that Rob would be "rescued". It is also appropriate to associate the work of the Cadet Tutors with this event as they instilled the ethos of self reliance into the cadet fleet

The final trophy is the Commodore's Trophy which is awarded to the person who is not on a committee who has made a contribution to the Club over a number of years. | was pleased to be able to give this to Bob and Elsie Anderson for all that they have done over a very long time for the Club. Bob is well known as a measurer for the Solo fleet, and he with Elsie have over the years improved the look of the sea wall with its spring daffodils as well as planting and maintaining the garden by the patio. All of this has been done at no expense to the Club and without seeking any recognition. Well done to all of the above and | hope that Chris Davies will have a similarly hard job deciding on the merits of next year's entries. Neil Pembleton Vice Commodore Clubhouse Cleaning Jan Morgan who has kept the clubhouse spick and span for the past three years has now given up the job to pursue other activities. Minutes of MSC Cruiser Fleet AGM 22TM Nov 2003 Apologies were received from Pat Black, Derek Kirby, Gordon Pewter, Julie Bloomfield Mick and Roger, Derek and Hilary Gardiner and Malcolm and Helen Shaft. Review of 2003 Sailing Season There were three winter meetings including a talk from the Port of London Authority, ICOM and a quiz. In May fifty six people attended the fitting out supper and eighteen boats went to Burnham. In June thirteen boats visited Brightlinsea and the Watercress Run on the 19th June was well attended with about nineteen boats and fifty people attending the evening barbeque. The ECPR was less well supported than usual this year and it would be nice to have more volunteers next year. Chris Davies announced that a sum in excess of £9,000 had been donated from the ECPR to the Cirdan Trust and thanked the cruiser fleet for their support. Nineteen boats locked into St Katherine’s Dock for the start of the summer cruise with fifteen going onto to Chatham where there was another successful barbeque. Fewer people than normal made it to Shotley this year with about sixteen boats locking in and only sixteen attending the Sunday dinner. Review of 2003 Racing Season Five races were held; the Doctor was run in conjunction with BURC, the Eagle trophy was run from the club to Burnham, while the Medusa finished by joining the rest of the club in Brightlingsea. The Steeple Bay trophy was new in joining catamarans and dinghies from the club, and the Knoll trophy was a new and successful single handed event. The diary for next year is still to be decided but will comprise five races maintaining the Jackpot and the single handed. There is also a possibility of a pursuit race. Winter Storage and Cruiser Haul Out Electrics. Roger asked Dave Payne to explain the electrical re-fit in the cruiser park. Dave Payne outlined the reasons for the refit due to non compliance of current regulations. The new system will ensure ample to supply to the far end of the cruiser park and that no one will be able to leave multiple electrical appliances plugged in for long periods. Six amp breakers have been installed on outlets with a welding socket on the cruiser garage, and on the winch hut. Bob Godbold was reassured that pressure washers would be able to be used in the cruiser park and Pete Bloomfield was assured that breakers in the engine shed would not trip. Mark queried why new bollards only had two outlets but Dave pointed out that outlets been over doubled. Mike Smith was told that if an appliance cut out there was a button on the outlet post to reset the club RCD. There followed discussion over the concern that boats that have their own electrical supply could cause, if live and neutral are transposed, their trailers to give off electric shocks. It was suggested that, until there had been further discussion at committee which would result in recommendations in Navigans, no one plug their electrical circuit into the club supply but use a wander lead instead. No plugs are to be left plugged into the main supply unless the owner is on Site. Plugs are available from Dave at a cost of £2.00

Tractors and Haul Out Murray was pleased that the season had started and finished with four working tractors. The club is looking to replace the four wheel drive tractor in the near future. (Since the AGM, the hydraulic winch engine has failed and is to be replaced with an electric motor.) Roger thanked Murray and this was endorsed by members. Moorings Peter Clayton mooted several options to cut down workload on mooring laying and lifting. These were discussed but a majority voted for the continuation of the present system for reliability reasons. There was a discussion about the logistics of the make up of mooring teams as some had been found to be excessively onerous. This will be investigated. Murray urged people to inspect their moorings during the winter and not to wait until inspection day. There was a discussion about the need to weld shackles. Chain Don Holdsworth has shackles for sale at £3.00 for % and £2.00 for 5/8. He urged people to change to heavier chain for their risers which he has available at a cost of £1.75 per foot for 14 mm. Paint Gordon Preston will sell paint and stated that prices will be more or less maintained. Details will go in Navigans as usual. Delivery will probably be a week later. Programme 2004 There will be no winter meetings due to the expense of hiring the Chelmsford MASC rooms. There is a possibility of a bowling evening in February and there will need to be a spring meeting at the club. The fitting out supper is booked for 8" May and the season will continue as follows: Burham on 29/30/31" May with a meal in the Swallowtail on the Sunday. Heybridge on 19" June. Brightlingsea on 3/4" July. ECPR 24'/25" July. There is a need for more cruisers. Ramsgate, Dover, Chatham week beginning 31° July August Bank Holiday with Shotley as a start. No restaurant is being booked this year so it was suggested that people book up the Shipwreck for themselves. Cock Up Trophy There were several contenders but, as is traditional, only those who attended the meeting know the results. Any Other Business Neil Pembleton thanked Frank Burgess and Roger Camp for their efforts. Letters & Articles 2003 Winner of the Mamgu Trophy “Three men and a Boat — the tale of a yacht delivery” It all started last summer. Paul a long suffering friend had a garden party to celebrate his sons 21* birthday, and as is the practice, good food, sun and plenty of alcoholic lubrication lulled one into a sense of self satisfaction and total happiness with the world. Paul is a bit smart and obviously spotted this and in a moment when my guard was down approached me with a proposition. | have known Paul for more years than | care to remember so | have become accustomed to some strange requests, but that might be another story. On this occasion Paul asked if | would be able to help him deliver a yacht he was buying. Details were sparse, or perhaps| just forgot them in the alcoholic haze but it seemed like a truly excellent idea, a few weeks in the Mediterranean delivering a sailing boat to Turkey, you would be mad to say no! | checked with my social and domestic manager (Wendy) who gave it the thumbs up, and the deal was signed with another kebab and a bottle of Becks. That was that for a few months while Paul went off and organised the purchase a decision that | am sure required something stronger than Becks when the time came to sign the cheque. Around January this year we started to make plans, routes were planned; holiday booked the usual sort of thing one does when delivering a yacht from France to Turkey as we all know! Regular weekly updates then started as the due date drew nearer, we see sawed between France and Croatia as our start point, as the manufacturer seemed unsure as to where they were in Europe they were going to deliver the yacht. Paul seemed not to worry about such minor details, perhaps still smarting from the cheque being cashed. In the end we left Luton airport on sunny March day enroute for the French Riviera, in order to take delivery of “JASSPER’ so named after Jenna, Alix, Sue, Sam Paul, Early Retirement! The plan being to be ready to sail on the 1°‘ of April, somehow the significance of this date passed both Paul and myself by. From Nice airport a taxi took us to Antibes marina, where we met Chris the owner of “Top Yacht’, who would be taking Paul’s boat on for charter use. Chris seemed happy as he told us that “we” had a small problem, which was that the mast could not be stepped due to a problem with the forestay, so poor Paul's first sight of his yacht was of one without a mast. No problem said Chris, if we can’t source the part locally one of his guys would be fly out from the UK Tuesday with the new piece. Nothing could be done so we sent Chris off to buy supper, and we eventually tucked in to a pizza with some other intrepid charterers. So, our start date looked already to be in serious jeopardy. Undaunted we booked into a small French hotel and made acquaintance with Brian who was to be our skipper/navigator for the two week journey, hoping to leave on the Wednesday. Brian was an experienced Ocean sailor, having sailed the BT Global challenge Southern Ocean leg, surely a skill not needed in the med! Read on. Trying to put a positive slant on things we decided to use the time to plot our course, provision the boat and get a sun tan, not necessarily in that order. This meant lots of sitting around drinking coffee, Ok and the odd beer, carefully scrutinising charts, and making a shopping list. The chart piece was easy when compared to 3 men planning to shop for food for a 2 week trip is not the sort of exercise that one should expect to go with out it’s problems. The first of the shopping problems was simply where to go, and it was then that Frank (pronounce this in a heavy French accent as Fraank for best effect) came into the story. Fraank wasa taxi driver with a difference, you could not book Fraank but you could make an appointment, which Fraank would then negotiate with you as he “may be a /eetle late, or he may not”. Frank also had an aversion to coins and liked to round up his fare, which was OK as he did have a Mercedes people carrier with TV and DVD, and he needed to pay for those sharp suits. He also needed to pay for his fuel as Frannk was keen to take short cuts, which included a trip to his parents apartment on one occasion, (they were not in but on holiday in Dakar we were informed), and on another occasion to pass by Fraanks own apartment, of which he was particularly proud. Fraank also had an interesting driving technique which involved often stopping just to talk to people, some he knew some he thought he knew but didn’t, and of course the meter was always running, “Gentlemen, (long pause for thought) shall | round this up to 25 Euros’?” became a familiar phrase of Fraanks. You will by now have established that we spent a lot of time with Fraank, and not much sailing. The shooing trip itself was an adventure; we had our list, carefully prepared by Brian, who sensibly had decided to stay with JASSPER to check charts (Brian did a lot of chart checking). So Paul and | picked up our two trolleys and set off. It took us many hours to shop and got some strange looks when we got to the checkout as the mix of produce was heavily in favour of drink. We both agreed if the bill was too much the bottled water had to go, in preference to the wine, beer and spirits. The new part needed to allow us to step the mast did actually have to come from the UK and arrived on Tuesday, so we booked a slot to have the mast stepped on the Wednesday and started to get excited at the prospect that we may soon have a complete yacht. So Wednesday came and after lots of activity in the boat yard, the mast was put up, but that then meant that the yacht needed significant work to the electrics and other bits, and all of a sudden she was engulfed with riggers and Paul, Brian and myself were surplus, indeed seemed to be in the way! So nothing for it, we needed another taxi trip to the Carrefore for essential provisions, while Brian finalised his chart work ready for the big off. This time the essentials entailed electric drills, boat shoes (they were such a bargain lets have 2 pairs!), a few pairs of trousers, yes another bargain, and assorted other bits of hardware to allow Paul to fit another piece of electronics, he had acquired. On this trip, Fraank decided to just stop and have a little chat with a little old lady and her dog, someone he thought he knew but actually did not! Never mind the traffic jam he caused finding this out. Paul had a doze as we flew through the back streets on a detour, “to save time”. Stopping off on F Fraanks parents house again to check the plants were OK. More on Pauls’ interesting ability to doze almost instantly and anywhere later in the story!

8 In the end the boat was finally ready late Wednesday evening, but by then the weather had changed and sailing was not an option our skipper told us with some authority, after listening attentively to weather info on channel 68 and studying the synoptic chart from the Capitainaire, Paul and | nodded with agreement. We did manage two brief shake down sails on the Thursday and Friday and decided to “go for it” early Saturday morning, the real adventure was about to begin. So it was that at 05:50 on Saturday the 5" of April, JASSPER with her three intrepid crew left Antibes on route for Turkey. Our plan was to sail down the eastern coast of Corsica, through the La Magdalena straits and then on to the heel of Italy, then Athens and finally Bodrum in Turkey. This was ambitious in the time left but fair winds and 24 hour watches might just make it possible, we convinced ourselves, but contingency was made to stop at Athens and let another crew take over. We soon learnt that having a contingency plan was an extremely sensible idea. All went well, for day one we had good breeze as we watched the French Alps disappear slowly from view and then we were alone in the Tyrannian Sea, with just the dolphins for company. We decided to eat around 6 that evening, ready for the watch roster and sat down on deck to enjoy hearty servings of Hot Spaghetti Bolognese, not from a tin or a packet, Oh No! All fresh. Brian our skipper describes this as “Good Scoff’, Paul and I had shopped well at Carrefore and we felt smug! We had set ourselves a 3 hour on 6 off watch pattern, and my first night watch went OK, | was on from 21:00 to 00:00 hours and enjoyed a wonderful sunset and a starlight night under a new moon. With great excitement| watched the odd freighter or cruise liner pass in the distance. The dolphins were still with us and one could see them leave a phosphorescent trail as they sped through the water only inches from JASSPERs hull. The next day saw sunshine and the good winds holding for us, as we headed for Bonafacio, at the southern end of Corsica, we had been told that this was an impressive sight and as the cliffs slowly came into view it was confirmed. The cliff tops were crowned by a magnificent fortress which just seemed to be hanging on the edge, really impressive. The sight was so delightful that we decided to stop over for a brief break and get over the slight bout of Mal de Mere from which | was suffering, | can thoroughly recommend Stuggeron tablets and | don’t know why but regular nibbles of Ginger Nut biscuits, also helped as a remedy. We stayed just long enough to have lunch, refill with fresh water and discover that the fuel station was closed, as were most of the shops, it was a Sunday but we had by now lost track of the days. So refreshed, off we went with the next planned stop to be Reggio in Southern Italy some 4 or 5 days solid sailing was ahead of us. The wind had freshened but was steady and the sun stayed with us as we left Bonafacio. We really started to sail the yacht now, as we had quite a swell and could surf down the waves, good old dinghy tactics. After a little play Brain set our compass bearing and we and headed for the La Magdalena straits between Corsica and Sardinia. Careful chart work was needed here as we picked our way through the many impressive but dangerous looking rocks, Brian pawed over his paper charts while Paul checked his electronic versions on the array of kit that had been fitted and was constantly being added to by Paul as a new bit of wizardry came out of no where! After a few hours we started out into open water saying good-bye to France and Sardinia, this was to be our last sight of land for quite a while. That evening we again dined on deck, | can’t remember the exact meal but seem to recall it had a high pasta content, and again was “good scoff’ according to Brian, just the stuff to keep your energy up, looking back perhaps Brian was psychic, because we certainly needed our energy in the next 36 hours. The wind died a little and we decided to use the motor to keep our speed over ground up to the desired level if we were to make the passage on time. It was around 20:00 hours that the wind picked enough for us to hoist the main, unfurl the jib, then turned off the motor to enjoy another spectacular sunset over Sardinia, as she disappeared from view. All was well in the world and as the winds got up slightly Paul started to really sail his boat and was like a dog with two tails when he saw the boat speed hit 10.44 knots as he surfed us down the waves, great fun. Both Paul and Brian went below to get some sleep and | took watch at 21:00. It was at about 22:00 that the wind came round to right on our stern and JASSPER was on a dead run, not comfortable but OK provided concentration was kept up. At around 23:00 hours the wind was veering and in order to avoid constant Gybes and waking the two down below, it was necessary to bear away from our true course, the boat speed was averaging about 8 knots as the wind started to freshen even further. Then at precisely 23:30 hours, yes | remember this time exactly, the Depth alarm started to scream at me, we had (it said) only 2.4 metres of water below us! With a 2 metre keel | was as you might expect just a little concerned. Logic said it was a fault, especially as a similar incident had affected Paul’s watch the night before. We were at least 40 miles from any land, and nothing was shown on the chart, but the alarm kept on screaming. But what has logic got to do with decision making! Brian was woken by a couple of crash gybes and came on deck, to see what was occurring, we tried to reset the electronics but without any success. No alternative but to get Paul up, as he was in charge of all things technical simply because he had read the manuals, and he liked to play with these things anyway. After much fiddling, checking of manuals, lots of cursing from Brian, it was decided that the depth gauge had had it. Paul went back to sleep, we had already learnt that Paul could wake up instantly and fall asleep just as quickly, it was an art that Brian and | both had not mastered. Anyway, we settled down and Brian took over his watch, and | decided to stay on deck and have a nap, it was a warm evening and this seemed sensible rather than go below and feel seasick again! Just as well that | did because at around 01:00 hours the winds started to really pick up to over 20 knots and Brian thought it would be wise to put a reef in the main, which we did. | was wide awake by now so stayed on deck and in just 30 minutes we had second reef in as the winds had built even further and the boat was beginning to become over powered. The depth gauge may have given up but the anemometer was working as we had 30 knots of wind showing and a very “confused sea” to contend with, or as the Italians described it “Molto Mosso”. Two reefs did not help we were screaming along so we had no alternative but to drop the main. So in rising seas | went below, struggled into my oilskins and was then soon battling on the foredeck tidying the main while Brian struggled with the helm. Paul slept soundly below! As | put the last of the sail ties around the main | knew what it must feel like to be in a washing machine, which was not set to the delicate programme, while riding a roller coaster. So here we were running just under headsail, averaging something like 10 knots, and still the wind built. The sensible thing now would have been to put up the storm jib. | am sure this is entirely possible but perhaps not sensible as the boat was now in 18ft seas and | am no mountain goat. So instead we furled the headsail to give us just enough steerage

9 and control, well everything is relative! It needs to be said that at this stage Brian had been at the helm for some 5 hours and that despite all this activity Paul was sleeping soundly in the sea berth below, which must be a record of some sort. During all this | tried to maintain the hourly log which at 04:00 hours showed us as having F9 winds, | gave up at 05:00 hours and simply put in that the log was not completed due to extreme weather conditions, an understatement as just then the squall came the stars disappeared and we recorded a gust of 42 knots! Suddenly | wished we did not have such a comprehensive set of instruments on deck! By now Brian and | were both pretty tired, the winds had died back to 25 — 30 knots as Paul emerged from below asking if we wanted tea! Paul duly took the helm and Brian got some well earned sleep. As | mentioned earlier, Brian had done the Southern Ocean leg of the BT Global Challenge and he remarked on the similarity of conditions, albeit the Med was just a little bit warmer when the waves broke over your head! | was feeling much worse for wear now, having been up for more hours than | can remember | went below feeling decidedly sick! As Paul and Brian soldiered on, not sure of what else to do, but in the end they decided we were not going to out run this storm, which we later found out was officially recorded a strong gale, so they turned JASSPER round and headed for a safe haven. After 12 more hours we finally out JASSPER into Punta Santaldia on the North West coast of Sardinia, for a well earned rest and hot shower, much relieved to have survived. Cruising in the Med is not meant to be like this! Our schedule had been severely jeopardised, and was not going to improve until the weather did. We ended up spending 3 days in Punta Santaldia, which would have been nice, if it wasn’t the off-season, everything was closed, and only the Brits cruise the med in April it seems! Anyway we amused ourselves by tidying the boat and getting to know the Cape and his staff in the harbour masters office. The weather did not improve and in order to stop ourselves going crazy we hired a car, mainly as a distraction and means of seeing the island, which it has to be said was very beautiful if a little rugged, real bandit country. However with a means of travel, Paul decided we must have a NavTech so we can get some real weather information, much better than relying on the VHF forecasts, so off we set in search of one. Two towns and 3 chandlers later no luck but we had some nice Pizza in one of the restaurants we found! Here is a snap of the motley crew, from left to right Brian, the skipper, Paul the owner, and myself, crew. After three days we had a window in the weather, the harbourmaster told us, that with a “Cape like Brian” we would be OK. Brian and the harbourmaster had built up a mutual respect for each others seamanship, even though the Cape as he was affectionately known to his staff seemed more at home in his sports car. We decide to go that very afternoon. So we waved good-bye to Sicily and set a course for Reggio in Italy, some 3 days sailing. The winds held and we made good progress for a day, but we needed to make good headway, as the plan now was to leave JASSPER in Reggio and let a replacement crew take her on to Turkey. A reluctant decision but the three of us had run out of holiday and really wanted to get back to the UK for Easter. Whilst in Punta Santaldia Paul had contacted the charter company and they were sourcing a crew, and his other contacts, namely his daughter Jenna who was organising transport for us back to the UK. Out of contact we just had to hope the jig saw fitted together. The first land we sighted was the volcanic group of islands dominated by Mount Stromboli, and we could clearly see the smoke rising from its peak as we passed less than a mile from it’s shores. Amazingly the side of the mountain was speckled with houses and other dwellings, clearly the possibility of an eruption held no fear for some! It was as we passed Stromboli that we encountered a British warship, which we happily hailed on the VHF to check the weather and also to ask for an update on the Iraqi conflict. The weather info was readily forthcoming but the response on the war was just a little guarded, but we gathered that Baghdad had fallen, but not much more. As the winds died we had to start the engine and power sailed our way to Italy, as the med changed from a maelstrom into mill pond, it seems we had had any wind owing us, and got it all at once! The sea was dead calm as we entered the straits between Italy and Sicily as the sun started to set. We needed to stay alert as the chart warned of whirlpools and sure enough we saw these spiralling off our port side, quite strange We finally made it to Reggio about 21:00 hours on day 13, and picked our way into the little harbour, finally mooring amongst an assortment of cruising and racing yachts. The final evening meal on board was prepared by my good self and contained pretty much everything, Brian again described this as good scoff and made an entry in the log to show that my cooking had at last improved! Early the next day caught a taxi to the railway station, we planned to travel to Naples and fly back to Stanstead only to be told that the railways were on strike! Luckily the Italians seem to be very selective when striking, they either didn’t know about it or they decided not to strike on the Eurostar. So it was with a heavy heart that we said our goodbyes to JASSPER, and Brian, who was staying on an extra day to greet the new crew, and Paul and | headed off to Naples for our flight home. The adventure ended at midnight as we touched down in the UK, and already | was missing the experience, how quickly one forgets the misery of sea sickness, the feeling of being totally saturated, and the experience of not being able to stand up. | arrived home at 1.00 a.m. and am sure | had a grin on my face for at least a week as | recalled the journey and the things we had gone through, do it again, yes without a doubt. For those who need to know the yacht we sailed was a Bavaria 36 (but measures nearly 38 ft!) and, she is fitted out with 6 berths and has very spacious accommodation, which includes a good kitchen and head, with shower. Well appointed with all navigation electronics and CD player etc. She is available for charter and Paul has selected Top Yacht to manage all arrangements. If interested visit the web site on www.top-yacht.com or call them on 01243 520 950. | can testify she is a good boat, she, and Brian’s exceptional seamanship, saw us through one hell of a storm Les Hurrell-Smith

10 News First Aid Course for Support Boat Crews You may recall that the Club decided to pay for RYA standard first aid training for members who regularly serve as Support Boat Crews, in order to enhance their skills in this area. The first of these courses will be delivered at Bradwell, on Sunday 15 Feb 2004, by Bradwell Outdoor Education Centre. | have contacted all those who have previously expressed an interest in this course, unless | have forgotten anyone, and the course is now nearly fully subscribed. However there are still one or two places available and anyone who would like to avail themselves of the course on this date should let me know asap. John Salmon [redacted] [redacted].fsnet.co.uk Seamanship Trophy Nomination Nick Miller Rob Mead Background: Early evening second week of camping Wind East 4 Tide Ebbing 2 hours before LW Conditions rough in channel due to wind over tide Several Pico’s were sailing in the general area off the club just outside the moorings. The rig came down completely mast and sails in the water on the Pico sailed by Rob Mead. | took the workboat over with Roy Hardwick and Grant Strong as a jumper if needed. By the time we got to the incident the boys had recovered the rig, made it secure and had the disabled Pico in tow with the other one sailed by Nick. This all achieved under sail; each boat single handed and with no damage or loss of gear. They received no assistance nor needed any. A very difficult task under sail. Well done to them. Peter Clayton View from the Rear With the recent expansion of the Executive team to include two rear commodores, it may take a while to settle into who writes what for Navigans. | hope that, as explained elsewhere, the clear division between the sailing sub committee on my side, and the ECPR and social events on Clive’s will become apparent as time progresses. My sincere thanks go to John Salmon and Dave Williams for all their hard work in managing the sailing sub in the time that | have been a fleet captain. | hope that | can continue their good work. | would also like to welcome to the sailing sub committee John Nisbet, who takes over the role of Solo fleet captain and Dave Ball, stepping in once again for the Handicap fleet. Also, welcome to Dave Hewes, taking over from Dave Williams as Sailing Secretary. Elsewhere in Navigans you will see the fruit of the sailing sub committees labours - support boat rostas are in place, contact details for drivers and crews are under constant scrutiny. Please take the time to check the list, and enter your duties into those lovely new diaries and calendars that you got for Christmas. If you find that you are planning well ahead and can't manage a duty, or that our information about your contact details are no longer accurate, then please accept our apologies and let Les know. You will also find, when you receive your yearbook, an exciting and varied sailing calendar for 2004, which we hope you will enjoy. You will see that we have two open events never before seen at Marconi: the Byte circuit will be visiting us for a Saturday-only open and Ospreys will be joining us for club racing, both over the first May Bank Holiday. The Cruiser fleet have a comprehensive cruising and racing programme, to include, following the success in 2003, the Jackpot, and a proposed pursuit race back from Brightlingsea. | can't wait to see the start out of the harbour for that race! Watch out in Navigans for details of smaller boat cruising events which we hope to introduce this season. 10

El If you started reading from the front of Navigans (I always start at the back - | don't like to be surprised by the ending), then you will already know about the three initiatives that we wish to pursue over the next year. Of most interest to the sailing sub is the initiative named ‘Foresail’. We will be taking a step back and looking at the sailing that we do in the club, what we do well, what we would like to do better, where we get the most from our club and its' facilities and where opportunities are being missed. This is a very wide agenda, and will take a lot of work. It is by no meansa criticism of what we do currently, as | believe we have a comprehensive programme of sailing. Rather it is taking the opportunity of our club's new found status to review what must be the most important aspect of a sailing club. All views and comments are welcome, both now and throughout the season. As we brainstorm, and work ideas up, expect to see the results here and to hear them from your fleet captains. If you have any thoughts or ideas on this initiative, do let me know - numbers and email address below. All the best for 2004. Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 2 Club Notes Commodore’s Comments What better way to work off the excesses of Christmas than by watching other people exercise? Combine that aim with water, barges and Morris men and you inevitably find yourself drawn towards Maldon Quay for the post-Christmas Rowing Race run by Maldon Little Ship Club in support of RNLI. The weather was not so good for the latest running of this excellent event but the usual large crowd turned out to support the hardy souls who actually go on the water and row or paddle the whole 3.5km course. Just by way of scene-setting: the thrill of skating down the paths from the car park is replaced with feelings of wonder at the decorations around the swimming lake, followed by amusement at the Christmas Trees atop the barge masts and then a variety of more individual emotions as you finally encounter both bag-piper and aforesaid Morris men as you press against the breeze on to the crowded quay. Once again MSC was represented in the race by Claire Davies (Rear Commodore), Jenny Ball (past Rear Commodore) and David Ball (son of Vice Commodore). Now, two thoughts cross my mind; the first is that you do not need to have a connection with the Executive in order to compete and, secondly, this trio (assisted by Lucy and Sarah on many occasions) have been the sole MSC representative team for some years. They've done a great job — they have even won prizes for their fancy dress — but they might welcome a bit of club support on the water. So how about a few more MSC entries next year — a Cat Fleet Team, a Cadet Instructors team, a gender-specific team, a Caterers team ... and so on? | will put up a suitable trophy for the winning MSC boat judged on speed over the course, style (rowing), style (sartorial) and nerve. This outing provides a good opportunity to meet up with MSC friends, many of whom, as ex-rowers in this event, are keen to pass on last-minute tips to the present crop of competitors. They do not seem at all perturbed by the fact that they are totally ignored. So we just revert to the inevitable chat about how many sat down to Christmas Lunch, how much alcohol was consumed and how long the visitors plan to stay, whilst admiring the inevitable crop of new hats, jackets, scarves and gloves. Ray, Maureen, Ron and Mary rattled the RNLI collecting buckets and added to the £8000 or so raised for the lifeboats by the event. Of course the sadder ones amongst us managed to conduct some Club business along the way. Neil updated me on some correspondence, Malcolm gave me some useful ideas for the Homepride project and Clive and I inspected the surface of the car park in pursuit of some ideas we have for the Stansgate site. My close-up photography of the roadway seemed to earn Barbara a few sympathetic smiles from the more caring members of the Maldon community. Then back home for Turkey sandwiches — as all good things must come to an end. Happy New Year. Chris Davies Vice Commodore - IT’S HERE! THE FIRST 2004 WORKING PARTY The first working party of 2004 will be held on Sunday 29" February (an easy date to remember). (For the unattached gentlemen amongst us, this is your opportunity to do a runner to Stansgate before the lady in your life has the chance to propose to you!) There will be a variety of works to get involved in both inside and outside the clubhouse. Please bring the usual working party tools of hedging, ditching and digging implements (spades, forks, rakes, pickaxes, hedgecutters, etc) plus appropriate protective clothing. Also a mix of DIY tools are always useful on these occasions. Expect the unexpected! Within the clubhouse there will be a general cleanup as this was not done at the end of last season. Please bring some cleaning gear and your rubber gloves. Maureen will arrange a supply of cleaning materials. As usual, refreshments (soup, rolls, and hot drinks) will be served to the merry band of workers. | am grateful to a number of members who have agreed to manage some specific, larger projects in the clubhouse and around the site. These people will be recruiting assistance from members outside the formal working parties. Please lend a sympathetic ear and, hopefully a hand, if asked. As the electrician said, “Many hands make light work ... .” If you require any more information please give me a call. Thanks in anticipation. Ray Ball Vice Commodore (Clubhouse and Precincts) [redacted]

Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 3 Safety Co-ordinator At sea or on the river, we all rely on good seamanship, experience and our mettle to get us through the tasks ahead. The ultimate goal is to reach our destination safely. Mother Nature is a fickle thing and she can throw up all sorts of challenges before us. As Sailors we are all too aware that we have absolutely no control over the elements whilst in the course of sailing. Naturally this can add to the enjoyment of being out on the water. Fortunately where we can control safety issues is back on land at the club ground. By their very nature boat yards are extremely hazardous places but with good husbandry from us all, we can significantly reduce hazards resulting in consigning risks and unsafe practice to a thing of the past. We all have a duty to ensure that operational equipment is in good serviceable order. Ladders are a prime example we should all be mindful that an incomplete/structure-fatigued ladder is a hazard and has the potential to cause harm. Badly positioned (untidy) chain, buoys, metal poles, ropes, hard core etc. can easily be made safe just by inspection and resiting. We can all exercise good practice; there were a few near misses last year due to various reasons. We need to work to a 100% safety factor and should members have any safety concerns please contact me via the spoken word, letter or email. Safety should concern us all. Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 5 Letters & Articles COMMODORES REPORT TO THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING, 23 NOVEMBER 2003 Two years ago when | was elected to succeed Clive Shenton as Commodore, | did not expect to be involved in buying the site however remote that possibility was. We all owe a great debt of gratitude to Clive and the team he assembled, which included Pat Black, Frank Bennett, Dave Thomas, John Bird and others, who produced "The Lifeboat Plan". All that we have achieved this year stems from that forward thinking and early basic ground work. During the latter part of last year as the crisis within the MASC unfolded, | was extremely fortunate to have the skills of the Executive Committee of Pat Black, John Bird, Dave Payne and John Salmon to help map out the way through the tangled mess. We in turn owe a great vote of thanks to Dave Thomas who was on the MASC Main Committee and ensured that the Sailing Sections interests were not overlooked. Once it was apparent that we would need to buy the site, we were able to find a wealth of talent and expertise within the Club to assist. Amongst many people who helped the Executive were Simon Dawkins, Simon Elwell, Chris Davies, Julian Royle and Nick and Jan Bevins (I dare not think of the lost hours of sleep that | caused Nick and Jan by asking them to send out letters to you all). In addition there were two anonymous people who both offered to provide immediate short term funding to buy the site if necessary. We all owe a great debt of thanks to Julian Royle who dealt with all the legal matters and John Bird who handled all the financial negotiations with the bank.. In addition | would like to thank both their wives who not only put up with my incessant chasing but did not complain (to me anyway) during the last frantic week or two when they were on holiday. Finally the most important element in our success was you, the ordinary members. The support that you gave us at the Special General Meeting not only boosted our confidence but also sent a clear signal to the MASC and the bank that you were determined to succeed. This support was turned into tangible evidence by the response to the Members Loan Scheme. |, and | am sure that | speak for all the Executive, thank you for this whole hearted support. Any criticism that we heard always came as positive suggestions with no negative thinking at all. As a result of the activity this year, | have not been able to pay as much attention to other aspects of the Club as | would have liked. Dave Payne and Clive Shenton masterminded the new electricity supply to the Clubhouse and the subsequent rewiring of the cruiser park. In doing this they were delayed by our inability to place an order with the contractor until the site purchase was complete. In turn the contractor was then asked to come on site with very little notice. Again many thanks to the cruiser owners for their co-operation and to the rest of the club for tolerating the disruption at this time of year. Over this winter it is intended to finish the rewiring required in the Clubhouse (mainly the Dell Bar) and then we will be issued with the certificate showing that we have a Safe and legal installation. Murray Bates and his team have so far managed to keep all our equipment running. Of special note must be the strip down, repair and rebuild of the hydraulic pump engine in the last couple of weeks. | would like to thank all those who work under the taskmaster. In addition Howard Griffiths and Robin Lovett have replaced the PA system. | understand that they still have some work to carry out over the winter but it is a great improvement. Pete Clayton, in addition to master minding the moorings, continues to fire up the team which trains our cadets. In conjunction with Les Hurrell-Smith and Chris Davies yet another successful cadet week/camping fortnight took place. Many thanks on behalf of all who attended to everyone who helped them. Dave Williams and the Sailing sub committee mater minded the excellent sailing programme and co-ordinated all the necessary support duties. They even managed to get the weather in on the act; its many years since | have enjoyed such a succession of dry and warm sailing weekends. Chris Davies and the East Coast Piers team again put their impressive organisational skills to good use and achieved a record donation to the Cirdan Sailing Trust. Fenella Thomas and her team continue to expand an already highly successful social programme and | know she is already working on ideas for next year. No praise is too great for Belinda Dowley and her team in the galley. Even us cruiser owners are seeing the benefit, a cup of tea and large slice of home made cake on our return to the mooring is very welcome (until my wife comments on my waist line). Amongst many others who help, a few are Nick and Jan who maintain the membership records, Matt Willis who edits Navigans, Mike and Maggie Boreham who stuff Navigans into envelopes and send it to us, Mike Smith who despite our best endeavours to drink the bar dry keeps it stocked, Derek Kirby who represents the Club on BACSPA and at the MDC River Users forums, the fleet captains, the grass cutting team, and many others who assist on subcommittees and around the site. You will be aware that John Salmon retires as Rear Commodore and Dave Williams as Sailing Secretary at the end of this AGM. Both of them have served the Club well during their time in office. | would especially like to thank Dave for all the extra work that he, and the rest of the Sailing Sub Committee, have done during this last year whilst John has been involved with the site purchase. | must pay special thanks to Dave Payne. | first came across Dave at an Annual General Meeting during my previous term as Commodore. What a pain in the backside, in the club ten minutes and wanting to rewrite the rules totally, reform the club and goodness only knows what else. Would he go away - no chance. Then two years ago on a cold December morning he nearly removed my car from the road as he swept out of the Mundon turning. | followed him to the club and thought the time had come to deal with him so asked him to be co-opted as Vice Commodore. To my surprise and slight concern he accepted. During the last two years, he has not only provided much sound advice and comment on the Executive but has transformed the galley, ensured that all the damage caused by the gale last year has been rectified at the insurers expense and driven forward the electricity project,. | hope that he will stick around the club and maybe he will return to the Executive at some future date. | thank everyone for their contribution however small to making this year such a success.

Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 6 | hope that like me, you have enjoyed your sailing and the company of other friends at the club this year, and for myself | have been overwhelmed by the support for the Club during the year which must stand us in good stead for the future. | wish Chris Davies, his team, and all members of one of the most friendly sailing clubs | know all the best for the future. Neil Pembleton Solo Sailors Sail Together Solo sailors are always fiercely competing against each other during the season. However, this autumn, over the weekend of 25/26 Oct, all rivalry was put aside as six of us sailed together. (Roger Smith, John Salmon, Malcolm Stuart, Steve Ash, Martin Hall and Dennis Dear). Roger had chartered a Sigma 36 "British Beagle"(complete with skipper, well he might come in handy), from Portway Yacht Charters at Shotley Marina. We met there at 18.00 Friday evening and after collecting our oilskins we stowed all our gear aboard. After a good meal, some fine ale, enthusiastic chat in the nearby restaurant, we all bunked down on board for the night. Next morning saw us all up at 07.00 washed, shaved, breakfasted and casting off by 08.00. Once through the marina lock, sails up, we had the ocean before us. Well, we sailed into the Orwell, passed the Parkstone quay dock area and into the North Sea. Already the skipper was dispensed with, (or was he guiding us on the course and sailing technique) as solo sailors took the helm with Malcolm giving us some cheer as he displayed the use of his satellite navigation direction finder. The plan was to sail into the Deben, which needed to be entered with a good flowing tide, as there is a massive sand bar across the mouth. Charts were consulted often and a very strict channel was followed which was very circuitous. We all enjoyed calling out the ever decreasing depth of water below us until the words "ready about —ho " were hollered. With excellent navigation by the skipper and good helmsmanship, we were into the river and heading up passed the Felixstowe-Bawdsey ferry. We were now, we thought, free to sail in the Deben, but this is a narrow river. With John at the helm, the channel followed, he neatly steered us through the many moored boats. We were very lucky with the weather and under a blue sky the river is a very interesting and attractive one. We stopped for lunch not far from Waldringfield (good practise here for the helm and crewmembers to perfect the art of catching a mooring and tying off). Although the pheasant and port had been left behind, we filled ourselves with food from the many boxes which Roger had supplied (a great favourite were the "Kit Kats"). We were soon Sailing again, new helm, Steve | think. After some time we expertly picked up a mooring off "The Ramsholt Arms" where we moored until the next morning. The inflatable dinghy was pumped up and two intrepid explorers rowed ashore to see if the natives were friendly. There were cheers of delight when they returned, declaring that we had all been booked in for a meal that evening. The only difficulty was that there were seven of us and the dinghy only held three. However at the appointed time, three trips were made, those rowing doing sterling work and soon all were ashore with the inflatable stored. After some excellent meals, good ale and more banter the clock told us it was time for those three journeys back to the boat. After more excellent night time rowing we could safely retire to our bunks. As cruiser sailors are well aware the size and shape of berths vary enormously. Whereas Roger had a "cabin" all to himself (well he did organise it) John volunteered to take the "letter-box (conjure up your own image of the size of that) and the rest of the crew had something mid-way in luxury. The Sunday morning started with a hearty breakfast of either grilled kippers or egg, bacon, fried bread and toms. Only kidding, it was cereal, toast and a piping mug of tea, which filled us up plenty. Turns were taken with the "provisions" duties (which included the dreaded wiping up). Soon the sails were set and we were retracing our course to re-cross the bar. As we approached the mouth there were dozens upon dozens of Lazers sailing out to sea for what must have been a very large open meeting (there could have been a hundred boats) As they formed up for the start they looked a very fine sight. We were once again in the unrestricted sailing area of the sea and Martin took the helm and put the boat through some parallel coast sailing. Our heading was northwards, towards the mouth of the Alde, with a fair breeze. After a while, having seen Bawdsey manor, the clouds started to gather and the wind strength rose. At this juncture John said he would make us all "a nice cup of tea" and disappeared down to the warm below. He obliviously anticipated the torrential rain and even stronger wind, which lasted for some twenty minutes. Most sat (racing cruiser style) with their legs dangling over the side as the boat roared along at tremendous speed while on her side. After the rain stopped and the wind slackened up popped John saying "the teas nearly ready”. Later, after surviving a hailstorm, viewed the desolate row of houses at Shingle Street it was time for mugs of soup (and of course kit kats) .We had sighted the mouth of the Alde and it was now time to turn south and head towards the marina. Although the wind was reasonable it was noticeable after some time that we were not actually making headway. Engines were switched on and an uneventful journey was made back to Shotley, except for once incident. Not far from the marina we tried to pull another cruiser into deeper water as we assumed she had gone aground. We could not move her and had to leave. When we arrived back in the marina we were informed that she had snagged a submerged buoy. They had to get the big boys out to free her (at a hefty charge for Sunday afternoon | suspect). Mooring up in the boat's berth, it was a case of all mucking in to clean throughout the boat.
