Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 10 ‘Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Forty Two - Tonga to New Zealand. We motored through the off lying reefs surrounding Tongatapu on the afternoon of Saturday 3rd November 2001, closely followed by ‘Arganauta’ with the prospect ahead of a 1200-mile passage to New Zealand. A fairly modest distance but what had been occupying our thoughts for some time was that this was a notoriously difficult trip. As we headed south we were coming out of the trade wind belt and heading into an area of relatively unpredictable changeable weather, similar in many ways to the situation you're in when setting out across Biscay. As you approach New Zealand you run the gauntlet of a series of fronts crossing the Tasman Sea from Australia. The perceived wisdom seemed to be to hang back while a front passes through, then go like the clappers, motoring if necessary, to get there before the next one gets you. As we were comparatively slow and didn't like motoring, | reckoned we would just have to take our chances. | had made my first contact with Des on Russell Radio the night before and he had indicated that it was a reasonable time to head at least as far as Minerva Reef, 250 miles away. Minerva Reef, like Beveridge Reef on the way to Tonga, is a reef-lined lagoon with no land. the only difference is that, unlike Bereridge, Minerva is partially uncovered at low tide. There are in fact two reefs, North and South Minerva, both of which provide relatively secure anchorages and an ideal place to await a weather window. Our plan was to head for Minerva and then decide where to stop. Having cleared the pass we set sail and were soon romping along in a fresh north easterly In the early part of the night the wind went to dead astern and we were in constant danger of gybing, so we dropped the main and set the downwind rig of yankee and genny, poled out on either side. Our repaired Monitor self steering got back to work without any fuss. Our 'repaired' autohelm had fallen apart again as soon as we had set it up so we were relying on our wind vane. The next 2 days were very straightforward with steady winds from the north east and by Monday afternoon we were fast approaching North Minerva Reef. 'Arganauta' had arrived there earlier that day and we reckoned we could get in by nightfall. It was tempting to stop, especially as the New Zealand-based weather guru Bob McDavitt was advising people already in Minerva not to leave before Thursday morning at the earliest to avoid a low currently passing below Minerva. My concern was that if we waited until then, the next window would not be big enough for us and we would be caught out. | therefore reasoned that we might as well keep going and get a head start, and gamble with this current low. So we kept going. We passed quite close to South Minerva in the dark. By morning the rain started as we hit the front and it didn't really stop for at least two days. By the evening the wind had backed to the north west and we had to dismantle the downwind rig. | was on watch at the time and had gone below briefly. When | came back on deck, something just didn't feel right and then | realised we were heading in the wrong direction! Early on Wednesday morning we crossed the 180 degree meridian and we were back in the eastern quadrant for the first time since before we had left England. Now there really was no doubt that we had come half way round the world. By that evening the wind was up to 35 knots and we were down to reefed yankee, staysail and trysail. With the wind just aft of the beam we were sailing really comfortably at 6 to 7 knots. With the increase in wind, the rain had also become torrential. By this time the boat was beginning to fill up with wet clothes. Another problem was that, moving into higher latitudes after all that time in the Tropics, we were really feeling the cold, especially when we were wet. Soon after midnight on the Wednesday the wind suddenly dropped and went into the south west. We managed to keep sailing. By the morning the wind was just east of south. We put the main back up and were sailing in calm seas and brilliant sunshine, only slightly off course, at up to 4 knots. The wind dropped further overnight but we kept on sailing - just! By Friday the seas were still calm, the sky still blue, but the wind was up to a south easterly 10-15 knots. We had a superb day's sail until about 10.30 that night when the wind dropped completely and we resorted to our first spell of motoring. By the morning the wind had got up just enough to get us sailing again and give us yet another glorious day. Once again at night the breeze died but we persevered until it had deserted us completely. At one point our GPS showed us making 3.1 knots in 5.8 apparent wind. That's pretty good for us! On the Sunday the wind did not get up as expected so we had our first day of motoring. The sea really was like a millpond. That evening, Des on Russell Radio, told us about an intense low developing in the Tasman Sea that was expected to give winds further down of 40 or 50 knots plus. He was advising boats in our area to go back above the 30 degree south line. It seemed silly to take unnecessary chances so we drifted all night and when conditions allowed in the morning, started sailing slowly northwards. Pat and Olivia on 'Aldebaran' had left Tonga 3 days before us and had stopped at Minerva Reef, coming on a couple of days after we had passed. When Des advised us to stop, they were about 100 miles behind so we gradually got quite close, though we never actually saw each other. We did get a couple of sightings of other boats as we all jilled about. It was actually quite pleasant as the sea was almost totally calm and the weather warm and sunny. We spent the time cleaning up and making sure everything was well tied down and in good order. With no wind it was like being at anchor. During this time 'Arganauta’, 'Stella' and ‘Maritime Express' that had left Minerba Reef a couple of days after ‘Aldebaran' were gradually catching up. After a couple of days the front had moved through but had not been anything like as bad as had been expected. Winds had got up to about 30 knots from the North West which would have suited us fine. As it was, when given the all-clear we headed south only to run into 36 hours of 30 knots from the south west, right on the nose! Desperate not to lose too much ground we held up as close to the wind as we could. The seas were decidedly lumpy and, with the wind, the rain returned and we were back to soggy sailing. After a couple of days the wind dropped and for a while we enjoyed some good sailing again. Then on the Friday the wind had gone completely and we had little choice but to motor. By the afternoon the breeze filled in enough for us to have a very pleasant sail. This kept up until the early hours of the morning when it headed us and died. In truth the whole trip was characterised by this stop-start, all or nothing, type of sailing. We started the engine and motored towards the Bay of Islands, getting our first sighting of New Zealand at about 6 in the morning on Saturday 17th November 2001. We were getting all sorts of ominous forecasts as we motored in a flat calm across the Bay. As the Bay opened up it kept reminding us of the Fal that had been our last sight of England 2 % years earlier. We started seeing other yachts and then we were approaching the Customs Dock, almost exactly 2 weeks after leaving Tonga. Not one of our fastest passages, but certainly one of the most varied. We couldn't believe how often and quickly we had seen the ocean change from flat calm to highly confused and back again. We almost had a nasty incident as we came alongside the Customs Dock when the throttle cable on the engine chose that moment to disengage itself from the engine. We drifted into the dock without a problem however, and were greeted by the very efficient but friendly officials. They confiscated some foodstuffs, but not nearly as much as we had been led to believe they would. “They” proved to be surprisingly relaxed about the whole process. They were training a sniffer dog that previously only worked at the airport, so we were treated to the fascinating spectacle of this dog enthusiastically examining every locker on the boat! Within an hour or so we were secure in the marina, our first marina berth for well over a year. We had our first walk that evening on New Zealand soil. We had arrived. Mona's Travels. Part Forty Three - North Island, New Zealand - Bay of Islands After our arrival on 17th November 2001 in the Bay of Islands, and the reality that we had actually arrived had begun to sink in, we began to settle down to life in New Zealand. First of all we had to survive the arrival celebrations! For the last few days of the passage, Terry on 'Stella’, who was just behind us and gaining fast, had been threatening a rum-drinking session on arrival. They arrived just a few hours after us so there was no escape! A number of boats that we had got to know across the Pacific arrived either just before or just after us, so all in all there was much merriment and conviviality. The focal point for most of this activity was the Opua Cruising Club situated next door to the marina. It proved to be a really friendly club complete with bar and good food. In spite of having a reputation for being the most expensive marina in New Zealand, we found Opua Marina to be extremely good value, particularly by English standards. We soon discovered that if we paid for three weeks we could stay for a calendar month. The total cost was the equivalent of what we had paid for a week in a marina in Poole just before we had left England. Being in a marina for the first time for over a year gave us the opportunity of having a really good clean up and for tackling some of the jobs that urgently needed attention. Not least of these was the exhaust system on the engine, which had caused a fire in Bora Bora 10

Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 11 and could have been extremely nasty. Although | had repaired the system as best | could, | had been extremely concerned about it. Luckily, even before we had arrived in Opua, Richard on 'Fair Hippolyta' had given me the name of a diesel mechanic who not only knew all about Perkins Primas but also actually liked them! | quickly made contact with Brian who gave the engine a good going over and fabricated a new wet exhaust system as a replacement for the one that had given us problems. We took out the flexible water tanks from the bilge. Water from these tanks had tasted a bit nasty for some time. Taking them out allowed us to give the bilges a really good clean. All in all it was good to have the opportunity to give everything a good going over. A slight complication was that two weeks after our arrival in New Zealand our youngest daughter Jenny and her boyfriend Rob flew in to New Zealand for a three month stay. This had been arranged some time before and we were looking forward to seeing them. However, while on the one hand we still had plenty to do on the boat after a busy year, on the other hand, it would have been strange not to meet up straight away, knowing they were in the same country as us. In the event it all worked out well, but it just meant that they had two weeks in the marina at a time when they were understandably keen to get moving. They did manage to see quite a lot of the immediate area in spite of a spell of unsettled weather, which gave us rather a lot of rain. During this time we also had an overnight visit from Derek Hall from Marconi Sailing Club with his nephew, which gave us a chance to catch up with news from the club and prove that we could sleep 6 on the boat. | was slightly miffed that the club had found it necessary to send someone down to verify the fact that we had actually arrived in New Zealand! By the time our month in the marina had passed, we had had a pretty good sort-out and were looking forward to seeing more of the superb cruising ground that we were in the middle of. A number of locals commented on the fact that many long distance cruisers either went into the marina and stayed there, or set off down the coast, without really exploring the immediate area which has a reputation for being one of the best cruising areas, if not the best, in New Zealand. One advantage of Jenny and Rob arriving when they did was that it motivated us into leaving the marina comparatively quickly when we could have easily found a number of excuses for staying put. Almost as soon as we got out into the islands, the weather responded by brightening up and becoming warm and settled. We landed on Moturua and Urupukapuka. These islands were once home to numerous Maori tribes. They have been more recently farmed by European settlers. Now owned by the Department for Conservation, it is possible to take advantage of the many secluded anchorages and landing places. Whichever way the wind is blowing, there are always sheltered anchorages to choose from. We had a wonderful time basking in the warm sun, which at times felt as hot as in the tropics, and cooling off in the bracing clear water. Rob proved adept at collecting fresh mussels and oysters off the rocks which put him in Helen's good books very quickly. While in the marina Rob had done a repair job on Little Mu, our seahopper sailing dinghy, which we had carried halfway round the world without using as much as we thought we would. This was now the ideal time to make up for that. We sailed out to Cape Brett, the southern extremity of the Bay of Islands and, hovering off Piercy Island which features the infamous ‘Hole in the Rock’, prepared to traverse the hole on our RIB. Jenny wasn't too keen at first, so Helen went through with Rob at high speed. | looked on enviously. While we were in the marina we had got the local Yamaha agent to service the Yamaha 8 that we had bought second-hand in Panama. He had also fitted fins. The result was that our RIB would now plane with two on board (out of Helen, Rob or Jenny). If | wanted to plane, it was a solitary activity! Later on we polished the underside of the RIB with the result that Helen and | could plane in calm water. When Helen and Rob had been through and circuited the island, returning through a narrow pass between Piercy Island and a smaller rock, it was Jenny's and my turn. Travelling at a more sedate speed we experienced quite a swell while in the Hole. All in all an exhilarating experience that has become an important feature of the area. Several fast boats operate out of the resort of Pahia with the express purpose of taking people through the Hole. It was now fast approaching Christmas (2001) and the crew decided unanimously that we should have a get together with Laura who, almost since our arrival, had been working on a fruit and veg farm near Kerikeri. She had Christmas and Boxing Day off and so we picked her up on Christmas Eve and made our way to the Tua Puna Inlet just behind Kerikeri. We had a beautiful sheltered bay almost to ourselves and spent a warm sunny and lazy Christmas, swimming off the boat, sailing the dinghy and exploring the shore. Later in the day we had oysters (courtesy of Rob) and champagne (courtesy of Derek Hall) on the aft deck, before enjoying a superb Christmas dinner (courtesy of Helen). To cap it all, it was the first Christmas that Helen and | had spent with both Laura and Jenny for about 5 years. On Boxing Day we had a leisurely sail through the islands back up to Opua where we anchored in the bay opposite the marina. The next day Terry and Aerial from ‘Stella’ kindly lent us their car to take Laura back to the farm. The weather had broken and we returned to the boat to find Jenny and Rob becoming a little restless. Luckily the next day the weather improved and we set off for the outer anchorages once more. When we had first arrived in New Zealand | had contacted my cousin Ginny who | hadn't seen for more than 50 years and who had moved to New Zealand with her husband and 3 sons in the 70s. She reminded me on the phone that the last time she saw me; | was a chubby toddler with short legs. On hearing this Laura commented that in that case Ginny wouldn't have any trouble recognising me! | phoned Andrew, Ginny's eldest son, and he told me that his family always camped over Christmas and New Year at Matai Bay further up the coast from the Bay of Islands. | looked up Matai Bay on the chart, thought it looked interesting and decided that it would be the place to aim for in the New Year. Sailing out of the Bay of Islands for the first time we headed up the coast and negotiated a course through the Cavali Islands. it was a bit shallow in places but there were no real problems. By this time, with the wind heading us, we were motor-sailing. We skirted Flat Island and bore away for the narrow entrance to Whangaroa. This entrance is very difficult to spot from any distance off. The wind suddenly got up to 25- 30 knots and Rob caught a fish. In the midst of the confusion we located the entrance and steamed in. It was like entering a fjord. The narrow entrance with towering cliffs either side opened up into a long sheltered lagoon. Sufficiently shallow to anchor almost anywhere you wanted to, the water was deep enough for most yachts right up to the sides. A perfect anchorage. The next day we set off early with little wind, heading still further north. As we motored across the wide expanse of Doubtless Bay in brilliant sunshine, the wind gradually increased right on the nose. We tried sailing for a while but progress was so slow that we reverted to motor sailing. As we closed the headland on the far side of Doubtless Bay, with Matai Bay just around the corner, there were some isolated rocks to negotiate, and then we were in the bay. The bay is divided into two by a mini headland and we chose the southernmost of the two bays, as it appeared to be the most sheltered in the northerly wind that we were experiencing. Since speaking to Andrew a few weeks before, | had lost his mobile phone number. Consequently we had no idea exactly where to find them. From the boat, the camp looked fairly extensive. Having launched the dinghy we made our way ashore. After wandering around for some time we found the camp warden who took us straight to Andrew and his family. Andrew and his partner Shiree and their children Kiri and James, camp there every year with Shiree's three sisters and their families and their father George. It was quite a group and we had a great reunion. The next day was New Year's Eve. Andrew and Shiree and some of the others came out to the boat. George in particular kept marvelling at the way in which we had all come together. That night we had a superb party ashore, culminating in seeing the New Year in from the top of the Headland, illuminated by a full moon. A magical night. After a couple more days we bid our farewells and made our way south across Doubtless Bay in a flat calm. Although the sky was completely clear, in the distance we could see a fog bank obscuring the coast to the south of Doubtless Bay. As we neared it, the line became even sharper and we could see boats disappearing into the bank. We carried on with some trepidation, but just before we hit the fog bank it lifted just enough for us to pass below it. We went through the narrow entrance to Whangaroa and anchored alongside 'Stella' who had come up from Opua a couple of days earlier. A little later, ‘Theresa Two’, another Canadian boat, came up from Opua and a party was soon in full swing! We ended up staying in Whangaroa for two weeks. After a couple of days Jenny and Rob caught the coach south to Auckland to stay with Andrew and Shiree, before hiring a car to start exploring the rest of New Zealand. Helen and I had a pleasant week in the company of ‘Stella’ and for a little while ‘Theresa Two’. We climbed up to a rocky outcrop known as the Duke's nose, did some fishing, walked on the beach, found a waterfall and a spot of socialising! Then we had a lovely sail in company with ‘Stella’ back to the Bay. Sailing up to Opua was beginning to feel 11

Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 12 j| like coming home. After a few days at anchor we moved back into the marina and set about tackling more jobs that hadn't been done for quite a q while, like replacing all the toilet piping and cleaning out the holding tank. This had been necessitated by a complete blockage which occurred, % fortunately, when we were on our own. As it was, the business of replacing the old system made me persona non grata for a couple of days. People would approach along the pontoon and then rapidly back away! Some time before, we had arranged a trip with Malcolm and Margaret from Marconi Sailing Club. They were visiting their son and his family in Australia and Margaret had arranged the sailing diversion with us in the Bay as a surprise for Malcolm's birthday. When she heard about this, Laura asked if it was meant to be a pleasant surprise! It all worked out extremely well. They only had about 5 days with us but we all had a really good time in spite of the fact that it rained on a couple of days and Malcolm has a serious aversion to rain! One rainy day was spent hiking round the island of Urupukapuka, quite a distance, and on another we visited the township of Russell. In the days of the whaling ships, Russell had a reputation as the hellhole of the Pacific, full of brothels and alehouses. Malcolm was disappointed to find that it is now a rather twee little place. In between the rain we basked in the sunshine in some lovely anchorages, while Malcolm got quite serious about his fishing and Margaret soaked up the atmosphere. After they had gone Helen and | went back into the Bay for a few days. We then made the momentous decision of doing a bit of exploring away from the boat! Leaving Mona well secured in the marina we caught the coach to Auckland where we stayed with Andrew and Shiree in their beautiful house. We made good use of their swimming pool and sauna and finally met up with my cousin Ginny. We had a really good time getting to know each other. We hired a car in Auckland for eleven days and set off on a tour of the Coramandel Peninsula and the central thermal area of the North Island. The scenery was breathtaking and the geothermal activity startling. We basked in thermal mineral pools, walked across heath land with bubbling mud pools and towering geysers. We got back to Mona just in time to welcome Helen's cousin Michael and his wife Susan whom| had first met when we had stayed with them in Toronto during our Canadian excursion. My introduction to Michael had been, in fact, being whisked across Canada in his tiny Cherokee Piper, initially flying low over hills to the east of Montreal under a building storm and then following the St Lawrence down to Toronto. During our stay in Toronto Susan had done a wonderful job of taking us round all the sights. She had been fascinated by our ‘Mona’ trip but confessed to a deep fear of the sea and boats. It was therefore with some trepidation that we approached their visit! The challenge was to provide enough excitement for Michael and a minimum of frights for Susan. Initially we weren't helped by an uncharacteristically swelly sea in the Bay. Susan was stoical however and we reached a sheltered anchorage without too much alarm, even when a squall temporarily reduced visibility to a minimum. We had several peaceful days in the islands with the weather co-operating for the most part. Towards the end of their time with us there was one last chance to visit the infamous Hole in the Rock. Michael was predictably keen, | got the distinct impression Susan preferred the option of moving to another quiet sheltered bay. In the end we decided to head out towards the Hole in the Rock and see what conditions were like. Unfortunately a swell had built up again. It's a fair way out to Cape Brett, off which Piercy Rock with its Hole lies, and with Mona's ever dirtier bottom, progress was decidedly slow. As we approached the Hole | was alarmed to see white water breaking in the entrance. We decided to go round the rock to what was today the leeward side to see what conditions were like there. It was still very swelly and | had a real skipper's dilemma. If things went wrong | would be responsible for a very nasty situation, if| backed down would | be able to live it down? | decided to take a closer look. Michael and | donned lifejackets and got into the dinghy. | approached the hole with caution and then decided to go in. The swell was quite bad so | accelerated and was through. As | looked back the water was breaking behind us so we rejoined 'Muna' by motoring round the rock. From Internet: The Hole in the Rock, off Cape Brett, has been etched by wind and wave in the Bay of Islands north of Auckland, New Zealand. Boat cruises in the Bay of Islands may attempt to sail through the Hole in the Rock, more like the eye of a needle, when the tide is ‘ight. As well, there are jetboat rides that bring you through the Hole in the Rock in a heart-stopping rush. Most cruises depart from Paihia. Soon after Michael and Susan left us it was time to lift 'Muna' out of the water, which we did at Ashby's yard just upstream from Opua Marina. We knew the bottom was bad but it was still a shock to see oyster shells and barnacles four inches deep on the keel. We then started refitting in earnest, particularly in the galley area. After 3 weeks we closed up shop and headed down to Auckland to fly back to England for our first visit since leaving nearly 3 years before. Malcolm Shaft 12

Club Notes Commodore’s Comments | know that many of you will be beavering away at home with a variety of decoration, repair and improvement jobs that you fully intend (honest) to get out of the way before the sailing season starts. It is certainly like that at Chez Davies. Down the road at Stansgate, similar things are going on or are about to happen. The committees and those who work on them have been busy over the last few months deciding on the priority issues and working out how to deal with them. Work is about to start in a number of areas and | want to share the good news with you. The Ladies changing area is to be given a face lift with the installation of new vanity units (smart bowls in a counter top) and re- tiling of the shower cubicles. Steve Glynn will lead a volunteer gang in installing these items, which are paid for out of our normal maintenance fund. We have responsibility for maintenance of the access road to the site (with a small contribution due from the farmer) and have instructed a contractor to undertake repairs to the badly deformed section of road close to the Eagle gates. This will be done during early March and is to be paid for out of our normal reserves. It is important that this work is done before this section deteriorates any further. We have been concerned that our tractor fleet — essential to the general maintenance of the site, handling club boats and moving member's boats — should not be compromised by the failure of the big four wheel drive tractor. It hasn’t happened yet but, if it did, spares are almost impossible to source. Paradoxically, that tractor has a fair value (to those who value vintage farm machinery) so long as it is running. So the decision has been made; using reserves built up for the purpose, we have bought a replacement machine and sold the old one to a good home. Many thanks to Peter, Derek and Murray for their efforts in identifying and tracking down a suitably ‘low-tech’ machine to suit our purpose and our pocket. Another concern has been the appearance and condition of the road and ground around the east side of the clubhouse. It has deteriorated slowly over the recent past and has been seriously affected by the general wear and tear caused by the electricity work. Simple making good was not the whole answer. Drainage has been so poor that some wag has posted a sign announcing the Windsurfer Training Lake at the bottom of the road.... and we have lived for years with a terrible hump in the entrance to the Cat field. Improving this area will be a significant step towards addressing some of the issues that underlie our Homepride initiative — protecting our investment, improving our environment and making ourselves more attractive to visitors and potential new members. Accordingly, we have issued invitations to tender and awarded work to renewa section of the road, install new drainage, remove the Cat field hump and install Grasscrete (load bearing concrete with grass inserts) to wide flanks on either side of the new piece of road. You might need to see it to understand exactly what | mean but you will understand, | feel sure, that the overall appearance and usability of the area will be improved. This work will be funded from excess monies generated through the Members’ Loan scheme and should be completed by mid March. Thanks to everyone for all the thought and effort that is going in to these important projects... and to the rest of you for all you will do at the Working Party at the end of February. Now, back fo that tiling..... Chris Davies Vice Commodore By the time you read these notes the February working party will have been and gone. The clubhouse and precincts should look a lot better. Thank you in anticipation for your contribution. The committee is continuing to look at ways of making the site a more enjoyable and convenient place for all. The groundwork to improve the road near the seawall (to get rid of the ‘windsurfers training lake’), the clubhouse approach and the entrance to the cat field (to get rid of the hump) are still receiving attention. Hopefully we will be able to see some activity in that area soon. Please be patient if you are temporarily inconvenienced by these works. Similarly some major work on the road between the Eagle gate and our site entrance will also be taking place shortly. Pat has put up a notice at the Eagle gate announcing this work. Again please be patient and you will have fewer potholes to drive round. On the same theme of improving things, please avoid the carpeted area of the lounge when you are wet or muddy. This small area is intended for people with clean and dry clothes and shoes. It is nice to have somewhere comfortable to take guests or for people to sit and watch the activities on the water, but of late it has become very dirty. Some improvement has been made with vigorous vacuum cleaning and it is hoped to take a shampooer to it before long. Nuff said. By popular request the hot drink area has been restored using facilities in the upstairs bar. There is another article elsewhere in this edition of Navigans about this. | would like to thank Mike Smith and his team for clearing the bar of drinks and glasses and giving it a good clean up to enable this facility to be restored. Enjoy!

Debbie Glynn [redacted] e-mail [redacted].com Racing ..see the Cruiser Fleet Calendar on the Navigans Noticeboard News Proposed New Wind Generator Arrays On the 10 February | attended a special meeting of BACSPA held at the Tollesbury Sailing Club. Not only regular representatives from the Blackwater clubs attended but representatives from other associations including the PLA as well as the RYA were there. The DTI are in the process of formulating their plans for phase 2 of wind generation of electricity in the Thames Estuary. There will be an extension to the Gunfleet site and generators will be placed on the Inner Gabbard and Galloper banks. The most controversial new site is the proposed London Array. They plan to have wind generators extending from the Long Sand across the Knock Deep to the Kentish Knock. The site also butts up against the navigable channel in Fishermans Gat, which is now used by commercial shipping. It will result in the loss of Foulgers Gat. This is a narrow gutway used only by small craft and is part of one of the safest routes across the Thames Estuary. It keeps commercial shipping and small craft apart. The cables carrying the electricity generated may well be brought ashore between Jaywick and Walton with inevitable areas of prohibited anchoring in the Wallet. This could have implications for the mother craft in the ECPR. The DTI will have the power of the Electricity Act, which will enable them to deny the right of navigation in any channel they consider necessary. At this stage the DTI plans appear ill informed of nautical considerations for all types of marine traffic and not just sailing boats. It is essential the RYA receive our support in representing our interests. To achieve this they need to know the strength of feeling in the member clubs. If you have ambitions to sail round to Ramsgate or Dover or if you are likely to cross the North Sea to Ostend or Flushing write to the RYA and let them know your feelings about the proposal. If you take part in or support the ECPR write to the RYA to make them aware of the effects that areas of prohibited anchoring could have in the conduct of the

8 race. Let us ensure that arrays of wind generators are installed and located where they will not be a hazard to small craft under sail. Note that the cut off date for comments to the RYA is 1Mar.’04. Please contact Don Holdsworth on [redacted] Ray Ball (on behalf of Don Holdsworth) View from the Rear At this time of the year, you would think that the Sailing Sub Committee would have nothing to talk about. The programme is in place, support boat rotas are published and getting a little fine-tuning, and the race officer rota is complete (you will have seen it elsewhere in this Navigans — time to get those diaries out again). And yet we have plenty to talk about. The ‘Foresail’ initiative that | mentioned last month has gripped the Sailing Sub’s imagination, and a recent brainstorming session has left us with a huge list of ideas to try and make some sense of. We are actively looking for more ideas: if you have a view on our current sailing activities, their strengths and areas of opportunity, your fleet captain wants to hear from you! We will, | am sure, be working on ideas in a fairly abstract way for the next couple of months, with the aim of presenting a set of proposals to you later in the season. So far we have looked at racing, cruising, interaction between the fleets, exposure to the wider sailing community, and class and sailor development. There are sure to be other areas to look at that we haven't got to yet. If you have one in mind, let your fleet captain know. On a less idealistic note, the club will again be funding a number of members in achieving their RYA level 2 Powerboating for support boat purposes. If you are interested in doing this course at Bradwell, please let me, or your fleet captain, know. The more competitive sailors amongst you will know that the Marconi Challenge Cup, a remnant of BJRC dinghy series of yore, has been one of the less popular events in our programme. It has always been run as an open event, although we haven’t had any visitors for several years, and it’s Saturday timing doesn’t really draw in the punters. In 2004, the Marconi Challenge Cup will run as a club trophy event on Sunday, 6" June, to a new format. But what format? The Sailing Sub are trying to devise an event that will be out of the ordinary for our sailors, and one that is truly a challenge. We havea few ideas, but if you would like to add to them, we’d love to hear from you. So that’s the big vision, initiative stuff out of the way — now it’s back to getting the boat ready for next season! Club Notes Commodore’s Comments Maintaining membership levels is an important part of our plan for survival as an independent club. Improving membership levels will enhance our security and, in the longer term, allow us to improve our facilities. Open Day on Saturday June 5" will therefore be an important event for the new club; important as an opportunity to showcase our facilities and activities to potential new members and important as a vehicle for publicity for the club in a range of media. So, even if it snows on the day, we will maximise the attention we can get for the club just through publicising the event far and wide. If Open Day is going to work it will have to be a whole Club event — with everyone possible involved in some way or other. Our visitors will need to be met at the gate, greeted at Reception, showed round the facilities, briefed on safety, taken afloat, fed and watered, entertained and signed up. The site will need to look the best we can make it and there will need to be a lot of activity both on and off the water. We don’t know how many people our advertising and PR activity might attract but there is something that almost every one of us can do to swell the numbers: bring a friend! Most of us will know someone — a neighbour, friend or colleague who is a potential club sailor. Don’t worry about whether they will join now, in the near future or whether they will necessarily join at all — if they are interested, will enjoy an active, fun day out and above all will talk to their friends and colleagues about MSC and what a good Club it is, they are the people we need to target. Please give all the support you can to this important event. Don’t wait to be contacted — if you have an idea speak to Fenella Thomas(Social); Claire Davies(Fleets); Ray Ball (Premises) or Simon Elwell (Publicity) — their contact details are in the year book. Recent attendance at an RYA Regional Forum (a perk of this job!) was an interesting and worthwhile experience. It prompted a couple of thoughts about our own situation. The presence of our late twenties Rear Commodore gave some balance to an event where the average age, including Claire, was mid-sixties. It underlined the value for me of the small steps we have taken in recent years to balance the age profile in our own committees. We need to do more. Mark Bulkely our very own Olympic hopeful names Marconi SC as his home club on a website at www.gbrtornadogold.com. Keep an eye on this as the preparation programme progresses. We have been in contact with Mark to tell him of the interest and support we have in and for his efforts. A surprise for me this month was the news that Patrick Black intends to stand down as Club Secretary - once we have found and bedded in a replacement for him. My personal disappointment at losing the services of someone who has served with distinction in an important role for a good number of years has to give way to the recognition that Pat has earned the right to enjoy his membership without the distractions of office. He has my hearty thanks for all he has done and will continue to do — at least for a while longer. Chris Davies MARCONI SAILING CLUB LTD VACANCY FOR COMPANY SECRETARY Due to the impending retirement of Patrick Black we have a requirement for a new Company Secretary to assume the role as soon as possible, following a period of instruction and familiarisation. The role is voluntary and essentially involves working closely with the Board of Directors (Executive) and Management Committee to ensure that all matters of administration and compliance are correctly dealt with and that proper records are maintained. There is no requirement for formal qualifications but the role is ideally suited to someone with good administration skills, an eye for detail, patience and people-handling ability. Above all, an interest in protecting and advancing the reputation of the Club will be an important attribute. Interested? Please call Chris Davies, Commodore on [redacted] for an informal chat or e-mail me at [redacted].net

Vice Commodore CLUBHOUSE CLEANING | am pleased to announce that we have now ‘signed up’ our new cleaners. They are June and John Rogers from St Lawrence. Please make them feel welcome at the club and help them in their task by thoughtful use of the clubhouse. They have started at a difficult time as the groundwork at the site is still going on and a lot of dirt is tending to tread into the clubhouse. Hopefully ‘things can only get better’. Now where have | heard that before? We have been without official cleaners since last November and the fact that the club has stayed reasonably clean in that time is due to various people taking the trouble to do a bit of mopping and sweeping from time to time. | don’t know who you are, but thank you. WORKING PARTY Many thanks to all of you who turned out for the working party on 29" February. It was very well attended and a wide range of jobs was tackled both inside and outside of the clubhouse. | know that a lot of the tasks were physically demanding particularly in the scrap metal and tyre area and no doubt a few pounds were sweated off. We were lucky with the weather; the bitter east wind and the sleet only making an appearance when the last few die-hards were clearing up as dusk fell. The site looks a lot better for all the hard work. Well done and thank you. WASTE NOT WANT NOT (OR, PUT ANOTHER WAY, YOUR WASTE IS NOT WANTED) A concerted effort has been made recently at the working party and other ‘events’ to remove waste from the site. This is expensive both in financial terms and for the amount of members’ time and physical effort involved. It is accepted that certain large items present their own problems of disposal, but please assist as far as possible by taking your waste away with you. For example | have recently taken someone’s old battery to the recycling centre and another has now appeared by the skip. If you bring a new battery down for your boat, please take the old one away. (Your recycling centre will take it.) Similarly, at the last count, | found six old sailboards on the site. If you have finished with your old sailboard, dinghy or what- have-you please dispose of it yourself (off site). Other than domestic waste for which we use the Waste-eater we don’t have a waste collection service at the site. If we did, or if legislation forces us to in the future, it would have to be paid for out of subscriptions. If you feel that you have finished with something which could be a real asset to the club please approach a committee member before bringing it down or leaving it at the site. This is to ensure that what you have to offer is likely to be useful without adding another maintenance task to somebody's list of duties; or cluttering up the place for years before it gets used. Even a seemingly generous gift can have maintenance and safety implications. GROUNDWORKS The groundwork to improve the site near the clubhouse is progressing well. The area has been fenced off to ensure safety and to prevent disturbance of the newly laid concrete. The fencing will remain in place for some time after the contractors have left site to ensure the concrete has fully hardened before we (or worse, the various delivery lorries that visit the site) drive over it. Please do not move any of this fencing even if it looks as though the work has all been finished. The experts tell me that a newly laid road needs a couple of weeks to harden properly. We don’t want to undo any of the good work. This may cause a bit of inconvenience at the start of the season, but hopefully not too much. SAILING Rumour has it that some people will start sailing from the club soon. Weird! (Yes | know that the sailboarders never really stop but they are made of sterner stuff than the rest of us.) | hope that you (we) all have a good season. Happy sailing! Ray Ball Vice Commodore (Clubhouse & Precincts) The new carpet fitted in the lounge has been badly soiled. As a general request would all members take to heart that much work, money and effort is expended in keeping the clubhouse and surroundings to such a high standard. Please respect the work that has been done. Editor

Solo Matters On a Dark and Chilly evening in January, the Solo fleet and their wives or Partners (to be politically correct) met at the Two Brewers Pub, which was warm and inviting. After several drinks and various topics of discussion, ranging from who was going to the Dutch Nationals & Nations Cup at Lake Garda, the UK National Championships in Plymouth, what format the 'Marconi Solo Open’ was going to take and finally what was going to happen to 'Snow Goose’ the Club Solo? These topics carried on being debated during the meal. 'A Special Menu' provided by the Landlord having a variety of courses and dishes which catered for all tastes. The food was excellent and enjoyed with fine wine by all. There was also a serious side taken by some of the more competitive Soloists in the Fleet by avoiding the dessert menu, to assist their performance for the fast approaching Spring Series!! Several members are already boasting weight loss and so soon after Christmas !! (lets hope for a Windy start to the season for the rest of us). John Nisbet Solo Fleet Captain [redacted] [redacted].co.uk Solo Bowling Evening Saturday evening 21st February saw Solo members and their wives arrive at “Eddies” the bowling centre in Billericay. Three lanes were used and it was not long before strikes were being scored. Two games of very competitive bowling were played on all lanes. With all the exercise everyone was very hungry and as if on cue our basket meals arrived. There were claims that no practise had been carried out since last year; but I’m not so sure. The winner of the ladies trophy (Marie Dear) and the men’s winner (John Burgoyne) were the same as last year. The runners up were Kath Smith and myself. Dennis Dear Cruiser Fleet Thanks to everybody who turned up for the club working party. Most of the work was completed, the rest of the water hose reinstatement will have to wait until boats have been launched to get access. The tender rack is almost finished and tenders can be returned to their numbered slots, i.e. your mooring number is your tender storage number. As always, if anybody has a problem, please ring me. The next function is the cruiser fitting out supper on 8” May, the menu form is in last month’s Navigans. Also in May, we have our shakedown cruise to Burnham on the Bank Holiday weekend of 29"/30'/31"' May and | will be putting up a list on the club noticeboard for the marina and the menu slip will be at the end of these notes. At this time of year | am reminded of all the unsung heroes of the club who repair and maintain club equipment. | am not going to name them as | am bound to miss somebody out but to all of you who go down the club when it’s cold and wet and just get on with it, a big thank you from the rest of the club. Although most of the electrical posts are 6 amp there is a 16 amp socket on the last post by the pillbox and 32 amp sockets on the cruiser garage and winch engine room. | have a 32 amp adapter which | will hang on the cruiser garage wall or you can buy your own from Edmunsons, Dukes Park Industrial Estate, Chelmsford for about £8. As the season approaches, thoughts turn to the laying of moorings and the launching of boats. Along with the usual reminders about not obstructing the movement of boats in the cruiser park, | will be putting the “no unattended parking” sign up again, although it is a bit bent as | think that somebody parked on it last year! We had a few problems last year with unsuitable and badly maintained trailers and owners being unprepared and without a suitable number of helpers to launch and recover their boats. Whilst the duty tractor drivers will help if they can, they are primarily there to operate the machinery. The launching list is now on the club noticeboard and after you have put your name down, make sure that you contact the designated tractor driver for the day. | appreciate that some club members are new to launching and may be unsure of how to go about it, even after reading their cruiser notes. Please ask any tractor driver for advice and although this will be freely given, it is the owners’ ultimate responsibility to carry out the operation in a safe manner. Everybody is responsible to operate safely when launching operations are in progress. Make sure that the warning signs are in use, be aware of the winch cable and make sure that nobody is between a boat launching and the sea. Non cruiser owners may not be aware of the loads and dangers involved and although dinghy members are meant to use the west side of the yard when launching operations are in progress, they tend to wander to the east side sometimes, especially when coming in from a sail. If this happens, politely ask them to move over and point out the dangers involved as last year we had a runaway due to mechanical failure of the winch. Fortunately, nobody was between the boat and the sea at the time.

Letters & Articles A big "Thank You" from The Cirdan Sailing Trust The Cirdan Sailing Trust have written to thank the members of Marconi Sailing Club for the large donation received following the 2003 East Coast Piers Race. Enclosed with their letter were copies of letters received from many of the young people who were able to take part in sailing with the help of a bursary received from The Cirdan Sailing Trust - the bursaries made possible by fund raising events like the ECPR. Here are some extracts: Thank you, Marconi Sailing Club, for your kind assistance in helping the Children’s Care Campaign to take a group of children sailing in September 2003. The children that we provide activities for would not get the chance of experiencing life on a sailing barge if it were not for people like your-selves. The children we work with are all social worker referred and come to us for a number of different reasons; this may be from a simple lack of money in the household to children who live in difficult situations. From our diary: Time to set sail. We could not have wished for better weather, plenty of sun and enough wind to make it interesting for the kids. Once they got the hang of what to do on the Barge they even started to work as a team. On Sunday morning all of the kids, and some of the adults, had the chance to climb the rigging which we all enjoyed. Country Care Children’s Home, written by Emma. Thank you for an excellent week with the Cirdan Sailing Trust. It was a really uplifting week and really helped to build my confidence and self-esteem. I was given a real sense of responsibility on Duet and it left me with a great feeling of achievement. The staff on the boat made it a really enjoyable week; they were really understanding and aware of all our needs! The week really made me think about sailing as a possible career and I would love to be able to go away on Duet again next year. The Essex Autistic Society Thank you so much for awarding us the bursary that enabled a group of students with Autistic Spectrum disorders to enjoy the experience of sailing on the ‘Xylonite’. We travelled from Wolverstone Marina on Tuesday to Stone Point at Walton on Thursday. Despite the rather rainy weather it was a very valuable experience for all concerned. Judgemeadow Community College — Leicester | am writing to express our thanks to Marconi Sailing Club for their kind sponsorship of our recent sailing trip. Adventure activities play an important part in the development of our young people and provide them with the opportunity to acquire skills and abilities that will prepare them for the future. At Judgemeadow we make alternative curriculum provision for students for whom GCSE courses are not suitable. This provision is called Future Pathways and includes a wide range of activities aimed at developing the life skills of these young people. Our group consisted of 12 students from years 10 and 11. Learning outcomes that were achieved by participating in the sailing trip. e Able to work as a team member To do tasks when asked Doing tasks that need to be done without being asked Different lifestyles in different environments Taking leadership roles and getting others to follow instructions Plus — the entire group (including the staff!) gained a competent crew award. Adolescent Outreach Team — Suffolk County Council We would like to thank Marconi Sailing Club for their kind assistance to enable a group of young people to experience the adventure of sailing on board the sailing vessel Duet. Without the help of the bursary, these young disadvantaged people would probably never have had such an opportunity. The trip allowed the continuation of our group work in building self-esteem and confidence whilst learning how to work as a team. All the young people have gained from the trip in many different ways. Even from just being away from home for the first time. For more information about The Cirdan Sailing Trust visit their web site at www.cirdansailing.com

Bass Strait News (or Rays Ramblings) Well we have been away for 6 months now and we are glad to read in Navigans that you are all busy back home with working parties and fitting out so we thought it was time to send news from Down Under. September We arrived to a drought and water restrictions which was somewhat odd as it did not stop raining for days. So after checking that Cats Chorus was still alright, as we had left her for 7 months, we opted for a quick ski trip and a long weekend walking in the Grampians. | think we needed a bit of a holiday after the last few hectic months in the UK. October Still raining and cold but work commenced on the boat, having two hulls to rub down and antifoul instead of one made for a very grumpy Jackie. Funny how Ray always seems to disappear and have urgent technical jobs to do at the onset of any nasty, manual work! One gentleman in the boatyard was so concerned that he lent Jackie his mask. We hit a slight problem when Ray inspected the fuel tanks and discovered that they were afloat in 150 litres of water! It seems that the angle the boat had been left sitting on the trailer, the inspection hatches, sealant and unusually high rainfall associated with the drought had given us our first problem. That took the rest of October! November Finally all the underwater jobs were completed and we were ready to launch, a very familiar experience involving a tractor, trailer and winch. Unfortunately we did not float off with the afternoon tide even with some pushing and shoving as it was inches away from leaving the trailer. This meant that when we did float off it was at 4am in the morning, what do you do when it is pitch black, misty and you are in a mangrove creek? Ray decided that it would be a good idea to attach your prop to the anchor chain of a nearby mooring, which was very effective! So in to the not so warm, muddy, crab infested creek he went to sort out the mess. By Thursday 13" we had moved to live onboard at last and were extremely happy to be in Hastings marina, Western Port, our home for the next 3 months. Work commenced on installing the new hydraulic steering system which seemed to involve a lot of crawling around and getting in to tight spaces in order to fit 50 metres of copper tubing around the boat. We also fitted an emergency steering system. The marina is on the Mornington Peninsula so we had a few trips out to the local vineyards or wineries as they call them to commence the task of provisioning. This involved several visits and much sampling in order to stock up the wine locker, which sadly is already nearly empty and we have had to resort to Chateaux Cardboard. December Our first visitors arrived and as we still had no steering it was sad that we could not take them out sailing. So we had to improvise and do tours of the peninsula and undertake further provisioning. On 19" we bled the hydraulics, yet again, and set off for our first test sail of the new steering, which involved a short 80 nm hop around to Port Philip and Sandringham Yacht Club. We spent Christmas with Ray’s family and on Christmas morning with Cats Chorus decked out in tinsel we had 12 on board for breakfast, swimming and a short sail. In 25 degrees with blue sky and perfect weather everyone had a magical time but it did feel a bit odd and not really like Christmas. For New Years Eve we decided to go in to Melbourne to watch the fireworks, us and 350,000 others, all of who it seemed were trying to get on the same train home, it was not a good idea! At Sandringham we were moored for several days in front of another British yacht called English Rose so Ray chatted to the skipper and 3 months later we have just realised who he was. It was John Ridgway, the sailor and adventurer who rowed across the Atlantic with Chay Blyth. January

9 January in Melbourne is race month so we entered our first regatta at Western Port, SOMHR, Southern Ocean Multihull Regatta, little did we realise that we would be the only cruiser and most of the other boats were out and out racing cats and tri’s. Race 1 — We missed it due to sailing back from Melbourne Race 2 — We were the only boat out there in 40 knots of wind as race control had cancelled the heat after we has already departed. Race 3 — We had our best race, on some tacks we were alongside other boats and did not come last. Race 4—We had a great start and were oddly in the lead with the fleet behind us, we were just savouring the moment and taking photo’s when we heard over the VHF that we had to do a restart or be disqualified because we were over the line at the start! After much protesting from Ray we learnt that Aussie rules involve a 1 minute gun so back we went. Race 5 — Things went from bad to worse, we were rammed and nearly holed by a tri as we both tacked for the start with 20 seconds to go. Then the rig of the boat in front of us collapsed so we retired and became a rescue boat! It was a fun week and we made many new friends, it was very windy and hit over 35 knots most race days, but we did learn a lot about handling our new boat and we did hit our top speed to date which was 16 knots so it was not all bad. At the Regatta dinner we were embarrassed to be called up and given the trophy for winning the cruiser class, as we had been the only cruiser racing but it was a good evening and very amusing as the skipper & crew from each boat had to do a turn, after enough alcohol of course. February/March On Friday 13" February we finally unplugged from the electrics, handed back the marina key had a long shower and set off to go cruising! We had decided that Tasmania would be a good place to start so we said farewell to all our new friends from the live aboard pontoon, and as they waved us off and wished us well we were so excited to be departing at last. There is so much to say about our first month cruising Tasmania that | do not know where to begin, it had been a truly wonderful experience and we have been overwhelmed by people’s friendliness, generosity and hospitality everywhere we have been. Highlights have included: e Covering over 120 nm on our first day sail from Hastings to King Island Doing over 14 knots as we surfed across the Bass Strait in huge seas and swell, at times we are both scared and exhilarated at the same time, the boat just seems to want to go faster and faster but we keep reefing down at the moment to control our nerves! Exploring Tasmania by boat and visiting; Smithton, Stanley, Devonport, Launceston and the Tamar River. Crossing from King Island to Tasmania Ray was muttering that he could not get the jib to set and | replied "We are doing 12 knots to windward, in 35knots of wind with a choppy sea” that seemed to stop him complaining! Lowlights have been few apart from one incident in the Flinders Islands where we managed to anchor to a rock and it did not want to let go! Ray had to snorkel to 10 meters in 20 knots of wind to attach a trip line but we did escape. We have now crossed back to the mainland and are planning to head north for the winter. Best wishes to all our friends at Marconi, have a great summer sailing. Love Jackie and Ray P.S. As you can see we keep a very strict log! 1] View from the Rear The season is soon upon us, and by the time you read this many of you will have braved the icy Blackwater already. | look forward to being able to report on the activities as they get under way. At the moment, | seem to be spending more time looking outside the club than in. Like many of you, | spent a happy day (and quite a bit of money) at the RYA Dinghy Show a few weeks ago. Apart from catching up with old acquaintances, | made a few new ones as | trawled around the class association stands to find out what events are happening in our area. The answer was ‘hundreds’! There are so many opens and regattas going on | don’t know where to start, but | suggest anyone interested could start with their fleet notice board, where much of the information will end up. Or, of course, ask your class association, who are all very keen. Of course, for some hardy souls, the opens have already started. Just ask Nick Miller and Tim Dowley how many boats they got through in their determined attempt to complete the Hoo Freezer... Despite the carnage, their determination paid off, being amongst only 22 finishers in a fleet of 69. They brought themselves to the attention of the race officer (probably by confusing them with the number of boats they sailed in!), and were awarded the Race Officer’s prize for endeavour. Well done Nick and Tim. | also hear rumours of trips abroad for European and even World championships for our intrepid Byte and Solo sailors during the season. | look forward to being able to tell you more... You will have read elsewhere about the planned Open Day. This ought to be a great day for the club — fun for the members and fun for the visitors. Please do lend your support. Some people may be approached for specific tasks, but generally your fleet captain will be able to let you know what needs covering. And now for a few notices: e When returning your dinghy to the dinghy park, please ensure that your details are entered in the corresponding slot on the plan in the clubhouse. If you have any difficulty finding or choosing a space, please contact Barry Hutt, Dinghy Park Secretary on [redacted] It would be helpful if dinghy owners could ensure that their boats are removed to the dinghy park before Easter; e Accidents will happen... As we return to the site and the water, please can all sailors of all vessels and boards please ensure that they are considerate of other members property both on and off the water. If there is any incident, you must report it to the OOD. If there is no OOD available, make an entry in the log in the lounge recording what happened. In any situation, it is all our responsibilities to make every possible effort contact the owner of any vessel we may inadvertently damage. Thank you. e We need more race officers! And we need them soon... If you are interested in training as a race officer, please contact me or Dave Hewes, Sailing Secretary. We will organise training and ensure that you get full support in your first couple of races. See you on the water! Club Notes “s Commodore’s Comments We're off! Its official, the season is under way: dinghy racing has started; a successful Open Meeting has been held; on site camping has been endured; Trumpeter, Cariad and Boogey are on their moorings — and all is right with the world! Well almost....... we do need to ensure that the contractor finally and satisfactorily finishes the concrete works; we need to finally clear Skip Central to a more appropriate off site location ... and so on. Once the concrete is finished we will need to continue the tidy up in that area. So watch out for re-imposition of parking restrictions, note that there is to be No Entry for any vehicles (tractors or cars) either way through the Race Reception entrance to the Cat Field and expect the skip to be re-located to an equally convenient but less prominent location. New smart signage will appear on and around the Club just as soon as we have finally agreed typefaces and colours. There are no plans to fiddle with the logo. We emerge from our winter hibernation with the need to acknowledge the special efforts of a number of people who have driven and executed a number of projects aimed at maintaining and improving our lot. Thanks to everyone who has done any thing at all and special mention for: e Peter Clayton and Pat Black for their concrete block moulding and installation works — making the slipway a safer place to be. Tim Dowley for his scrubbing work — making the slipway a less slippy place to be. Tim Dowley for his excellent efforts to keep the Orkney in service after its breakdown Steve Glynn, Tim Dowley and Kevin Dowley for the retiling of the Ladies’ showers and installation of vanity units. Maureen and Ray Ball for clubhouse cleaning during the absence of cleaning staff. Gerry and the Pacemakers for all their hard work in the major installation job on the winch hydraulics. New members get together For the purposes of this exercise a new member is anyone who has joined the Club since last New Members’ evening. The intention is to give you an opportunity to meet and chat with members of the Main Committee and Executive who should be able to answer all those questions you have been meaning to ask if only you could find someone with a few answers. It is most definitely not an occasion for us to trawl for new committee members — so come along with a light heart! | have written individually to (hopefully all) new members to explain that this year’s even will be an informal meeting at the end of Open Day on June 5"" _ not the date originally published in the Year Book. If anyone else would like to be involved and hasn’t heard from me please give me a call on [redacted] — | will confirm the arrangements and you will be very welcome. No Entry Please note that it has been decided that no vehicles (cars or tractors) may be driven either way through the Cat Field entrance adjacent to the flagpole and Race Reception. Please respect this rule at all times which is intended to address safety concerns and reduce wear and tear on the turf. Car Parking Designated Car Parking Areas are in the Cat Field to the right of the entrance gate and in the field to the left of the entrance gate. Windsurfers may park in their designated rigging area. During Camping Fortnight, East Coast Piers Race and other events other areas may be made available; signs and notices will direct members as appropriate. Cruiser owners may park cars alongside their parked boats but must not leave these unattended (in case access to other boats and trailers is impeded). Cars may not be parked in the vicinity of the clubhouse other than for loading and unloading by caterers, bar managers, cleaning staff and so on. Cars must be removed as soon as loading or unloading is complete. This rule will ensure that essential access for boats, pedestrians, tractors and emergency vehicles is maintained. Provided that sensible precautions are observed, cars are allowed on to the hard for loading and unloading only. The must not be left unattended. Do not allow guests to park their cars outside the Club entrance. Bring them through the gate and remember to include their vehicle details when completing the signing-in book Please pay attention to these basic rules and be prepared to comply with any necessary changes of arrangement that occur from time to time — watch out for notices and respond positively to polite requests! | am planning to give our new boat Fandango a taste of the water this weekend. Give me a sympathetic wave as you sail serenely past and snigger at my attempts to cope with new and unfamiliar rigging systems — but, above all, enjoy your sailing. Chris Davies

VICE COMMODORE’S NOTES - CLUBHOUSE & PRECINCTS os PROGRESS ON THE GROUNDWORKS At the time of writing there is still some work to do to complete the groundwork. The soil and seed in the grasscrete has settled and needs ‘topping up’ and the areas surrounding the new concrete need levelling off with roadstone. The contractor is due back to do this work and by the time you read this it should be done. However we are already seeing benefits from the work. The more observant of you will have noticed that the recent heavy rain drained away, as it has been designed to do, without leaving a lake - sorry kids! Also the cat sailors are appreciating not leaving their wheels behind as they used to when pulling their boats over the hump. This should get even better when the grass becomes established in the grasscrete. NO SPEED HUMP - NO CARS OR TRACTORS PLEASE . Having removed what one observer called the speed hump into the cat field at the clubhouse (north) entrance | have now noticed that cars and tractors are attracted to this way in. This is turning the grass abutting the new grasscrete into mud which is rather spoiling the effect of the new work. This has been discussed in committee and it has been decided that this entrance should be for cats, dinghies and tenders only. There is no need to use this entrance as a short cut for cars and tractors. Please use the top (club gate) entrance to the cat field for vehicles or, if you are going to work on your cruiser, the cat field entrance at the east end of the cruiser road. Similarly it has become common practice to drive cars onto the cat parking area either to work on boats or to park near the cadet hut or race cabin. Again this is turning some areas into mud or leaving deep grooves in the soft ground. There will be times when this is necessary, but please avoid it as far as possible just as we try not to have cars in the dinghy park area. SKIPS RUS Sorry for the rather prolonged presence of the two large skips on the hard. Hopefully they will have been removed by the time this issue of Navigans hits the streets. Some people have found that they provided useful shelter from winds from the south when watching the sailing. Perhaps we should have kept them! DOGS MESS IN THE CLUBHOUSE Sorry folks but, except for using the formal clinical term, there is no nice way to put this. On arriving for one of their morning cleaning sessions our cleaners were met with dogs mess in the clubhouse; and it had not been trodden in if you follow me. Although removing doggy-dos is most certainly not in their job description they were good enough to clear it up. This was a nasty thing to happen at any time but happening so soon after they started working at the club our new cleaners must have wondered what they had taken on! | think it very unlikely that the culprit was a member's dog. It was more likely one of the stray animals that seem to like roaming around our site. It may even have got itself accidentally locked into the clubhouse overnight. Maureen had to evict a stray dog from the clubhouse recently. There is little that we can do about other peoples’ dogs coming onto the site but | would ask all members to do the following: If you bring your dog to the club please observe the club rule and do not allow your dog to go anywhere in the clubhouse. If there are no doggy smells maybe the strays will be less interested in the building. If you see a dog in the clubhouse firmly shoo it out. \f you are shutting up the clubhouse please have a quick look around (including upstairs) to make sure that you are not locking in any unwelcome guests. Happy Sailing. Ray Ball Solo Matters The Sailing session has started and we had a good turn up following the Russian Evening without too may hangovers apparent. It was a shame the Sailing was cancelled due to High winds! Since then we have had two days of racing with an ever improving start line. Well done Mike and Roger for completing the race on weekend of the 4th April when so many others retired it was good to see the Solo fleet out on the water with a strong start line. Thank you Malcolm and John for volunteering to do the Jack 'B' rescue duties in the afternoon - If you had not I'm sure | would have stayed drier and warmer in the Club House!

John Nisbet Solo Fleet Captain [redacted] [redacted].co.uk Solo Fleet's Russian Evening Saturday evening (20th March) saw many solo sailors and their wives dressed as Russians descend on the club house. There was a Striking array of colour and a multitude of furry hats. All things that night were Russian, starting with a picture quiz_hung around the walls. While we were in the warm, Malcolm and Steve were outside cooking the meal. What a sumptuous dinner was served up. We started with Borsch (beetroot soup for the uninitiated), followed by Beef Stroganoff with a desert of Varenyky (sweet dumplings) .A tremendous amount of hard work was carried out by Malcolm in deciding the menu, co-coordinating the pre-cooking at home by solo members and overseeing the whole meal on the night. After the meal and the answers to the quiz were heard, everyone was divided into three teams. Russian titled games were then played (" Lenin's lying in state" and "Off to Siberia" being two). The evening ended with each team acting out a sketch entitled "From Russia with love" which included some excellent Cossack dancing by all the teams members. This was a really good evening and thanks go out to all who helped. Next year will be another theme but don't wait till then, buy a solo now and join in the fun.
