Page 9 of 17 Marconi alla Italia by Roger Smith Winner of the 2005 Mamgu Trophy for Best Log. It’s a well known fact that sailing on Lake Garda in Italy is the acme for the small boat sailor, so when the Dutch Solo Association arranged the World Trophy meeting at Fraglia della Vela di Riva del Garda we just had to go. We being John Salmon and Roger Smith, intrepid Solo sailors from Marconi. So 6.30am one Saturday morning saw John’s car loaded with the sailors and their wives Margaret and Kath, a load of luggage and a borrowed trailer with two Solos on, setting out from Billericay towards the Dover ferry terminal. We are making a holiday of it – not like some of the Solo jockeys who had to get back to work as soon as the sailing finished. That first day saw us across France to an overnight stop in Nancy. The navigation is going to be tricky – there are 3 maps in the car and every road junction results in a committee discussion on which way to go. I take my first driving stint; John can’t bear to watch and promptly falls asleep – no navigation assistance here then! Perhaps a word of explanation here for those not fortunate enough to sail the Solo. The class is quite old (Jack Holt design from 1956 in fact) and really only caught on in the UK and the Netherlands with a few in Australia. The World Trophy is sailed each year between the Dutch and British with each country taking turns to host the event. However there has been a little resurgence lately and there has been attempts to increase the spread of the disease - er hobby, further within Europe. The Dutch guys take the biscuit however by arranging to have their World Trophy meeting in Italy at the fabulous Lake Garda where we were told the morning is peaceful to recover from the hangover or take the sun and at 1.00pm the Ora sets in from the South with a force 4 to make exciting sailing. Back to the plot: after a short detour for coffee in Kayserburg, Alsace – Albert Schweitzer’s birthplace and very quaint, day 2 sees us taking to the country roads in Switzerland; picture book scenery, mountain pastures complete with bells with cows on them, pretty chalet style houses with window boxes all with the backdrop of snow capped mountains. Roger bursts into “The Hills are Alive…” but they all say “That was Austria – shut up”. As we entered Switzerland we had to pay a nice lady €30 for a vignette to use the Swiss auto-routes, and we had to pay another €30 for the trailer. As we start to move off Kath shouts STOP! – The nice lady was still carefully affixing the vignette pass onto the trailer. We wonder where the money goes as the first thing we encounter is a traffic jam and what seems like continuous road works in Basle. We finish up in Lugano where Roger tries a bit of mountaineering in John’s car in an effort to reach the hotel car park: stalls it: tries again and again resulting in a red face for Roger and the acrid smell of burning clutch plates! Later that evening he tries his newly aquired Italian only to be met with blank looks from the waiter – not his day! Other entertainments that evening were the European Cup soccer final and watching the staff arrivals at the night club next door. They were Polish girls going to do Russian dancing – or was it Russian girls doing pole dancing? Either way Margaret was lucky not to get her soup in her lap as the waiters ogled these scantily clad ladies arriving for work with their sugar daddies. Day 3 sees us through the 17km long St. Gotthard tunnel and into Italy where we immediately notice a deterioration in the road quality as well as the scenery as we descend into the Lombardy plain which is the industrial workshop of Italy. Soon however we get our first glimpse of Lake Garda – Roger tries “Arrividerci Roma” and is told to shut up again – how about “Just one Cornetto?” No? We find the sailing club quite easily and also a few familiar faces from the travelling Solo crowd, dump the boats and then get to our apartments which are about a 20 minute walk from the sailing club. They are modern, clean and comfortable - but what shall we do? - there is no teapot! Zut Alors! – oh sorry that’s a bit of French! Margaret’s face drained of blood immediately until alternative means of making the cup that cheers were suggested and agreed. o The 54 Intervela; the Regatta of which we shall form part also includes events for the 470 and Finn class which have attracted sailors from various nationalities seeking to hone up their heavy weather sailing before the Olympics. We watch a team from Slovenia unload two 470s and a RIB for the coach, but John says he forgot to pack our support team! We plan to do a bit of sightseeing on day 4 but we get to the ferry terminal and there is a strike! The strike ends at 17.30 but there is a ferry to Torbole at 1.30pm! So we adjourn to a local café and chat to other Soloists also caught out by the strike. So far the wind does just what the books say and this is true also on day 5 when they craftily put on a practice race. John gets out on the water and completes the race in rather testing conditions resulting in damage to some boats. Thursday is the first day of the Regatta proper. The start is delayed due to light wind until 2.30pm rd when we do get off. Its Roger’s birthday – yes really – and he is in 3 place after the first lap! But the luck does not hold and the wind collapses completely and they can the race! Although the wind picks up a little that’s the end for the day. A big bonus though is the free pasta and bottle of water laid on by the club to recharge the energy levels of the athletes (eh em!). So, Belinda – you know what we expect now! The Marconi Rescue boat crews will be interested to know that the windward mark was in 380 metres of water for that race! The committee boat has a concrete block for an anchor and lowers it on a big reel of plastic covered wire and recovers it - with some difficulty one imagines. But the race marks are laid with a breeze block type of anchor connected by a lot of bio degradable string – and when they come to remove it they just cut it away. Day 6 and its blowing a lot from the South and the lee shore we find tends to exaggerate the wind force. We are all wondering whether to go or not and those with ‘B’ plan sails decide now is the day! It really worked well and I was in front of several people with full sails after the beat and gybing was a breeze. Unfortunately it tore on its first outing as a result of the boom and gooseneck parting company

Page 10 of 17 on a gybe resulting in a capsize while trying to fix it and missing the next two races. John gets out for the second two races and completes them both without event – well done. Later the Dutch Solo Association had arranged a meal at a delightful restaurant on the outskirts of Riva which was thoroughly enjoyed by all. The race committee is getting worried now and start us at 0900 (where is this lay-in?) for day 7, the third race day, however the wind is light from the North but we get a race in the morning and again in the afternoon in a light Southerly. Its barbecue time tonight at the sailing club, although the meal is served in their large events room and it is all cooked in their kitchens, red wine served in flagons etc. None of your half oil barrels here! The sailing club itself is a very well organised institution with full time secretariat, catering and bar staff and people looking after the st nd boats etc. The building had a nice lounge, internet access, roof terrace and this enormous function room complete with the 1 , 2 and rd 3 podium. Every morning the cadets were out in Optimists and the bigger ones in Lasers in the afternoon, we even saw a group of cadets performing physical jerks and press ups in the marina one morning prior to their sailing. A new chore for cadet week? Having said that I feel the Solos were the poor relations of the 470s and Finns despite having a fleet of 62 boats. We tended to get shorter courses, nearly always sausages to fit in with the other classes, despite all that lovely reaching wind. So we move onto the last day of the regatta; 0900 start again and we are launching just after 8.00am with a gentle Northerly to sail about three miles down the lake to the committee boat with ominous, lowering clouds over the mountains to the North. By the time we get there it’s a force 5 and rising and the RO is reluctant to set a course. So we all retreat to the shelter of a small bay on the East side of the lake. Soon we see why: the clouds are harbingers of a massive thunderstorm and winds reported to be up to F8. Some of the Solos who started to go back to the club are caught in it resulting in one dangerous incident. One Solo capsized on the way back and apparently the boat cart-wheeled away from the helm several times. No rescue boats around and the helm was getting quite distressed as he was not used to conditions like that. Luckily another Solo, helmed by a Dutch girl, came to his rescue and with good seamanship picked him up and sailed two up to his boat which had a broken mast where the rescue services caught up with them. The Dutch Solo Association rightly presented her with a commendation at the prizegiving. It is amazing how you can sail right up to the side of the lake with centreboard right down and not see the bottom. The down side is that while stooging around I get a reverse blast of wind off the cliff face and the boom hits my head and I am swimming – Oh bother! Eventually the storm passes after an hour or more getting colder and colder in the rain (is this Italy?) and we manage to get in three races starting with a good F5 but moderating as the sun warmed us up. So it’s pack up the boat time and go to the prize-giving. We remark on the size and fitness of the Finn sailors (Honey Monsters according to Paul Kimmens) and the slim athleticism of the 470 crews - that’s the men and the women. Then the Solos got their prizes. Ian Houston won – well he lives in Switzerland so he didn’t have so far to travel. The winners are a bit self conscious about the podium thingy! The Dutch Solo President sums it up when he says that if they have the World Trophy just across the Channel they only get half a dozen guys from England but if they go 1000 miles into Italy they get about 45. So I guess next time it might be in Australia! Its Monday now and we clean the apartment and prepare for the journey home. We travel back a different way via Austria, Germany and Belgium and start with the Brenner Pass. Here I claim the altitude record for a Solo dinghy (mine was on top!) of 1,374 + 1.5m. We pay for another vignette for the car to use Austrian roads but it does not seem to help as every time we stop we seem to have to pay another €8. Scenery in Austria is superb once again, in particular the road engineering with massive high viaducts and cantilevered roads out from the mountainside. Roger tries “Castenegger Bogle–by–the Sea” as it sounds a bit Austrian like a town we just passed but is told there is no sea here – see here. The journey home is marred by the inability of the ViaMichelin web site routes to provide navigation over the last mile of each day. Tonight we stay in the town of Friedrichshafen on the shore of Bodensee but as we follow the directions we come to a dead end at a pedestrian precinct and ferry terminal! Roger does the first of his road runner impersonations and legs it down the road past the Zeppelin Museum to the hotel, where they issue him with a pass to drive through the precinct to the hotel. Despite rather alien weather we enjoy our short stay in this pretty town, in particular an excellent meal of Schwabian beef in a small beer kellar. Roger has to try the famous cloudy German Wiesbier – a good cure for constipation! Day10 brings us through Germany; destination Koblenz. The final part of the journey is a detour along the Rhine river and we marvel at the amount of traffic on this artery of Europe. Large cargo barges with the bargee’s motor car on top, hotel cruise ships, ferries and smaller commercial traffic all bustling along the river. Roger quotes from the Pied Piper of Hamelin “The river Weser runs deep and wide with grassy banks on the Southern side….” but gets told that is not this part of Germany (Poor Roger!). Our hotel location crisis today is highlighted by the bizarre sight of John and Margaret asking directions of a passing lady in German and her responding in English! She had more trouble with the directions than the English. Her directions were excellent; unfortunately she did not know that the last bit of one road was completely blocked by some sewer excavations so Roger did the road runner bit again to find a diversion. We generally found good quality, good value hotels and restaurants along the way – at least when we eventually found them. Next morning the route is to follow the route of the Moselle river before turning onto the Autobahn to get us into Belgium for the last stop of our adventure. It was very pretty with small villages and towns sporting cute churches and houses, a schloss or three all amid the famous vineyards of the Moselle region. A short stop for John to buy up the output of one of the vineyards and we are off again. More trouble finding the hotel which calls itself a resort, but we can see no reason to justify this status. Finally we are off to Calais and after a short drive we are soon boarding an earlier than planned ferry home. Roger starts “We are sailing” as the ferry starts to vibrate noisily but gets told a) it has not left yet and b) it does not sail but motors! A great trip and good holiday. Thanks to John for using his car and to John and Margaret for good companionship and good humour throughout making the trip enjoyable for Kath and myself and to Kath for her constant support with the trolley, food, water etc. Roger Smith.

Page 11 of 17 Extract from RYA Research into Dinghy Entrapments - March 2005 For the full document see www.rya.org.uk INTRODUCTION Over recent years, public awareness regarding the risk of getting trapped has grown. In addition there have been a few well-publicised ‘near misses’ and one or two incidents involving foreign sailors. Whilst the statistical risk appeared to be very small, no clear records of this type of incident appeared to exist. In response the RYA has logged incidents through the RYA website. Air gap tests have been carried out under a range of boats, and a range of techniques for rescuing a trapped sailor tested. As well as holding discussions with the major dinghy manufacturers, the RYA has looked for good ways to prevent or reduce the problem. SUMMARY OF FINDINGS There are no clear patterns in the cause of incidents, which occurred in a wide range of conditions and boats. Neither the experience of the sailors nor the equipment used suggest a single dominant factor in the incidents recorded. The statistical risk to a dinghy sailor of becoming dangerously trapped is tiny, but sailors should be aware that these incidents can happen. Rescue can be difficult in the time available and staying calm contributes to the chance of escape. INCIDENT RECORDS Incidents were logged over two seasons via the RYA website, following publicity to all affiliated clubs and centres: it is impossible to judge what proportion of those which took place were recorded, and how many were missed. No historical data appears to exist, so it is difficult to tell if incidents of this type are more frequent in recent years. Despite the low statistical risk, there is sufficient range of incidents to suggest it is worth making sailors aware of the problem. Of the incidents reported, only a small proportion required medical treatment, but over one third were serious i.e. potential threat to life. The biggest risk results from complete inversion of the boat with the sailor tangled or stuck underneath. The probability of an incident seems unaffected very much by the conditions, since a number of incidents were recorded in light winds. The speed of inversion can increase the risk: some designs invert faster than others, but most will invert quickly if capsized to windward whilst sailing downwind. While approximately a quarter of sailors recording a problem were in their first year of sailing, approx a quarter had sailed the class of boat less than 5 times. There was a similar figure for those who had sailed the class more than 3 years. The incidents were spread fairly evenly across recreational sailing, racing and coaching/training. A very wide range of boats were involved. The vast majority of recorded incidents occurred without a spinnaker. Approximately one third of incidents involved ropes caught around the sailor. Just over one third involved other fittings or equipment, and one third involved trapeze equipment. There is no doubt that the ability to stay calm under water enabled a number of people to clear themselves. EQUIPMENT DESIGN The bulk manufacturers of modern dinghies were involved in discussions and all contributed ideas. Design considerations leading to inversion are extremely complex, with a number of significant trade-offs to be taken into account. Sealed masts do appear to have some effect in reducing the speed and likelihood of inversion. Some manufacturers have made masthead buoyancy available as an option. Most modern designs have a raised cockpit floor to enable self-draining. An inverted boat of this type will therefore have a lower ‘ceiling’, and a smaller air void. In the case of sailors trapped in the cockpit, most self draining boats have no useful air void, though there may be an air void if the water is calm. In larger waves, neither traditional nor self-draining boats were found to have a useful air void. (It is worth noting that self draining boats are probably less prone to multiple capsizes, and therefore arguably safer.) New trapeze equipment is becoming available but its reliability is untested: Several manufacturers have releasable hooks available and one system dispenses with the hook and ring entirely. It is essential that a trapped sailor can find the release mechanism instantly by feel. PREVENTION It is clear that untidy boats with unnecessarily long or tangled control lines increase the risk. Good housekeeping reduces the risk. The best defence amongst sailors is probably widespread awareness of the issue. Masthead flotation may be useful in training centres, or when learning to sail a new high performance boat. A great deal of time and energy can be saved if the boat will not invert, but will float on its side while the crew recover. 30 – 40 litres of air at the masthead appeared to prevent inversions in a range of boats and conditions during trials, with no evidence of masts breaking. The impact on sailing performance is minimal for basic training and coaching. Undoubtedly significantly less buoyancy would be effective in many boats, but a fast windward capsize can result in very rapid inversions. 20 litres was insufficient on many classes. • Sailors are therefore advised to: • Keep control lines short and tidy and maintain elastic so it does its job • Carry a very sharp, easily accessible, preferably serrated knife • Practice good housekeeping If RYA recognised Training Centres feel there is a significant risk due to the nature of the boats, the students, or the conditions on the day, they may use masthead flotation for certain tasks. It is not mandatory or normal practice on courses involving beginners. If it is employed on such courses, the instructor should remove the buoyancy and demonstrate inversion to the course members. Ordinary good practice, such as competent group control and setting tasks appropriate to the group, make the sport as safe for learners as it has always been.

Page 12 of 17 RESCUING A TRAPPED SAILOR If someone is actually under water there is very little time for rescue, with or without a safety boat. A wide range of approaches and boats were tried over several sessions in several locations. The fastest reliable rescue technique which worked for all boats was found to be two heavy sailors aboard the inverted boat, pulling on the centre board. Nearly all boats could be righted consistently inside thirty- five seconds in a range of conditions. This can also be achieved using a RIB tow or push, which immediately increases the risk to the trapped sailor (whereabouts usually unclear) from the propeller. A variety of new and established methods involving the powerboat were tested. A number of established techniques failed in some circumstances, and no technique was faster than the basic one using leverage from sailors to right the boat. Instructors and safety boat crew have shown a tendency to dive under the boat to attempt to free the casualty. This may or may not involve a knife. This is a risky approach which has no guarantee of quick success. It would be better to right the boat as quickly as possible. While an air gap can be created by picking up one end of a light boat (e.g. Feva, Topaz, Pico) it is important that the rescuer know which end to pick up, otherwise the casualty may be forced deeper. There is a significant risk of injury to the safety crew in attempting to raise one end of heavier boats, particularly from an unstable platform such as safety boat in waves. This is therefore not recommended. There have been cases of sailors entangled above water but under a boat, who were forced under water as the safety crew stepped onto the hull to right it. A sharp, serrated knife was used in some rescues; this is now a requirement for safety boats in RYA recognised Training Centres.

Page 10 of 14 Danbury A414 Closure From 11 April 2005, essential maintenance work on the A414 in Danbury will involve the road being closed for approximately 12 weeks. With average traffic flows of around 22,000 vehicles a day, the A414 is a primary route across the county. Currently, the whole length of the road is in a very poor condition. The scheme is therefore vital, but for work to be carried out safely, closure of certain sections is necessary. Phase 1 of the £2.7 million improvement scheme started in November and has involved replacing street lighting, resurfacing footways and installing new bus stops. Phase 2 involves work to highways drainage systems, as well as essential resurfacing work on the majority of the carriageway. Travelling in the area The map shows the different stages of the work. The first closure, which is due to last approximately 8 weeks, will stop traffic travelling along the A414 between the A12 interchange and Eves Corner. After this section is completed the second closure, which is due to last approximately 4 weeks, will stop traffic travelling between Eves Corner and the Royal Oak Roundabout. Whilst these closures are in place all through traffic will be directed to the signed diversion routes. These follow north and south alternatives, and although they are longer than the normal route, they have been chosen as they are suitable for all types of vehicles, especially HGV'S. The north diversion from Maldon follows the B1019 through Hatfield Peverel to the A12. The south diversion from the Royal Oak Roundabout follows the B1418 to South Woodham Ferrers, then onto the new A130 Southend Road via the A132 to Rettendon. All traffic should expect delays and you should allow for longer journey times. If you are able to make arrangements, car sharing will reduce the expected congestion at peak times. The closures will also have a significant effect on local public bus services and possibly cause longer journey times. The information on the other side gives more details of the revised routes. Those students on affected school contract services will be contacted individually about how the work will affect them. Further details about the work and how journeys will be affected are being made available locally, but if you need more information, including revised bus timetables, contact the Essex Traffic Control Centre on 08456 000110. It was good to know that Ken had such excellent support from both the professionals and his friends but the outcome is no less sad for Bob, his family and all of us who knew Ken. Ken was great to have around and always interesting to talk to. One abiding memory for me will be his recent Talent Night performance; Ken explained to us all that he had decided to revive long-lost brass band skills in order to entertain us. He played for us (I hope that I am not doing him an injustice here) the bugle call he had worked hard to re-learn and soaked up our applause for his talent and his efforts. I am sad that we will now be denied his planned offering for Trafalgar Day. Ken told me that had plans to add a few more tunes to his repertoire and could deliver some suitably inspiring readings to match the mood of the occasion. CRUISER RACING NEWS 2005 The Doctor Trophy Conditions and course for the Doctor Race were almost identical to last year. A nasty day with a dodgy forecast, winds gusting over force Force 7 and a long 6 hour course via the Colne and Knoll greeted Marconi yachts as they joined the BJRC fleet for the Brown Cup. The return beat into the Blackwater was very hard with winds gusting to Force 8. Mike Turner made a welcome return to racing in Sea Brume crewed by the ‘Killaras’, plus Peter Ward racing Macgregor, Colin Leveridge in Bluster and myself. Colin wisely retired, Peter battled through, to a good finish and a close fought battle between the Hustlers settled by line honours for Mike and a handicap win for Ocean Slipper. Each team consists of 6 people (3 Tickets are available now priced £32.50 from me at: helms and 3 crew) in 3 identical boats who sail matches against other such teams in the same type of boat. , A ‘match’ between two teams means that 6 boats are on the water in each individual race and (usually) follows a ‘best of three races’ format. Basically, each individual race provides you with three ‘1-on-1 match race’ encounters going on at the same time between the two teams. Races are short (about 10 minutes each) on a Don’t forget to include your name and address when single triangular course right in front of the spectators. sending payment for tickets. The action is fast, furious and always changing. Racing is frequently accompanied by much shouting, calling for Wendy Hurrell-Smith perceived sailing ‘rights’ and frequent ‘on-water protests’ which are adjudicated upon immediately by on-water umpires who are very close up to the action in their RIBS. In each individual race, points are awarded with 1 point (for 1st place) down to 6 points (6th place) and the team finishing with the least total number of points wins the particular race. With 6 boats in the race, you can see that there is a total of 21 points to be awarded, and the aim is to make sure that your team doesn’t score more than 10 points. It is thus important that each team member is very aware of (i) the position of their own and their other team boats and (ii) the acceptable finishing combinations needed to secure a (team) win e.g. 1st , 3rd and 6th (10 points) beats 2nd, 4th and 5th (11 points). HOWEVER, a boat doesn’t necessarily want to finish before they are absolutely sure the other boats in the team are (a) holding a winning combination or (b) capable of improving into a winning combination. The leading boat of the team might have to delay finishing in order to assist the team in pushing a boat from the opposition further back down the finishing order. Just how you do this makes all the difference between being the World Champions – or not! Mind you, the teams who finished 2nd, 3rd and 4th in the World’s are pretty good at it too. Coxswain Glenys Credit: Les Hurrell-Smith The last Sunday in October saw our sailing season come to an end with the aptly named “Final Fling”. After 5 years serving us teas, lunches and cakes, Glenys Monks has decided to hang up her cake knife and apron. Whether you were a racer, cruiser or visitor to the club, you were always guaranteed a welcome smile and often a hearty laugh as Glenys happily made sure we were all fed Suited and booted at the laying up supper Credit: Les Hurrell-Smith and watered. So she will still continue to look after us but in a different way.

Page 6 “Return to Jassper!” by Les Hurrell-Smith Winning Entry of the 2005 Mamgu Trophy Some of you will recall my previous jottings recounting my exploits in the Mediterranean while delivering a Bavaria 36 from Antibes in France to Reggio in Italy. Well two years on and JASSPER made it to Turkey and has been happily paying her way as a charter boat for Top Yacht, it was high time we made use of her so a blokes jolly was organised for late May this year. Four of us were to take advantage, Paul the owner, his son Sam and good friend Richard with myself making up the crew. It was to be a holiday which we had convinced ourselves we needed and duly started at Gatwick with full English and a few lagers, our flight was 7:30 in the morning, a little early for a beer, I think not! The flight was OK indeed less traumatic than the taxi ride from Dalaman. We were lucky in as much as the taxi was fairly new and certainly had a new horn which the driver seemed to constantly use as we climbed through the hills that made up the coast road to Gocek, where Jassper was berthed. When we left the taxi we were hit by a wall of hot air, 36 degrees was a shock but luckily once we had put our bags on board Jassper we were just 100 yards from a welcoming cold beer at the local tavern, so decided that was to be our base for the afternoon while we planned ahead. The people at top Yacht were very helpful and once back on the boat they paid us a visit to help us plan out sailing over the next 7 days. Next stop was for provisions and as before we made sure we had enough room for the beer in the trolleys, it is all about prioritisation! We spent a leisurely evening in town had a really good meal and then meandered around the local market, all very colourful Day 2 and it seemed we had a split in the camp, Richard and I were keen to get going, both being early risers, but Paul and Sam seemed to be in a coma, indeed they slept through the local Mosque calling to prayer the townsfolk. My memory went back to the last time Paul and I sailed together and his legendary sleep, through a force 9 gale, so very little chance of getting him up until he was ready. He was ready by 11 so we then readied ourselves for the first sail, and got going at midday deciding that first stop would be Sarsala, about 15 miles or so across the bay. Gocek Marina Dolphins The breeze was a perfect force 3 – 4 and as we made our way out into open water we were soon joined by a pair of Dolphins who stayed with us for 30 minutes or so, sweeping under the boat and jumping up around the bow as if to say hey guys bet you can’t do this. It was quite spectacular to watch. The breeze remained steady and we made good time, taking turns to helm and get familiar once again with Jassper. We just made the most of the open water and spent a good few hours reaching across between headlands. But the wind patterns around Turkeys coast are strange and seem to switch on and off at predefined times so as we neared Sarsala the wind started to drop and was almost nothing as we silently crept up between rising cliffs on both sides, as we entered a tiny bay on our way to Sarsala. As we approached the scene was very picturesque, with flags fluttering across the quay and numerous yachts already moored up alongside the ramshackle quay, which was made up of old tree stumps and branches covered in planks. The restaurant owner was on hand to help bring the stern in and in hardly any time at all we were nicely sandwiched between two other yachts. No charge for berthing up but one is expected to eat at the owners restaurant which is no hardship at all, the food is always good and drink plentiful and often entertainment is provided, which this evening was to watch people stagger on and off a large Gulet, a local style of boat, often with always has masts but rarely any sails! This particular one was being used for parties, disgraceful that people should let drink get the better of them!

Page 7 Sarsala Quay Jassper at Sarsala Day 3 and the despite the local cockerel making a real din, Paul was the last to rise, clearly tiring work this being the skipper of your own yacht. No matter the water was crystal clear and we decided that an early, well earlyish morning dip was in order so one by one (except Paul who was asleep) we dived off Jassper to discover that it might be clear but it was cold, you have never seen 3 guys enter and exit the water so fast in your life. This wasn’t so bad until we noticed the Germans who were happily treading water about 100 yards from the shore! Anyway, after a pancake based breakfast we set about planning our next leg. Fethiye was to be our destination again a 10 – 15 mile sail. Rather than waste the breeze we cruised back and forth across the wide bay dodging the Gulets who seemed to totally disregard all others. Our plan was to sail for 4 hours then make our way into Fethiye bay in time for a swim before sunset. Right on time at 4 p.m. the wind started to drop and we slowly sailed into Fethiye, past the holiday homes on the cliffs, past the marina and on to what was the working end of the town. As we came up to the quay we were looking for the usual bow line to pick up but just could not see it, after a few attempts were helped by ex-pats Roger and Sally who pointed out that the bow line had sunk! So we needed to drop our anchor and slowly motor back towards the quays, suddenly we had become the afternoons entertainment as heads popped up from boats to have a look at our efforts. Luckily all went well and our ex-pat friend saw us nicely back and we simply jumped off and tied up, like true professionals but it could have been so different! This was the commercial end of the town, with numerous boatyards building the tradition Gulets of varying sizes, but quayside facilities were OK, swimming pool, restaurant close to hand so all looked well for a pleasant stay. We spent the evening in a local bar watching Liverpool play football on a dodgy TV, an entertaining game made all the livelier by the Turkish commentary and the antics of the locals whenever a goal was scored. I never new so many Liverpool supporters lived in Turkey! Day 3 dawned bright as ever to much hammering and general boat yard noise, but not enough to rouse Paul before he was ready! Quick breakfast and then we caught the local Dolmas (bus) into town as it was market day. Fethiye is a really interesting town, the market sprawls for what seemed like miles and all manner of things are on sale, and clearly looking like tourists we were prey to all the sales pitches you could imagine. We were offered leather goods, jewellery of dubious heritage and quality and even T shirts in three styles, short and long sleeved as well as “Rambo” which to us was a capped sleeve. All very colourful and interesting and certainly a good way to spend a day as it was mostly under shade. Also in abundance was food and I have to say the kebabs certainly tasted better than those traditionally eaten at 2 in the morning after a nights clubbing! On the way back to Jasper we decided to try a Turkish bath a great way to get rid of the days grime and relax before the evening meal. How right that was, We found a suitable venue and four tired and grubby men went in and a few hours later four squeaky clean and very relaxed guys hovered out with skin that was a smooth as the proverbial! Brilliant! We meandered back to the boat and on the way stopped to watch one of the larger Gulets being launched, a really physical task, to do that is not watch. It seemed as if everyone from the many boats yards was involved, many giving clear and precise technical insights while others, wielding large pots of engine oil smoothed the way as the great boat inched its way to the waters edge. Slowly, ever so slowly she got to that point of no return, hesitated and then as if by magic tottered over an invisible edge and then rushed into the water, steadied by great ropes until she settled down to float. Quite a magnificent sight to see and also like magic crates of beer emerged and all those involved each had an open bottle and were toasting the achievement.

Page 8 Gulet being launched at Fethiye Richard struts his stuff Day 4 and for a change a reasonably early start, the boat yard being the hive of industry it was, was too much for Paul, so we had breakfast and readied the yacht for a full days sailing. This time we decided to make our way to Coldwater Bay, so called because it is fed by fresh water springs, and has a feel of a pirates cove, though we did not see any I hasten to add. We were told this was where one could see some ancient ruins and also do a little cliff diving! Can’t wait! This was a more challenging sail, the wind picked up and we sailed in flotilla with another Bavaria yacht, I am sure they were trying as hard as us as we tried to increase boat speed as we both tacked on each other great fun! After 4 hours of good sailing, oh yes the other Bavaria gave up clearly not up to the challenge and peeled off as we turned the last headland with some 4 miles to go before Coldwater Bay. Once again and almost as if a switch had been turned the wind died and we were forced to turn on the motor to keep moving. A bit of a shame but it did not spoil the sights as we crept along the coast with towering hills both sides and nested within the sparse tree line we could easily see the ancient ruins were had been told about, lots of building and a few temples some apparently just hanging off the side of the hill, we decided to explore these later on. So into Coldwater Bay, which was a tiny bay large enough for about eight yachts and we were the th th 8 to arrive, surrounded on three sides by high rock walls, and on the 4 by a tiny shingle beach which led up the hill to the mandatory restaurant. No quayside here so as we motored in we were greeted by the owner in his motor boat who took our stern line and tied it to the rock wall as we laid out our anchor, and he welcomed us with some dried fruit, pointing out the route to the restaurant, which seemed to be guarded by a Donkey! It was a hot day, and the water was very clear so in we all dived for a refreshing swim, but luckily the option of cliff diving was not for us simply because a large yacht was moored very close the landing spot, real shame that! Time for dinner so out came the tender and we made our way ashore, as we landed the Donkey eyed us up, but didn’t seem to bothered by us at first then he let out an almighty BRAY which went on for ages, we later found out that he didn’t like females for some reason or other, perhaps Richards belly dancing efforts had a longer lasting effect than we first thought! In actual fact we had been followed ashore by 2 couples and it was this group that the donkey took umbrage at! So after a brisk climb we made it to the restaurant and settled in for the evening, great food but we were soon attacked by the largest mosquitoes you have ever seen and no amount of arm flailing could deter them from there supper US!

Page 9 Donkey at Coldwater Bay Looking down on Coldwater bay Next Day we were greeted by a small rowing boat offering us fresh fruit and pancakes for breakfast, the Turkish equivalent of food to go I guess. Anyway we decided to motor around the headland and explore of the local ruins, so off we went, followed by the rowing boat, clearly he was on a commission basis! Once safely off of Tersani Island with our anchor down and the stern line tied to a tree! This was a great spot surrounded by Byzantine ruins and was so peaceful. We spent time snorkelling and fishing while another enterprising Turk asked us if we were going to visit the ruins, and if so we had to pay! Seemed reasonable so we did, but later found out that we were conned and that we should have paid the officials who looked after the island! The ruins were spectacular, at some time the island had been a hive of activity, lots of dwellings, temples and even more burial mounds were scattered around on all side, but the best of all was the view from the top absolutely stunning. All around were mountains surrounded by clear blue waters with the odd sailing yacht dotted around. Well worth the effort of climbing what was a large hill but felt like a small mountain in the 38 degrees of heat! *Pancakes for Breakfast at Coldwater bay Wake me up before you Go Go! Reluctantly we left the island for our next anchorage some 10 miles away, which was to be Kapi Creek in another small bay which was serene and absolutely proof from the wildest storms although it never looked like anything other than sun during our stay. Kapi Creek is surrounded by pines and olives and is the home to Memmet's restaurant, which had fresh lobster (choose you own from the cage) as well as an abundance of local specialities on the menu. The usual drill applied, stern line to the quay ably helped by one of Memmets people soon had us snuggled up against other yachts. Through the crystal clear water we could see the fish happily swimming around so Richard decided that it was an ideal opportunity to do a little fishing. One of the local children was also fishing using a simple line and hook and seemed to be very successful pulling a few out as we watched. So Richard with his hi- tech collapsible fishing rod and multiplier reel was certain to catch the big one. Wrong! Not a nibble while just feet away the youngster was getting bored because it was too easy! So here we were at our penultimate day, and having to make our way back to Gocek, which we did but in a very circuitous route in order that we made the most of the wind and have as much sailing time as the wind allowed, boat speed was the order of the day and Sam managed to set a new Turkish record by hitting 8.7 knots. Right on time at 4:00 the wind died and we motored slowly into Gocek marina, stopping on the way to refuel ready for the next set of charters. Once berthed we tidied the boat and chilled out, only to notice that moored next to us was one

Page 10 Michael Buerk of TV fame. We were even more surprised when his wife came over and started to chat, we found out that Michael was also a Top Yacht charter owner and had been for some years now, and spent most of his free time sailing the med in one way or another. We had the side lockers open as we stowed away ropes and Christine, yes first name terms by now, was very interested in the small 12v outboard motor we had stowed below. We were soon demonstrating it and she called out to Michael to take a look as it was just what he wanted, from the look on his face it wasn’t! Anyway the jolly soon came to an end and we spent our last night getting rid of as much Turkish Lira that we could, as pounds sterling and euros seemed very popular and everyone could work out the exchange rate as quick as look at a £10 note! The journey back to Dalaman was just as interesting as the incoming one, but we got to the airport in plenty of time to join the mile long queue! Thoroughly recommend Turkey as a sailing venue, and (here is the advert) would also recommend Top Yacht and Jassper as a charter boat, If interested visit the web site on www.top-yacht.com or call them on . Page 11 Commodore’s Report AGM 2005 I will once again try to balance the requirement to convey the information demanded by the Companies Act with some less dry information on how the club has performed over the last year. Firstly, I am required once again to confirm that our principle activity during the past year has been the provision of sailing facilities to our membership. Ultimate responsibility for the activities of the club rests with the Executive Board. The board comprised six directors: • Murray Bates • John Bird • Peter Clayton • Chris Davies (Managing) • Claire Davies • Clive Shenton During the year, due to unforeseen circumstances, Claire found in necessary to resign her post and the board co-opted Chris Laing to take her place. John Bird has taken responsibility for finance matters and all other directors have specific operational responsibilities as Flag Officers of the Club. The board appoints an Honorary Secretary and during the past year that post was held by Ray Ball. Ray moved from a Flag Officer role to his present post on the retirement of Pat Black and has applied exactly the level of care and attention to detail that was expected of him. I am extremely grateful for his not inconsiderable efforts on behalf of the Board and the Club. I am no less grateful to Chris Laing for the effort and insight that he has brought to his unexpected role as Claire’s replacement. Two Board members will retire this year and I would like to pay tribute to them for the significant contribution they have made in different ways to the life and wellbeing of the club. Clive Shenton steps down for a well-deserved rest after 11 consecutive years on the Executive and will, I know, continue to be an active contributor to club life. John Bird, who did so much to ensure a smooth transition from MASC control to our independent ownership of the Club, has found it increasingly difficult to devote as much time to the Club as he might wish and has decided to move on also. Both Clive and John have our grateful thanks for all that they have done. The board met formally each month since the last AGM and has conducted such other meetings of sub-groups as have been appropriate from time to time. The Management Committee has also met monthly throughout the year and there have been regular meetings of the various sub-committees that deal with specific areas of activity. I am grateful to all those people who have been so active and so supportive in their work for the board and all the committees. I acknowledge here too the huge amount of work that is done by a large number of members who operate outside the committee structure but who get things done in a thousand different ways. I mentioned last year the importance of ensuring that we properly filled all our committee posts and ensured that duty rosters were fully operated. I think that we have had a pretty good year so far the rosters have been concerned – although there is always room for improvement in this regard. Recruitment of members into posts of responsibility continues to be an issue that concerns me. You will note that we are lacking nominations for several posts this year. This arises either because those of us who are already involved have been unable to identify replacements or because members have failed to put themselves forward to be those replacements. Or both. I have no complaint with anyone about this. I understand that some people have already done their bit and earned a rest. I know that many have extremely busy lives elsewhere. I know that a great many members undertake or assist with duties, projects or tasks that are not elected posts. However, if we are to function efficiently and without too great a burden falling on the shoulders of any one individual (or group of individuals), we do need to identify people to fill these roles. We need a full complement of members on the Management Committee and Executive in particular in order to ensure that we have proper continuity in managing club affairs from year to year. We do need people and will need people so do consider and encourage others to consider when you might formalise – perhaps just for a short time – your undoubted commitment to the functioning of the club. Having extolled the benefits of committee involvement I suppose that, in the interests of balance if nothing else, I need to admit to and acknowledge the less pleasant and most difficult work that the committees get involved in when dealing with issues arising out of members overlooking, disregarding or openly challenging Club rules and practices. These occur only infrequently, are not pleasant situations to deal with and it is rare for anybody to get any satisfaction out of them. In our duty to protect the interests of the general membership, however, we do from time to time find it necessary to point out to individuals the error of

Page 12 their ways; I am happy to confirm my belief that such activity is carried out as fairly, as clearly and as discretely as the circumstances allow. The members concerned are not always happy with our interventions – but that’s life, I suppose, and we do work hard to try to achieve the best outcome for everybody concerned. I am required to mention any political or charitable donations made during the year. I am proud of our ongoing work in support of the Cirdan Sailing Trust and can confirm that, through ECPR, we were able to donate over £9000 to that charity. We also donated relatively small amounts to RNLI and to Essex Air Ambulance. However, all these sums were raised during events and were not paid from club income. We may not have been altogether obviously active in terms of addressing a number of important issues regarding the fabric of the club. Whilst we have enjoyed the new-found benefits of the enlarged Dell Bar with its improved access, we have not visibly moved forward on other desirable improvements to the layout and fabric of our buildings. However, I can assure you that this aspect has not been overlooked and a considerable amount of work has been done in the background to give proper consideration to these matters. We expect shortly to be in a position to finalise a maintenance and development plan for the site that will provide a blueprint for the protection and improvement of our property that will enable us to move forward in a considered and structured manner. I suggested in my report to you last year that we would maintain the cautious approach adopted in our first year of financial independence and this is again reflected in the figures already circulated to you. Notwithstanding such caution, we have once again: • Enjoyed, through Wendy Hurrel-Smith’s efforts, a strong and innovative Social Calendar. • We have had a full and varied sailing calendar with some innovation and more to come. • Maintained and extended the range of Open events held here. • Enjoyed another excellent ECPR and an outstanding Cadet Week • Seen MSC sailors active on the circuits on a Europe wide basis. • Maintained our levels of membership. • Continued to improve equipment in the cause of safety, efficiency and convenience. On balance then another active, interesting and involving year in which the club has thrived and progressed. I look forward to further progress being made in the next twelve months. Chris Davies November 2005

If you have not put your name down please contact Dennis Dear on Dennis Dear Fast Cat / Medium Cat Report The new season is approaching fast and both fleets have the potential for some more close and competitive racing - certainly in the fast cat class where we saw some exceptionally fast and close races between Daniel K / Anthony Monks and Mitchell Glynn / Nick Miller sailing their respective F18 Nacras Both pairs also represented the club at the F18 Nationals at Worthing in August 2005. Although it was our “nationals”, it was spiced up with the 3 Nissan Pro-team boats from France, Holland and Germany which I have to say set the standard for the week. If you take the Yachts & Yachting you may have seen their promotional antics trying to compete with surfers by sailing their Hobie Tiger down the face of incoming rollers or their speed trials at St. Marie de la Mer, where they were sailing down a narrow channel in 35 knots of wins when the unfortunate French boat pitch-poled with such force the wind lifted the 180 kilo Tiger completely clear of the water! Thankfully apart from being shaken and bruised, there were no injuries. CAT A.G.M. We are very grateful to Fenella Thomas for finding and booking a new venue for us. For those who wish to stay on for a meal, we will move into the adjacent restaurant after the meeting. Should you only wish to join us for the meal, it will be about 8:45 – everybody is welcome. Page 2 of 15 Commodore's Comments Important progress from I promised back in January to give you more news on the work done by the PUDS group and the outcomes that were beginning to flow from their hard work and deliberations. By way of a refresher for you now, I wrote then- I mentioned …. that we had not overlooked the need to plan for improvements to and maintenance of the fabric of the Club. Our plans to date were centred around the finances needed to purchase the site and to survive as an independent entity; those plans were well put together and have brought us to a point at which can and must look at the sort of actions we need to take to protect and improve our investment. During 2005 a group affectionately referred to as PUDS have been working quietly on an analysis and report on the present state of the Stansgate site and how it might be improved over a period of time. The group ………told us clearly that there were two areas for improvement that are head and shoulders above the rest. The first is for the provision of toilets and changing rooms that are of adequate size and with facilities that are on a scale and of a standard more in keeping with a modern club. The second is for buildings and site layout that give a better overall facility and visual appeal – as opposed to the rather messy and ramshackle appearance that applies to some of our current operation. Since writing that quite a lot has happened, with Michael Taylor further developing some of the design-work that he had undertaken for us, and the Executive and the Management Committee giving a lot of thought to what is feasible, desirable and likely to be affordable. Dealing with affordability first, we are as confident as we sensibly can be that we have a proper understanding and control of our finances in the relatively new circumstances that we operate. Membership levels are encouraging and we have no reason to believe that they cannot be maintained. We are creating sensible operating excesses of the sort that will enable us to invest in improvements and developments over a period of time. We need to accept, however, and plan for the fact that we will need to undertake the work involved in stages, as funds become available. It the light of the above, it has seemed to us to be important to create a Development Plan to which we can commit now and against which we can organise our capital spending over the next several years. That plan is more than just a wish list; it is a clear statement of intent concerning the improvements that we mean to make to the site and buildings and the order in which they will be carried out. Here is a brief summary of the key elements of that plan in priority order: Pontoon This assumes perhaps a slightly higher priority than might otherwise have been the case because consideration of the job pre-dates the PUDS operation. Nevertheless, this is an important addition to our facilities and impacts on issues of safety, efficiency, accessibility and general amenity. Changing Rooms and Toilets Universally agreed to be our most urgent priority. The need to create a facility that properly caters for the number of women members active in the modern club, to create facilities that are more in keeping with modern standards of presentation and amenity (and are easier to maintain in a good clean condition) and to make proper provision for disabled people and families with young children are all important factors. They are especially relevant to our efforts to maintain membership levels. Tractor Shed We have recognised a need to make the site more visually attractive and a key issue here is the location and storage of vehicles, equipment, plant and materials. We have had our attention very forcibly drawn to the fact that the tractor shed is in the wrong location. We knew that it had become inadequate for our needs, but Michael also pointed out that it was remote from the areas in which the tractors most often operate – but, more importantly, the fact that tractors and their towed accessories made frequent journey across the track in front of the clubhouse, seriously impaired the safe and quiet enjoyment of that area by members. We propose to build a larger shed, capable of absorbing the contents of our two containers and

Page 3 of 15 the concrete garage as well as the tractors and their equipment, in the cruiser field. It will be an agricultural style building located and designed to fit the background. The existing tractor shed, containers and garage will become redundant and release space when they are removed. The existing fuel stores will be relocated, too. Boat Shed The existing garages are barely adequate for the storage of the support boats and, again those boats have to be dragged across the width of the clubhouse to access the slipway. By creating a purpose-made boatshed behind the sea wall and on the concrete pad to the E side of the seawall gate, we remove the impact on the front of the clubhouse, we move the boats closer to where they are needed, we tidy up what is currently a rather unattractive storage area (and absorb the existing hydraulic pump house) whilst creating a more accessible boat storage facility of adequate size (to accommodate larger craft if appropriate in future). The additional floor area released in the clubhouse will be a welcome bonus also. Viewing Deck and lounge improvements We have one of the best views for miles around but are not always able to make the most of it. There is widespread agreement that a deck extending out from the N side of the clubhouse and across the full width of the lounge, accessible from French doors to replace the existing windows, would be a most welcome and enjoyable improvement to our facilities. The re-location of the tractor shed and rescue boat storage make this entirely possible. Upstairs Bar and Galley improvements The present Dell Bar is a great facility but it is lacking in two important respects: it is somewhat dislocated from the lounge area and it does not have much of a view. By extending above the existing changing rooms we can create a bar with a view that is hard to beat, with a roof terrace extending from the viewing deck, an enlarged and improved galley and an overall improvement in useable space at first floor level. The last two items in this priority list may be some time away but by planning for them we give focus to our spending priorities and avoid costly mistakes that arise out of undoing or redoing work unnecessarily. Of course, we already have planning permission for the pontoon, have the funding in place and the work is in hand for a two stage completion with the whole job being finished in the 2007 season. We are now moving towards the submission of a planning application to cover the Changing Rooms enlargement and improvements, the Tractor Shed and the Boat Shed and at the same time working to get prices for the work needed. Assuming that we can get the necessary permissions, the timing of the commencement of construction of the Changing Rooms extension is dependent on funding considerations. In the hope of avoiding any unnecessary delay we have determined to make a bid to a number of potential funders for grants to cover the value of that work. We believe that we can make a strong and acceptable case for this type of support but know that success is by no means guaranteed. If we can’t get that kind of ‘kick start’ to the Development Plan we may have to wait a little while. In the meantime we would like to give all members the opportunity to see in more detail all of the plans that have been discussed here. To that end we will be mounting an Exhibition in the area of the Dell Bar on each of the Viewing Days that are planned for June 11th, June 25th and July 9th; in this way both existing and prospective members can see what we believe are exciting and forward-looking plans that will both improve and protect our investment. The exhibitions will be available for viewing throughout each of those days and will be manned for a minimum of a couple of hours at lunchtime to enable you to discuss matters with a member of the team. We look forward to sharing our proposals with you. Chris Davies May 2006

Page 10 of 11 Mona’S VOYAGE TO VANUATU FROM OPUA, NEW ZEALAND, 2005 As May 2005 saw the start of Autumn, and the end of our second eighteen month stay in New Zealand, it was time once again to set sail in Mona, our Ebbtide 33 steel cutter. Two years previously we had sailed to Fiji for the full six month winter season, a superb experience which had convinced us that what suited us best was being able to enjoy a place at a leisurely pace. The plan this year was to head for Vanuatu for the winter and then head over to Australia for the first time. Prior to sailing into the Pacific in 2001 I don’t think we had ever even heard of Vanuatu, and were only vaguely aware of its old pre 1980 name of the New Hebrides, given to it by Captain Cook in 1774. We were determined not to rush the experience as we had heard favourable reports from other yachties, as to it being one of the least changed and most interesting of the Pacific Island groups. It is just on a thousand miles from the Bay of Islands to Tanna, the most southerly, bar one, of the Vanuatan islands and the one where we were hoping to make landfall, as it is the first where you can clear customs. It is an extremely difficult passage to predict, weather wise. The usual technique is to leave on the back of a low which should give favourable south westerlies for at least the first two or three days. After a short wait this is exactly what we did, and were rewarded with a lively and lumpy but fairly efficient start. Having not been offshore for eighteen months we were a little rusty to say the least, and took a while to acclimatise to being at sea again. As we sailed out of the Bay of Islands with a brisk twenty five knotter up our tail, I set the Monitor self steering only to have the link chain come away. After a few anxious minutes sitting on the stern, while I seriously considered turning back, I managed to re-engage it. With just two of us on a longish trip, the self steering is a pretty important member of the crew. An increasing number of people seem to rely on electronic autopilots these days. We carry one for when we’re motoring, but we find the Monitor much more relaxing and generally far more reliable, with the added bonus of no power drain. We left Opua on Saturday 4th June 2005. By the Monday after a boisterous couple of days, the wind was beginning to ease. I am quite often physically sick during the first couple of days if conditions are lively, and this trip was no exception. Fortunately I am usually able to carry on as normal. It usually takes us two or three days to settle into a proper routine. Just as we began to, I started to worry about losing the wind completely. Boats that had left Opua for the islands ten days before us had ended up motoring most of the way in a flat calm. We don’t carry enough fuel for that and in any event neither of us enjoy motoring for any length of time. The wind came round to the east and dropped to less than ten knots, but we managed to keep sailing, albeit slowly. Then on the Wednesday the wind picked up to over thirty knots, still from the east. This was now more wind than we needed but as it was on the beam, well reefed down we were making good progress. In addition it was much more comfortable than it had been with the wind astern. We had left New Zealand at the start of the winter and it was still pretty cold so we were hoping to warm up as we headed north. For the next three days the winds were consistently easterly between thirty and forty knots. Mona was sailing well, the monitor steering faultlessly, after its initial hiccup. Helen was keeping up her tradition of producing a good cooked meal before sunset every day. We had both settled into our three hours on three hours off overnight watchkeeping routine, and were sleeping pretty well. I was checking in daily on the SSB with Des on Russell Radio in New Zealand, who was giving me weather updates. It turned out that a squash zone had developed between a high over New Zealand and a low over New Caledonia. This was giving us the stronger than normal winds. By Saturday morning we were a week out of Opua. We had been steadily reducing sail, and that morning I stowed the last of the main so we were sailing under staysail and well reefed yankee. Though we were making good progress the continuous strength of the wind was getting a little wearing and we were eagerly anticipating a bit of a let up. Having being offered ‘more of the same I’m afraid’ for several days, on this occasion it was encouraging when Des predicted ‘another day of this followed by a gradual easing off’. An hour later I was sitting in the cockpit, when the wind in the space of seconds leapt from around thirty eight knots, to fifty eight. Suddenly all hell was let loose. The initial onslaught brought with it a wall of water which seemed to envelop the boat. The staysail, which admittedly was our remaining original sail, but built like a barn door, burst almost instantly. The rigid inflatable dinghy that was stored upside down on the foredeck was swept overboard, only remaining secured by its bow painter. A deckbag in which we stored oars, boathooks, spare tiller etc., was ripped from its ties and deposited in the sea. Surprisingly, the spare jerricans of diesel also stored on the foredeck, stayed put. As I attempted to furl up the yankee, the furling line was wrenched from my grip. By the time I had winched it in, the yankee sheets had worked themselves in a frenzy into a knotted mass, that a couple of days later was to take me a full three hours to unravel. With no sail up, Mona was lying ahull in a hove to stance, heading about thirty degrees or so off the wind. The tiller was threatening to smash itself to pieces, swinging wildly from side to side. I lashed it down, but was worried about the strain the rudder was obviously under, so substituted shock cord, which worked much better. The canvas named dodgers had torn several eyelets and were flogging themselves crazy so I lashed them to the rail. The clear screens round our newly installed cockpit hardtop seemed to be coping remarkably well, as were the three large solar panels mounted on top of the aft gantry. This was the first deep sea excursion for both modifications. My next priority was to try and sort out the staysail and the dinghy. Harnessing myself onto the jackstay that runs right to the bows, I crawled up the sidedeck. Somehow from an almost prone position and with waves breaking repeatedly over me, I managed to lower what remained of the staysail and get it under some sort of control. I then somehow retrieved the dinghy. This task was made possible by the fact that we were well heeled over. Back in Opua I had tied the dinghy down using the straps at the side. These had all been ripped from the dinghy. I then removed the remains of the staysail and got it back to the cockpit. By this stage I had been on the foredeck for at least two hours. Down below we were concerned by increasing levels of bilge water, some of which could not be pumped. Helen and I resorted to scooping it up in a bucket and depositing it down the toilet. By this time I was feeling rather weak. Helen persuaded me to lie down. I went to sleep almost immediately only to be awakened by a torrent of water pouring through the dorade vent straight onto my stomach! Later on I could see the funny side of the incident, but at the time I must admit to having a bit of a humour bypass. I can still see Helen vainly holding a cushion up to the vent to save me from the deluge.

Page 11 of 11 The next step was to set the storm jib in place of the blown out staysail. This was an operation that also took an age. To give some sort of time frame, the really severe weather came on at about eight o’clock in the morning. It continued to blow at between fifty and sixty knots until well into the afternoon when it began to moderate slowly. It took me until four in the afternoon to set the storm jib, when we were able to get under way again. By the Sunday the wind was back to the thirties and we made steady progress under storm jib alone until, after several hours of unravelling the sheets, I was able to reset the yankee. By Monday afternoon we could see Aneityum, the most southerly of the islands of Vanuatu. It was annoying that we were not allowed to make initial landfall there, as it was reputedly a lovely island, and we could have been in by dark. As it was we arrived off Tanna in the early hours, and hove to for several hours, to wait for light, making landfall on Tuesday morning. We skirted a fearsome looking reef that, unlike many reefs, could be easily identified because of the huge waves crashing on it. It was a relief to get into the lee of the reef and enter Port Resolution, one of the many places in the Pacific named by Captain Cook. Dropping the anchor in four metres on soft mud we were able to relax and lick our wounds. Thanks in no small part to Mona’s design and solid construction we had come through relatively unscathed. Over the next few days we gathered that at least four boats had been lost during the same system, initially with no fatalities. Two of the boats lost had been anchored inside Minerva Reef, the isolated reef with no land attached that we had sheltered inside for a week on the way to Fiji two years earlier. Then the winds had been thirty to forty knots with one squall of forty eight. On this occasion the two boats, one of whom was a Japanese single hander that had been next to us on the wall in Opua, had dragged their anchors and ended up on the reef. Both crews were rescued by other boats in the reef. Of the other two boats one, a Swedish singlehander who we also know was rolled in the heavy seas. The skipper was lifted off. The fourth boat was crewed by a couple. In the heavy weather the husband was hit by the boom and suffered a severe head wound, which his wife apparently stitched up. They were eventually airlifted off and the boat abandoned. Much later we heard that another boat had disappeared without trace. We spent the next few days cleaning up the boat, getting to know our beautiful surroundings and generally relaxing. When we first anchored, Port Resolution, in spite of its name, had the appearance of a heavily wooded seemingly uninhabited bay. Captain Cook would have had no trouble recognising it today. Behind the trees however were several villages. The main village headed by Chief Ronnie, even boasted a yacht club which included a very basic three roomed resort, all owned and run by the village. We had lots of visitors coming alongside in their dugout, outrigger canoes. They were all incredibly friendly and fascinating to talk to. Any trading that we did was of a very relaxed nature. This set the tone for our entire stay in Vanuatu. We were never to run short of fresh produce. We were made very welcome in the village, which was a fairly large one, by local standards, of about one hundred and fifty people. There were quite extensive vegetable gardens around the village, mainly tended by the women who, what with general domestic duties, seem to be kept pretty busy. Like most of the places we were to visit in Vanuatu, the locals enjoy hosting visiting yachts and we soon got to know the Chief’s son Stanley who was adept at organising transport on the island. My first priority was local currency. When we left England six years ago, a major concern had been making sure we had sufficient cash. Since then we had got so used to arriving at various remote spots and going straight to an ATM machine and getting local currency, that we had long since stopped worrying. Now there was not an ATM in sight, only a bank that changed money on the other side of the island. Some Kiwis kindly lent us some money and a trip was duly arranged across the island to Lenakel. This was normally where you had to go to check in, but two days after we arrived, customs police and immigration arrived at the yacht club to check us in. The whole official process was very friendly and relaxed. to be continued…
