Page 8 of 9 Mona’S VOYAGE TO VANUATU FROM OPUA, NEW ZEALAND, 2005 - Continued However a trip across to Lenakel was still necessary to change some kiwi dollars that luckily I had with me, into the local currency vatu. A thousand vatu was equivalent to about fourteen kiwi dollars or just under five pounds sterling. I must admit to finding it rather confusing dealing in thousands of vatu. I went to Lenakel on a Friday which was payday. The small bank was a mass of humanity. The whole town was extremely lively. I was able to deliver the first of two boxes of date-expired medicines to the local hospital, that my doctor in New Zealand had asked us to bring. The European doctor at the extremely busy little hospital couldn’t believe his luck. The trip across the island to Lenakel was fascinating. I was surprised by the number of small villages we passed through. I was later to learn that many children grow up on Tanna, having never seen the sea. The first and last part of the track across the island was heavily wooded. In the middle of the island the trees and indeed the track disappeared and you found yourself crossing a flat volcanic plain. Most of the islands that make up Vanuatu are volcanic, and Mount Yasur is a particularly active one. Two days later we visited the rim of the volcano at sunset and it was an incredible sight, especially after dark. Every so often there would be a loud rumble followed by an explosion as huge red hot molten boulders were hurled high above our heads. We were invited to spend a morning at the Port Resolution Primary School. We were impressed with the enthusiasm and behaviour of the pupils. The teachers appeared to be achieving a great deal with very limited resources. The teacher of one of the youngest classes was very keen that we should teach the children a new song. Helen taught them ‘The wheels on the bus’, substituting truck for bus as there were several trucks around, but no buses. The children thought it was great fun and memorised the words very quickly. One morning Stanley took us on a walk into the interior to a Kustom village, where they try and maintain traditions that are slowly being lost. They generally wear traditional clothes, in the form of grass skirts rather than the westernised shorts and tee shirts that are the norm among the men and the voluminous ‘Mother Hubbard’ dresses introduced by the missionaries designed to conceal female curves, that are still favoured by the women. In some of the islands further north the traditional male dress is a namba or ‘penis sheath’ woven out of reeds. On Tanna the kustom dress was a more modest backless grass skirt for the men and grass skirts for the women. After a two hour walk we arrived at the Kustom village. Stanley saw the Chief who ran a gong and within minutes a group of men had gathered to give us an impressive display of Kustom dancing and traditional fire making. After nearly two weeks it was time to start thinking about seeing some of the other islands. The islands of Vanuatu are grouped roughly into a Y shape. In Tanna we were near the bottom of the leg. The next island up the chain was Erromango some fifty five to sixty nautical miles to the north. This was a difficult distance for us to daysail in the twelve hours of tropical daylight that we had. We don’t like motoring hard, and the last thing we wanted was to be trying to enter an anchorage after dark. Apart from anything else, although we have GPS and therefore generally knew where we were, the available charts were drawn long before the advent of GPS and so did not always show things as they really were. We have in addition to paper charts, MaxSea Electronic charts on our computer. Every so often a well used bay would show up accurately, surrounded by much vaguer contours. We decided to make an early start as we thought that Port Resolution Bay would be reasonably easy to leave in the dark. As it happened we were awake at midnight and there was a good moon so we decided to leave then. Having negotiated the entrance quite easily we set the yankee and settled in for a lively but fairly efficient downhill run in lumpy conditions, arriving at Dillon’s Bay Erromango at about eleven in the morning. Erromango is a larger island than Tanna, but has a much smaller population. Erromango was famous in the past for its sandalwood trees that were highly valued in China where it was used for incense. Enormous profits could be made from sandalwood so the traders were prepared to go to great lengths to obtain it. It became the cause of much discontent between the islanders and the traders and in the mid 19th century Erromango became known as a dangerous place to visit. As on all the islands blackbirding, whereby locals were rounded up for employment or virtual slavery abroad, was an ongoing source of discontent and bad feeling. In 1839 John Williams a missionary, unfortunately arrived five days after traders had murdered five islanders. He was told by the chief not to go any further than the beach, a warning he chose to ignore at his cost. After he was killed and before he was eaten, his body, which according to ‘The Lonely Planet’ guide, was short and stout, was laid on a rock, and its shape marked out. When we were escorted to the rock by a group of local children, I was rather upset to discover that I fitted the outline perfectly! I’m pleased to say our reception was a lot friendlier. On first landing we were given a guided tour of the whole village and taken up the lush river valley, stopping for a refreshment break of coconut milk. We were shown the extensive vegetable gardens and assured that unlike Tanna men, Erromango men do their share of work in the gardens! The rivalry between the islands has softened since the days when they would happily eat each other, but is still evident. Later we met the current missionaries and were able to give the local clinic our second box of medical supplies. We spent over a week on this beautiful peaceful island. It was wonderful being able to swim off the boat in crystal clear water. Money is virtually meaningless here. We were given all the fruit and veg we could possibly need. In return they were always grateful for clothes. Fish hooks were much in demand. A lone fisherman would come out to the boat in his dugout canoe and ask for a hook, then paddle way out to sea to fish, only to return at dusk often having caught nothing at all. Islanders would often paddle out to us just for a chat. For most of our stay we were the only yacht in the bay, and we were made to feel extremely welcome. We managed to get a fair way up the coast in the dinghy, finding some interesting little coves. From Erromango we did an overnight sail of eighty five nautical miles to Vila the capital of Vanuatu. It was another lively downwind sail. We arrived at the start of the twenty five years Jubilee celebration of the granting of independence in 1980. Prior to 1980 Vanuatu was known as the New Hebrides and was governed by an Anglo French Condominium Government,

Page 9 of 9 which had been set up in 1906 in response to German expansionism in the region. I must admit that my initial reaction to the concept of France and Britain governing together, was one of incredulity. At one stage Vila was home to an English Governor who spoke no French and a French Governor who spoke no English. Everything was duplicated. There were two police forces, two sets of schools, two hospitals. Any local unfortunate enough to be found on the streets of Vila after the official curfew set for locals, would spend the night in either the French or English police station, depending on who arrested him. At an exhibition set up to mark the anniversary of independence there was a superb photograph that for me, summed up the whole situation beautifully. It was taken at a crossroads in the centre of Vila just before independence in 1980. At the time there were still British and French police plus a new Vanuatan force. A representative of each force were standing together attempting to direct the traffic. They were each pointing in different directions! As Brits we were repeatedly told that without us they would never have achieved independence as the French wanted to keep control as they did elsewhere in the Pacific. A short walk up the hill from the very sheltered anchorage was the Parliament Building. Next door in Independence Park we watched some superb displays of Kustom Dancing with elaborate costumes from various islands, that were put on as part of the festivities. It was fascinating watching the reaction of the locals to some of the more revealing costumes. We spent some time in Vila sorting out our Australian Visas, then we were able to do some coastal sailing around Efate. Our first overnight stop was a small bay near Hideaway Island, from where we set off early the following morning to round Devil’s Point, a notorious headland which happened to be in fairly benign mood. We then sailed across Havannah Harbour, a large natural, almost totally enclosed stretch of water that was made full use of as a base, by the American Navy during the Second World War. Looking at it today it is hard to believe that it was once full of warships. Surprisingly there has been very little development since that time. It remains a pristine, virtually deserted, expanse of sheltered water. Its only drawback as a cruising ground is that it really is a deepwater anchorage. We had to nose right up the Boat Passage, a narrow cleft between an outlying island MASC and the main island of Efate, stopping just short of a shoal area before we found anywhere shallow enough to anchor in. to be continued…

Page 11 of 14 Mona’S VOYAGE TO VANUATU FROM OPUA, NEW ZEALAND, 2005 Continued After a couple of days in this idyllic deserted spot we headed out of Havannah Harbour for the offlying island of Nguma, arriving with twenty five knots on the nose. Making our way ashore we were given a guided tour of the village by the friendly chief. A lot of the villagers were absent as the island is near enough to the main island of Efate, for them to go there to work. After a less comfortable night than usual, we set off early on a wild downhill romp in thirty five knots with just the yankee set for a fast trip to the beautiful twin volcano island of Emae. Once there we spent well over an hour, and one or two harsh words, investigating the reef strewn bay before finally finding a spot to anchor in. Just as we got settled, Photon, a Kiwi boat we had met in Tanna, appeared and without any hesitation, anchored alongside us, telling us later that they had assumed we would have found a good spot! The next day we walked across the island with Janet and John (I kid you not) two of the crew of Photon, meeting up on this sparsely populated island with several locals who were typically keen to talk. We could never get over how well most of the islanders spoke English, as well as Bislami, a sort of Pidgeon English and in many cases French, as well as their local island language. A friendly chat would often develop into an in depth discussion of the political system or the history of the islands. By way of contrast, numeracy skills were from our observation extremely basic. Calculators were one aspect of modern technology that were much in evidence, even in the smallest and most basic of village stores. I would offer a one hundred vatu coin as payment for ninety vatu’s worth of fruit, only to have to wait as patiently as I could, while the change required was worked out on a calculator. If we were purchasing several items, the calculations could become quite protracted. If I dared mention the final price and was eventually found to have predicted the right figure, I was given some very strange looks. In Vila there was a sale of material that Helen was interested in for cushion covers, priced for one, four and ten metres. The cost worked out the same per metre regardless of length. Helen worked out that she needed three metres but the assistant was completely confused and said she could only have one or four metres. From Emae we had a lively sail to Epi where we anchored in Lamen Bay. Back in Vila we had discovered that the public library had a large consignment of school books donated by Ausaid that they were having difficulty in distributing because of the high cost of inter island transport. When we offered to take a box we were asked to deliver it to the school in Lamen Bay. When we landed in the dinghy with the books, Helen went off to find directions to the school. The first person she saw was a man working in his garden. He turned out to be the Headmaster! We soon found ourselves escorted by a large group of children to the school, where the box was opened with great excitement. Lamen Island lies some distance off the main island. There was much traffic across and this was the first place where we saw dug out canoes equipped with sails or in some cases well leafed branches from palm trees. Their upwind ability was a little suspect but downwind they went pretty well. Helen was disappointed not to see any sign of a dugong, a seal like mammal that feeds by hoovering up sea grass from the sea bed, that was supposed to be readily sighted here. From Lamen Bay we motored in a flat calm and blazing heat across to the Maskelyn Islands, a group of small islands in the south of Malekula, where we met up with Terry and Ariel our Canadian friends on Stella who, while we were in New Zealand, had been in the Marshall Islands north of the Equator. After a few days we motorsailed together up the coast of Malekula to Crab Bay, a deserted and beautiful coral enclosed bay, where I distinguished myself by running Mona firmly aground on an isolated patch of coral. Fortunately the water was flat calm. We induced a heel by taking a masthead line to the dinghy which Terry powered at right angles to the boat. This wasn’t initially successful but eventually just before dark when the tide had made a little, with the engine at full revs and the other dinghy adding its thrust, we were free. In fact we shot off with such gusto that we almost ran straight up the beach! After anchoring well clear of any coral we repaired to Stella for a much needed celebration. We spent nearly a week in Crab Bay. Our swims off the boat were a little briefer here as there had been a shark attack in Malekula a few weeks earlier. When we ventured ashore to what had been a plantation we quickly discovered how the bay had gained its name. It was difficult not to trip over them as they scurried across the path right in front of you. We dinghied around the bay and soon discovered just how extensive was the coral. From Crab Bay we had a short sail up the coast of Malekula where, in the large semi enclosed Norsup Bay we anchored in the lee of the little island of Suoro. We were visited by Chief Willy, who stayed on board while the paddler of his canoe ran errands ashore. Like so many of the islanders he was fascinating to talk to. We then had an extremely hot and calm motor sail (with emphasis on the motor) up to Luganville on the largest Vanuatan island of Espirito Santo, named by the Spanish explorer Quiros who discovered it in 1606, thinking he had stumbled upon the great Southern Continent. Motoring in to the anchorage off Luganville, an area that had been a huge American Naval base during World War Two, we passed by the wreck of the President Coolidge, a large American liner turned troopship, that had sunk in 1942 after hitting American mines. Somehow the Captain had been given faulty information and tried to enter through the wrong route. After the explosion the Captain ran the ship up on the reef where she stayed just long enough for all but two of the five thousand men on board to escape. Today the wreck is a big diving attraction. The little town of Luganville was largely built by the American army during the second world war. As many as half a million military were stationed here. Up to one hundred ships were anchored in the bay at any one time, and ashore there were at least forty cinemas. At the end of the war the Americans were prepared to offload surplus supplies to the Condiminium Government at a price of eight cents in the dollar. The Government held back, thinking they would eventually get everything for nothing when the Americans left. Out of frustration the Americans dumped everything from bulldozers, aero engines, trucks and jeeps to crates of coca cola and canned food into the sea, at a spot that for obvious reasons, became known as Million Dollar Point. This has become another popular dive as many of these things can still be seen today. I can’t imagine that many full bottles of coke stayed down there for very long. Today Luganville is something of a ghost town. The wide main street only has a few well

Page 12 of 14 spread out shops. There was a well stocked market where the service was so laid back you had to literally wake the vendor up to buy what you wanted. Villagers come in from outlying islands to sell their locally grown produce. They stay in Luganville for several days at a time. While they are there, the market is their home. They sleep under the tables. As in other markets in Vanuatu, prices were clearly marked on each item. Bargaining is virtually unknown here. It certainly made shopping a relaxed activity. From Luganville we did a short trip round the south east corner of Santo to Oyster Island. We were led in to the bay by Terry and Ariel on Stella who had been there before. To get into the bay you have to negotiate the deepest part of a reef which in reality meant swerving around isolated lumps of coral with literally a couple of inches of water under the keel. Once safely in you anchor in completely calm water just off a beautiful little resort run by an ex Parisian Chef, Jean Pierre, who produces the most incredible food, particularly seafood. While in Oyster Bay, Terry and Ariel were joined on Stella by Kiwis Stan and Karen who had flown up for a week’s holiday. We had all met two years earlier in Minerva Reef on the way to Fiji. Stan brought with him a Navman Autopilot, to replace the Autohelm pilot that although it wasn’t being used at the time, seemed to have died on the passage up from New Zealand. With Terry’s help and supervision we managed to get the new autopilot up and running in a couple of days, celebrating with the most amazing seafood platter for six we have ever seen, courtesy of Jean Pierre. We dinghied up a narrow river to the Blue Hole where we swam in deep crystal clear fresh water right over a spring. Nearby we found the surviving runway of Fighter One, one of four American wartime airfields on the island. We then had a lively sail up the east coast of Santo to Port Orly, making good use of the new autopilot. Port Orly is another beautiful tropical anchorage that totally fails to live up to its name. Sheltering behind an island with white sandy beaches that is also home to a beautiful freshwater lake, it is almost unbelievably picturesque, We discovered a beautiful secluded beach only accessible by dinghy where we were able to swim in complete privacy. The local village is mainly French. While there we were persuaded by a couple of locals to join them ashore for an evening of kava drinking. We went ashore with Stan and Karen, Terry and Ariel having decided to stick to alcohol for their evening’s entertainment. Vanuatan Kava is far stronger than the Fijian variety that I had previously sampled. It turned out to be a really good evening. One of the locals had a guitar and we soon had a lively sing song going. I thought that I was in fine voice but on the dinghy ride home Helen kept reminding me that kava is supposed to have a calming effect whilst the opposite appeared to be the case. In the morning I was feeling rather sorry for myself when the two locals came out to see us. ‘I thought you said there are no after effects from kava’ I challenged them. ‘I’ve got a terrible headache!’ ‘Me too’ one of them replied ruefully, the other one nodding his head in agreement. Stan and Karen left Stella at Port Orly, to make their way back to New Zealand. Stella and Mona then headed north to round the cape at the top of Santo, to enter Big Bay, as its name suggests, a huge chunk out of the top of the island. We headed for a tiny bay, christened ‘On Your Own Bay’ in one of the cruising guides we had on board. When we got there, another boat we knew was already there, but as it was very calm we attempted to anchor. It took both boats quite a while to get settled as the water was very deep close to the shore with very little anchoring room. Eventually we managed to anchor right on the edge of a steep drop off. I am normally very cautious as far as anchoring goes, and I wasn’t very happy as we couldn’t afford to set much chain as we could have swung on to a reef. It was such a lovely spot and as the weather appeared settled, we decided to chance it. Helen and I rowed ashore and found yet another deserted beach round the corner. When we got back the other boat had left and we enjoyed the surroundings over a drink on board Stella before turning in for the night. About half past one in the morning Helen woke me to say she thought we were dragging. I checked the GPS and sure enough we had moved about a quarter of a mile. It was a very dark night but eventually we made out the shape of the cliff right above us. Amazingly enough in the light southerly breeze that had sprung up, we had drifted right along the shore without running aground and had hooked up on something. I sat at the chart table checking our position for well over an hour until suddenly we were moving again. We started the engine and Helen steered gently away from the shore while I got the chain in. We then hovered offshore until first light when we motored into Table Bay, a very straightforward anchorage in the south eastern corner of Big Bay. Terry and Ariel joined us a little while later, having felt a little insecure especially after waking up to find Mona gone. From Table Bay we did a three dinghy expedition up the Jordan River no less. The entrance was quite exciting, with several twists and turns that was a bit like a miniature Deben Bar. Having entered with some difficulty against a strong outgoing flow, we very quickly ran out of water. However we managed to get some distance, and give a local a lift across the river, before we disembarked for a picnic on a small island. Back at the anchorage we explored ashore. The local village was making a worthy attempt to set up a nature reserve, to preserve the thickly forested area in its natural form. We took a guided walk deep into the rainforest which was very informative. When we set off from Table Bay we left early as we were hoping to cover the sixty miles back to Luganville in one hop, to renew our visas. We motored through Big Bay with very little wind, soon to be surrounded by large numbers of friendly dolphins, with Helen leaning under the pulpit encouraging them. By the time she had finished she looked as if she had been swimming with them! The wind picked up enough to give us a good motorsail around Santo to Luganville. After renewing our visas and restocking in Luganville we had a lively sail in thirty knots or so, with the wind ahead of the beam, to Ambae where we anchored for the night before setting off for Asanvari on the island of Maewo. Asanvari turned out to be one of the highlights of our trip. We anchored just a short dinghy ride from a natural waterfall where we could swim, wash our clothes and shower often in complete privacy. We quickly got to know Chief Nelson who supervised the Yacht Club as well as leading the village. The importance of a chief in Vanuatu is generally measured by how many pigs they have to kill at a major festival. Nelson was a thirty pig chief, which put him well up the rankings. Nelson and his son Nixon arranged a superb display of Kustom Dancing. Nelson’s other son Codie was the Headteacher of the village school. On one of our walks through the village to the other side of the island, he invited us into the school. He asked us if we would like to hear his class sing. When we said that we would, without any hesitation they launched into an amazing display of harmonic singing. Codie was organising a school concert for

Page 13 of 14 the parents as a fundraiser and asked us if we thought that the yachties would like to watch and perhaps contribute to the funds. We were sure that they would. After many years of organising and watching school events, this one has to rate as one of the best I have witnessed. The singing was superb, and the junior Kustom Dancing and pole dancing very impressive. In this type of pole dancing, several pairs of children each hold each end of two parrallel poles, a few inches off the ground, moving them apart and together in time to the rhythm of a drum while other children hop over them down the line. Codie told us that he didn’t mind yachties joining in except that they kept breaking his poles. Helen decided that it was probably safer all round if this was one dance I didn’t attempt. There was also a totally non politically correct ‘Miss World Contest’ put on by the boys which was absolutely hilarious, particularly one very tall gangly lad dancing in a voluminous missionary approved ‘Mother Hubbard’ dress, as Miss Vanuatu. While we were in Asanvari we went out fishing with Nelson and Nixon. The first thing Nixon caught was a 25hp Yamaha, much to everyone’s amusement. We walked up the hill through dense forest to the site of a deserted village that had apparantly been the scene of black magic, before the entire population of the village were banished by the Chief to a neighbouring island. The chiefs still wield an enormous amount of power, in spite of the fact that Vanuatu now has a Westminster style Parliamentary Government. We certainly felt extremely safe the whole time we were in Vanuatu, and rightly or wrongly never felt the need to lock the boat in our absence. We certainly never heard of any yachties experiencing problems. From Asanvari we had a very pleasant day sail back to Luganville, where after refuelling and restocking, we moved across to a mooring off the Aore Resort. After four incredible months in Vanuatu, the maximum stay permitted, it was now time to prepare for the one thousand mile trip to Australia. We had been encouraged to sail with a free rally that runs at this time of year to Bundaberg. Although we had chosen Bundaberg as a suitable destination we decided not to wait for the rally. We have up to now studiously avoided rallies mainly because you have a pre determined departure time which may well not be the best time to go. Leaving independently you can usually reckon on at least two or three days of favourable weather. As it turned out we left with twenty five knots from the south east, aft of the beam which stayed with us for the first couple of days until dying down to a gentle ten knots or so, which made for slow but very comfortable and pleasant progress. After another three days the wind almost deserted us completely but it was so calm and peaceful that we were reluctant to motor. There was none of the usual rolling and slatting of sails that you often get in calm weather and with a favourable south going current and just enough wind to keep the sails still, it was at times almost like being at anchor. When the wind died completely we resorted to the engine long enough to make water before drifting again in complete stillness and swimming off the boat, always an exciting activity in these depths! After a week of generally slowish progress we still had a way to go, but overall we were enjoying the peace of it all, in spite of various problems with the new autohelm which couldn’t be solved, in spite of advice from Terry over the SSB. One evening when we were sailing in typically light conditions, Helen called me up because she didn’t like the look of the sky ahead. We rolled in the genny and suddenly we were in the middle of the most vivid electrical storm we had ever seen. Just as suddenly, the wind went from eight to forty five knots and the heavens opened. With just the mainsail up Mona set off like a scalded cat, until I reefed the main and hove to. Luckily the whole thing only lasted an hour or so, after which the wind dropped back to less than ten knots but stayed where it had come up from, the south west, dead on the nose. We stayed hove to until morning when we discovered that with the wind change, the previously favourable south going current had changed to a north going one, and we had lost about thirty miles. We started motoring only to find our progress was painfully slow. Eventually the wind picked up and settled in the north east which allowed us to get sailing again albeit slowly. Over the next twenty four hours the wind stayed constant at just under fifteen knots, but our speed increased from less than three knots to nearly eight knots, by far the fastest in the ten and a half day passage, as the current eased then turned back in our favour. We then had a cracking sail the rest of the way, so much so that on Sunday night we had to slow down to avoid arriving in the middle of the night. We still had to hover to await first light before entering the long lead in to the flattest land we had seen in a long time. Suddenly after several years of island hopping it seemed strange to be arriving at such a large land mass, whilst being able to see very little at all. Anchoring just inside the Burnett River just off Port Bundaberg Marina, we only had a short wait until being summoned to the Custom Berth, to be officially admitted to Australia and to set foot on Australian soil for the first time. Malcolm Shaft

GOCAEKGYCHTCLUB Page 7 of 11 JASSPER goes racing Les Hurell-Smith writes of his latest experience sailing in Turkey Gocek Regatta 2006  Having had a few successful and enjoyable years cruising the coastline of Turkey, and forgetting the challenging conditions the delivery itself in 2003 presented, this year we wanted to do something different, just to give our sailing a little focus. So the four intrepid sailors, Paul, Sam, Richard and your truly, collectively sometimes known as Old Gits (sorry Sam at just 24 you are honorary OG) decided to step up the ante. For the past 6 years a pre-season regatta has been held at Port Gocek, to blow away cobwebs and keep the tourists happy as well as allow some to show off nice yachts and dubious racing skills. Previous years have seen some 50 yachts ranging between 6 and 27 metres compete in a 6 race series. This year would see JASSPER resplendent with new spinnaker but same old crew as one of the entrants. Leaving early on the Sunday as ever the flight into Dalaman was not as traumatic as the taxi ride from the airport to Port Gocek, amazing what you can do in a Kangoo! We had one nasty incident where the driver had to swerve to avoid a very large tortoise crossing the road! I am sure it winked at us as we passed on the wrong side of the road, nice to know conservation is upper most in Turkish cab drivers mind, it certainly was in mine as we would our way up into the mountains and waited with trepidation for the inevitable decent .By the way we checked on the way back for tortoise shaped stains in the road but saw none, clearly the shell was BSI approved! So a little shaken and well stirred we arrived at the Port Gocek marina, quickly stowed our bags and headed for a well earned drink just to acclimatise, 26 degrees and sunny, it was going to be hell! We decided to use day 1 as an opportunity to try out the recently purchased and as yet unused spinnaker, while at the same time getting the boat and ourselves sorted. We didn’t rush, after all it was a holiday and the wind doesn’t pick up till early afternoon. Time well spent checking the foredeck. With the help of the Top Yacht team the spinnaker and its snuffer bag were rigged and it looked like it would work, so off we went to sail in the bay to test it out. After several re-rigs (it looked ok in the bag!) we finally managed to hoist, drop, and gybe the very large and very blue spinnaker. Satisfied with our exploits we headed back to Gocek, to ready ourselves for the evenings entertainment at the yacht club. As with all such things registering JASSPER and the crew were essential on day 1 which Paul, the owner readily did, and came back happy with his bag of goodies, including our race numbers, class flags. We were in division 4 it seemed. And with our newly acquired ISAF rating were down as the fastest boat, clearly ISAF does not take account of crew ability! So with these formalities out of the way the next task was the pre-regatta briefing, which was an experience. Admittedly we arrived a few minutes late (Turkish directions) but were a little surprised that the topic on most people lips was not the racing rules, courses, or indeed anything to do with yachts. It was about the hospitality and what would happen when the free beer ran out at the various parties that the race committee had organised for competitors (and numerous hangers on). It got a little agitated when we were told that for the last night party each of us would be given a pre-paid card for drinks, how much do the beers cost, what do we do when we have spent our quota? All serious stuff, but as it turned out it wasn’t a problem, Turks do know how to have a good time, but more of that later. So that out of the way we were off to enjoy cocktails and meet the other competitors at the “Blue Bar” aka Gocek Yacht Club drinking hole, not quite Royal Yacht Squadron standard but pretty good and a lot warmer, the weather that is not the cocktails! Food

Page 8 of 11 was good, plentiful and free, and we soon got into a heavy conversation with one Brit who was a geologist (lots of rocks in Turkey) and another who after Gocek was off to Greece in his Yacht and after than the US crewing, hard life for some. This guy actually had a “Little Ships” sweat shirt, but when asked it was a club based in London near Southwark bridge for wayward sailors to meet up, not as I though our Maldon watering hole of the same name, still it made us a new friend Day 2 of our holiday, and Race day 1 started sunny and still, as usual, with much activity on the pontoon, as boats readied for the first two races. One of the bigger boats in the regatta was throwing off its sails as a brand new set of Mylar ones had just been delivered, all liveried up by the Turkish Bank, some clearly took this serious. The “Mylar Boys” as we christened them certainly did as we soon found out on the water. Sadly things were not so good with us, as poor Sam, had developed a nasty ear infection on the flight over and was feeling quite rough. Nothing for it but medical treatment and again the Top Yacht shore crew helped out and soon Sam and Paul were off the have it looked at. This meant a slight change to plans as it was unlikely that we would make the start for race 1, so Richard and I readied the boat, bought some provisions before wandering around the marina to check out the many yachts. Suddenly we both felt very inadequate, some of these boats were bigger than houses, clearly cost a fortune, and looked as if they were rarely used, such a shame. Around midday Sam returned having been prodded about by local doctors, suitably reassured that it was not terminal but needing antibiotics, oh and by the way don’t get the ear wet! He was keen to get, so off we went to join the fleet for race 2, but first the obligatory team photo! The race course was a few miles off so we motored in the general direction, partly to make up time and partly because the wind was so light sailing was not a real option.? Where was the 11- 4 breeze we have come to expect? After about an hour we found the fleet, made ourselves known to the committee by sailing up to the committee boat and letting them have a good look at us, we expected someone would be taking race numbers, instead they were either taking a beer or a nap, perhaps one led to the other who knows, anyway pretty relaxed. So we then waited for instructions, and watched the flags, and we waited and waited, and we watched and watched. Seems that the race committee were also waiting for the breeze to fill in. The start line was not huge some 150 yards and the area was quite busy so we stood off and took stock, listening to the vhf banter. Clearly we were not the only ones feeling frustrated, the radio was soon alive with the plumby English tones … “Committee boat this is yacht Grand D’artagnan what is the hold up?” After some delay the curt reply was “we are waiting for the wind”. A long pause before we heard the response from Grand D’artagnan ”In my considerable experience sailing these waters if the breeze hasn’t arrived by 3 p.m. it won’t be coming!” The silence! Eventually the committee boat replied “We understand but are still waiting for the breeze!” Grand D’artangnan had left the VHF channel open so we could all hear the muffled response which sounded very much like “fools, were off” or words like that anyway. Suffice it to say that not long after the race was abandoned. Not an auspicious start for Jassper, one race missed, one DNS, oh well always tomorrow. Back to Gocek marina for a well earned meal and drink, to reflect and plan, and get some sleep. Day 3. Up early determined to get to the start and make the most of the breeze for the two races scheduled today, the “Power FM and Becks Cup” Catchy titles. The start was split into two groups based on handicap. We went in the second group of 17 yachts, which gave us the benefit of watching how the professionals, including the “Mylar Boys” did it. Lots of shouting and general mayhem ensued but the fleet got away and then it was our 10 minutes gun, well actually it was a whistle, luckily we had VHF on otherwise I am sure we would not have heard it, We had made a practice run so knew the time needed to get to the line, in theory! We also had a plan, it just didn’t work as we started two thirds down the fleet, still we started clean and went off on starboard. The race itself was pretty uneventful except as we approached the windward mark on our second lap we met up with the “Mylar Boys” on lap 3, we were on Starboard, but so were they, albeit closer to the wind. We held our course not wanting to put in an extra tack, but then we saw the look of determination on the bowmans face, heard the various Turkish phrases not in the tourist book and our nerve broke, we tacked away, well Jassper is quite new and shiny, be a shame to dent her. Finished 6th. Race 4 followed after a spot of lunch a few beers and a th good look at the start line. A better start but the rest was fairly similar we think we finished 5 but were never quite sure. All in all a pretty good day, especially as up to now the rest of the crew had only really cruised, I apparently was the race expert, that is really worrying, still I did have the countdown watch! Rather than back to Gocek we had a treat and were going to enjoy the Power FM party, with we hoped free Becks beer!

Page 9 of 11 So the fleet went in to Kapi Creek for the night to be welcomed by the local restaurant owner, clearly Christmas had come early, lets hope they had ordered extra beers! The boats tied up alongside each other so it was generally friendly as we clambered across each other to get to the rather rickety pontoon. We saw some aftermath from the race start apparently a few boats were a little too friendly, protest flags were flying and much rubbing of chins, great spectator stuff, especially over a cold beer or two. Anyway the evening was set fine as the food was free, a live salsa band played for us, and did I say it was all sponsored by Becks, yes we had a few! This is a rare picture or Richard standing up! Day 4, a special day today, it was the Sunbird Offshore Cup, a race of some 20 Nautical miles 10 miles to the windward mark, in a straight line that is! Which just happened to be a small island, so should see that OK! Much better start this time top half of the fleet but really not enough breeze to make it exciting. We settled down to a long slog deciding to follow an offshore line as we had been told of the “banana” wind which bounced back off the headland, best to avoid that we were told, on reflection though it was at Bar Blue and the beers were free, had we misheard? Anyway we held our position and settled down to a long slog, It was sometime after lunch that we could, using binoculars, just make out the turn mark, that would be the island then. But more worrying than the fact that it was some miles off, bearing down on us, resplendent with spinnakers flying were the fleet leaders these guys had set out just 10 minutes before us! Clearly the expensive suits of sails were paying off. We soldiered on and it was late afternoon when we could clearly see the turn mark, about a mile off, it was at this time that the wind decided to slowly turn off! Almost teasing us as we were so near but so far, to keep morale up we needed a few cold beers and perhaps a little snack., as we crept ever so slowly towards the goal, the halfway mark and it was about 4 o’clock, we had been sailing some 5 hours or so. Luckily the Mediterranean does not suffer tides or I am sure we would have made the turn only to find that that it too was against us, as it was we seemed to be getting sucked towards the island,, which was home to a whole lot of swooping and noisy sea birds, clearly not happy with us disturbing them. Eventually we made it, and turned for home, Port Gocek, only some 10 miles away in a straight line! What wind we were enjoying was behind us so up with the spinnaker! Hurrah! Now watch us go! , Wrong! We did pull away from the following boats but it was hardly knife edge stuff, still it looked pretty! Did I mention that the race had a 10 hour time limit, well it did, and we needed to average 2 knots to finish inside the time which was 9:20 to be precise, I was wishing I hadn’t noted our start time, and indeed it was the only race that started on time, easy you might say, well if the wind had not dropped I would have agreed, as it was we were struggling. But giving up was not an option, we kept on, and on, and on, then it was time for tea. Beers and snacks as the sun started to set, quite prophetic really as it was only that morning I had asked Richard if he had ever done a night sail, well it looked more and more like he would get his chance and very soon. The wind continued to drop but we kept our average speed up, and crept towards where we suspected the finish line was. Had they waited for us? A quick radio call to the committee boast was left without a response, which added to our doubts, it was 10 hours we did start at 11:20, it was still Wednesday, wasn’t it? It was then very dark and the minutes ticked by, You could have cut the air with a knife, Actually if you did it would have at least created a breeze to fill the spinnaker! Onward, we went, then yes could just make out what we hoped was the committee boat, then we heard it, they were having a party! I should say that the committee boat was very, very large, and by the sounds of it the crew were very very drunk, would they even notice us. They would if we went close enough! Which is what we did and with 15 yes 15 seconds to go we crossed the finish line to a welcome whistle and lots of cheers from the crew of Jassper. Really strange but it really seemed like a major success, event though we were clearly last boat in , but we carried on and finished. So all that remained was the motor into Port Gocek, tidy the boat, and then find somewhere to eat. We ended up easting at 11:00 in the now very famous (to us) Kebab Hospital, strange name but highly recommend for great food and drink and a waiter who looked like Gollum and had for some (strange) reason taken a liking to Paul. We believe it was not a serious relationship but we did get free coffee most evenings when we ate there. Day, 5, and the last day of racing, just one race today, which was a bit of a shame, we were now getting into our zone, a few more weeks of this and we were confident to be Americas cup standard. So for the last time we donned our racing T Shirts and

Page 10 of 11 headed for the line, in what was the weeks best breeze, and it had come in early. The race sponsors today were Hillside Country Club and that is where the regatta prize giving would be, and we had the promise of free beer once again, courtesy of Becks and Efes. This was going to be hard. Anyway we had finely tuned our racing skills over the week, and were up for it, one last chance to get that great start we knew we were capable of. And we did it, more wind top play with and we powered across the line in the top half dozen, with hardly a kebab separating us. This was a one lap race around a triangular course, so everything to go for. At the first mark we had made up 1 place and approached this mark level pegging with a Bavaria 40, he was glancing nervously over his shoulder, as his crew smiled and took snaps of Jassper powering down on him. We held our nerve and our course, he panicked and at the last minute stuck himself head into wind, one more down! Sam was jubilant, Paul said he felt sory for him as he i=7la.! struggled to make the mark. No time for sentiment and we took aim on our next victim, oh I meant competitor, so on to mark 2, we sailed high hoping to avoid traffic and setting us up for what we expected to be a spinnaker leg, we were powering along, catching the leaders, you could smell the adrenaline (or was it the dodgy bananas?, that’s another story) At mark two we rounded neck and neck with another yacht, too busy to check the name, ooops too tight we nearly broached, steady Paul, a fast boat usually has it’s mast in the air. Paul soon settled the boat and we started towards the finish line, just astern of two boats. The wind had changed direction and it was too tight for the spinnaker but who cared. We drew level with a very nice 38 footer, they looked at us, we looked at them, and then very very slowly we edged past, we were ahead! If only we knew what we were doing right. So next one to take was Cloudy Bay, we had socialised with this crew at Kapi Creek, fellow Brits but ex pats and they knew the waters very well. The boat we had just passed was desperate to get back at us, and hoisted the kite, a little to close to the wind we thought but they got away with it just and started to make ground on us, but had to bear away to keep the wind. Cloudy Bay was still ahead but we seemed to be catching them, we were just feet, OK yards, off the transom, but they remained just out of our reach, defending there sailing line and they powered through the finish line ahead of us. What a race! Both crews cheered and thanked each other for what we though was the best race of the week Shame it had to end, One more lap we would have had them I am sure!!! So racing over and now to find the Hillside Club, to berth up and join the evening festivities. It was a spectacular sight as we rounded a headland to see the hotel nestled in the rock face, some huge yachts were moored off shore, perhaps a little surprised to see the fleet bearing down on their tranquil spot. Once moored up we simply chilled out with lunch and a few zzzz to be ready for the evening. I was still recovering from the dodgy banana, honest it was the banana, I just didn’t want to be to far from certain facilities just now, so the rest was very welcome, and was to set us up for the evening festivities which had the potential to far exceed any of the hospitality we had enjoyed so far, Hillside clearly as major sponsors wanted to make an impression, and they certainly did. Then to our slight worry be saw that our friend in the Bavaria 40 was coming alongside, lets hope he doesn’t hold a grudge, then we spotted the German flag, oh dear this had the potential to get a little messy. As it turned out he was fine and perhaps didn’t realise it was us who had given him grief earlier in the day. As is usual we watched the boats tie up, which in this instance was interesting as it meant putting very long lines out and then attaching these to the rocks, luckily we were all assisted by Hillside staff. Paul then happened to remark that the transom seat on Jassper was foam filled in case it went over board, it would then float, not sure why he said this, but strangely our German friend then decide to drop his over the stern of his yacht, hey it wasn’t foam filled, how did we know, it sunk in 15 feet of water! He got it back with the aid of snorkels!. As evening came we were ferried ashore by one of the club RIBs we received out complimentary Regatta T shirt, day pass and the all important drinks card, loaded with credit! Hey Ho hard life this sailing. Before canapés at 7 we enjoyed the waterside bar facilities and then made our way to the amphitheatre for the prize giving. Usual Turkish time keeping meant it was an hour late but that just gave us time to banter with other sailors, especially the crew of Cloudy Bay. Apparently when we were racing they were in control and had not the slightest worry we would pass them, yea alright, next year Pal! Like the old salts we had become we exchanged tales, and pondered the rules while we waited for the prize giving to begin. The prize giving was an amazing experience, hosted by someone who clearly in a previous role had been a late night game show host on local TV. We were entertained by him slipping in and out of Turkish and English, inviting people down to be hugged, kissed and paraded on front of hundreds of spectators, while generally getting himself excited at seeing old friends receive another trophy, it could have been the Americas Cup, not sure how Denis Connors would have reacted though! It really ended what had been a great weeks racing. That over it was time to eat and get some more free beer. The buffet was excellent and we enjoyed a beach bonfire and firework display late into the night. Eventually it was time to go back to Jassper, which

Page 11 of 11 meant a short RIB ride from the quay. Unfortunately Richard, who had maximised the use of his beer vouchers, seemed to miss the RIB as he stepped off the Quay. Almost in slow motion he was watched sliding into the clear water, in a perfectly straight decent only to come up Sans glasses. And they were expensive glasses, oh dear. He took it well and the next morning tried to get a diver to retrieve them, but it was a needle in a haystack task, so somewhere at Hillside Club lie under 15 feet of water are a pair of Zeiss glasses no reward for a safe return. So racing over time to relax, and we decided to spend a day a Fethiye a short sail to a friendly Quay and restaurant, once moored up we spent a leisurely afternoon in the sun along side a varied assortment of boats who clearly did not move far. In the evening we ate at the restaurant where we were remembered from the previous year, we were the Brits who watched the European Cup Final ‘til midnight amongst a large bunch of locals, Liverpool won I seem to recall, and Richard was the guest belly dancer. Next day we took the obligatory Turkish bath and then totally at peace and relaxed we gently sailed back to Port Gocek, to spend our last night with our new friends at the Kebab Hospital, we never did find out what was wrong with the kebabs but understand they have made a full recovery! Another great experience and to remind you, Jassper is on charter to Top Yacht, she is a Bavaria 26, with 6 berths, a well appointed Galley and Head and has full Navigation facilities, well worth a charter, so if interested contact Top Yacht on or visit the web site www.topyacht.com.

Ray Ball Dave Steward www.bacspa.org.uk The Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association The last meeting for this year of BACSPA was held at the Maldon Little Ship Club on 30 November. These are brief notes on the meeting but the full minutes should be available around February of the new year. At the September meeting I raised the issue of the water ski race held on the 10 September. Our club was not properly notified of this race and it appears that other clubs were also not notified. The race caused chaos and danger on the river for other users. A report from the representative of the Stone Water Sports Club indicated that the race had not been held at the location intended by the club. Any future race would be held in St Lawrence Bay, which would leave the fairway clear. Personally I believe that power boats moving at 60 knots and towing a water skier cannot be mixed safely with sailing dinghies and other small craft such as are to be found on any Sunday in the summer on the Blackwater. The MCA are seeking a change to the high court ruling that personal watercraft (jet skis) were not vessels and were not obliged to comply with the collision regulations. The PLA will provide a guide for leisure users of the Tilbury Traffic Scheme. This will be modelled on the leisure guide provided by the Harwich Harbour Authority. The IMO have approved the revision of the Sunk Traffic Separation Scheme. The Essex Estuaries Marine Site has foundered for lack of finance. The EU had supported it but this money has now run out and the appointments to sustain it have disappeared. The lights for the London Array wind farm do not conform to the Collision Regulations. This is due to conflicting requirements between the lights required for warning civil aviation and lights required to warn vessels. The construction of the Gunfleet wind farm will not start before 2008. The exclusion or safety zones for wind generators will be 500 m during construction and 50 m during operation. This would not apply to vessels in distress or vessels going to their assistance.

Ashore at Stansgate £13250 For inspection and inventory call Ray Ball Commodore’s Report AGM 2006 I am required under the provisions of the Companies Act to confirm once again that our principle activity during the past year has been the provision of sailing facilities to our membership. There are other equally important but similarly dry facts that must follow but I will hope to balance them with some more interesting information and observation on how the club has performed over the last year. Firstly, I must remind you that ultimate responsibility for the activities of the club rests with the Executive Board. The board ordinarily comprises six directors. Last year members elected: • Murray Bates • Peter Clayton • Chris Davies (Managing) • Simon Elwell • Chris Laing and there was one unfilled vacancy at the time of the AGM. Chris Laing has taken responsibility for finance matters – and has done an excellent job in his new role - and all other directors have specific operational responsibilities as Flag Officers of the Club. Fenella Thomas agreed to be co-opted as the missing fourth Flag Officer and completed what I believe is a team that is hard-working, knowledgeable, caring and talented. The board appoints an Honorary Secretary and during the past year that post was held by Ray Ball. I am extremely grateful for his not inconsiderable efforts and real diligence on behalf of the Board and the Club. The board met formally each month since the last AGM and has conducted such other meetings of sub-groups as have been appropriate from time to time. The Management Committee has also met monthly throughout the year and there have been regular meetings of the various sub-committees that deal with specific areas of activity. I am grateful to all those people who have been so active and so supportive in their work for the board and all the committees. I acknowledge here too the huge amount of work that is done by a large number of members who operate outside the committee structure but who get things done in a thousand different ways. The year has been a successful one in almost all respects. Others will report shortly on the details regarding our financial well- being and on membership levels. We have managed to achieve and maintain a level of financial control that can give us real confidence about our future but underpinned this with a degree of sensible caution that characterises everything we do as a club. So far as membership is concerned, we do not necessarily look for significant growth in overall numbers but we do need to be confident of our ability to attract new, active members to replace the natural wastage that occurs every year as people move out of the area or out of sailing. During 2006 we replaced our departing members in record time and continued to recruit new members across all fleets right up to and beyond the end of the sailing season. The site is busy and there are more boats, newer boats and larger boats. This does mean we need to look carefully at the layout and use of the site and a small committee is due to start work shortly with a view to making recommendations for change and improvement. Shortly after the AGM last year we did, as promised finalise a maintenance and development plan for the site that, as we said at the time, will provide a blueprint for the protection and improvement of our property for the foreseeable future. Things have moved on, through a design and membership consultation phase, through the rather lengthy LA planning application process to the point at which we have recently had confirmed planning permission for the creation of a changing room extension to the

Page 6 of 13 clubhouse, the building of dedicated enlarged safety boat storage facilities immediately adjacent to the sea wall entrance and the construction of a barn that will house tractors, attachments, equipment and all the other kit that is currently distributed, often untidily, around the site. We are now updating our costings on these proposals and beginning to explore the funding options that are open to us in order to start to move these plans forward with a minimum of delay. We cannot at this stage commit to a timetable against which these improvements will happen – but we are agreed on two things: • They will happen as soon as they sensibly can. • We have a robust plan for the development and protection of the site to which we are committed for the long term and which will guide all our future maintenance and development activities. Out on the water, around this site and away from it, we have enjoyed another busy and successful year in so many other ways. Not everything was easy, of course; Cadet Week was cursed with persistent high winds, the same high winds that saw a large fleet of MSC Cruising boats trapped for the whole week in Ramsgate Harbour. George Vs famous two word put-down of Bognor could equally apply to poor old Ramsgate for most of us who suffered that particular hold-up. But both events were successful because we adapted to the conditions, enjoyed each others company and made the very best of the opportunity. During the early part of the summer we enjoyed much better weather and some excellent club racing and the usual crop of Open Meetings. As ever, some members travelled far and wide to compete and a particular mention must be made here of the particular achievement of one young man – the youthful Nick Milller, always an effective and competitive dinghy sailor – who became the 2006 Byte National Champion. Elsewhere another young member – a not inconsiderable dinghy sailor in his own right - continues to make weekly newspaper headlines with his startling achievements in seeing off older and more experienced competitors – but Alex Dowsett is doing this on his bike! Camping Fortnight, Cadet Week and East Coast Piers Race are, deservedly, highlights in the Cub calendar. They are greatly enjoyed by all who attend them – and for very good reasons. But such events also pose a particular challenge, bringing as they do so many people together in one place at one time. The physical needs can be planned for and dealt with; what is not quite so easy to predict is the behaviour of people. The Board is determined that these events can and should continue as the large scale successes that they are seen to be but will act positively to ensure that proper standards of conduct and behaviour are encouraged and maintained for the general comfort and well-being of all. The Board accepts that this will occasionally give rise to accusations of ‘nannying’ but are clear that this is a small price to pay to ensure that we preserve our well deserved and hard earned reputation as a safe and family-friendly club. All clubs change. What members wanted five years ago may not be what they want today. But there is no guaranteeing that they won’t want it - whatever it is – back in two years time. It is just human nature and I am the last one to complain about that. However, it is just worth, from time to time; reflecting on the nature and extent of change is worthwhile. We have recently been considering, for example, the impression that we seem to be a bit less interested in racing and rather less interested in some of our social events than has been the case in years gone by. I use the word ‘impression’ because it is not always easy to distinguish a one-off disappointment from an established downward trend – finding the real fact is often difficult. We need to review some of the things we do and every member of the club needs to play their part by making their views known when they asked – and even when they are not asked. The Club did not make any political or charitable donations during the year. I can confirm however, that this year ECPR raise £9800 for Cirdan plus a further £1000 for the Essex Air Ambulance. Given that this report marks the end of my period of office as Commodore, I would like to end this report on a personal note. I have belonged MSC for a long time and have always been proud to be a member. I have been particularly proud to be Commodore and it has been a particular thrill to be in the role at a time of real change. I am confident that what we have all achieved in recent years since we achieved independence means that we have an even greater future to look forward to. Chris Davies November 2006

Page 7 of 13 “Big Cat” Cruising in the Caribbean By DereK & Hilary Gardner, Killara 2 Mike & Rosemary Turner, Feeling The Pinch With the idea of eight people sharing a sailing boat in a hot climate our thoughts turned to a “Big Cat” as Mike & I planned our 60th birthday celebrations set for February 2007. The Sunsail 45 foot long and 25 foot beam Lagoon 440 appeared to fit the bill and the trip to the British Virgin Islands was booked. “ACBOS” our home for the next week was amazingly capacious for us all, our excessive amounts of clothes (we were not to wear anything more than tee shirts and shorts all week) and the copious food and liquids we had ordered ahead. Everything disappeared into the humongous fridges, cool boxes, cupboards & lockers. Still we had not even investigated the two forward berths in each of the hulls! The 10 ton + boat & all the electrical gear was driven by twin 40hp engines & separate generator to handle the power requirements of the aircon and electric winches etc.! The boat along with its 170 gallons of fuel and 160 gallons of fresh water was all driven along by a massive sail area of 1,250 sq ft. Up on the raised steering & sailing station, around 4 metres above the water level, nervous clammy hands gripped the twin throttles as we edged out of the marina for the first time, following the tortuous channel to avoid the breaking water on the surrounding reefs!   ACBROS our Lagoon 440 Tortola from the air Hoisting sail sounded easy using the electric two speed winches! BUT.. Standing on deck you could only just reach the underside of the boom and the mast seemed to reach up into the clouds (of which there were not ANY)!We learned eventually that motoring at about 6 knots directly into the wind was necessary to get the thing up. This would take around 5 minutes longer than on Killara 2. Once up it looked and was HUGE with a massive roach. Now, engines & generator off we set sail, unfurling the genoa as we sped off at a steady 8-9 knots in a light breeze to our first destination Virgin Gorda Sound only about 12 miles away. Getting the mainsail dropped was also a challenge with the full length battens getting jammed frequently in the lazy jacks and the massive sail falling out of the bag. Anyhow with four of us we could get it down and stowed eventually, just before the beers got too warm to drink! Driving the “Beast of ACBOS” for the week was great fun! The unresponsive hydraulic steering was a bit like driving a big red London bus. It could plainly be seen when snorkelling in the exquisitely clear water that the miniscule rudders on the aft end of each hull could not get much of a grip to turn the beast in the desired direction. Being monohull sailors beating with the beast was disappointing. Tacking required specials skills to keep her actually moving. Even we experienced sailors would find she would stop dead from 8 knots when going through the eye of the wind – all quite embarrassing! Leeway took on a new meaning. Instead of possibly 5 or 6 degrees on Killara we were faced with about 20 degrees leeway and tacking angles of around 120 degrees! The reaching however made up for this so the passage plans were made dependant on wind direction. We did not realise though here in the Caribbean the wind would blow always from the same direction for months at a time – never mind, the occasional beat was a challenge! We soon got to grips with her likes and dislikes. Anchoring was a breeze with all controls operated from this raised “fly bridge thing”. Picking up moorings required a certain skill and was preferable with at least 3 people on the trampoline to pick up and secure to the bridle. The windage was vast so you had to combine all possible skills to get her where you wanted her. Coming alongside in marinas was fun. But we had plenty of fenders and no bumps or damage was sustained at all during the week. The vast amount of space was simply the best (good name for a group?) thing. We never thought that you could actually be alone with 8 people on a boat, but apart from our own cabins with our own showers/heads, the massive saloon to seat at least

Page 8 of 13 10, the spacious covered after deck seating also ten, the steering platform seating (5 or 6) the trampoline and seats on each bow we also had a jaccuzi! This was a welled seating area in front of the main cabin for about four to five that you could fill with water – not that you needed to as the access from each hull to the sea provided superb access to the warm sparkly water for swimming and snorkelling. Sunsail did us proud. ACBOS was less than a year old, well equipped for hot climate cruising and we had superb service from them at our one time of need (more of that later in the year). The BVI`s were just an amazing cruising ground. Winds up to force six blew steadily day and night. The temperature during the day was around 30 – 32 and just the same at night, so we never wore a pullover even once whilst away. We visited the very flat off lying island of Anegada (The Drowned Island) about 15 miles away where we ate massive lobsters in a wonderful idyllic white sand palm fringed bay. A 20 mile reach to Monkey Point on Guana Island gave an exciting sail and we were rewarded with a wonderful quiet mooring where we barbequed on board amongst the multitude of feeding Pelicans and fish with absolutely no light pollution visible anywhere. Next it was Ladies Day! The men pretended to be asleep on the trampoline as the ladies took over for the run down from the Eastern end of Tortola to the island of Jost Van Dyke to the North West of Tortola. We made it in one piece, but the island had run out of water so we could not replenish our dwindling water supplies. We had plenty of beer, but a beer shower was not too appealing, so we drank it instead! Anchoring in yet another idyllic bay – White Bay – we went ashore to explore the delights of the Soggy Dollar Bar. The “Painkiller” a potent cocktail, was originated in this bar and consists of Pussers rum with a splash or two of various fruit juices. This just had to be tried and tested several times to check we approved of it – by late evening and a hearty meal to soak it all up we decided they were quite good! We presented them with a Marconi Sailing Club pennant to hang with the others in the bar, so look out for if you visit there. Next day Water was needed and a yearning for another Painkiller, to lay the dust. This took us to Sopers Hole on the mainland of Tortola. This was the only civilisation we saw all week. It is also the home of Pussers rum and we have photos to prove it. After taking on the necessary fluids we sped off to the small Norman Island for another memorable night. Snorkelling was terrific with the fish inquisitiveness thrilling us all. The mobile boat shop was irresistible. Three smiling, pretty & scantily clad girls run the boat shop “The Deliverance” and we all bought the most expensive ice creams of the holiday – wonder why!! The Valentine Day supper that evening was memorable. This was made even more fun when Barbara scattered and hid literally millions of small red hearts everywhere (literally) around the boat. Sunsail are probably still finding them in all sorts of corners and places! What made this holiday so special? The locals were genuinely friendly, helpful and so laid back they were almost horizontal! The BVI`s are truly unspoilt (not like the USVI`s nearby) Not cheap, but then you had to admire the way that they got their living from tourism. There was no profiteering, no real Western wealth, just happy fun loving people making a few dollars to keep food on their tables for their families. What a revelation compared to our society of today! The cruising grounds were just absolutely perfect in every way. Small perfectly formed Caribbean islands surrounded by azure blue warm sea within easy reach of each other or larger islands or longer sails if you prefer, all designed to make the perfect boating holiday. Would we go again –YES YES YES, but for longer next time as we only scratched the surface of this wonderful cruising ground. DereK & Hilary Gardner. Killara 2 Mike & Rosemary Turner. Feeling The Pinch    It’s a long way up there! Enjoying a “PainKiller”

Keith Murray (Iolanthe and JP) I thought my recount of a recent incident on the hard while recovering our cruiser might help others. Jan and I were standing by the main winch having a chat with various people in one of those quiet moments that often happen when several boats are being recovered. I thought that a ladder that was resting on the side of our'Gazelle¹ needed moving promptly as a tractor was going to move the boat before I could get there. Jan set off at a fast walk to move the ladder and, because the taught winch wire was so close to us, she did not see it and fell over it. We discovered early the following Sunday morning that she had fractured her forearm. So if you are in the working area when cruisers are being recovered maintain your awareness especially if movements seem to be in a lull and you and others are taking a break. Best perhaps to take a break away from the working area to relax a bit then go back into the area with renewed vigilance... Regards, Nik Beavins
