Ladies and gentlemen Before I turn my thoughts to the sailing season, just closed; I’ll dwell first on some important aspects regarding the business of the club. May I remind you that, when we bought the Stansgate site from Marconi, we formed a limited company; and as MD of the company I should like to confirm to you that our principle activity during the past year has been the provision of sailing facilities to our members. Responsibility for the company and thus the club rests with the board – elected here by you each year. The board during the last financial year comprised six directors: Myself (Simon Elwell) – I act as managing director and chair Peter Clayton – whose responsibilities cover moorings and equipment and cadet training Murray Bates – Murray looks after premises and the site Fenella Thomas – Fen has responsibility for sailing activities at the club Chris Laing – our treasurer and; Pat Shaw – Pat joined the board this year with responsibility for events and social activities and has proven a valuable addition to the board…bringing with him (as do all our directors) a wealth of experience from outside the club. Ray Ball is the honorary secretary for the company and club and it is his meticulous attention to detail that steers us through the events of the corporate year. I’m sure that you join me in thanking these individuals who give so generously of their time to run the club on your behalf. The board has met regularly throughout the year – as has the management committee. Additionally a number of sub-committees meet to manage and organise the day-to-day activities and events of the club. There are few weeks in any year that don’t see members giving up their valuable free time. I won’t dwell on finances, as you’ll have a chance to hear our honorary treasurer make his report in a few moments. I will, however, say that we are ahead slightly of where we expected to be when we drew up the plan on acquiring the club site and would like to thank Chris and his team for keeping us on the straight and narrow financially. The 2007 sailing season was preceded by a winter that saw the club bar open on alternate Sundays; thanks to Frank Burgess. Sunday lunchtimes in the bar proved such a success that Frank is repeating the exercise this year – and at the moment is opening every week. May I

Page 11 urge you all to take your Sunday constitutional down at the club if possible and support this initiative. Other social activities were organised through the closed season – notably the cruiser fleet v cadet fleet bowling evening which I sincerely hope will become a fixture in the calendar, as it brings together two of the most diverse elements of the club. In the early season we enjoyed (think back) the hottest April for 350 years. Unfortunately after that it all went rapidly downhill weather-wise, with some very ropey sailing conditions right through till August. Bryan Spencer, however, ignored the weather and started to run a series of extremely well attended cadet training and sailing days. Aimed at getting youngsters on the water more regularly than has previously been the case, these days were an unqualified success. On your behalf I should like to thank Bryan, ably assisted by Cadet Captain Lois Dowsett as well as Richard Dixon, Roy Hardwicke and a number of others. The early May bank-holiday saw a visit from Walton and Frinton Yacht Club and, whilst some of our own early season rallies were affected by the poor weather, the season culminated in successful trips to Ipswich and Heybridge basin. I won’t dwell on the racing season – Dave Hewes will say more about that in due course. In July the ECPR was once again a resounding success thanks to the hard work of Clive Shenton, Derek Kirby and their willing team. This year saw the Royal Navy provide our committee boat and Commodore Jim Patrick – commanding officer Eastern Region - was our starter. This year saw the first ever Marconi winners of the main race – Steve Monks and Clara Hurrell-Smith. The social side of the club was somewhat quieter this year although the New Members’ evening was well attended, as was the Caribbean evening. As a result of steadily falling numbers we decided not to hold a black-tie Laying Up Supper this year. I’m very keen to ensure, however, that it’s a short break only; as I think the Laying Up supper is one of the few events which can bring members from the whole club together to celebrate the closing season. We requested, and were granted, an extension to the number of days camping we are allowed during the year – we now have 32 days. Many members enjoyed camping as usual this year and we were particularly pleased that measures announced to address some of the behavioural issues at camping we largely successful. The board was disappointed to note however that late-night revelry without due regard to everyone on site still managed to engender complaints. As we move into next year; I see three major risks that as a club we have to mitigate: Firstly it will come as no surprise to you to know that we have an aging membership. The current age profile shows that over 60% of members are over 50 years of age; and more than a third are over 60. This manifests itself in two ways – our ability to attract and retain members in the younger age groups and in the amount of knowledge about the club and its systems and equipment that resides in the heads of our senior members. We will continue with the succession planning work that was begun by previous boards and, at the same time, make every effort to win new members in the younger age groups. The second major risk is linked to this: Our clubhouse and premises have, over time, ceased to compare favourably with other clubs – both sailing clubs and other sports clubs. This affects our ability to attract members – particularly the younger members to which I referred some moments ago. You will know, through the consultation that took place in 2006 and from my comments in Navigans recently that we have been planning to address our major shortcomings in this area – and this will require us to invest in the future of the club. I will return to cover this subject in more detail in a few minutes The final risk I perceive is that the organisational and financial foundations of the club are laid on the principle of members continuing to take on roles and jobs around the club to get things done. Each year we need to attract volunteers and bring new faces into the group of people who are active in the club. I’m sure that in this regard I’m telling you what you already know:, because the subset of our members who bother to come to the AGM are, by and large, the same group of people that make the club tick. Belonging to Marconi Sailing Club can be even more rewarding when we take the opportunity to make an active contribution to the life of the club; - so please encourage others to join in with committees and activities. Now back to plans for the site. You may remember that last year, Chris Davies spoke of our plans to transform our facilities as a result of the consultation and analysis that took place during 2006. I have to say that things have moved on less rapidly than the board and I had hoped – not least because of the considerable amount of pre-work that is required to mobilise a significant building project. You will be aware that we plan to extend the clubhouse and refurbish the changing and showering facilities to allow equal space for men and women and provide an accessible facility for those with mobility needs. During 2007 we successfully applied for planning permission for all our proposed works and retained professional architectural advice to develop a specification that could be issued as a tender document.

Page 12 Complex legislation now covers what 20 years ago would have been a DIY job and only recently, following asbestos reports and the involvement of health and safety specialists have we been able to go out to tender. Having reviewed our timetable, the board now sees great risk in attempting to start and complete works during this close season and we now expect to complete the commercial discussions and apply for such grant-aid as we are able with a view to commencing as soon as the 2008 season closes. I confirm that whilst the club made no political or charitable donations during the year we did raise, through the East Coast Piers Race a substantial amount of money for the Cirdan Trust and Essex Air Ambulance. During the course of the year three members submitted entries for the Mamgu trophy, which, as you know, is awarded for the best log of a cruise. The board judged the entries this year and independently of one another were unanimous in awarding the trophy to…. Rory Ash. I have one other award to present as part of this report. As commodore I have the honour of awarding the commodore’s trophy to a club member who has made an outstanding contribution to the club this year. I have already mentioned Bryan Spencer and his outstanding work with Cadets; I was also mindful of Pete Clayton’s long-haul stint running cadet week which came to an end this year. I should also say that John Weedon was very much in my mind – John has been race officer on Wednesday evenings for longer than anyone can remember and next year takes a well-earned break. I felt, however, that this year’s award should go to an unsung club member who has given significant amounts of time and effort to create the fantastic pontoon that now adorns our waterfront – that member is John Chisnall. Ladies and Gentlemen – I sincerely believe that the club is on a sound footing that enables it to face the challenges I have outlined today. I look forward to facing those challenges with you and should be delighted to answer any questions you may have. Simon Elwell November 2007

Page 2 Club Notes Commodore’s Comments Pete. An enthusiastic and competent sailor with a sense of humour. Our thoughts and sympathies are with Kelly and As I write this, January is all but over - 2008 is well and Pete’s family and friends. truly under way! We spent the day today sailing on the Orwell in unseasonably warm weather. It was our first sail In Memory of Pete Sayer by Mike Silvey of the year, and has fully confirmed that we have the "winter sailing bug" from which many of you also suffer, Peter and I were friends since living near to each other for and which sees Marconi club members competing in over 30 years. His first introduction to sailing was in a frostbites and winter-warmers around the South East. Torch dinghy that I sold to him. He joined Tollesbury SC with me and he sailed his boat with Kelly. Marconi Sailing Club Ltd Managing Director’s (Commodore’s) report to the 2008 AGM 30th November 2008 Ladies and gentlemen Before I turn to the substance of this report; I’ll dwell first on some important aspects regarding the business of the club. May I remind you that, when we bought the Stansgate site from Marconi, we formed a limited company; and as MD of the company I should like to confirm to you that our principle activity during the past year has been the provision of sailing facilities to our members. Responsibility for the company and thus the club rests with the board – elected here by you each year. The board during the last financial year comprised six directors: Myself (Simon Elwell) – I act as managing director and chair Peter Clayton – whose responsibilities cover moorings and equipment and cadet training Murray Bates – Murray looks after premises and the site Fenella Thomas – Fen has responsibility for sailing activities at the club Chris Laing – our treasurer and; Pat Shaw – Pat has taken responsibility for events and social activities and ECPR Ray Ball is the honorary secretary for the company and club and this year, as much as ever, I should like to thank Ray (ably supported by Maureen) for his unfailing support to the board and his patience with the rest of us. The board has met regularly throughout the year – as has the management committee. Additionally a number of sub- committees meet to manage and organise the day-to-day activities and events of the club. On your behalf I'd like to express our thanks to all those whose service in this way makes the continued running of the club possible. Finance is the subject of a separate report to be delivered by our Honorary Treasurer in due course. I should confirm, however, that the club is on a financially sound footing and should like to thank Chris and his team for the diligent hard work they put in each year to ensure we meet our corporate obligations. Before I talk about the club's activities, I should like to ask you to remember a number of friends and fellow members who have passed away this year. I don't propose to list them all but I'd like to acknowledge the contributions made by Ray Hampson, Peter Bloomfield and Peter Sayer in particular. Once again last winter, Frank Burgess organised the opening of the club bar on Sunday lunchtimes; and it proved very popular. This winter offers a double opportunity – socialise with fellow club members, at the same time see how our building work is progressing. The cadet v cruiser bowling evening took place once again in the closed season and saw our first lady winner – Jackie Camp. As always, some started their sailing season early this year. It was not just the usual hardy dinghy sailors, either. Derek Gardner and Mike Turner celebrated birthdays by hiring the famous Gipsy Moth IV for a cruise; and it is Derek's account of that trip that wins this year's Mamgu trophy for the best log. Once again this year, Bryan Spencer has done an outstanding job with the cadets and as a direct result of his enthusiastic work, we were approached by the RYA and asked host a Mirror class training event. I support, whole-heartedly, what Bryan is doing with young people at the club and I'm sure that the closer links with the RYA will prove mutually beneficial. Cruising this season was characterised by mixed fortunes weather-wise. Actually it was a lousy summer. A number of us got stuck in various places, pinned in by poor weather and when it wasn't raining it was cold! The season was enlivened, however by the innovative idea of the “pressed buoys” breakfasts – I'll leave you to ask a cruiser fleet member about them. Peter Ward proposed the idea last year and it turned into a popular and entertaining series of events. Peter also took his boat “McGregor” racing regularly and won not only the Marconi Challenge Cup but the BJRC series too. It is in the light of both his contributions to cruising and cruiser racing that I've decided to award Peter the Commodore’s Plate for an outstanding contribution to the club. It also falls to me to award the Seamanship Trophy, which this year goes to a club member who whilst unable to render personal assistance, showed great presence of mind and calmness under pressure to coordinate a life-saving rescue of fellow [redacted]s using the VHF to vector emergency services to the casualty. This year's seamanship trophy goes Gordon Preston. I won’t dwell on the dinghy racing season – Dave Hewes will say more about that in due course. In July the ECPR was once again a resounding success thanks to the hard work of Clive Shenton, Derek Kirby and their willing team. The High Sherriff of Essex started the race and whilst we didn't repeat last year's feat of supplying a Marconi winner, we showed well in the race and as usual the Jenny Ball (Colne Point) trophy was won by – Jenny Ball. January 2009 Navigans 8

Socially the club had a successful year – a number of barbeques were held and the social activities especially on camping weekends and cadet week were well attended. I'm delighted that the winter dinner / dance now in its new slot at the end of January is a complete sell-out and I'm looking forward to a bright night out long after the Christmas and New-Year sparkle has faded. We have a special agenda item coming up about the current development works taking place at Stansgate. I don't propose to dwell on the subject here other than to remind you that in my report last year I announced that we were proceeding to tender. Our applications for grant aid proved fruitless – the availability of public money was severely constrained in 2008 and so additional time in the tender process was required to negotiate an affordable solution. Some of you have asked me why we didn't wait until this meeting before committing ourselves to a course of action. Quite apart from the wisdom (or otherwise) of making decisions in a room of 150 people; it was only by starting as soon as the season ended that gave us a chance to complete the bulk of the work with minimal disruption to the start of next season. I'll leave this as a subject now until the later agenda item. I'd like to acknowledge the fine work done by Andrew Dowley who volunteered to take on the role of webmaster for the club's website. More and more new members find us via the website and the information it contains is a useful repository of knowledge and history about the club. In recognition of the contribution made by the website the board decided to create a new seat on the management committee for the club website manager. Unfortunately this year I need to echo my incessant nagging in Navigans about security. Most of you know that an organised theft of our support boat engines took place in the summer and a number of smaller, but no less outrageous thefts have taken place before and since. We have, for some time now, guarded against the casual thief. We have to accept that is is now organised theft against which we need to be vigilant and the board has sanctioned a number of steps in this regard. I should like to pay special tribute to Roger Camp, our clubhouse manager, who having obtained quotes for a cctv system realised that he had acquired sufficient knowledge to undertake the work himself and, in the very best traditions of the club, purchased and installed himself a far better cctv system than we would otherwise have been able to afford... many thanks Roger. You will also be aware of the two containers that we purchased to house our support boats. They're not pretty, I admit, but we will address that and they do do the job. My final vote of thanks this year go to those who have served on our club committees, giving selflessly of their time to ensure that the club continues to function on behalf of others. I should like to mention, in particular, Fenella Miller our Rear Commodore for sailing and Pat Shaw who looked after events for us. All stand down this year after some years of service. Their contributions will be greatly missed. I confirm that whilst the club made no political or charitable donations during the year we did raise, through the East Coast Piers Race sum of £18,969 for the Cirdan Trust and Essex Air Ambulance. Ladies and Gentlemen; last year I outlined what I saw as three risks facing us as a club. The first was our aging membership profile The second was the gradual deterioration of our clubhouse facilities and The third was the need to keep a fresh supply of volunteers flowing into key club roles. I'm delighted that during the last year we have addressed all three. The work being done by Bryan Spencer with the RYA will help us attract and retain younger members. The work on the clubhouse will contribute also to that agenda, at the same time safeguarding one of our key assetts. Finally during this year we have again seen new people step up to take on important club roles and to all those for whom this is the start of a new position in the club, I say “thank you” on behalf of all members and welcome to the mad-house! I don't think the challenges have changed that much – although we can add a very uncertain economic climate to the overall list of things to worry about. I sincerely believe, however, that the club is on a sound footing that enables it to face these challenges. I look forward to facing them with you and should be delighted to answer any questions you may have. Simon Elwell – Commodore November 2008 January 2009 Navigans 9

Membership Renewal Guide 2009 1 Classes of Membership A FULL MEMBER - Shall be a single person over the age of eighteen. Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall have one vote. A FAMILY MEMBER - Shall include a married couple or couple living together as a family, one of whom is over the age of eighteen, or a single parent over the age of eighteen; and all their children under eighteen years of age. The family unit shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall have one vote exercisable by one person over the age of eighteen. A YOUNG ADULT MEMBER - Shall be a single person who at the commencement of the subscription year is aged eighteen and is under the age of twenty two. Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall have one vote. A JUNIOR MEMBER - Shall be a single person who at the date of election or at the commencement of the subscription year is under the age of eighteen and joins the club other than as a Family member. They must be supported by a sponsor who is a full or family member and who will be accountable for his or her conduct. Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities but may not purchase alcoholic drink or cigarettes from the bar and shall have no vote. A SENIOR LIFE MEMBER shall be a single person who is over the State Retirement age, has been a FULL or FAMILY member for the a minimum of the preceding fifteen years, has paid the senior life member fee, does not keep a boat at the Club and shall have one vote. Any member over the state retirement age shall be entitled to a discount of 50 % of the full fees paid for Full or Family Membership subscription as appropriate. 2 Annual Boat Permit Fee - All craft incur a Boat Permit Fee. The first boat of a member is always deemed to be the craft incurring the highest fee. Subsequent craft less than 10ft in length (tenders) are free of charge. 3 Winter Storage. Storage Fees are payable in advance at these rates on boats, trailers and cradles to be kept at Stansgate during all or part of the period 30th November to 1st March following the date of renewal. th Any person who has a boat, trailer or cradle on site after the 30 November, and has not paid the appropriate storage fee will be liable for payment of a penalty fee in accordance with rule 2.3. 4 Trailer Storage Fee. A summer and winter storage fee is payable (as specified below) on second or subsequent trailers not associated with a boat for which a boat permit fee has been paid. Per winter or summer season: Cruiser trailer £45.00 Catamaran trailer £41.00 Monohull dinghy trailer £33.00 (A dinghy or catamaran is permitted to have one launching and road trailer on site before incurring the summer storage fee.) 5 Car Stickers A car sticker will be supplied free to each member, which should be displayed on all cars parked at Stansgate. If extra (free) stickers are required please specify the number required. 6 Resignations Persons wishing to resign their membership at renewal must indicate so on the form and return it together with all MSC Ltd keys by the end of January to the Registrar. 7 Late Renewal Renewal fees are due on 1st January and are payable by the last day in January. Renewals received after this date will incur a Penalty Fee; rule 2.3. 8 Is Our Data Correct? Will all members please fill in your boat details and amend any printed information that is incorrect, so that we may keep our database up to date. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Mamgu Trophy 2008 – The Winning Log 2008 Log of our Gipsy Moth IV Experience!!!! by Derek Gardner Fastest Voyage around the word by any small vessel Longest passage made by a small vessel without port of call for 15,500 miles More than twice the distance of the previous longest passage by a singlehander – 15,500 miles Twice broke the record for a singlehander`s weeks run by more than 100 miles Set a singlehanded record by covering 1,400 miles from point to point in 8 days Twice exceeded the singlehanded speed record for a long passage, more than 130 miles per day for 226 days Third TRUE circumnavigation by a small vessel via Cape Horn At the age of (nearly) 65 years old, and having overcome cancer, in 1966 Francis Chichester set off in Gipsy Moth IV and arrived back in Plymouth after sailing for 226 days and nights. He said that GM IV “was cantankerous” and “ needed an elephant to move the tiller”, “ needed a 3`6” chimpanzee with 8ft long arms to get about below and work the gear”, etc. His final comment was that “What GM IV needs is a gallon of paraffin and a box of matches”!! For those that have read his book “Gipsy Moth Circles the World” you will appreciate some of the hardships and problems he battled against during his long lonely voyage. GM IV was laid up for 37 years in dry dock, until a campaign was launched in 2003 to save the rotting boat from total destruction. Since this very expensive refit she has again completed a second circumnavigation, but this time with underprivileged youngsters with various professional skippers. This is another interesting story that is well summarised in the book “A Legend Sails Again” Mike Turner and I passed our 60th year and a present from our families Gipsy Moth rounds Cape Horn in 1967 gave us the opportunity to sail on GM IV for a weekend in March this year. The forecast on our way to Cowes to meet up with the boat was SW 8 and outlook for Saturday SW 8 increasing 9. We imagined the trip would be cancelled, but no chance. On Saturday morning with our skipper, Lars, we manoeuvred the 16 ton, 54 feet long, 10 ft beam and over 7ft draft, graceful lady out from her berth at the UKSA. With a healthy breeze we hoisted staysail and mizzen as it was too windy for any more sail, and set out into the Solent. Just to be there on board and experience the motion, the feel and the smell of such an amazing piece of history was magical. She was everything that Sir Francis said she was, and that was with our full crew of six! She rolled alternately her Port and Starboard gunwhales into the water and kept this up unceasingly with water pouring along the side decks. No spay hood on this baby! We made a Westerly course up the Solent hard on the wind, and then turned for Portsmouth now a beam reach. This called for the mainsail! Reefing was fun as the main was rolled around the boom using the entire original reefing gear. How the great man managed this alone I will never know. We six struggled and we only had about 30 to 35 knots of wind. He often experienced more wind and heavier seas that we had! Our speed picked up Reaching towards Portsmouth - 2008 to a maximum of 9.5 knots as we surfed and rolled continuously, our way down to Portsmouth. Boy was it a wet boat! Even with our modern oilies, boots, hats etc. it was impossible to keep dry. This was a mixture of heavy rain and lots of salt water! I wonder how the original skipper managed some 42 years earlier. What a hero? We all took turns to helm. One hour was sufficient for each trick, even for the strongest of us! She was an absolute PIG and required a strong pair of arms to hold her on course. The tiller was about 1.50 m long and even with this leverage she took some controlling. I can see now why Sir Francis made the comment about needing an elephant to steer! Also consider this was AFTER the rudder had been modified by Chichester in South Africa and again during her re-fit where the application of modern science had investigated and modified her rudder for the second time. Alas, to no avail! It was all part of the GM IV experience! March 2009 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk We took a lunch break and made “Cuppa Soups”. Well, eventually anyhow, after we managed to light the famous cooker that Sir Francis referred to frequently in his book. Mike became the expert at this. It was akin to an old fashioned blowlamp. Methylated spirits had to be poured down a tiny tube and then lit. When you thought it was hot enough the paraffin pump was started. Flames leaped in the air and we had visions of the precious GM IV being cindered there and then. Thankfully the paraffin vaporised, caught light and the kettle was boiled and part of the countries heritage was saved. We know that when at sea the cooker was impossible to use and Chichester survived without hot food or drinks for weeks when it could not be used due to too rough weather conditions. It was difficult enough for us at anchor! The wind picked up again, and because we were modern day wimps we voted for the comfort of a marina berth and drying rooms for our clothes and ourselves for the night. We sailed back to Cowes now hard on the wind again, and yes, the F 9 did arrive as we thrashed (literally) our way back! We were bashed and rocked and soaked when we arrived in after an amazing day sail. What about tomorrow we considered, but the forecast was better much to our relief. Very wet outside we felt we needed to complete the experience by getting a little wet on the inside also! A hearty meal ashore, then we spent the evening in the snug saloon of this famous lady. Unfortunately the Whitbread beer pump and gimballed chair had not been replaced after the refit (Sir Francis had a keg of Whitbread beer on tap to help him on his voyage) so we had to make do with Scotch. It was a very poignant and surreal evening just to sit in the cramped, damp smelly (our clothes were hanging all over) atmosphere and to look at exactly same instruments that HE navigated his way around the world with. (It is true that modern GPS etc. are hidden away under a lift up panel that houses the now old redundant, non functional original instruments) It was magic. One of the other crew read some passages from one of his books and it made your spine shiver. To think that we were privileged to be there is HIS boat recounting his tales of knockdowns in the Southern Ocean, rounding Cape Horn in a storm and how he got really annoyed that a Navy vessel was there to “escort” him round, when all he wanted was to be on his own. There are so many details in the book, read them if this whets your taste buds at all? A few drams later, so to bed. We slept in the main saloon. Getting in was fine, getting out was a real problem after a days sail when the bodily stiffness sets in! The pipe cots were so narrow there was no chance of even turning over during the night. It was just like sleeping in a sling! (or a casket as some sailors had One for the record books! referred to them!) A call of nature in the night proved almost an impossibility! We were not altogether certain that there was not a ghost of Sir Francis on board as strange woody type creaking noises were heard as she “talked” to us during the dark hours! Maybe it was just the Scotch? We will never know! Morning came and the sun was shining. Today was to be so different! We managed to set all sail and had fun downwind sailing with the VERY large cruising chute. We felt so honoured to feel the admiring looks and pointing and photographing and to have the boat being admired by so many people on other boats. Well she is probably one boat that most people have heard something about. We cut a fine picture as we gracefully sailed up the Solent and even felt the warmth of the Spring sun on our backs. She still constantly needs a lot of TLC and money to be spent on her to keep her in this condition and it is thought that she may become a non sailing floating museum piece eventually in a new maritime museum that is in the planning, which would preserve her for many more years to come. We felt very honoured to have had this weekends sailing and living on board this piece of our marine heritage. We loved the experience and will be able to recount these and many more memories of the weekend for many years to come. A BIG thank you to our families for making this trip possible. Derek Gardner March 2009 Navigans 11

Minutes of Marconi Sailing Club Ltd Annual General Meeting held at the MASC Beehive Lane Chelmsford on the 30th November 2008 1 Apologies for absence Apologies for absence were received from J Ball, D Russell, R Jephson, J Bloomfield, C James, P Shaw, E Cockerton, F Bennett, R Davis, D Thomas, K Kirby, D Williams, P Playle, G Flemons, G Jackson, L Jackson, C Jackson, A Russell, S Ash, R Ash, J Townsend, R Dixon, N Miller, C Burrow, D Burrow, K Murray 2 Minutes of the 2007 AGM The minutes of the 2007 AGM were accepted as a true and accurate record. Proposed by N Pembleton, seconded by C Davies. Carried unanimously. 3 Matters arising from 2007 minutes. There were no matters arising. 4 Reports 4.1 Commodores Report: The Commodore, Mr S Elwell, presented his report. Questions: None Acceptance of the report was proposed by C Davies, seconded by F Miller. Carried unanimously. Commodore’s Trophy. The Commodore presented P Ward with the Commodore’s Trophy in recognition of his contribution to cruising and cruiser racing. Mamgu Trophy. The Commodore announced that D Gardner had been awarded the Mamgu Trophy for his log of a cruise on Gypsy Moth IV. 4.2 The Honorary Secretarys Report. The Honorary Secretary, Mr R D Ball, presented his report. Questions: In answer to a question by B Hood on last years membership levels the Secretary stated that there were 432 members at the time of the 2007 AGM. Acceptance of the report was proposed by C Shenton, seconded by C Hennah. Carried unanimously. 4.3 The Honorary Treasurers Report. st The Honorary Treasurer, Mr C Laing, presented the Financial Statement up to 31 August 2008. Questions: In reply to a question from B Hood the Treasurer explained that ‘Cash at bank and in hand’ represents cash held in the bank and ‘Retained surplus’ represents Club assets. Acceptance of the report was proposed by C Wardell, seconded by R Camp. Carried unanimously. 4th November 2009 Page 3 of 6 Issue 1

4.4 Sailing Secretarys Report. The Sailing Secretary, Mr D Hewes, presented his report. Questions: None Acceptance of the report was proposed by D Ball, seconded by R Smith. Carried unanimously. 5 Presentation on Site Developments C Davies gave a presentation explaining the background to the Club’s development plan and the actions that have resulted in the present situation where building work on the clubhouse extension has started. The Treasurer followed with details of the financial arrangements which have allowed the current developments to proceed. Questions: M Turner and C Hennah asked about the affordability of future developments such as the balcony. C Davies replied that the balcony was not costed in to the current developments and the Treasurer added that it may take 5 or 6 years for the Club’s capital to improve before new major works could be considered. M Taylor (architect) stated that the current plans allow progression to future developments. M Balfe and B Hood asked what security the bank has. The Treasurer replied that the bank already has a charge over the site and had sent a valuer to site before granting the new loan. M Balfe asked if a new issue of members’ loans had been considered to finance the current work. The Treasurer explained that time scales had precluded this course of action at this time but it could be considered for the future. The Commodore asked for an informal show of hands of members who would consider taking out additional members loans if offered. The majority of members responded positively. The Commodore invited members to view the development display at the back off the back of the room and to discuss the plans after the meeting. 6 Proposals 6.1 Resolution 1 Election of J Bloomfield to Honorary Life membership The late Peter Bloomfield was an active supporter of the Club and at the time of his death in 2008 was serving on the Management Committee as a Vice President. The Board is, therefore, pleased to recommend that Julie Bloomfield be elected an Honorary Life member. Proposed by the Board of Directors Carried unanimously. D Kirby thanked the membership on behalf of Julie Bloomfield who was unable to attend the meeting. 6.2 Resolution 2 Election of F Bennett to Honorary Life membership Frank Bennett has been actively supporting the Club over many years and in many different roles. In particular he was Treasurer at the time that MSC purchased the Stansgate site and designed, installed and maintains the Clubs access system. The Board is pleased to recommend that Frank Bennett be elected an Honorary Life member. Proposed by the Board of Directors Carried unanimously. 6.3 Resolution 3 Election of C Davies to Honorary Life membership In addition to his work with the MSC Board, cadets and the ECPR, Chris Davies has been running the Club’s development programme from its early stages of identifying how the site is used and directing a team that prioritised potential developments to the stage where building work has now started. The Board is pleased to recommend that Chris Davies be elected an Honorary Life member. Proposed by the Board of Directors Carried unanimously. Chris Davies thanked the membership. 4th November 2009 Page 4 of 6 Issue 1

6.4 Resolution 4 Amendments to membership categories to introduce the Overseas class of membership Proposed by the Board of Directors, supported by the Management Committee Questions: J Salmon asked how many members were likely to be in this category. D Kirby suggested six or seven. M Hellewell asked if Overseas members would view Navigans electronically. The Commodore and D Ball confirmed that they would. Carried unanimously. 6.5 Resolution 5 Revision of membership subscriptions and fees Proposed by the Board of Directors, supported by the Management Committee Questions: In response to questions about the proposed increases the Commodore confirmed that increases were to cover inflation. The Treasurer stated that increases were based on an inflation rate of 5% and amounted to 4.7% overall. The recent decrease in the VAT rate does not affect subscriptions and fees. Carried unanimously. 6.6 Resolution 6 Appointment of Honorary Accounts Reviewer Mr D Thomas to be appointed Honorary Auditor for the 2009 accounts. Questions: None. Carried unanimously. 6.7 Resolution 7 Election of the Club President Mr Tony Benn to be appointed Club President. Questions: None. Carried unanimously. 6.8 Resolution 8 Election of Vice Presidents N Pembleton, P Black, C Shenton Questions: None. Carried unanimously. D Payne agreed to serve as a Vice President after the closure of nominations and will be co- opted on to the Management Committee. 6.9 Resolution 9 Election of Executive Officers S Elwell, P Clayton, M Bates, B Spencer and C Laing Questions: None. Carried unanimously. The Commodore advised the meeting that there was a rear commodore vacancy which it was hoped to fill by co-option. 6.10 Resolution 10 Election of the Management Committee Questions: None. Acceptance of the proposed management committee nominations was taken as a block. Questions: None. Carried unanimously. The Commodore advised the meeting that there was a committee member vacancy which it was hoped to fill by co-option. 4th November 2009 Page 5 of 6 Issue 1

7 Any other Business M Yeoman, R Hardwicke and D Gilbey asked questions about the condition of the Club road, the roadside hedges and the hazardous conditions at the junction of Stansgate Road and Bradwell Road. The Secretary confirmed that he had recently written to Essex County Council about the dangers in turning out of Stansgate Road and had received a reply that the junction was under review. The Secretary encouraged other members to write to ECC. It was confirmed that the Club road and the hedges belong to the farmer. M Bates agreed to ask the farmer to cut the hedges. The condition of the road surface and the encroaching verges are being kept under review. M Balfe asked about the Club’s child protection policy, offering the services of his wife who is involved with the child protection programme at the RYA. The Commodore replied that the Club insists that parents or guardians remain on site with their children while they are involved in MSC activities but this may not be sufficient under future legislation. J Ball has agreed to be the Child Protection Officer. The Secretary stated that the Club does have a child protection policy document. M Boreham expressed concern for the security of the replacement outboard engines being purchased and suggested they should be ‘distressed’ to make them less attractive to thieves. C Davies stressed the challenges that had been faced in 2008 and thanked the Commodore for his work for the Club during the year. B Hood thanked the Commodore, C Davies and C Laing for the information and presentations on the development plans. There being no further business the meeting closed at 12:15hrs. R D Ball 4th November 2009 Page 6 of 6 Issue 1

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The Single Handed Fleet Visit London 21st July to 2nd August 2009 Roger Camp (Southern Hey) was organising a Club cruise to St Katherines’s Dock in London this year and a number of single handed boats were interested in joining in. However they all had previously experienced the thrills and spills of the “Well oiled system” for locking into and out of St Katherines’s. Unanimously they decided that their collective hearts could not stand the stress and trauma of another such experience so decided to go to Limehouse Marina. In addition they decided to extend the duration and take in a visit to other anchorages as well. Thus it was that Pat Black (Tamarisk), Bob Godbold (Icarus), John Chisnall (Charlotte), Bob Whittaker (Chappie) and Neil Pembleton (Trumpeter) found themselves leaving the Club on Tuesday 21st July in a steady ESE 4 and assembling at Brightlingsea on the first leg of the trip. Later a planning meeting was held ashore over a leisurely pint at which it was agreed to depart at 04.30 the following morning so that there would be sufficient water in the Spitway for Tamarisk. So on Wednesday 22nd July departure was made at 04.15 and with a SSW 4 blowing good time was made to the Spitway. Once through sails were stowed and iron topsails engaged for the run down the East Swin. The wind steadily increased and by the time that Blacktail Spit was reached an indicated SW 5-6 was shown on more than one windspeed indicator. This made for very interesting motoring across to the Medway Channel, passed the Montgomery and into Queenborough, which proved surprisingly sheltered so moorings were picked up by all with no problems around about 11.00. In the evening Tamarisk and Icarus provided a very efficient rubber duck taxi service to the shore where we indulged in a meal at the Flying Dutchman. As we had already been caught by the Harbour Master and paid our overnight fee, we agreed to depart the following morning at 07.45 to avoid paying for a second day. (Note for the uninitiated, the fee is payable from 08.00 to 08.00 the following day or any part thereof.) Thursday 23rd July saw the fleet depart as planned at 07.45 on the next leg to Erith Yacht Club in a SW 2 which gently increased to a 4 during the day. Arriving at Erith at 12.30, moorings were once again easily picked up. However one of the party did discover that finding the vacant mooring with the clean new strops was not the best of ideas. As we all assembled on Trumpeter and were enjoying a pot of tea, we were hailed by an Erith boat and had to move the one of our party to another mooring. The moral is to find the mooring with no strops, or at least strops so weed encrusted that when on board the foredeck is covered with interesting sea life. Once again in the evening Tamarisk and Icarus provided the taxi service ashore to the Folgefonn which is the clubhouse for Erith YC but soon to be replaced by a new shorebased building. We were made very welcome and as we enjoyed a beer, Frank Burgess (who had initiated the contact with Erith) and Murray Bates arrived. Frank was in his element amongst old club members and we all enjoyed a very convivial evening. If you are intending to go up the Thames, it will be well worth contacting Erith YC in advance and asking to use their moorings, especially on a Thursday which is their Clubhouse evening. Friday 24th July saw a leisurely start at 12.30 with a forecast W 4-5 becoming SE 3-4 and mainly fair. As the group moved up the Thames the sky became more and more overcast with a light drizzle setting in as we passed through the barrier. Passing the Greenwich Dome a vicious squall swept through with quite heavy rain but only lasted 3 or 4 minutes. On entering Greenwich Reach, Trumpeter called Limehouse Marina who wanted to take three boats in the first lock and two in the second. On the basis of the (un)democratic decision made by Trumpeter, Icarus and Chappie were assigned to the second lock. Passing Hilton Pier another call was made to Limehouse who confirmed that the lock was ready for the first boats and the second group would be able to enter within ten minutes. On entering the lock, we each received an envelope showing a plan of the marina with our berth highlighted and additional information inside. Clearing the lock, we heard the second group being called in and saw that they had only waited eight minutes. We were all berthed by 14.30 approx. It must be said that throughout our stay the staff were extremely helpful, friendly and being a pre-booked party we enjoyed a club rate of £19.00 per boat per night regardless of length. In evening we had a meal at the Cruising Association headquarters before adjourning to the “Grapes” for an evening of gossip. Saturday 25th July we made a tour of the area around Limehouse, locating Tesco’s, a couple of restaurants, and the Docklands Light Railway station. In the afternoon using our Oyster cards (reduces the cost of travel) we made our way to Canary Wharf and the London Docklands Museum which at £3.00 each proved excellent value especially as the ticket is valid for one year and multiple visits. After eating on board, a pilgrimage to the “Prospect of Whitby” was made which was followed by a nightcap on Icarus. Sunday 26th July was the day the “Other Fleet” would arrive at St Katherines. The crew of Trumpeter and Charlotte were first to reach St Katherines and attempted to have some lunch in the Dickens, after waiting over an hour in a not very busy bar, we left and found another café – we ate but only just. The others joined us about 16.00 as we saw the first of the Marconi boats arrive outside the lock. We were amazed to discover that St Katherines were using radio to check and collect the details of boats as they arrived. Just a pity that they did not use it to call the boats one at a time into the lock reverting instead to type with then usual free for all scrum as the lock opened. Just over half the fleet made it into the first lock as we went round to help them berth in the East basin. After the eternal wait they came into view, berthed and we were offered light refreshment on Shell Seeker while waiting for the remainder who finally made it about an hour later. December 2009 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk It was agreed to meet at “The Pommelers Rest” a Wetherspoons pub just over Tower Bridge for a meal in the evening and then the single handers made their way back to Limehouse while the others set off along the Embankment in the light rain. Monday 27th July saw our group doing our own thing, while Icarus, Charlotte and Chappie visited Woolwich Arsenal Museum, Tamarisk enjoyed a lazy day in the sunshine on board and Trumpeter visited an old work colleague. In the evening Icarus, Tamarisk and Trumpeter enjoyed a meal at the local Italian (La Figa) which was excellent value with a main course which we struggled to finish and a bottle of wine. Later we all met up for a night cap on Charlotte. Tuesday 28th July was to be our last day in Limehouse before departing for Chatham the next day to join up with the St Katherines fleet so a leisurely day was spent in preparation etc.. Then early to bed. Wednesday 29th July we all listened at 0520 to the forecast which indicated that the wind would increase to a SW6 about the time we would enter the Medway. In view of our experience on the trip from Brightlingsea to Queenborough, we very easily made the collective decision to delay our departure until the following day. With the benefit of hindsight, this may not have been the best decision. The marina once again were extremely helpful indicating that we might need to move Icarus but that proved unnecessary as the regular berth holder conveniently stayed at Teddington rather than return. Thursday 30th July found us listening to a forecast suggesting an initial SW5-7 decreasing 3-4 so we decided that we would depart at 06.45. This meant punching the tide for the first hour or so before the ebb set in but we estimated would get us to the Medway channel as the tide turned to flood and help us to Chatham. As it happened we had a WSW 3-4 down the river allowing us to motor sail under genoas. All went well until we turned into Sea Reach with the tide still under us. As I reached the Mid Blyth buoy, I could see dark menacing clouds gathering behind us. Rapidly donning wet gear, reducing the size of the genoa and putting the washboards in the hatch, I waited for it to arrive. Minutes later we were enveloped in a heavy rain and hailstorm, after the windspeed indicator showed 32 knots, I decided that I was not going to look again. Luckily with the tide still under us and the wind virtually dead astern the water was quite smooth. As I reduced the genoa still further, the sacrificial strip at the foot was torn off for about three feet. Luckily as we approached the Nore Swatchway the wind eased and the decision was taken to stay at Queenborough overnight knowing that an early start would be made the following day to return to Brightlingsea (Nothing to do with Queenborough only wanting £8.00 compared with the unknown but much higher MDL fee at Chatham.). The harbourmaster managed to collect our fee but also transferred two cans of fuel from Icarus to Chappie, perhaps they do have a heart after all. Friday 31st July found a forecast of SW 3-4 backing SE 4-5, slight, fair, good being issued so we departed at 07.45 (avoiding the harbourmaster on his early morning rounds). The wind initially was SSW 0 and gradually filled to a steady S 3 occ 4 as we headed down the East Swin, through the Spitway and into Brightlingsea arriving at 13.45. The other fleet from Chatham started to arrive about 15.00 with Shell Seeker being the last. On our way to Brightlingsea, I had contacted Winkies to see if they could accommodate us only to find that they had a party of 19 due to sit down at 21.00. They offered us a 19.30 booking on condition that we left by 21.00 which we did. Needless to say the party at 21.00 comprised the crews of the other fleet. Saturday 1st August was a quiet day with a lunchtime visit to “The Rosebud” which in the past had provided excellent pub grub at a very reasonable price. However it has changed hands and has moved its food up market (£6.50 for an open sandwich) but the beer is still good. During the early afternoon Tamarisk, Chappie and Charlotte departed for the Club. In the evening Icarus and Trumpeter decided to try the restaurant at “The Yachtsmans Arms” which proved to sell excellent food at a reasonable price so may well see further custom from us. Sunday 2nd August found Icarus and Trumpeter departing Brightlingsea at 08.50 headed for our home moorings at the Club swiftly followed by a number of boats from the St Katherines fleet. After a brief sail the wind progressively died and the iron topsail can into its own yet again and the mooring was picked up at 11.50. So ended the singlehanded fleet’s trip to London. Ten days of varied weather and sailing, ten days of enjoyable and relaxed company, ten days of memories for the winter months ahead and planning of next year’s trips. On the negative side it was unfortunate that we did not join up with the other fleet at Chatham and missed their meal at Winkies. Neil Pembleton – Trumpeter. December 2009 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Round The Island Race 2009 A flurry of snow swept across the garden as we enjoyed a post Christmas drink with family & friends and talked of the sailing season to come. “Let’s do the Round Island Race next season…” I suggested! What is it all about? I only knew it was the biggest yacht race in the world and that it was around the Isle of Wight. Internet to the rescue. Everyone seemed to think it was a good challenge so off we went. This was the start of what was to be an exciting day’s race for us all. As we are not familiar with the Solent or the IOW research was done and by mid January I had bought charts and signed up to compete on 20th June The Island Sailing Club in Cowes on the IOW organises this race and has been doing so since its origin in 1931. 2009 was to a record entry with 1,779 boats being entered and an estimated 20,000 people participating on board the boats. “Why not raise some money for charity as we race” we asked ourselves? We chose to raise cash for RYA Sailability. They use the money to give disabled people the opportunity to try out sailing. We enjoy our sport, so why should not other people less able than ourselves also enjoy it? So a page was set up on justgiving.com and the funds started rolling in – albeit slowly at first! A lot of planning was needed to enable us to enter a reasonably competitive race. A lot of advice and information was obtained from Island Sailing Club web site and even a beginners guide was available! The tides in the Solent are complex, so a study of these was also very necessary. The course is fairly simple. Start at Cowes and go anti-clockwise round the IOW. There is only one official passing mark as such Bembridge Ledge Buoy on the South East corner of the Island. But then who would in heir right mind would dare to go inside the Needles?! We also read articles about previous races and talked to people to glean what knowledge we could. Crew selection took place and our two daughters Alice & Nicola with Damian Boreham, Mike Turner and Conrad & Heather Barnard signed up. It was great, as Conrad has also recently retired so he agreed to help sail the boat there and back with me, ably assisted by Nicola and Mike Turner. The Sailing Instructions duly arrived in early June. No time to back out now! One book called the “Safety & How it affects You” made chilling reading….. How to handle a helicopter rescue, how to call for help, a list of all the hazards en route !! Maybe we will retire before we start?.... Well possibly not, but all good stuff to know about. One sentence even quoted “ If you finish the course without a bump and your gear intact, and no-one has put in a protest against you or even shouted a rude remark, Congratulations”!!! The finish lines and how to text our declaration seemed complicated, but with eight people on board it should be easy, shouldn’t it? Somewhat nervously we headed off on Sunday 14th June with little wind and managed to reach Dover for the first night. We would only day sail as we did not know the waters at all and also being of retirement age it is difficult to stay awake during the day never mind the night! A good decision, as we encountered mile after mile of lobster pots on the trip, although they were quite well marked. From Dover we passed the landmarks of Dungeness, where we were intercepted by the Lydd firing range warden who told us they were using live ammunition for their firing practice. We decided to stay well offshore to avoid holes in the mainsail! So, on we sailed to Eastbourne for the second night. This was a pleasant experience, as we found a lovely pub and managed to quench our thirsts whilst Nicola went for a “cheap” half price hair do! As the tides were not in our favour for a long push we took in another night at Brighton and from there straight to Cowes via the Looe Channel. The 3 knot tide was with us so this aided our speedy arrival in Cowes. I can see the attraction of the Solent – calm waters, sparklingly blue and lots of choices of places to go to – albeit at a cost! In fairness Shepherds Quay only cost us £23 per night so we stayed for two! We made shore visits to the Island Sailing Club (the organisers of the race) where we discovered not only a superb local bitter, but found them to be very welcoming. On our second, or was it our third, visit we befriended the Commodore ! It seemed that the other posh yacht clubs probably would not have let us in anyhow! Friday evening we were due to meet up with the rest of the crew coming down to the Hamble car. Poor Hilary had just been to the IOW all week with the children from her school so had a double journey for her pains. Our briefing took in our objectives. We wanted to enjoy ourselves, stay safe and minimise damage to the boat, but try and do well. This was to be quite a challenge in these unknown waters. Saturday morning and up at 0430, steady drizzle….oh dear what a start for the day . Dry mouth syndrome as we headed off to the start line. Hundreds of boats appeared to be going the same way. What a surprise? Our start was at 0810 - one of the largest fleets with 118 boats in total. The start line was not that long as the seconds counted down to the start gun. Where was the line? Could not see it or the ODM for boats. Oh well potluck, we cannot all be over the line! A radio countdown was a help to crank up the sailing speed for the gun. Then we glimpsed the large orange ODM well in front! Not a racing start, but as we all headed off with all the boats pinching wind from each other we suddenly saw a gap. What a wonder in all that melee of boats!! Maybe it was our after-shave? Our luck held as we beat up the Solent in a force 2-3. With sunshine becoming stronger. Some close encounters were inevitable but most competitors were sensible and did not want clashes of gunwales either. As we approached Hurst Castle the narrowest part the wind picked up and so did the tide. The next December 2009 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk fast boat fleet were now overtaking us (or trying to) as we sighted the dreaded Needles. The tide was whisking us, and the water, as we closed that familiar red and white lighthouse. “Keep the Coastguard hut above the Needles light” we were told, to be sure of not hitting the wreck of the Varvassi . Bits of it are scattered around on the shallow rocky ledge but we managed to miss it all. It was rather disconcerting to see the Lifeboat anchored just inside The Needles waiting for some unfortunate to crash onto the rocks or the wreck! Anyhow we rounded it safely. The fleet was busy hoisting spinnakers as fast as possible and the inevitable broaches were witnessed, as several had not realised that the wind on the South of the Island was stronger. We held off for a few minutes to clear away from the fleet before deploying our gaudy pink and powder blue cruising chute. Maybe it might frighten some contestants into submission? Away everyone blasted away on a reach for the next 12.8 miles – so time for FOOD! What a spectacle to see so many wonderful colourful sails both in front and behind us. Just wall-to-wall boats as far as the eye could see. Some took the inshore route, some took a long offshore route (not sure why) we went straight line route to St. Catherines point. The over falls when we got there caught many sailors out. Spinnakers had to be jibed, and several were seen to tear, many wrapped around the forestays and boats broaching everywhere. We took our chute in to let the mayhem pass so as not to get tangled up in the out of control boats, and remain more manoeuvrable in case we had to take violent avoiding action. Once relative calm had returned up the chute went again for the reach to Bembridge Ledge Buoy. Sail on for 12 miles then, carnage AGAIN as boats jockeyed for position at the mark. We rounded unscathed giving way to two boats on the inside of us. Many boats then sailed right into the shore across Ryde Sands, but the more cautious (us) decided to stay in deeper water. One of the forts – No Man’s Fort – was a rounding mark in previous years, but not this year. This meant that the causeway to the fort, only 1.5m above datum, would have to be crossed if you went inshore. We would not compromise the boat so had to go into the deeper water and hence the greater adverse tide. This was our Waterloo! We lost a lot of places on those boats inshore, but not knowing the local waters and seeing literally hundreds of boats beating along in the very shallow waters about a mile inshore of us did not tempt us to go in there with our 1.9m draught. The tide was strong and the winds now light. We made slow progress and the chart plotter even showed us doing a circle at one time! Not good enough, time for another ploy. We broke from the main fleet heading for Portsmouth side. Every time we tacked we seemed to get closer to the Spinnaker Tower not further away. Slowly we crawled our way towards Cowes. With Osbourne House visible in the gloom of early evening we closed the main fleet again as the finish line was spotted in the now gathering mass of boats. As the wind fell lighter the hundreds of boats drifted toward the line. As we closed the finish on starboard tack, this clot directly in front of us on port tack ignored our (initially pleasant) pleas to move out of our way. He ignored us so with cms to spare we crash tacked to avoid hitting him amidships. The jib sheet wrapped itself around Alice’s leg and as she rose from the deck she hurled (politely) the rulebook at him. He just ignored us as though we were not even there. So a few places lost, but we crossed the line 11 hours 46 minutes after we had left. Relieved, exhausted, elated were some of the superlatives used as we headed back to the Hamble for well-earned drink and food. Our Results: 31st in class – out of 52 686th out of total starters 1,779 In summary then: Did we enjoy it – resounding, YES. We were lucky to have weather to get there and back with only one lost day due to strong winds, especially knowing what weather was in store for the summer! Will we “do it again” next year? – Unlikely as it was quite expensive and took a lot of organising and person power to get boat there and back in the time schedule. Might be good to do it in a boat that is already in the Solent. We have so far raised £509.00 for RYA Sailability There is still time to donate see justgiving.com/derekgardner Thanks to all “The Lame Duck Team” as without everyone’s help it would not have been possible. (Why Lame Ducks? Well that another story!) Derek & Hilary Gardner December 2009 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Marconi SC Remarks to 2009 AGM Simon Elwell-Commodore 2009 COMMODORE’S REPORT LADIES AND GENTLEMEN As usual, I start my report by reminding you that our club is a company, limited by guarantee and that our principle activity during the past year has been the provision of sailing facilities to our members. Responsibility for the company and thus the club rests with the board – elected here by you each year. The board during the last financial year comprised six directors: Myself (Simon Elwell) – I act as managing director and chair Peter Clayton – whose responsibilities cover moorings and equipment and cadet training Murray Bates – Murray looks after premises and the site Bryan Spencer, our rear-commodore for sailing who has responsibility for sailing activities at the club Michaela Glyn, who as our second rear commodore is on point for the events programme and Chris Laing – our treasurer Once again Ray Ball has acted as honorary secretary for the company and club and, as ever, shoulders a significant part of the administration burden that the club generates. The board has met regularly throughout the year – as has the management committee. Additionally a number of sub- committees meet to manage and organise the day-to-day activities and events of the club. On your behalf I'd like to express our thanks to all those whose service in this way makes the continued running of the club possible. We will hear shortly from Chris Laing, our treasurer. You may already be aware that Chris is stepping down as treasurer after 5 years at the financial helm of the club. Firstly may I say that I fully understand why he’s stepping aside. It’s important that people can take up roles within our organisation, and step down when it’s the time to do so. Chris has helped us navigate a complex minefield of financial challenges, from the time when the club became an independent company, helping us navigate the worst recession any of us can remember and still enabling us to fund our strategic plans in an affordable way. We will miss his sure footed handling of our finances and I, personally, will miss his counsel and level-headed approach to any problem. Chris leaves the role with the club in a sound financial position - no small thanks to his skilful management of our money. Well; it’s been an interesting year. 2009 started with the clubhouse in ruins (well half of it anyway) and the fight to get our renovations completed in time for the new season. The snow in January and February was a major blow to our timetable, and unforeseen problems with the clubhouse roof and waste disposal systems meant that we failed in our initial objective of finishing all the work in time to start the season. I must pay tribute to the stoicism and resilience of the early season sailors who unselfishly agreed to put up with spartan conditions for the month of April so that we could get the clubhouse finished. And finish it we did. In May, after literally years of talking, planning and a winter’s building; we opened the renovated toilets and changing facilities to members. Since that time, both our members and visitors to the club have commented favourably on the new facilities despite some initial teething problems. This brings me to the first presentation I’d like to make this morning. The Commodore’s plate is an award made to someone who has made an invaluable contribution to the club. Traditionally it’s not given to a committee member or officer; but this year I am going to make an exception to that tradition. You will be aware, I’m sure, that a major project such as our extension and refurbishment requires coordination and a significant amount of time. In this case I think it’s not an exaggeration to say that without the efforts and sheer persistence of the individual concerned, the renovations wouldn’t have got off the ground, let alone completed when they did, with as few problems. In addition, he found time to get creative and had the vision to design and commission the pargetting that now graces the clubhouse. Ladies and Gentlemen - this year the Commodore’s plate goes to the man who almost single handedly project managed the building works on our side - Murray Bates. I won’t steal others’ thunder by going into detail about our sailing activities this season; I would like to say, however, that it has been great to see cadet training continuing with such success and the cruiser racing scene extending to offshore racing by some. Bryan Spencer again led our cadet training throughout the season, and ran another successful cadet week, whilst Clive Shenton and the ECPR team managed a difficult race, with a fog-affected start, that was nevertheless enjoyed by many racers and which enabled record levels of fundraising for the Cirdan Trust. Whilst the club made no political or charitable donations during the year we did raise, through the East Coast Piers Race sum of £19,360 for the Cirdan Trust. Some sailors found time not only to sail, but to chronicle their voyages; and two logs were submitted for consideration to win the Mamgu Trophy for the best account. They were two very different styles - one more descriptive, the other a factual account that would prove useful to anyone thinking of making the same trip. I had thought to make my life easier by asking two senior December 2009 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk committee members to share the judging duties with me... and I thank Clive Shenton and Derek Kirby for their assistance. Unfortunately they each picked a different winner; leaving me back where I started! I re-read both entries in the light of the judges comments and took a casting vote - so this year’s Mamgu Trophy for the best log, goes to Neil Pembleton for his account of a single-handed trip up the London River. This year’s social programme began with the Mid-winter dinner / dance held at the end of January. The traditional laying-up supper had been proving less popular, clashing, as it did, with Christmas events. The gathering was a sell-out and a huge success. I understand that Becki and Michaela have long-since sold out of tickets for this year’s event and I for one am looking forward to the evening as it falls in the middle of a social wilderness at the end of January and it’s great to see everyone in the middle of winter. This time last year, I had cause to dwell on the subject of security at the club. I’m delighted to say that the security measures we adopted have so far proved successful and the improved boat storage, combined with the security cameras and lights installed by Roger Camp have proved a sufficient deterrent for the most part. There have still been a number of smaller thefts this season, however; and I must caution against complacency. Take it home or lock it securely please! We are, as we speak, preparing to install a new security card system here at Stansgate to replace the one that has served us well for many years but which now requires more maintenance than is ideal. Andy Redman has been working on the new system for us and I’d like to thank him for the time and effort he’s invested. I hope too that the new card system will address one area of misuse - that of nonmembers using our facilities. We all occasionally bring visitors to the club, but it has come to our attention that a number of members regularly permit nonmember friends to use the club and even lend them access cards. I’m sure I speak for the vast majority of us when I say that this is unacceptable and I ask you all to be careful about allowing just anyone to follow you through the gate. Ask them to prove they’re a member and if someone challenges you - please don’t get annoyed! At the AGM in previous years I have set out what I feel are the key challenges for the club; and we’ve been addressing them through our plans and investments. This year in addition to the ever-present need to attract and retain members and to maintain our clubhouse and site; I’d like to re-visit the ambition document that the board produced some years ago. Some of the elements of that vision have now been achieved; others are in train whilst a couple are still dreams. I want to ensure that we have a contemporary vision for the club going forward so I invite anyone who is interested in contributing to the discussion to email me. I’ve already sought the views of the board and vice-presidents but feel it’s time to widen the net and canvass broad opinion. I conclude as always by thanking all of you who have contributed to the running of the club this year - either through service on a committee, in a specialist role or by helping to do the never ending list of tasks that the club generates. I was asked, earlier this year about my own continued presence as Commodore. In the absence of queue of people wanting the role, I undertook to stand one more time and, if re-elected in a few minutes will gladly serve in that capacity again this year; but I will step down at next year’s AGM as I feel that the club will benefit from a fresh perspective and new ideas. I thank you for your kind support this year and I’m happy to take questions. December 2009 Navigans 14
